Section 1
Introduction

         This manual provides a complete reference for all Executive Control Language (ECL)
         and File Utility Routines/Program File Utility Routines (FURPUR) statements and
         describes the purpose, format, options, and individual fields of each statement.
         Examples appear throughout the manual to help you understand the various uses of
         these statements.

         The primary audience for this manual is any OS 2200 user. This includes system
         programmers, site administrators, and general users.

         Before you begin using ECL, you should have some familiarity with the OS 2200
         environment.

         Note: This document might have more recent updates and the latest version is
         available on the product support site. Enter the part number of the document to
         search and view the document.

         https://www.support.unisys.com/common/epa/DocumentationLibraries.aspx?PLA=
         OS2&NAV=OS2

Notation Conventions
         This manual uses the following conventions to describe messages and statements:
            Commas, periods, and parentheses must be keyed in as shown.

            Letters, words, and symbols in italics represent variable information that changes,
             depending on the circumstances. Letters, words, and symbols that are underlined
             represent user input in computer dialogue.

            Uppercase letters indicate a keyword or a required word. LEVEL in the following
             example is a required word:
                LEVEL,product_level ;

             Unless otherwise noted, uppercase letters can be coded in uppercase or
             lowercase.

            Lowercase italic text indicates a variable or information that the user must supply.
             product_date and product_time are user-supplied values in the following
             example:
                TIME,product_date,product_time




7830 7949–031                                                                                 1–1
Introduction




           Ellipses (...) indicate a variable number of entries.

           Brackets ([ ]) surround an optional field, expression, or value. The following
            example uses brackets:
               LOAD_FILE_PACK_ID type,pack[,pack,...]

           Braces indicate you have a choice between two or more values. A vertical bar
            separates the choices. The following example uses braces and vertical bars:
               LOAD_FILE_SECURITY { NONE | KEYS | PRIVATE }

           The Ʌ is the start-of-entry (SOE) character. The Exec places an SOE character on
            the screen to let you know that the system is ready for your input.

           Changes made since the last version of the manual are shown with yellow
            highlighting in the online version (and appears as shading in the printed version).

Section 2
Using Control Statements

         Control statements are the means by which you make requests to the operating
         system to perform services. Control statements include Executive Control Language
         (ECL) control statements, FURPUR control statements, processor call control
         statements, and unformatted processor call control statements.

         ECL control statements let you initiate and control demand and batch runs, create and
         use mass storage and tape files, print information, generate and execute programs,
         send messages to the system console and other terminals, and control certain
         terminal characteristics. ECL control statements are the interface between you and
         the Exec system software portion of the OS 2200 operating system.

         FURPUR control statements allow you to control and move data within OS 2200 files
         and elements.

         Processor call statements are calls to compilers and system programs that perform
         various functions. See Section 6 for the processor call formats.


2.1. Control Statement Format
         All control statements consist of a recognition character called the masterspace (@)
         and four major fields, as follows.

         Format



                    [ label: ]   mnemonic [ ,options ]   field-1,...field-n   [ . comment ]

                  Label Field      Operation Field       Operand Fields       Comments

         Start all control statements in column 1 with the masterspace (@), which indicates that
         what follows is a control statement and not data. You can use spaces after the
         masterspace.

         Label Field
         The label is not necessary, but you can use it to name a control statement. The label is
         1 to 6 characters from the set A through Z and 0 through 9. The first character must be
         alphabetic. If you specify a label, follow it with a colon ( : ). You can use spaces after
         the colon.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  2–1
Using Control Statements




        A label statement is any control statement containing a label but no operation or
        operand fields. A label statement consists of the masterspace (@), the label, the colon
        ( : ), and, optionally, a comment. Here is an example:
            @TAG:
            @MARK:
            @LAST:XQT PROGX

        In this example, the @XQT statement can be referenced by any of the labels TAG,
        MARK, or LAST, which are attached to the @XQT statement by label statements.
        As each label statement is encountered, no operation is performed and runstream
        processing continues until a control statement with an operation is found.

        If the same label appears more than once within a run, the first forward occurrence
        from the point of reference is taken as the proper label.

        You can specify a label for almost all control statements. The one exception to this is
        the @EOF statement, which cannot contain a label. The label provides the means to
        skip portions of the runstream and pass control to the statement having a particular
        label. However, you cannot pass control with labels on the @ENDF and @FILE
        statements because these statements are not entered in the runstream. Although
        control statements have only one label, you can attach additional labels to a control
        statement by using label statements.

        Operation Field
        Unless you plan to use the control statement only as a label statement, you must
        always specify the mnemonic name associated with the statement in the operation
        field. The mnemonic specifies what component of the operating system is to be called
        and what function is to be performed. The mnemonic on all ECL control statements is
        1 to 6 characters from the set A through Z. Terminate the mnemonic with a space or (if
        you want to specify options) with a comma.

        The options are alphabetic characters, which you can specify in any order. The option
        field must start with a comma (,) to separate it from the mnemonic.

        You must separate the operation field from the operand field with a space or a series
        of spaces.

        Operand Field
        Use field-1,...,field-n to specify information associated with the operation field.
        Separate fields with commas. You can use a space or spaces after the comma.

        The content and number of fields and whether they are required or optional depend on
        the statement. Some examples are
            Names of files or elements within files
            File specifications
            Messages
            Run-IDs
            Account numbers


2–2                                                                                7830 7949–031
                                                                    Using Control Statements




             User-IDs

         Fields, in turn, can contain subfields that are separated with a slash ( / ). You can use a
         space or spaces after a slash. For the most part, subfields are optional within a field.

         The relative position of a field or subfield determines its meaning.

         If you want to include a field that is preceded by optional fields you are not using, you
         must provide extra commas ( , ) to indicate that the preceding fields are blank. You do
         not need to include the extra commas if they occur after the last field you are
         including in the statement. Optional fields left blank assume system default values.

         If you want to include a subfield that is preceded by optional subfields you are not
         using, you must provide extra slashes ( / ) to indicate that the preceding subfields are
         blank. You need not include the extra slashes if they occur after the last subfield. Any
         optional subfields not specified assume system default values.

         Example
             @CAT,P MAILSAVE,F///500

         In this case, the extra slashes indicate the position of subfield 500; the subfields
         between F and 500 are not used and assume system default values for file allocation.

         Comments Field
         You can add comments to control statements. Comments follow the operand field.
         Start your comment with a space-period-space ( . ) and then enter your comment.

         The comment can contain spaces and any character except the semicolon ( ; ), which
         is the continuation character. The comments field is optional.

         Examples
             @RUN GHT,847120,ACCT-REC . Place comments after period

         @RUN is the mnemonic; there are no options; and there are three operand fields:
         GHT (a run-ID), 847120 (an account number), and ACCT-REC (a project-ID).
             @ASG,A ACCT-MASTER.

         @ASG is the mnemonic; A is an option; and there is one operand field: ACCT-MASTER
         (a file name).
             @COPY MO-TRANS.,AUG87-TRANS.

         @COPY is the mnemonic; there are no options; and there are two operand fields:
         MO-TRANS and AUG87-TRANS (both are file names).
             @FIN

         There are no options or operand fields, just the mnemonic itself (@FIN).




7830 7949–031                                                                                    2–3
Using Control Statements




        Continuing Control Statements
        The maximum length of a control statement is 84 characters per line for Fieldata and
        80 characters per line for ASCII. In batch mode, statements exceeding this length
        cause your run to terminate. In demand mode, statements exceeding this length are
        truncated when input. A control statement requiring more than one line can be
        continued.

        You can continue a control statement to another line by entering a semicolon ( ; ) at
        the end of the line to be continued. You can split a statement at any point in the
        statement where spaces are allowed or following a delimiter.

        You can start the next line in any column, with one exception: Do not place the
        masterspace ( @ ) in column 1 of the continuation line.

        You cannot continue the following control statements:
            @END
            @ENDF
            @ENDX
            @EOF
            @FILE
            @FIN
            @RUN

        A file name or element name is legal for certain control statement fields. But a file
        name cannot be continued at any of the statement subfields. If the period that
        distinguishes the file name is not encountered before the continuation character, an
        element name is assumed.

        The following @ASG statements illustrate the possible coding combinations that result
        from applying general default rules. Since control statements are freeform (fields are
        not required to be in specific columns), you can align the label, operation, and operand
        fields to improve readability.
          @ASG FILENAME
          @ASG,A FILENAME,,REEL1
          @ASG FILENAME,26N///4
          @ASG,T FILENAME,26N//,REEL1;REEL/;
           REEL2/REEL3
          @ASG,A FILENAME,///6
          @TAG1:ASG FILENAME,,REEL1




2–4                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                Using Control Statements




2.2. Transparent Control Statements
         Normally, control statements and data images in a runstream are processed
         sequentially and are processed only when directed to by the Exec, FURPUR, or an
         executing program. However, a special set of control statements (transparent control
         statements) are processed immediately after you enter them at a demand terminal.

         Transparent control statements can be entered at any time. Since they are processed
         immediately, you cannot store them in a file as part of a runstream.

         There are two types of transparent statements:
            Transparent ECL control statements
            Demand symbiont control statements

2.2.1. Transparent ECL Statements (@@)
         Transparent ECL statements are double-masterspace (@@) versions of selected ECL
         statements. Transparent ECL statements follow the same general rules for syntax and
         format as their single-masterspace counterparts (with the exception of @@PASSWD).

         These are the transparent ECL statements:
             @@ASG
             @@BRKPT
             @@CAT
             @@FREE
             @@HDG
             @@LOG
             @@MODE
             @@MSG
             @@PASSWD
             @@QUAL
             @@START
             @@SYM
             @@USE




7830 7949–031                                                                             2–5
Using Control Statements




2.2.2. Demand Symbiont Control Statements
        Another type of transparent control statement is the demand symbiont control
        statement. It is a special statement that controls the way the Exec handles your
        terminal. Unlike transparent ECL control statements, demand symbiont control
        statements have no corresponding single-masterspace (@) statements. Another
        difference is that you do not see a system response for some symbiont control
        statements.

        The demand symbiont control statements are

             @@CM                        @@INQ                          @@SKIP
             @@CONS                      @@INS                          @@TERM
             @@CONT                      @@NOPR                         @@TM
             @@CQUE                      @@PMOD                         @@TOUT
             @@DCT                       @@PRNT                         @@TTY
             @@END                       @@RLD                          @@X
             @@ESC                       @@RLU
             @@FUL                       @@RQUE
             @@HOLD                      @@SEND


2.2.3. Guidelines
        Follow these guidelines for using transparent control statements:
            Use transparent control statements only in a demand run.
            Wait for the transparent control statement to finish processing before you enter
             another one from your terminal.

        Transparent control statements can be entered at any time. To enter a transparent
        control statement, do the following:
        1.   Enter the transparent control statement following the start-of-entry (SOE)
             character (Ʌ) that the system provides. If the system is sending output to your
             terminal, press the MSG WAIT (break or interrupt) key first.
        2.   Press the transmit key again to get back an SOE character.

Using Files and Elements

         A file is an organized collection of data, treated as a unit, which is used to store
         programs or data. An element is a discreet entity within a special file called a program
         file.

         This section includes the following information on files and elements:
            Classification of files
                Mass storage and tape
                Cataloged and temporary
            File size
            Naming files and elements
            File cycles (F-cycles)
            System-created files
            Print files
            File formats
            Types of program file elements
            The table of contents for a program file
            Multireel tape files




7830 7949–031                                                                                 3–1
Using Files and Elements




3.1. Classification of Files
         Files are either on mass storage or on tape.

3.1.1.   Storage Classification—Mass Storage Versus Tape Files
         Mass storage files are files stored on magnetic disk. They can be read and written
         sequentially or randomly. Magnetic tape files can be only read and written
         sequentially.

         The basic concepts that you must understand to create and manipulate tapes and tape
         files are as follows:
            A volume is the same as a reel.
            A multivolume file is a single tape file so large that it takes more than one reel to
             store it. A multifile volume is a single tape reel that has more than one tape file on
             it (see Figure 3–1).




                Figure 3–1. Multivolume Files and Multifile Volumes

            The load point is the position near the beginning of a tape where the reading or
             writing of data begins.
            When more than one file is on a tape, the files are separated by a hardware mark
             called an end-of-file mark or EOF mark.
            After the last file on a tape, two consecutive EOF marks are used to indicate that
             there is nothing else on the tape.




3–2                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                      Using Files and Elements




3.1.2. Life Classification—Cataloged Versus Temporary Files
         Temporary files exist only for the duration of a run. When the run terminates, or if you
         release the file from your run, the file ceases to exist.

         Cataloged files are permanent files. They exist whether or not a run is active. If you
         want to get rid of a cataloged file, you must specifically delete it with the @DELETE
         statement (see Section 7.17).

         The technical difference between cataloged and temporary files is that cataloged files
         are recorded in a master file directory (MFD), whereas temporary files are not.
         Temporary files are only visible to the run that created them.

         An MFD contains information about all permanent files. Permanent files are cataloged
         in a master file directory.

         A master file directory contains the following information about each cataloged file:
            Complete file name
            Project number under which the file was cataloged
            Account number under which the file was cataloged
            Time the file was cataloged
            Time the file’s current assignment started or last assignment ended
            Time the file was last backed up (if applicable)
            Time of the first write after the file was cataloged or after the file was backed up
             by FAS or time of unload (only one can apply)
            Number of times the file was assigned to a run
            Usage authorization
            Recording mode (tape files only)
            Size of a mass storage file, in tracks or positions (see Section 3.2 for a description
             of tracks and positions)
            Information that describes the physical location of the file on a device.
            Number of tape reels or cartridges used for the file, as well as the tape identifiers
             used (tape files only)
            Number of disk packs used for the file, as well as the pack-IDs of the packs used
             (removable mass storage files only)
            F-cycle numbers of the existing cycles of the file
            Position on the tape where the rolled-out file is stored (only for mass storage files
             that have been rolled out to tape)
            Security attributes (if your site has Security Level 1 or higher)
            Cartridge Tape Library (CTL) pool name (tape files only)




7830 7949–031                                                                                   3–3
Using Files and Elements




        To examine the master file directory entry for a particular file, use the F option on the
        @PRT statement. See Section 7.48 for more information.


3.2. Additional Mass Storage and Tape File Topics
        Various increments are used to describe the size of files. Most of these terms apply to
        mass storage files. The most common terms used to describe data are explained
        here.

        A word is the smallest addressable unit of data; it consists of 36 bits. When used to
        store data, a word can contain either 4 or 6 bytes of data, depending on the format
        used. If the ASCII format is used, a word contains 4 bytes (9 bits each). If the Fieldata
        format is used, a word contains 6 bytes (6 bits each). (Fieldata is an older format for
        representing data; this format is used internally by the Exec. One disadvantage of
        Fieldata is that it does not let you represent lowercase letters.)

3.2.1. Mass Storage File Topics
        The following units are used in reference to mass storage files. I/O operations to mass
        storage files specify the size of the operation in sectors. The size of a mass storage
        file when it is assigned or cataloged is specified in tracks or positions.

            A sector contains 28 words.
            A track contains 64 sectors or 1,792 words.
            A position contains 64 tracks, which is equivalent to 4,096 sectors or 114,688
             words.
        When you create a mass storage file, the system automatically sets the maximum file
        size to your site’s default maximum (default_max_granules). If you think your file
        needs more than the maximum default, you can specify your own maximum, in either
        tracks or positions.

        Your system can be configured to allow large files. The maximum allowable file size is
        determined by your site’s installation (large_files_enabled). The values given are the
        maximum size the system can support, depending on the system configuration.


                  Maximum File Size (tracks)                    Large_files_enabled

                                                      FALSE                 TRUE
            Track granular                            262,143               262,143
            Position granular                         262,143               16,777,152




3–4                                                                                   7830 7949–031
                                                                      Using Files and Elements




3.2.2. Tape File Topics
         Tape files on unlabeled tapes are closed out with an end-of-file (EOF) mark written
         after the last data block in the tape file. The last tape file on a volume is closed out
         with two EOF marks, signifying the end-of-recorded data on the volume.

         Tape files on labeled tapes are surrounded by groups of labels called label groups.
         Two or more header (HDR) labels comprise the HDR label group and precede the data
         in a tape file. Two or more trailer (TRL) labels comprise the TRL label group and follow
         the data in a tape file. The first file on a tape volume also contains one or more VOL
         labels comprising the VOL label group that precedes both the data in the first file and
         the HDR label group associated with that file. The HDR and TRL label groups are
         separated from the data by EOF marks. The VOL label group butts against the HDR
         label group with no separator. Tape labeling is presented in more detail in the Exec
         Administration Reference Manual (7831 0323). The end of a file and the end of
         recorded area on a labeled tape are marked exactly as on unlabeled tapes; in other
         words, with one and two EOF marks, respectively.

         Upon receipt of an end-of-reel status, the statements that transfer files to tape
         (@COPOUT, @COPY) deposit an end-of-file (EOF) mark and a file continuation (swap)
         indicator on the "unlabeled output reel" if the entire file contents has not been copied
         to the output reel. An exception to this procedure is the quarter-inch cartridge tape,
         which lacks the functionality to backspace and handles only unlabeled tapes. When
         you copy to a quarter-inch cartridge and you encounter an end-of-reel status, the
         swap indicator is written before an EOF mark. This is critical for a copy from
         quarter-inch tape.

         The swap indicator has two forms:
            For labeled tapes, the operating system writes the information on the output reel
             in the form of end-of-volume tape labels.
            For unlabeled tapes, FURPUR writes one of two types of data patterns when it
             reaches a reel swap point, depending on the data format and type of copy.

         For all COPY,G and all nonquarter-word tapes of other copy formats, a 16-word block
         is written as follows:

         WORD 0                   0541600000000

         WORDS 1 - 7              0044105117122 ($EOR)

         WORDS 8 - 15             0000000000000


         For quarter-word format tapes, an 18-word block is written. This block is the same as
         the data pattern shown, but it is in quarter-word format.




7830 7949–031                                                                                       3–5
Using Files and Elements




        The statements that read tapes (@COPIN, @COPY, @FIND, and @MOVE) check for a
        swap indicator after the EOF mark for each tape file. For open reel and ½ inch
        cartridge tapes, if a swap indicator is not found after the EOF, the open reel or
        cartridge tape is backspaced (repositioned) for the next operation. Because
        backspacing is not possible for quarter–inch cartridge tapes, the statements must
        check each data block for a swap indicator during a read operation. The absence of the
        backspace capability for the quarter-inch cartridge tape also means that it is possible
        to receive a 012 I/O status if attempts are made to copy or move the cartridge tape
        past the double EOF sequence after the last file.

        Labeled tapes return a status code to FURPUR through the operating system when
        end-of-volume (EOV) labels are found.

        For unlabeled tapes, the data pattern written to the tape is checked for a swap
        indicator. If this block is not a swap indicator, the reel is backspaced and repositioned
        for the next operation.

        Table 3–1 summarizes the end-of-reel configuration for tapes that contain multireel
        files.


                      Table 3–1. End-of-Reel Configuration for Multireel Tapes


                              Tape                             End-of-Reel Configuration

            Labeled                                    File Blocks * EOV1 EOV2 * *
            Unlabeled                                  File Blocks * swap indicator * *
            Unlabeled, quarter-inch cartridge          File Blocks swap indicator *

        *    Indicates an EOF mark

        When you execute a move across reels for a multireel file, the EOF preceding the
        swap information on the first reel (or cartridge) is not part of the EOF count for the
        MOVE since it does not delimit an entire file.

        The @MOVE and @FIND statements are restricted when you use them with multireel
        files. They do not recognize reels preceding the one currently in use. However, they
        continue on succeeding reels. The @REWIND statement repositions the tape to the
        beginning of the first reel.

3.2.3. Virtual Tape Handler Files
        Virtual tape handler (VTH) simulates tape by using mass storage. The @ASG statement
        lets you assign virtual tape files to a run. You assign them in the same manner as a
        standard tape file, using an assign statement. Your access and manipulation of virtual
        tape files is the same as to standard tape files. Your control statements remain
        identical for a virtual tape as for a standard tape. Programs cannot tell the difference
        between a virtual tape and a real tape. The only tape functionality that is not
        supported is the Fast Tape Access (FTA) functions of cartridge tape subsystems.




3–6                                                                                   7830 7949–031
                                                                      Using Files and Elements




3.2.4. Omnibus File Format
         The omnibus file format is the superstructure upon which the program file, SDF, and
         many other data reference structures are based. This is the level at which the Exec
         supports the mass storage devices. It can be assigned in 1,792-word increments
         (track) and addressed in 28-word increments (sector). The assign granules (track) are
         not necessarily all allocated in succession in an active file.

         The @COPY and @COPY,G statements work with the omnibus format level and are not
         involved with the structures within the file. Those structures remain intact since the
         @COPY and @COPY,G statements view the substructure as data. This allows you to
         use the @COPY,G statement to transfer a program file to tape, or reload a program file
         on another OS 2200 system. MAP, MASM, and other processors work with the data
         directly.

3.2.5. File Sharing
         The order in which master file directories are searched depends on the system
         configuration. Systems without the file sharing feature naturally search only the
         standard master file directory. Systems with the file sharing feature can search either
         one or both of the master file directories, depending on the system configuration.


3.3. Naming Files and Elements
         The only part of a file name that is required is the basic file name, as follows:
           filename.

         All other fields are optional.

         In some cases, the period is optional; if you do not include a period, the system
         assumes that it is the name of a file. In other cases, if you do not include a period, the
         system assumes that it is the name of an element. To avoid confusion, include the
         period except for file names specified on the @BRKPT statement.

         The name originally given to a file is called the external file name. A file can also have
         an internal file name. See Section 7.68 for information on how to use the @USE
         statement to give a file an internal name.

         File Name and Element Name Format
           [[directory-id#]qualifier*]filename[(F-cycle)/read-key/write-key.element-name/
           version(S-cycle)]

         directory-id
           Shared files exist exclusively on an OS 2200 mass storage device that is shared by
           two or more OS 2200 systems. Shared files are different from local files, which are
           files that are stored on a specific OS 2200 system.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    3–7
Using Files and Elements




          The directory-id field is valid when file sharing is configured on the system. It
          indicates which master file directory contains the file. The directory-ID has two
          possible values: STD (standard) for local files on any system and SHARED for shared
          files.

          The # is a delimiter to separate the directory-ID and qualifier.

          This field is valid only for the following statements:
              @ASG
              @CAT
              @FREE
              @MODE
              @QUAL
              @USE

          All other statements that have a filename field cannot include the directory-ID in the
          file name. You can indirectly use a directory-ID for file names on these statements
          by either giving them internal names with the @USE statement or by specifying
          directory-IDs with the @QUAL statement, as in the following examples:
              @USE P1,STD#QUAL1*FILEX
              @COPY P1.,X.

              @QUAL,D SHARED#QUAL1
              @COPY FILE1.,FILE2.

          In the second example, the default qualifier (QUAL1) and directory-ID (SHARED) that
          were specified on the @QUAL,D statement are assumed in the file names on the
          @COPY statement.

          For more information on the @USE statement, see Section 7.68. For more
          information on the @QUAL statement, see Section 7.49.

          If you omit the directory-ID# from a file name and do not specify a directory-ID on a
          previous @QUAL statement, the system uses the director-ID value configured at
          your site. One exception to this is if a user is cataloguing a shared removable pack
          file, the system detects that it is a shared pack and uses the shared directory.

          If you include the #, but not a directory-ID, the system uses the implied directory-ID
          you specified on a previous @QUAL statement. If you did not specify an implied
          directory-ID, the system uses the directory-ID value configured at your site.

          The default directory-ID and default qualifier are the directory-ID and qualifier given
          on the last @QUAL,D statement performed in a run. The implied directory-ID and
          implied qualifier are the directory-ID and qualifier given on the last @QUAL with no
          options performed in a run.




3–8                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                                     Using Files and Elements




         qualifier
           The qualifier helps to ensure that file names are unique. Different files can have the
           same file name, as long as their qualifiers or F-cycles are different. User-IDs and
           project-IDs are commonly used as qualifiers, but you can create your own. The
           qualifier can be up to 12 characters long and can include any combination of letters,
           numbers, hyphens (-), and dollar signs ($). (The @QUAL statement, which also
           defines the qualifier, is described in Section 7.49.)

           If you omit the qualifier and asterisk (*) from a file name and do not specify a
           qualifier on an @QUAL statement, the system uses the project-ID on your @RUN
           statement as the qualifier.

           If you include an asterisk (*) but not a qualifier, the system uses the implied qualifier
           you specified on an @QUAL statement. If you did not specify an implied qualifier,
           the system uses the project-id on your @RUN statement.

         filename
           The basic name of a file can be up to 12 characters long and can include any
           combination of letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and dollar signs ($).
           Note: Do not use a processor name (ELT or DATA, for example) as a file name.
           The results will be unpredictable.

         F-cycle
           The F-cycle number identifies a file in a set of files that have the same qualifier and
           file name. Normally, you never have to include an F-cycle number with a file name. If
           you do not supply the F-cycle, you get the highest cataloged file cycle in the set.
           See Section 3.4 for more information on F-cycles.

         read-key/write-key
             Keys are like passwords that are required to read a file or write to it. Keys typically
             apply only to unowned files which are standard in Fundamental Security, but they
             can be used for owned files if the system is so configured. Keys are an easy way
             you can protect a file from unauthorized use. When you create a file, you can
             specify a read key, write key, both, or neither. If you use only a write key, you
             must precede it with two slashes to indicate that it is a write key, not a read key.
             Each key can be up to six characters long. You can use any characters but the
             period (.), comma (,), semicolon (;), slash (/), or blank.

             To change the read or write key on a file, or to add a read or write key to an
             existing file, use the @CHG statement as follows:
                @CHG filename/RK/WK,filename/RK/WK

             where filename1 is the file to be changed (including the current read/write keys),
             and filename2 is the file with its new or changed read or write keys. See Section
             7.5 for more information on the @CHG statement.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   3–9
Using Files and Elements




        element-name
          Is the name of the element. Element names can be up to 12 characters long and can
          include any combination of letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and dollar signs ($).

        version
          Is used to distinguish between elements that have the same name and type, but
          contain different information. Using version names is one way you can save
          different renditions of the same program. Version names can be up to 12 characters
          long and can include any combination of letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and dollar
          signs ($). If the element is an omnibus type, some processors can ignore the
          version.

          A combination of element name and version need be unique only within a file.
          Thus, .ELT1/VER1 and .ELT1/VER2 are two different elements (note the leading
          period). Then with different files, Q*F1.CH2/VER1, Q*F1.CH2/VER2, Q*F2.CH2/VER1,
          and Q*F2.CH2/VER2 are four different elements.

        S-cycle
          Is a number identifying a cycle of a symbolic element. Only symbolic elements can
          use element cycling. Element cycles are different stages a symbolic element goes
          through as it is updated by certain processors (U-option). Normally, you do not need
          to be concerned about element cycling and S-cycle numbers. Some processors,
          including IPF 1100, do not use element cycling. Processors that accept symbolic
          element input always default to the most recent cycle of a symbolic element. See
          Section 3.5 for more information.

          Only the basic element name is required; the version and cycle numbers are
          optional. Normally, different elements within the same file have different names.
          However, elements can have the same name, provided their element types are
          different (symbolic, relocatable, executable, or omnibus).

        File Name Examples
        ACCT-MASTER.

          ACCT-MASTER is the basic file name. The system uses defaults for all other parts of
          the file name:
             It uses the project-ID from the @RUN statement as the qualifier.
             It uses the current cycle of the file.
             No read key or write key is used.

        GL*ACCT-MASTER.

          GL is the qualifier, and ACCT-MASTER is the basic file name.

        GL*ACCT-MASTER/SESAME.

          GL is the qualifier, ACCT-MASTER is the basic file name, and SESAME is the read
          key.



3–10                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                                   Using Files and Elements




         PR*ACCT-MASTER//POPPY.

           PR is the qualifier, ACCT-MASTER is the basic file name, and POPPY is the write key.
           (The two slashes indicate that there is no read key and that POPPY is a write key,
           not a read key.) The current cycle of the file is used.

         GL*ACCT-BAL/SESAME/#%$&!.

           GL is the qualifier, ACCT-BAL is the basic file name, SESAME is the read key, and
           #%$&! is the write key.

         SHARED#DATA*BASE.
           SHARED is the directory-id, DATA is the qualifier, and BASE is the basic file name.

         Element Name Examples
         COLORS.RED,.BLUE,.YELLOW

           All three elements (RED, BLUE, and YELLOW) are assumed to be in file COLORS.

         COLORS.RED,.BLUE,YELLOW

           The elements RED and BLUE are assumed to be in file COLORS, while element
           YELLOW, which has no preceding period, is assumed to be in the TPF$ file.

         MAIN

           In this example, only the basic element name is used. Since a cycle number is not
           specified, the current cycle of the element is used. The version name is blank. The
           file container for element MAIN is TPF$.

         SUB1/APR02

           Here, SUB1 is the basic element name, and APR02 identifies the version of the
           element to be used. Since a cycle number is not specified, the current cycle of
           element SUB1/APR02 is used. The file container for element SUB1/APR02 is TPF$.

         When you specify an element name without a file name, the system usually assumes
         that the element specified is in TPF$, a temporary file automatically assigned to your
         run. An exception occurs when you specify a series of elements on the same control
         statement. If you include a file name with the first element name and put a period
         before the subsequent element names, the system assumes that those elements are
         in the first file named.

3.4. F-Cycles
        You can use file cycles (F-cycles) to manipulate a set of cataloged files.

        Each directory-id#qualifier*filename constitutes an F-cycle set. Each file within one
        of these sets of cataloged files has the same read and write keys, as well as the same
        directory-id#qualifier*filename. Each master file directory on a system can contain an
        F-cycle set with the same qualifier*filename.

3.4.1. Numbering
        When you create a file of a given F-cycle, a number is assigned to it. This number is
        called the absolute F-cycle number and uniquely identifies the file, along with its
        qualifier*filename. Absolute F-cycle numbers are unsigned integers that begin with
        1 and continue through 999, at which point the numbering recycles to 1. The circular
        assignment of F-cycle numbers does not cause conflicts since a maximum of 32
        consecutively numbered files can be retained in a set.

3.4.2. Referencing
        You can reference a file within an F-cycle set by its absolute F-cycle number or by a
        relative F-cycle number.

Relative F-Cycles
        Relative F-cycle numbers are signed integers in the range +1 to -31. Relative F-cycle
        number 0 (-0 or +0) refers to the cataloged file whose absolute F-cycle number is
        highest. Relative F-cycle -1 refers to the next highest, and so on. The highest is defined
        as having the highest absolute F-cycle number of any of the files in the F-cycle set,
        unless the absolute F-cycle numbers are at the point of recycling from 999 back to 1,
        in which case 1 is higher than 999.

        When a cataloged file is assigned with a relative F-cycle, the list of currently assigned
        files is searched to determine whether that relative F-cycle is already assigned to the
        run. If it is, that F-cycle is used. If the specified relative F-cycle cannot be found, the
        master file directories are searched to determine whether that relative F-cycle exists.
        If the relative F-cycle does not exist, the assignment request is rejected.

        If the relative F-cycle does exist, it is converted to the corresponding absolute F-cycle
        number and the list of currently assigned files is searched again to determine whether
        that absolute F-cycle is already assigned to the run.

        If it is assigned and it already has a relative F-cycle number associated with it, the
        request is rejected because a naming conflict exists when one absolute F-cycle-has
        two relative F-cycle values associated with it.

        If it is assigned and no relative F-cycle number is associated with that absolute F-cycle,
        then the absolute F-cycle is associated with the relative F-cycle.

        If it is not already assigned to the run, that relative F-cycle/absolute F-cycle is assigned
        to the run.



3–12                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                       Using Files and Elements




         When you specify a relative F-cycle, the file is known to the assigning run by both its
         relative F-cycle and the appropriate absolute F-cycle number. However, if you specify
         an absolute F-cycle, the Exec does not attempt to convert it to a relative F-cycle. In
         this case, the file is known to the assigning run only by its absolute F-cycle.

         The use of relative F-cycle numbers enables you to refer to a particular relative backup
         file. For example, assume a program required that a particular file always be created
         from an earlier cycle of the file. The relative F-cycle could be used to reference the
         earlier file each time the program is run. But, if an absolute F-cycle notation had been
         used, it would have to be changed each time the program was run.

Absolute F-Cycles
         To create the next sequential absolute F-cycle, you can use the relative specification
         +1. If files have been deleted, the relative specification +1 creates the highest
         numbered deleted F-cycle. When this +1 file is cataloged (by freeing the file or by run
         termination), its relative F-cycle number is set to 0 and other existing files of the set
         have their relative F-cycle numbers decreased by 1, thus maintaining consecutive
         relative numbering.

         If a file is created by its absolute cycle and the absolute cycle is not the next
         numerically sequential absolute F-cycle available, the sequence of F-cycles is updated
         to point at the newly created F-cycle. In addition, a buffer of noncataloged F-cycles
         exists between the newly cataloged F-cycle and the previously cataloged F-cycles.
         This increases the F-cycle range by more than 1.

         When a cataloged file is assigned with an absolute F-cycle, the list of currently
         assigned files is searched to determine whether that F-cycle is already assigned to the
         run. If it is, that F-cycle is used. If the specified absolute F-cycle is not assigned to the
         run, the master file directories are searched to determine whether that absolute F-
         cycle exists. If it does not exist, the assignment is rejected. If it does exist, that
         absolute F-cycle is assigned to the run.

3.4.3. Deleting
         Only one F-cycle can be deleted by the creation of another F-cycle. If the creation of
         an F-cycle causes more than one F-cycle to be deleted, the request is rejected.

         For example, if absolute cycles 36, 6, and 5 (relative 0, -1, -2) are the only cycles of a
         file cataloged, then cycle 38 cannot be created because cycles 5 and 6 must be
         deleted first. The creation of absolute cycle 37 deletes absolute 5, but absolute cycles
         37, 36, and 6 (relative 0, -1, -2) remain. Absolute cycles 38 through 68 can now be
         created because any cycle in this range causes at most one existing cycle to be
         deleted.

         The deletion of the last remaining file of a set causes all recognition of the set to be
         removed from the system.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    3–13
Using Files and Elements




        When the maximum number of files in one F-cycle set is exceeded, the record of the
        file with the most negative F-cycle number is deleted. If the file is stored on mass
        storage, the file’s text is deleted. The maximum number is 32, but you can change it
        with the MSCON$ Executive request. See the Exec Administration Reference Manual
        (7831 0323) for more information on ER MSCON$.

3.4.4. Internal Name
        An internal name can be attached (with @USE) to a file in the +1 condition. Then, if an
        @FREE,R is performed on this file, the resulting dummy item has no relative F-cycle
        value (null), but the absolute F-cycle value of the file is retained.

3.4.5. Temporary Files
        F-cycles for temporary files do not serve the functions previously described, but are
        allowed and can be used to uniquely identify temporary files that have the same
        qualifier*filename. When F-cycles are used in this manner, there is no correlation
        between relative and absolute F-cycles.

3.4.6. Examples
        Here are some examples using F-cycles.

        Example 1
        As an example of the correlation between the absolute and relative F-cycle numbering
        schemes, assume that the most recently cataloged cycle of a file has an absolute
        F-cycle number of 28. When referring to this file, the F-cycle could be either 28
        (absolute) or 0 (relative). Now, assume that a new cycle of the file is to be cataloged.
        Since the file has not yet been cataloged, its relative F-cycle is +1 and its absolute
        F-cycle is 29. When the new file is freed (cataloged)
           The absolute F-cycle remains as 29, but the relative F-cycle becomes 0.
           The file whose absolute F-cycle is 28 is now given a relative F-cycle of -1.
           The file whose absolute F-cycle is 27 is now given a relative F-cycle of -2, and so
            on.

        Example 2
        Here is an example of creating and deleting F-cycles by using relative specification +1:

        These statements create and catalog absolute F-cycles 1, 2, and 3 of the file
        QUAL*TEST, respectively.

              @ASG,C QUAL*TEST(+1).
              I:002333 ASG complete.
              @FREE QUAL*TEST(+1).
              I:002333 FREE complete.

              @ASG,C QUAL*TEST(+1).
              I:002333 ASG complete.




3–14                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                   Using Files and Elements




                @FREE QUAL*TEST(+1).
                I:002333 FREE complete.

                @ASG,C QUAL*TEST(+1).
                I:002333 ASG complete.
                @FREE QUAL*TEST(+1).
                I:002333 FREE complete.

         This @CYCLE command reports that three F-cycles of the file exist. It displays their
         absolute F-cycles: 3, 2, and 1.

                @CYCLE QUAL*TEST.
                  MAX-RANGE= 32        CUR-RANGE= 3
                  NO. OF F CYCLES=     3: 3, 2, 1

         These @DELETE commands delete two of the F-cycles, beginning with the highest
         relative F-cycle (absolute F-cycle 3).

                @DELETE QUAL*TEST.
                 END DELETE.

                @DELETE QUAL*TEST.
                 END DELETE.

         This @CYCLE command reports that F-cycles 2 and 3 were deleted, indicated by the
         *’s around the F-cycle number. F-cycle 1 is the only accessible F-cycle of the file.

                @CYCLE QUAL*TEST.
                   MAX-RANGE= 32        CUR-RANGE= 3
                   NO. OF F CYCLES=     1: *3*, *2*, 1

         These statements create another F-cycle of the file.

                @ASG,C QUAL*TEST(+1).
                I:002333 ASG complete.
                @FREE QUAL*TEST(+1).
                I:002333 FREE complete.

         This @CYCLE command reports that F-cycle 2 is still deleted.
         The new F-cycle is F-cycle 3, taking the number of the highest deleted F-cycle.

                @CYCLE QUAL*TEST.
                   MAX-RANGE= 32        CUR-RANGE= 3
                   NO. OF F CYCLES=     2: 3, *2*, 1


3.5. S-Cycles
         Symbolic data is represented in system data format (SDF). Complete information about
         SDF data is contained in the Data Structures Programming Reference Manual
         (7833 3481). There are several types of SDF data, but only the "general symbolic" type
         can contain the element cycle information that allows different versions of the



7830 7949–031                                                                               3–15
Using Files and Elements




           symbolic data to be contained in a single symbolic element. Processors that maintain
           element cycle information, such as ED, ELT, MAP, MASM, and PDP, update the
           element cycle information as symbolic data records are added and deleted.

           Note: Not all processors that update symbolic elements update the element cycle
           information. IPF is an example of a processor that does not update cycle
           information.

           For symbolic elements that contain element cycle information, you can use S-cycles to
           select which version of the symbolic data to reference. S-cycles are often referred to
           as element cycles.

3.5.1. Numbering and the Element Cycle Word
           Each symbolic element contains an element cycle word. This word contains three
           element cycle values:
              The maximum number of element cycles that can be contained in the element. It
               has a default value of 5 and can be changed to a value of from 1 to 63, inclusive.
               This value is referred to as max in the discussion of element cycles in this section.
              The current absolute element cycle number. It can have a value of from 0 to 62,
               inclusive. This value is referred to as cur.
              The number of element cycles present in the element. It can have a value of from
               1 to max. This value is referred to as num.

           The element cycle word can be displayed with the FURPUR @PRT,TL command (see
           Section 7.48.3). The following example is referred to throughout this section. It shows
           under the (CYCLE WORD) header the element cycle word values for an element ELT
           that has been initially created and then has been updated six times.

           Example
       @PRT,TLS QUAL*FILE$.
       STD#QUAL*FILE$(1) PF, 7/5000 elements, 29/256 tracks
                             ELEMENT TABLE

       D  NAME     VERSION    TYPE         DATE       TIME         NUMBER   SIZE    SIZE   MAX CUR NUM BITS   LOCATION
       *  ELT      VER        SYMBOLIC -Q 2014-10-01 16:14:58           1              2     5   0   1          1792
       *  ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            2              3     5   1   2          1794
       *  ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            3              3     5   2   3          1797
       *  ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            4              4     5   3   4          1800
       *  ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            5              5     5   4   5          1804
       *  ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            6              4     5   5   5          1809
          ELT      VER        ELT SYMB-Q 2014-11-12 12:11:38            7              4     5   6   5          1813
       NEXT AVAILABLE LOCATION-                                                                                 1817
       *File contains 6 deleted elements and <1 track of deleted text


           For the current ELT sequence number 7 max is 5, cur is 6, and num is 5.

           When a symbolic element is initially created
              max is set to the default value of 5
              cur is set to 0
              num is set to 1




3–16                                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                           Using Files and Elements




         When a symbolic element is updated
            max is not changed
            If cur is less than 62, it is increased by 1. If cur is 62, it is set to the smaller of
             max-1 and num.
            If num is less than max, num is increased by 1. If num is equal to max, num is not
             changed.

         The absolute cycle numbers contained in an element are cur-num+1 to cur, inclusive.
         For convenience, the lowest absolute cycle number cur-num+1 is referred to as low in
         the discussion of element cycles in this section. In the example, the current element
         ELT has the 5 absolute cycle numbers 2 (6-5+1) to 6.

         Once num reaches max, the element contains the maximum number of element
         cycles. When the element is updated, data records that were deleted at cycle number
         low are removed, and data records that were added at cycle number low are changed
         to indicate that they were added at cycle number low+1. In the example, if the
         element ELT is updated, data records deleted at cycle 2 are removed, and data records
         added at cycle 2 are changed to indicate they were added at cycle 3.

         Once cur reaches 62, the element is at the maximum absolute cycle number. When
         the element is updated, the absolute cycle numbers low to 62 are renumbered so that
         they fall in the new absolute cycle number range of 0 to max-1 (or 0 to num in the
         unusual case where num is less than max when cur is 62). Table 3–2 shows how
         absolute cycles are renumbered in the normal case when max is 5, cur is 62, and num
         is 5.


                     Table 3–2. Absolute Cycle Renumbering


                         Before Update                  After Update

                                58                            0
                                59                            0
                                60                            1
                                61                            2
                                62                            3
                                                    4 (new data records)


         After the element update, max is 5, cur is 4, and num is 5. This renumbering assures
         that element cycles always have only one range of absolute cycle numbers. This is
         unlike F-cycles (see Section 3.4.1), where there can be two ranges of absolute cycle
         numbers at the same time (lowest absolute F-cycle to 999 and 1 to highest absolute
         F-cycle).

         The FURPUR @CYCLE command (see Section 7.15.2) can be used to change max for an
         element to any value between 1 and 63, inclusive. Changing max causes the element
         to be rewritten when the new max value is smaller than num.

        In the example, the element ELT contains absolute cycle numbers 2 through 6. Note
        that sequence numbers 1 through 6 contain deleted versions of ELT that contain
        absolute cycle numbers 0 and 1. Until these deleted elements are removed from the
        file with the FURPUR @PACK command (see Section 7.42), the FURPUR @DELETE,U
        command (see Section 7.17.3) can be used to undelete any of the deleted elements.
        This can make additional versions of the symbolic data available for use.

3.5.2. Referencing
        You can reference different versions of the symbolic data contained in a symbolic
        element by specifying an absolute S-cycle number or by specifying one of the two
        available formats of relative S-cycle number.

Absolute S-Cycles
        Absolute S-cycles are specified as decimal numbers from 0 to 62 without a leading
        sign character (+ or -). The absolute cycle number that can be specified for an element
        is determined by the element cycle word values cur and num. The lowest absolute
        cycle number is cur-num+1 and the highest absolute cycle number is cur. If you do not
        specify an S-cycle, the default is the highest absolute cycle number cur.

Relative S-Cycles
        Relative S-cycles can be specified in two formats:
        Format 1
          (-cycle)

        Format 2
          (+cycle)

        Relative S-cycles are specified as decimal numbers from 0 to 62 with a leading sign
        character (+ or -). The relative cycle numbers that can be specified for an element are
        determined by the element cycle word value num. For both formats cycle is a decimal
        number from 0 to num-1.

        For format 1 the relative S-cycle number (-0) is the element cycle with the highest
        absolute cycle number, cur. Relative S-cycle number (-1) is the element cycle with the
        next highest absolute cycle number, cur-1, and so on.

        For format 2 the relative S-cycle number (+0) is the element cycle with the lowest
        absolute cycle number, num-cur+1. Relative S-cycle number (+1) is the element cycle
        with the next lowest absolute cycle number, num-cur+2, and so on.

        Note: S-cycles 0, -0, and +0 can represent different element cycles. 0 is an absolute
        S-cycle, and -0 and +0 are relative S-cycles. This is unlike F-cycles, where 0, -0, and
        +0 are all relative F-cycles and all represent the same file cycle (see Section 3.4.2).

        In the example element ELT, cur is 6 and num is 5. Table 3–3 shows the S-cycles that
        could be specified to select each of the five element cycles contained in ELT.

                  3                     (3)                     (-3)                     (+1)
