3.6. System-Created Files
         When you start a run, the Exec automatically creates up to four files for you: TPF$,
         READ$, PRINT$, and DIAG$. READ$ and PRINT$ are created only if your run is a batch
         run.

3.6.1. TPF$
         TPF$ is a temporary program file you can use as a working file during your run. Since,
         it is a temporary file, anything you store in it is lost as soon as your run terminates;
         use TPF$ only for data and programs you do not want to save. If there is something in
         the file you do want to save, be sure to copy it into a permanent (cataloged) file before
         terminating your run.

         Although the name implies that TPF$ is a program file, it could actually be either a
         program file or a data file, depending on how it is first used. (This is true for all files.)

         The system sometimes uses TPF$ as a default file when you do not provide the name
         of a file on a control statement. If you do not provide a file and element name for the
         output produced by a compiler or the Collector, the system uses TPF$.NAME$ by
         default.

3.6.2. READ$
         READ$ is used as the primary input file for batch runs. READ$ serves as a holding area
         for the runstream. During the course of the run, the Exec retrieves the control
         statements, data, and other images from the READ$ file and processes them in the
         order retrieved.

         Demand runs do not use a READ$ file. Instead, you type in all input directly from the
         keyboard of your terminal.




7830 7949–031                                                                                        3–19
Using Files and Elements




3.6.3. PRINT$
        PRINT$ is used as the primary output file for batch runs. The PRINT$ file contains the
        runstream statements from the READ$ file, as well as all output produced by the run.

        This output includes error and diagnostic messages, output generated by executing
        programs, and summary accounting information produced when the run terminates.
        After your run terminates, the PRINT$ file is queued to a printer, and this output is
        printed. This process is automatic for batch runs.

        Demand runs do not use a PRINT$ file. All output that is normally stored in PRINT$ is
        immediately displayed at your terminal. If you wish to direct output to a printer during
        a demand run, you must use the @BRKPT and @SYM symbiont statements.

        See Section 3.7 for more information on print files.

3.6.4. DIAG$
        DIAG$ is a diagnostic file used to store the parts of main storage that a program
        occupied when the program terminated. By analyzing this information, experienced
        programmers can determine what process has occurred. This can help them when a
        program terminates in error.

        To produce a printout or dump of the information saved in the DIAG$ file, use a
        PostMortem Dump (PMD) processor. For absolutes not collected with the TYPE
        NPEDIAG directive, use the @DAP or @PADS statement. For object modules, use the
        @PADS statement.

        It is permissible to use the @PMD statement following the execution of any program
        regardless of type. The Exec determines which PMD processor must be used based
        on the type of the last program executed. That processor loads and, if not @PMD,
        executes as if the ‘W’ option were present on the @RUN image.


3.7. Print Files
        When the system is configured, a default printer is assigned to each terminal. When
        no other printer is specified, the output from runs submitted from a particular input
        device is printed out on the default printer.

        For batch runs, the output generated during the run is normally stored in the run’s
        primary output file, PRINT$. Then, when the run terminates, the output stored in the
        PRINT$ file is queued to the default printer for the input device used. (See Figure 3–2)




3–20                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                                     Using Files and Elements




                            Figure 3–2. Normal Batch Output

         For demand runs, output normally is neither stored in a file nor printed; it is sent
         directly to your terminal. (See Figure 3–3)

         In spite of these differences in how output is handled for batch and demand runs,
         symbiont statements @BRKPT and @SYM perform the same basic function for both
         types of runs. The @BRKPT statement is used to direct output to a user-defined print
         file, and to redirect output back to the PRINT$ file (batch runs) or to the terminal
         (demand runs).




                          Figure 3–3. Normal Demand Output

         The @SYM statement is used to queue a user-defined print file to a printer. Unlike the
         PRINT$ file, user-defined print files are not queued automatically. You can also use the
         @SYM statement to queue the PRINT$ file to a printer other than the default printer
         that is assigned to the input device from which you submitted your run.

         Request output by using the @SYM statement (if the desired output is in a breakpoint
         file) rather than the SITE command from CTS, which would tie up your terminal.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   3–21
Using Files and Elements




        Figure 3–4 represents these print file concepts.




                  Figure 3–4. Breakpoint Output (Batch or Demand)

        You can breakpoint to either a mass storage file or a tape file. When you are
        breakpointing to a tape file, there is a technique you can use to breakpoint several
        print files to the same tape file. In addition to specifying the tape file you want to
        breakpoint to, you also specify a label or part-name to identify each print file (part) on
        the tape. Then, when you want to queue those print files to a printer, you include the
        name of the tape file and the labels (part-names) on the @SYM statement, to specify
        which print files (parts) you want to print.

        Although you usually queue a print file to a printer, you can also queue a file to a
        terminal or user-ID. If someone has queued a print file to your user-ID or terminal, you
        can receive the file by using the @@SEND statement after terminating your run with an
        @FIN statement. If a local printer is connected to your terminal, you can receive a
        printout of the queued file by entering the @@PRNT statement before you use the
        @@SEND statement. (See Section 7.47 for a description of the @@PRNT statement.)


3.8. File Formats
        This section describes the following file formats:
            System data format (SDF)
            Track-binary
            Track-binary: revised variant
            Element
            Program

3.8.1. System Data Format
        Symbolic data files are represented in system data format (SDF). Complete information
        about SDF data is contained in the Data Structures Programming Reference Manual
        (7833 3481). SDF files can be created by the symbiont complex, by products such as
        @DATA, and by your programs. SDF files can also be created from program file
        symbolic elements with the FURPUR @COPY,I command (see Section 7.13.2).




3–22                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                                               Using Files and Elements




3.8.2. Track-Binary Format
         The track-binary format is the representation of a mass storage file as a tape file.

         The @COPY,G statement produces the track-binary format on tape. Before the file
         contents are copied, a 28-word label block is written to tape, giving details of the
         copied file and the time when the copy was made. The format of this 28-word block
         follows.

                                                      ‘COPYG’
                                                     ‘BLKSEQ’
                                         Qualifier (2 words, left justified)


                                         File name (2 words, left justified)


                                                      F–cycle
                                Fieldata date in format month, day, year (mmddyy)
                             Fieldata time in format hours, minutes, seconds (hhmmss)
             Revision-ID                                                   Equipment Code
                                               Highest track written
                                0                                      Number of tracks in block
                                                     Always 0
                                                     Always 0
                                                     Always 0
                                                     Always 0

         Subsequent data blocks are multiples of 1,794 words and consist of a two-word
         header followed by 1,792 data words, a mass storage track.
              When "Revision-ID" in the label block is zero, then "number of tracks in block" in the
               label block is zero and subsequent data blocks are 1,794 words.
              When "Revision-ID" in the label block is nonzero, then "number of tracks in block" in
               the label block is from 1 to 16 and subsequent data blocks are 1,794 words times
               this value. The default number of tracks in a block is configured to 8 in FURPUR.
               This format is written when data compression is enabled for the output tape and
               when the D option is included on the @COPY,G statement (see Section 7.13.1).

        b                              Sector address of first sector in track
                           Checksum                                  Block sequence number
                                             1 track: 1,792 words




7830 7949–031                                                                                      3–23
Using Files and Elements




        The "b" is a one-bit "last track" indicator. When "Revision-ID" in the label block is zero,
        this indicator is 0 for all tracks. When "Revision-ID" in the label block is nonzero, this
        indicator is 1 for the last track in the file; this indicator is 0 for all previous tracks in the
        file.

3.8.3. Element File Format
        The element file format exists only on tape. It is created by the @COPOUT statement.
        You use the @FIND statement to locate specific elements within an element file. You
        use the @COPIN statement either to copy an element file to a program file or to bring
        specific elements or groupings of elements in an element file into a program file.

3.8.4. Program File Format Structure
        Program files are files that are formatted for storing independent collections of
        information called elements. To keep track of the elements, each program file
        contains a table of contents (TOC). The table of contents identifies each element in the
        file and describes significant characteristics of each element.

        There are three kinds of program files:
            Standard program files (PF) that have a variable-size table of contents and can
             contain up to 5,000 elements. Elements might have a maximum of 262,143 sectors
             of text.
            Large program files (LPF) that have a fixed size table of contents and might contain
             a guaranteed maximum of 26,146 elements. Elements might have a maximum of
             262,143 sectors of text.
            A large element program file (LEPF) can be initialized with the small, variable-size
             table of contents of a standard program file, or with the large, fixed size table of
             contents of a large program file. Elements can have more than 262,143 sectors of
             text.
        Table 3–4 shows the relationship between program file type, maximum number of
        elements and maximum element text length.


                                     Table 3–4. Program File Capacity


              Element Text Length         5,000 Element Maximum          26,146 Element Maximum

            Element text less than       Standard PF                   LPF
            262,144 sectors
            Element text of any size     Standard LEPF                 Large LEPF




3–24                                                                                     7830 7949–031
                                                                  Using Files and Elements




3.8.5. Types of Program File Elements
         Program files can contain these types of elements:

            Symbolic (includes procedure elements)
             Symbolic elements contain symbolic images or data. Symbolic elements can
             contain lines of a source program to be compiled, instructions (directives) for
             special processors (such as the Collector), data to be processed, or runstreams.

            Relocatable
             Relocatable elements are machine-language elements produced by some
             compilers. The Collector resolves intercomponent references in relocatable
             elements and generates absolute elements.

            Omnibus
             Omnibus elements are special-purpose elements that are not symbolic,
             relocatable, or executable. Omnibus elements are used to store information when
             a more flexible format is needed. For example, the Meta-Assembler (MASM)
             creates an omnibus element to contain the output of a definition mode assembly.

            Executable
             Elements that are ready for execution on a processor. These subtypes are
             associated with executable elements:

                Absolute elements
                 Absolute elements are executable machine-language elements produced by
                 the Collector, one of the system processors.
                 Absolute elements are created from user-defined relocatable elements,
                 together with elements from relocatable subroutine libraries.

                Object modules
                 Universal Compiling System (UCS) compilers, MASM, and the static linker
                 create these elements. They are directly executable; that is, you do not have
                 to prelink or collect them before you execute them.

                Bound object modules
                 These elements are special object modules created only by the static linker.
                 They cannot be linked to other bound object modules during a dynamic linking
                 operation, and can be linked to other object modules only during a dynamic
                 linking operation. For more information, see the Linking System Programming
                 Reference Manual (7831 0505).

                Subsystem definition elements
                 These are definition elements created by the subsystem definition processor.
                 They define the attributes of a logical group of object modules called a
                 subsystem. For more information, see the Linking System Subsystems
                 Programming Guide (7830 7451).



7830 7949–031                                                                              3–25
Using Files and Elements




        Symbolic procedure, relocatable, and absolute elements cannot be added to an LEPF.

3.8.6. Table of Contents for a Program File
        The table of contents for a program file consists of five tables: an element table, three
        procedure tables, and an entry point table. To examine the table of contents listing for
        a particular file, use the T and L options with the @PRT statement.

        A table describing the entry points within object modules is located in the element
        text area. The table of contents contains a pointer to the start of this table, if it exists.

Element Table
        The element name table contains an entry for each element in the program file. In
        addition to identifying the element name, version name, and type, these entries
        provide the following information about an element:
           Relative starting location within the file
           Size of the element
           Subtype of the element
           Time and date that the element was created
           Auxiliary information about the element

Procedure Tables
        The table of contents also includes three procedure tables: one for COBOL
        procedures, one for FORTRAN and PLUS procedures, and one for assembly language
        (MASM) procedures.

        A procedure is a set of instructions that is stored separately from the rest of the
        program and then copied into a program when needed. Procedures are used most
        often when the same instructions must be included in different programs. Entries in
        the procedure tables are created by the Procedure Definition Processor (@PDP). See
        the PDP Operations Reference Manual (UP–10070.1–A) for more information.

        Each entry in the procedure tables contains
           The name of the procedure
           A link to the element that contains the procedure
           The location of the procedure
           Procedure name tables




3–26                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                     Using Files and Elements




Entry Point Table
         The last table in the table of contents is an entry point table, which is used when a
         program is generated to link separate subprograms into a complete program. A
         program file can contain two entry-point tables. One table identifies the entry points
         for relocatable elements, and the other identifies the entry points for object modules.

         The @PREP statement adds entry points to an entry-point table. Thus, when
         relocatable elements or object modules are created or copied into a program file, the
         entry points within these elements are not inserted into an entry-point table until you
         enter an @PREP statement. See Section 7.46 for more information on @PREP.

Large Program Files
         Compared to a standard program file, a large program file has a larger capacity for all
         tables. For a standard program file, the table of contents is the first 28 tracks of the
         file; for a large program file, the table of contents is the first 629 tracks of the file.
         Table 3–5 shows the maximum number of entries that can be inserted in each table in
         a program file. The number of files can be less, depending on the types of elements
         contained in the file and the order in which they were created.

           (4-word)
           COBOL Procedure                430                   2,446                 32,686
           (8-word)

3.8.7. Large Element Program Files
        The large element program file (LEPF) format can contain symbolic and omnibus
        elements with text larger than 262,143 sectors. Relocatable, absolute, and symbolic
        procedure elements cannot be placed in an LEPF.

        Creating, accessing, and updating LEPFs are supported by the SYSLIB Program File
        Basic Service Package (BSP) routines and by FURPUR and PCFP. LEPFs are not
        supported by the Exec Program File Package (PFP) or by the ECL commands that
        accept element names, such as @ADD, @CHKPT, @RSTRT, @START, and @XQT.

        To specify that a file is formatted as an LEPF you must use the @CHG,E command. The
        @CHG,E command can be used only on newly assigned or erased files. See Section
        7.5 for more information on @CHG.

Section 4
File Security

         The OS 2200 security system ensures that only authorized users have access to
         information in your computer system. It protects sensitive data from both
         unauthorized use and inadvertent or unintentional disclosure.

         Unisys offers security software in several levels:
            Fundamental Security
            Security Level 1
            Security Level 2
            Security Level 3
            Security Level 3 Controlled Access Protection Environment
            Security Level 3 Trusted Environment

         This section gives you instructions on how to apply security mechanisms to your files.
         For an overall understanding of OS 2200 Security, see ClearPath OS 2200 Software
         Security Overview (8205 7282). For more details, refer to the ClearPath OS 2200
         Apex Help (8207 4154).

         The term "security management product" implies one of the following products:
            Apex is a web application for managing the OS 2200 operating system. It
             consolidates administrative tasks that have traditionally been performed using
             various Unisys provided and user developed utilities and processes, such as
             Security Administration for ClearPath OS 2200 (no longer supported) and
             Repository for ClearPath OS 2200 (UREP). Apex includes a command line utility,
             SECMGR, that was previously released as part of Security Administration for
             ClearPath OS 2200.
             As an administrative user, you can manipulate the current state of the OS 2200
             system or request historical reports of data from the OS 2200 system. From the
             Apex web application, you can perform the following:
                    Administer all aspects of user, account, and file security.
                    Run reports that support internal security audits and check for users who
                     are out of compliance with your security policies.
                    View and modify the configuration of the Apex OS 2200 agent, the
                     Configured Password Profiles authentication module, the OS 2200 Exec,
                     the security environment, and network authentication.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 4–1
File Security




                      View information about the installed OS 2200 software products and the
                       OS 2200 Exec.
              As a non-administrative end user, you can use Apex to view your own
              environment.
              As a database administrator, you can view the following:
                      Current UDS application group configuration
                      RDMS objects such as schema, table, and storage-area definitions.
              For more information, see the ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154).
             Site Management Complex (SIMAN) is the TeamQuest interactive software
              product that provides a tool with a screen-oriented, menu-driven interface for
              creating and maintaining security and resource control in an OS 2200 system. You
              can set up security for the whole system, for a particular application, or for
              personal security. For more information, see the TeamQuest Site Management
              Complex (SIMAN) Administration and End Use Reference Manual (TQ-01151).

4.1. MAC and DAC
         File protection is divided into two categories: mandatory access control (MAC) and
         discretionary access control (DAC). The MAC and DAC security mechanisms you can
         use for a file depend on whether the file is owned or unowned, as shown in Table 4–1.


                                      Table 4–1. File Protection


             File Type                                    DAC Protection

             Owned           Public or private access list or ACRs
                             Read-only/write-only files
             Unowned         Public/private by project-ID or account number
                             Read-only/write-only files
                             Read/write keys
                             Owned or unowned ACRs (Options 1, 2, and 3 only)


4.2. Protecting Unowned Files
         Files can be unowned in systems with Fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2, and
         3, except in a Security Level 3 Trusted Environment or a Security Level 3 Controlled
         Access Protection Environment, where the files must be owned. Unowned files can
         be protected using
             Read/write keys
              Keys are similar to passwords that you need to know to read from a file or write
              to it. For example, if a file has a write key on it, you cannot delete it, erase it, or
              overwrite it unless you know the write key.




4–2                                                                                    7830 7949–031
                                                                                        File Security




             If your site has Fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the file is
             unowned, the following applies:
                When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its read key,
                 write key, privacy mode, or all three overridden by privileged runs. Only the
                 unconditional delete file system privilege overrides the G option.
                If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read or write keys
                 for the file set are obscured by ‘////////////’ from all users. If a particular F-cycle
                 of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the privacy mode and either the
                 project-ID or account number under which the file was created are also
                 guarded.

            Read-only or write-only mechanism
             You can create your files as read only or write only. If a file is read only, you can
             only read it; if a file is write only, you can only write to it. To make a file read only,
             specify the R option when you create it with the @CAT, @ASG,C or @ASG,U
             statement; to make a file write only, specify the W option. (See Section 7).

            Private by project-ID or account number
             An unowned cataloged file can be private by project or account, depending on
             how your system is configured (check with your security officer or site
             administrator). Note that the definition of private for unowned files is different
             from the definition of private for owned files (private by owner).
             To make a file public, use the P option on the @CAT, @ASG,C, or @ASG,U
             statement. To make a file private, omit the P option. A private file takes on the
             project-ID or account number that you are executing with during file creation.
             Only users who have either the same account number or project-ID as the private
             file can access it.

            Owned or unowned access control records (ACR) (Security Levels 1, 2, and 3 only)
             Unowned files are made ACR-controlled through SECMGR, Apex, Security Admin
             Client, or SIMAN, which must be used to attach an ACR automatically. See the
             ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154) for more information.


4.3. Protecting Owned Files
         If your system has Security Level 1, 2, or 3, files usually have owners. The user
         creating the file is its owner.

4.3.1. Mandatory Access Control
         Files have security records that contain their security attributes. Those attributes
         include the file’s security level, which is the combination of its clearance level and its
         compartment set.

         When you create a file, it automatically takes on your executing clearance level and
         compartment set. (Compartment sets are available only in systems having Security
         Level 2 or higher).



7830 7949–031                                                                                       4–3
File Security




         The types of access a user is granted to a file depend on the comparison of the user’s
         mandatory attributes with the file’s mandatory attributes. For this reason, you must
         carefully consider your security level for a session before you sign on and create or
         access files (see the ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154)).

         The security system enforces the following validation rules for files:
             Read and execute access
              The mandatory access rules allow read and execute access to a file if
                  Your executing clearance level is greater than or equal to the clearance level
                   of the file, and the file’s clearance level lies within your clearance level range;
                   or the clearance level of the file is zero.
                  The compartment set of the file is contained in your executing compartment
                   set. Note that NULL is always a member of a compartment set. This rule
                   applies only to Security Levels 2 and 3.
             Write and delete access
              The mandatory access rules allow write and delete access to a file if
                  Your executing clearance level equals the clearance level of the file.
                  Your executing compartment set equals the compartment set of the file.
                   This rule applies to Security Levels 2 and 3.

         Note: When a file has a clearance level of 0 and a null compartment set, it is
         considered "unclassified." Every user has mandatory read and execute access to
         unclassified files. You still must have read access through the access list attached.
         To have write and delete access, your executing clearance level must also be equal
         to zero and your executing compartment set must be null. This applies only to sites
         with Security Level 2 or higher. For sites with Security Level 1, an unclassified file
         is a file with a security clearance level of 0.
         Examples of MAC Validation
         1.     Your clearance level range = 20-25
                Your executing clearance level = 22
                Your executing compartment set = personnel, payroll
                File’s clearance level = 18
                File’s compartment set = personnel, payroll

                You are denied access because the file’s clearance level is less than your
                minimum clearance level.

         2.   Your clearance level range = 20-25
              Your executing clearance level = 22
              Your executing compartment set = personnel, payroll
              File’s clearance level = 22
              File’s compartment set = personnel, payroll

                You have read, execute, delete, and write access to the file because your
                executing clearance level equals the file’s clearance level, and the file’s
                compartment set is the same as your executing compartment set.



4–4                                                                                    7830 7949–031
                                                                                 File Security




         3. Your clearance level range = 20-25
            Your executing clearance level = 25
            Your executing compartment set = personnel, payroll, financial
            File’s clearance level = 20
            File’s compartment set = personnel

             You have read and execute access to the file because your executing clearance
             level is greater than the file’s clearance level, which is equal to your minimum
             clearance level. The file compartment set is a subset of your executing
             compartment set.

         4. Your clearance level range = 20-25
            Your executing clearance level = 22
            Your executing compartment set = personnel, payroll
            File’s clearance level = 20
            File’s compartment set = financial, accounting

             You are denied access to the file because its compartment set is not a subset of
             your executing compartment set.

4.3.2. Discretionary Access Control
         Over and above the protection provided by mandatory controls, you can give your files
         protection with discretionary controls, either with default or explicit action.

         When creating a file, you must decide whether to give it a public, private, or
         ACR-controlled access list. ACR-controlled files can be considered as having
         semiprivate access as they can typically be accessed by a limited number of people
         apart from the owner. The type of access list you choose depends on who needs
         access to your file. Table 4–2 shows the three access list types, how to give them to
         a file, and who has access.

                             @ASG,U                                    delete

         Access to a file is allowed only if a user passes both mandatory and discretionary
         control validation.

         Always create files with the least amount of access permitted, and relax restrictions
         only if necessary. That is, always create private files and then change to
         ACR-controlled or public if necessary.

Access Control Records
         An access control record (ACR) allows you to restrict access to your files or other
         objects. An ACR identifies the users that have access to a file and the access types
         permitted. For example, an ACR could be used to limit user-ID XYZ or Account ABC to
         read access.

         An ACR can specify one or more of the following access types:
            Read
             Allows full read access to the file and automatically grants execute access.

            Write
             Allows write access to the file.

            Delete
             Allows deletion of the file.

            Execute
             Permits access to programs in the file.

            Delete ACR
             Allows deletion of the ACR if it is unowned.

            Modify
             Permits modification of the ACR if it is unowned.




4–6                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                                File Security




         The ACR also identifies the users who can access the file using one or more of the
         following types:
             User-ID
             Account
             Project
             Time of day

         The relation parameters EQ (equal) and NE (not equal) are used to include or exclude
         users from the group that is allowed to access the file. The following expression
         includes users assigned to account 123456 and excludes all others:
             ACCOUNT EQ 123456

         The relation parameter NE excludes account 123456 and includes all others:
             ACCOUNT NE 123456


                                               Caution
                Be careful when placing the project-ID Q$Q$Q$ in any ACR. This project-ID
                is available to all users on the system. You can easily compromise the
                security on your file even though you create other restrictions.



         The key words AND and OR are used to connect the parts of complex expressions.

         Separate the parts of a complex expression with OR when only one of two or more
         conditions must be true. The expression
             ACCOUNT EQ 123456 OR PROJECT EQ PROJECT-X

         grants access to any user associated with account 123456 or project X. This group
         consists of all users who meet one or both conditions.

         Use the word AND to connect expressions that must both be true. The expression
             ACCOUNT EQ 123456 AND PROJECT EQ PROJECT-X

         grants access to users who meet both conditions. It excludes users who meet only
         one or neither of the conditions.

         Parentheses are required in some complex expressions. The expression
             PROJECT EQ X OR PROJECT EQ Y AND USERID EQ BJSMITH

         is ambiguous and requires parentheses for precise interpretation.

         The parentheses are placed as follows if user BJSMITH is to be given access only if
         using project X or project Y:
             (PROJECT EQ X OR PROJECT EQ Y) AND USERID EQ BJSMITH




7830 7949–031                                                                                 4–7
File Security




         In this instance, both conditions must be true. Users of project X or project Y that
         have a user- ID other than BJSMITH are excluded.

         A different placement of parentheses alters the meaning of the expression:
             PROJECT EQ X OR (PROJECT EQ Y AND USERID EQ BJSMITH)

         In this instance, there are two conditions that are independent of one another. All
         users of project X are included, as are all users of project Y who have the user-ID
         BJSMITH.

         You can also designate a file public, which lets any user-ID have the access types
         associated with the condition.

         Creating an ACR
         You can create an ACR for your own user-ID and, if you have sufficient privilege, for
         other user-IDs. The security officer for your site determines the number of ACRs that
         can be created for your user-ID. When you create an ACR, the number allocated to
         your user-ID is decreased by one. You must always have at least one ACR available for
         your user-ID.

         Use your security management product. See the ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help
         (8207 4154) or SIMAN Administration and End Use Guide (TQ-01151) for additional
         information on creating ACRs.

         Attaching an ACR to a New File
         To attach an ACR to a new file, specify the ACR on the @CAT, @ASG,C, or @ASG,U
         statement.

         For example, attach the ACR named RDPUB to the file DEPT*PERSONNEL:
             @CAT DEPT*PERSONNEL,,,,,RDPUB

         For more information on attaching an ACR see the @ASG (Section 7.2) and @CAT
         (Section 7.4) statements.

Attaching an ACR to an Existing File
         You can attach an ACR to an existing file or replace an ACR with a new ACR by using
         the following:
             @CHG statement, as in the following example:
                @CHG,K filename.,ACR-name

             SECMGR keyword syntax interface as in the following example:
                @SECMGR
                Update file = filename.
                Attached_ACR = ACR-name
                ACR_Owner = your-userid




4–8                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                                                   File Security




            Apex Security  Files  <select file>  General  Access

            Security-Admin Client Update Catalogued File Security

            SIMAN keyword syntax interface as in the following example:
                @SIMAN,B
                Update file = filename.
                Attached_ACR = ACR-name
                ACR_Owner = your-userid

            SIMAN full-screen mode, Cataloged File Security Maintenance menu.

         See the ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154) and your security management
         product documentation for additional information on attaching ACRs.

         Deleting an ACR
         You cannot physically remove an ACR from the system. Deleted ACRs are marked as
         not in use. Deletion of an ACR does not increase the number allocated to your
         user-ID. You can recover a deleted ACR by retrieving it with your security
         management product and updating its contents.

         Updating an ACR
         The ACR name and owner cannot be changed, but there are no other restrictions for
         owned ACRs. You cannot update an unowned ACR. You can recover an ACR that is
         marked for deletion by updating the ACR.

         See the ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154) or the SIMAN Administration and
         End Use Guide (TQ-01151) for additional information on updating an ACR.

         Note: Modifications to the content of an ACR have no effect on users who have
         current access to a file or other object. If the changes to the ACR remove a current
         user’s access, the restriction does not take place until the file is reassigned. The
         only exception is a TIP user who has accelerated access to a TIP file. If the user’s
         access is revoked by changing the ACR attached to the TIP file, access is denied the
         next time the user attempts to access the file.

Making Files Read Only or Write Only
         The read-only/write-only mechanism, when applied to files at the time they are
         created, does not protect files from deletion, but it does prevent someone from
         inadvertently or intentionally reading or overwriting them. Create files as read only or
         write only by using the R or W option on the @CAT, @ASG,C, or @ASG,U statements.

         Do not use the read-only/write-only mechanism as a substitute for ACRs. The read-
         only/write-only mechanism protects only a single cycle of a file set, but ACRs protect
         an entire file cycle set. Read-only mode prevents users from writing to a file cycle.
         Write-only mode prevents users from reading a file cycle.

         You might want to access a previously created file as read only, so you do not
         accidentally destroy data in it or delete it.



7830 7949–031                                                                                 4–9
File Security




         Use @ASG,AR to assign a previously cataloged file as read only. The file could be
         originally cataloged as not read only, but you can still assign it as read only by using
         the R option. The A option indicates that the file is already cataloged and ensures that
         it is not treated as a temporary file. The R option write protects the file and prevents
         its deletion.

         The read-only assign mechanism merely reinforces read accesses specified in an ACR
         or the read access usually allowed by the owner of the file.


4.4. Changing Your File’s Protection
         You might need to change a file’s protection so that other users can see the data,
         or because the security sensitivity of the file’s data has changed.

         You can change some security attributes of a file you own; you must have a privilege
         to change other attributes.

4.4.1. Modifying Mandatory Attributes
         To modify a file’s clearance level or compartment set, or to set the ALL flag (gives the
         file the system compartment set and all future system compartment sets), you must
         be the file’s owner and have the privileges to change a file’s security record.

         See your security officer if you want to make any of these modifications.

4.4.2. Changing Access Lists
         To change a file’s access list, use the @CHG statement with the K, P, or Q option,
         as follows:

            @CHG,K
             Sets ACR-controlled access list (you must include the ACR-name parameter).
            @CHG,P
             Sets public access list.

            @CHG,Q
             Sets private access list.

         Another method of setting the ACR-controlled access list is by using your security
         management product.




4–10                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                                 File Security




4.4.3.   Changing or Clearing the Read-Only or Write-Only
         Mechanism
         To change or clear the read-only or write-only mechanism on a file, use the
         @CHG statement with the appropriate option:

            @CHG,V
             Sets the file as read only; clears write only.

            @CHG,W
             Sets the file as write only; clears read only.

            @CHG,Z
             Clears the file as read only and write only.

4.4.4. Changing Other File Attributes
         To give your file a different owner, the security attributes of the new owner must be a
         superset of the file’s attributes and a subset of your attributes. In other words, the
         file’s attributes must be a subset of the new owner’s attributes. To set special
         handling flags, you must have certain privileges. See your security officer if you want
         to make these modifications.

         $$OPEN Statement

5.2. Accessing the System
         The amount and type of information you supply the system when signing on depends
         on how your system and your user-ID are configured. The following subsections tell
         you what kinds of information the system can solicit and how you supply the
         information.

         Before you sign on the system, you need to know the type of applications you can
         perform. The application modes are as follows:
             Demand (interactive) run
             Batch runstream
             Transaction Processing (TIP)

         Your user-ID can be configured to access the system only in certain modes. Your site
         administrator or security officer determines which application modes your user-ID is
         allowed to access.

5.2.1. Demand Sign-On Modes
         When your security officer or site administrator registers your user-ID with the
         system and lets you work in demand, you are assigned one of three sign-on modes
         for accessing the system in demand. The three modes are just different ways to begin
         a terminal session. The difference lies in how much information you supply the system
         on the @RUN statement and how much information the system already has at hand.




7830 7949–031                                                                               5–3
Getting On and Off the System




        These are the three sign-on modes:
            User entered @RUN statement
             You must enter an @RUN statement after signing on. See Section 7.55 for
             information on the @RUN statement.

            System generated @RUN statement
             The Exec automatically uses the @RUN statement configured for your user-ID.
             You do not have the option of starting your own run by entering an asterisk before
             your user-ID. If you try to start your own run, the system ignores the asterisk.

            User entered or system generated @RUN statement
             You do not have to enter an @RUN statement to start a demand run; the system
             does that for you, using the information configured for your user-ID. You can
             bypass the automatic @RUN statement if you want to enter your own @RUN
             statement. To bypass the automatic @RUN statement, enter an asterisk ( * )
             before your user-ID when responding to the sign-on request.

        Your site administrator can configure your user-ID for automatic @RUN statement
        generation so that a program such as Interactive Processing Facility (IPF) is
        automatically started when you sign on, or so that your run-ID is different from your
        user-ID.

        If your site requires you to have a user-ID and password, the system displays one of
        the following messages, depending on whether or not your system requires a
        clearance level:
            Enter your user-id/password and clearance level:

            Enter your user-id/password:

        Precede your user-ID with an asterisk (*) if you want to prevent the system from
        automatically generating an @RUN statement for you.

        For example, this is how you bypass the automatic @RUN statement if your user-ID
        has a configured @RUN statement but you want to enter a different @RUN statement:
            Enter your user-id/password and clearance level:
            *user-id/password clearance-level
            *UNISYS 1100 Operating System Lev. 49R3
            @RUN,/B run-id,acct-id/user-id,...
            *BATCH RUN MODE - ENTER RUN STREAM*

        This example shows a batch mode run starting, but bypassing the automatic @RUN
        statement is done the same way when signing on to the system to use demand
        mode. At this point, enter the rest of your runstream.




5–4                                                                             7830 7949–031

5.2.2. Signing On to the System in Demand
         Your user-id might be configured for single sign-on so that you do not have to enter a
         user-ID and password combination. In this case, the multi-factor authentication that
         established your identity at your workstation combines with Kerberos, NTLM, or
         TLS/SSL certificate authentication to securely identify you to the OS 2200 system. If
         your user-ID is not configured for single sign-on, you must sign on to the system..

         The operating system issues the following sign-on requests:
           Enter your user-id/password and clearance level:

           Enter your user-id/password:

         Format
         The format of your response to the sign-on prompt is
           [*]user-id/password[/new password] [clearance level]

         Enter an asterisk ( * ) before the user-ID only if you are allowed to enter your own
         @RUN statement instead of using the one configured for your user-ID.

         user-id
             The user-ID is a unique identifier that your site administrator or security officer
             assigns to you. It can be up to 12 characters in length and can consist of the
             characters A through Z, a through z, 0 through 9, the hyphen ( - ), and the period
             ( . ).
             The slash ( / ) is the delimiter character used to separate the user-ID from the
             password.

         password
             Your password is a character string that you must specify when you sign on to
             the system.
             The first time you sign on to the system, use the password assigned to you by the
             site administrator or security officer. Change your password immediately after the
             initial sign-on to prevent unauthorized use of your user-ID.
             The procedure for changing your password depends on the configuration of your
             system. If the machine-generated password feature is implemented at your site,
             the system generates a new password for you when you request a change. If this
             feature is not in use, you can specify your new password.
             See Section 5.3 for more information on changing your password.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   5–5
Getting On and Off the System




        clearance level
            If your system has Security Level 1 or higher, the security officer establishes the
            clearance levels for your system. They can consist of numbers between 0 and 63
            or of symbolic names. (Symbolic names are available only with Security Levels
            2 and 3.)
            You can supply a clearance level after you enter your password (or a new
            password). You have a clearance level range associated with your user-ID, but you
            can run with only one clearance level at a time.
            If you do not specify a clearance level, the system gives you the lowest level in
            your clearance level range, called the minimum clearance level.
            If you enter an illegal clearance level, you receive an error message and the
            system gives you the following prompt for a new clearance level:
              Enter your clearance level (0-63; <XMIT>=default):

5.2.3. Sign-On Security Measures
        If you enter an illegal user-ID or password or both when signing on, the system
        response depends on how the system is configured:
           You can continue receiving the sign-on request.
           The system ignores any sign-on requests after a configured number of incorrect
            user-ID/password combination attempts occurs, but the system continues
            soliciting entries.
           You can experience an increasing delay time between each successive invalid
            attempt to sign on with each successive prompt taking about 4 times as long as
            the previous one, and after the maximum allowed attempts, the system disables
            your terminal. Once a site-ID has been disabled, the sign-on prompt is not
            displayed to the terminal. To use the terminal again, the system operator must
            re-enable it.

            Approximate delay times are displayed in the following table:


                Number of Invalid
                   Attempts                           Delay Time

                          1–3           Almost unnoticeable
                          4             64 seconds
                          5             4 minutes
                          8             Terminal disabled


        Depending on the configuration of the terminal emulator you are using, when you type
        in your sign-on response, the characters you type at the keyboard might not show up
        on your screen. This is a security measure to prevent someone from looking over your
        shoulder and stealing your user-ID and password.




5–6                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                              Getting On and Off the System




         For demand sign-on, the following message indicates that you have successfully
         completed the sign-on process:
           *UNISYS 1100 Operating System Level 49R3 ...

5.2.4. Providing Compartment Information in Demand
         If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, your system can have an added security
         feature called compartments. The compartment feature places groups or categories
         of information from the same interest or topic area into compartments, and then limits
         access to those compartments. For example, compartments on your system can
         include medical, legal, personnel, financial, or payroll. Several compartments can be
         associated with one file.

Compartment Sets
         Table 5–2 shows the four types of compartment sets you need to know about.


                              Table 5–2. Compartment Sets


           Compartment                                Definition
               Set

           System             All the compartments on the system.
           User               All the compartments listed in your security record. The
                              user compartment set is a subset of the system
                              compartment set.
           Executing          The compartment set with which you are executing. This
                              can be your entire user set or a subset of it.
           Default            The compartment set the system automatically uses if you
                              do not specify any compartments when you sign on. Either
                              you or your security officer can set up your default set.


         Your security officer specifies your user compartment set in your user-ID’s security
         record. The system checks this record whenever you sign on.

         You can access data associated with any compartment that is specified in your user
         compartment set, as long as the compartment is also in your executing set.

Rules for Entering a Compartment Set
         Your system can be configured so that you do not receive a solicitation for
         compartments, but instead, you automatically receive a default set established for
         you. Your administrator can change your default to a different set by using your
         security management product, as long as the default is a subset of your user
         compartment set.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 5–7
Getting On and Off the System




        Your system can be configured so that you receive the following solicitation for your
        compartment set after you sign on:
            Enter compartment set (or NULL, MAX, <XMIT>=default):

        You can respond in several ways:
            Enter the compartment set you choose as your executing compartment.
            Enter NULL if you only want to access system resources that have no
             compartments associated with them.
            Enter MAX if you want your user compartment set as your executing
             compartment set. Your security officer might choose to define your user
             compartment set as the entire system compartment set.
            Press the <XMIT> key if you want your default compartment set.
        Follow these rules and examples when entering your user compartment set:
            A comma must separate the names. Spaces are allowed before or after the
             commas. You can use uppercase or lowercase characters or a combination.
            If the names all fit on one line, transmit after the last name. The system then
             checks the compartment names you entered against your security record. If the
             names you listed are included in your record, validation passes.
            If the names do not fit on one line, use a semicolon ( ; ) as the continuation
             character. Press XMIT after entering each line of compartment names. Each time
             you transmit, the system checks the names you listed against your security
             record.
             As long as you keep entering the continuation character, and the compartment
             names on each line are in your record, the system responds with the following
             prompt:
               Continue entering compartment set (or <XMIT>):

            When you are finished entering compartment set names, press XMIT after the last
             line (do not include the continuation character). If you discover, after you have
             already transmitted a line with the continuation character, that you are through
             entering compartment names, press XMIT without any names in response to the
             "Continue entering compartment set (or <XMIT>" prompt. Compartment set
             validation is now complete.
            If you enter a name incorrectly, or if the compartment you listed is not in your
             security record, you receive the following message:
               Input was ignored. An illegal compartment was entered.

             Either the "Enter compartment set (or NULL, MAX, <XMIT> = default)" prompt or
             the Continue entering compartment set (or <XMIT>): prompt is displayed,
             depending on whether you have just entered your first line of compartment
             names or were transmitting a continuation line. You can then correct the line that
             was in error by retyping all the compartment names on that line. You do not need
             to retype compartments validated on previous lines.




5–8                                                                               7830 7949–031

             Example
             In this example, the user executes with FINANCIAL, PAYROLL, LEGAL, MEDICAL,
             and PROCUREMENT, but not with PERSONNEL.
                Enter compartment set (or NULL, MAX, <XMIT> = default):
                FNANCIAL, PAYROLL, LEGAL
                Input was ignored. An illegal compartment was entered.
                Enter compartment set (or NULL, MAX, <XMIT> = default):

                Continue entering compartment set (or <XMIT>):
                PERSONNEL, MEDICAL, PROCUREMENT
                Input was ignored. An illegal compartment was entered
                Continue entering compartment set (or <XMIT>):

             If you enter a compartment name and it is validated, but your security officer
              happens to change the name while you are entering other compartment names,

              You are then given this prompt:

              and you must start over your entering of compartment names.

5.2.5. Providing an Account Number in Demand
         After you sign on and provide compartment information (if required), you might be
         prompted for an account number before you or the system generates the @RUN
         statement.

         If you are not prompted for an account number, the system automatically takes the
         account number the site administrator or security officer has placed in your user-ID
         security record, or it takes the default account number 000000; however, you can still
         override the account number in a demand session.

         When you are prompted for an account number, your response depends on whether
         you are allowed to use only one account number or can choose from several or all of
         the valid account numbers on your system.




7830 7949–031                                                                                5–9
Getting On and Off the System




        If you can use only one account number
           You cannot get any prompts, and the system automatically supplies your default
            account number.
           You can receive the following prompt:
              Enter your account number:

            Either type in the number and press XMIT, or just press XMIT to receive your
            default account number.

        If you can choose from several account numbers
           You can receive the account number prompt. Enter any valid account number.
            For example
              Enter your account number:
              599210

             If a default account number resides in your user-ID security record, you can
             accept your default by pressing XMIT. You might have the ability to change your
             default, depending on the capabilities given to you by your security officer.

           You can be asked to select one from an index of up to five account numbers.
            The index number corresponds to the account numbers as displayed on your
            security management product screen. If you receive the account number prompt,
            press XMIT, and then you receive another prompt that asks you to choose a
            number from the account index. For example
              Enter your account number:
              (XMIT)
              Choose your account index (1-5):
              3

        If you receive only the account index prompt, answer it by typing an index number.
        See Section 7.55 for information about supplying an account number on the @RUN
        statement.

5.2.6. Providing a Project-ID in Demand
        A project-ID is a method of classifying a run for file access. If your system is
        configured for project-IDs, how you supply a project-ID depends on whether your
        @RUN statement is automatically generated by the system or whether you enter the
        @RUN statement yourself.

        If you sign on, but are entering your own @RUN statement, you must provide the
        project-ID the @RUN statement (see Section 7.55). You must also supply a project-ID
        on the @RUN statement if you are entering a batch run using @RUN with the B option.




5–10                                                                          7830 7949–031
                                                             Getting On and Off the System




         If your @RUN statement is automatically generated, you might have to supply a
         project-ID when signing on the system. Depending on how your user-ID is configured,
         you supply the project-ID by using one of the following methods.

            Select a project-ID from a list of up to five project-IDs. For example
                1. PROJA 2. PROJB 3. PROJC 4. PROJD 5. PROJE
                Choose your project-identifier index
                (1-5; <XMIT> = Q$Q$Q$):

                The range of indicators on the second line corresponds to the number of
                project-IDs listed on the first line. Your response to the prompt must be the
                one-digit number of your selected project-ID (spaces are ignored).
                If you respond to the project-ID index prompt incorrectly, the project-ID list and
                prompt are displayed again.
                If you press XMIT without entering a number, the system gives you default
                project-ID Q$Q$Q$.

            If you receive a project-ID prompt that displays only the default project-ID your
             security officer has established for your user-ID, either accept the default by
             pressing XMIT or enter any valid project-ID on the system. For example
                Enter your project-identifier (<XMIT> = PROJA):
                ABC

             The project-ID displayed after <XMIT>= is the default (PROJA in the example). If
             you have no project-IDs assigned, the project-ID displayed is Q$Q$Q$. You can
             respond by either transmitting a blank line (accepting the default) or entering a
             project-ID (ABC in the example).
             If you respond to the project-ID prompt incorrectly, the project-ID prompt is
             displayed again.

5.2.7. System Response
         After you complete the sign-on process, you might receive one or more "messages of
         the day" on your terminal; this is one method the site administrator uses for contacting
         all the users of your system to inform you of special developments concerning your
         system, or other appropriate information.

         Following the messages of the day, the system informs you of your current session
         number and the date and time of your last sign-on to the system.

         Your current session number is the total number of valid sign-on attempts to the
         system for your user-ID. Initially 0, this value can be reset to 0 after you have made
         999 valid sign-on attempts.

5.2.8. Authentication and Session Initiation Subsystem (ASIS)
         Demand sign-ons may be affected if ASIS is used. See the User Authentication
         Administration Guide (7850 4586) for more information.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 5–11
Getting On and Off the System




Site Does Not Have ASIS Registered
        If ASIS is not registered, session initiation proceeds as normal, unless a user-ID with a
        nonzero authentication type is encountered. If the Exec is set to allow traditional
        authentication passwords, all users with traditional passwords can sign on.

        If the Exec is set to not allow traditional authentication passwords, only the security
        officer is allowed to sign on using a traditional authentication password. Other user
        receives this error message:
        The Authentication Subsystem is not available. This sign-on is rejected.
        Contact your site administrator.

Site Has ASIS Registered
        If ASIS is registered, it processes the sign-on attempt with the help of authentication
        modules (AMs) that have been linked into ASIS. ASIS can respond with several
        different statuses:
            If ASIS declines to authenticate the user-ID/password, then the Exec processes
             the user-ID/password text that ASIS has solicited.
            If ASIS processed a successful authentication, then it has several ways to indicate
             the clearance level to use. If ASIS returns a valid clearance level, then there is no
             further solicitation. ASIS can also ask the Exec to supply the default (minimum)
             clearance level for the user-ID. ASIS can also supply no clearance level, in which
             case the Exec prompts the user with the message "Enter your clearance level."
             The Exec and ASIS cooperate to make sure that the user-ID exists, that it has not
             been disabled previously and that the user-ID has access to demand.

            If ASIS processed the sign-on attempt and returns a failed authentication with no
             retry, the Exec performs the usual hacker frustration on the user-ID and the
             terminal, and then may terminate the session.
            If ASIS processed the sign-on attempt and returns a failed authentication with
             retry, then the Exec performs the usual hacker frustration on the user-ID and the
             terminal. The Exec does not terminate the session unless the maximum attempts
             have been reached, but allows ASIS to process the next sign-on attempt.

        If the user authentication failed, the Exec terminates the session. If it has failed due to
        bad user-ID, the Exec generates this console message:
            Sign-on security error at site: terminal-id attempt # nnnnn userid: uuuuuuuuuuuu

        and generates a log entry for this bad user-ID sign-on.

        If the ASIS returned a message saying that authentication failed for any other reason
        and the Exec is configured to allow terminal messages, then the Exec displays the
        following message:
            You have entered invalid authentication data.

        If authentication retry is allowed, the Exec logs the authentication failure and institutes
        hacker frustration as configured.



5–12                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                              Getting On and Off the System




         If session initiation processing requires additional information, then the user receives
         the regular solicits for clearance level, compartment set, account number or index, and
         project-ID or index.

ASIS Not Available
         If a demand mode user tries to sign on while ASIS is temporarily not available,
         the Exec sends to the terminal the message
           The Authentication Subsystem is not available. This sign-on is rejected.
           Contact your site administrator.

         The session is not immediately terminated, but session timing continues and the
         session might eventually time out. The demand user can enter a @@SOLI command
         that causes a traditional solicit for a user-ID/password. All users who are allowed to
         enter traditional authentication passwords can sign on. If traditional authentication is
         not allowed, only the security officer is allowed to sign on using a traditional
         user-ID/password.

5.2.9. Signing On to TIP
         If you are a TIP user, you might need to sign on to TIP before running any application
         programs. Signing on to TIP is similar to signing on to demand. If your user-ID is not
         configured for TIP access, you see the following message after entering your user-ID
         and password:
           Your user-id has no access to TIP.

         When you sign on to TIP, the system establishes a TIP session during which you can
         enter input to application programs. The session continues until you sign off the
         system or until you time out by failing to enter input. If your system requests that you
         sign on with a user-ID/password, then TIP Session Control is configured for your
         system. While TIP Session Control is active, you cannot override the default account
         number for that TIP session.

         If you have the appropriate security attributes in your security record, you can change
         your timeout period with the @@TOUT statement (see Section 7.65). During a TIP
         session, @@TOUT is the only transparent statement that you can enter.

ASIS
         ASIS affects TIP sign-ons the same way as demand sign-ons. See the earlier
         subsections "Site Does Not Have ASIS Registered" and "Site Has ASIS Registered. For
         more information, see the User Authentication Administration Guide (7850 4586).

ASIS Not Available
         If a user tries to sign on to TIP while ASIS is temporarily not available or not accepting
         new authentication requests, the Exec sends to the terminal the message:
           The Authentication Subsystem is not available. This sign-on is rejected.
           Contact your site administrator.

         The session is immediately terminated.
