5.3. Changing Passwords in Demand
        Passwords are an important mechanism in your security system. Your password
        restricts the use of your use-ID and helps prevent unauthorized access to the system.
        You must specify a password when you sign on to the system unless your user-ID
        has been configured to use single sign-on, in which case you have already been
        authenticated to your PC and your authorization and identity are securely passed to
        the OS 2200 host.

        At most sites, you must change your password at regular intervals. Changing your
        password is an important part of maintaining a secure environment. You can receive a
        message indicating that your password has expired and a prompt to choose a new
        password. Your user-ID can be disabled if you fail to change your password when
        prompted to do so. Only you or an administrator with permission to change your
        user-ID record or the security officer for your site can change your password.

        Your system is configured for one of the following options:
            Machine-generated passwords
            User-specified passwords

        The procedure for changing your password depends on which option has been
        implemented at your site. Check with your security officer if you do not know which
        option is implemented at your site.

5.3.1. Changing a Machine-Generated Password
        If the machine-generated passwords feature is configured, your system generates a
        password when you request a new password at sign-on.

        Use the following statement to request a new password:
            userid/old_password/

        The second slash in the statement signals the system that you want a new password.
        The system ignores any characters after the second slash because only
        system-generated passwords are permitted.

        The system responds to a request for a new password as follows:
            Your new password is: xxyyzzzz (xx-yy-zzzz)
            Enter your new password (or transmit to request another password):

        The new password can consist of 1 to 18 characters, depending on system
        configuration.

        You can now enter the new password to verify the change, or press the transmit key,
        to request generation of another password. If the new password is successfully
        entered at the prompt, the system displays the following message:
            Your password has been replaced.




5–14                                                                          7830 7949–031
                                                              Getting On and Off the System




         If the user enters the new password incorrectly in response to the prompt, the
         following message is displayed:
             Re-enter your generated password (or transmit to request another password):

         If a user-ID is allowed to ignore solicitation for a new password, the following
         message is displayed:
             Do you wish to change your password?

         If the user enters Y or presses the transmit key, a new password is displayed. If N is
         entered, sign-on continues with no change to the password.

         Note: You cannot use the @@PASSWD statement to change your password if the
         machine-generated passwords feature is configured at your site.

5.3.2. Changing a User-Specified Password
         If the machine-generated passwords feature has not been configured at your site,
         you must specify a new password when you make a change. You can change your
         password when you sign on to the system, or you can use the @@PASSWD
         statement (see Section 7.43), unless the system configuration prohibits the use of
         @@PASSWD.

         Your security officer specifies the length of passwords on your system (1 to 18
         characters if the Exec passwords are used, or 1 to 32 if your user-id uses Configured
         Password Profiles, one of the ASIS AMs) and how often you must change your
         password.

5.3.3. Guidelines for Choosing a Password
         Follow these guidelines when choosing a new password:
             Choose a password you have never used before.
             Avoid repetition of characters.
             You can use any characters on the keyboard for your password combination
              except the slash ( / ), comma ( , ), and blank ( ) characters.
             Use variable lengths for your series of passwords, which makes them harder to
              guess.
             Remember that long passwords are more secure than short ones.
             You cannot use the same sequence of characters as your user-ID for your
              password.
             Avoid initials and names that others might connect with you.
             If you must record your password, lock it up.
             Do not reveal your password to anyone.
             Change your password if you think some else knows it.
             Do not sign on if someone is looking over your shoulder.




7830 7949–031                                                                               5–15
Getting On and Off the System




        If your user-ID's authentication method is Configured Password Profiles, you must
        comply with additional rules established by your security officer. For instance, you
        might not be allowed to reuse a number of past passwords or your new password
        might have to have a combination of upper and lower case letters, numbers, and
        special characters.

5.3.4. Changing Your Password at Sign-On
        You can change your password when you sign on to the system by specifying a new
        password in the statement as follows:
          userid/old_password/new_password

        If the system accepts the new password, the following message is displayed:
          Your password has been replaced.

        If your user-ID uses Configured Password Profiles authentication, you might have to
        enter your new password twice, as a safeguard against a typing mistake becoming
        your new password.

5.3.5. Changing Your Password Using @@PASSWD
        The @@PASSWD statement lets you change your password in demand mode on all
        systems where the system configuration allows it. Attempts to change your
        password on a system that does not allow @@PASSWD returns the error
          System configuration disallows password changes by @@PASSWD.

        The format is
          @@PASSWD old-password/new-password

        For example
          @@PASSWD QMKE/PAX01

        changes your password from QMKE to PAX01.


                                              Caution
             The password specified in an @@PASSWD statement is visible to
             observers. Security can be compromised if you execute this statement.
             The most secure way to change your password is during sign-on.



        You can change your password when you are working in batch mode by using the
        @PASSWD control statement (see Section 7.43).

5.4. Run Termination
         Run termination is a state that can be reached either normally or abnormally.

5.4.1. Termination Actions
         A number of actions occur at either normal or abnormal run termination, including the
         following:
            Summary accounting information is entered in the print file, including run start and
             termination time, standard units of processing (SUP) used, pages printed, and
             pertinent console messages.
            Symbiont output files are closed and queued for printing/punching in batch mode.
            All facilities allocated to the run are released back to the system facilities pool,
             with the exception of mass storage space being retained in a cataloged file.
            Temporary files are freed and disappear from the system.
            Cataloged files are freed and are retained, unless you specify assignment options
             to the contrary. Any exclusive use interlocks are released.

         A demand run terminates normally when you enter @FIN. A demand run terminates
         abnormally when you enter @@TERM or $$CLOSE without entering @FIN first, or as a
         result of an operator keyin.

         A batch run terminates normally when it reaches the end of the runstream (@FIN).
         An abnormal termination occurs in a batch run when one or more activities terminate
         in error.

         Batch runs that terminate because of an @FIN statement can have files assigned with
         the C or D options, even though there are error contingencies set in the control word
         for the run. See the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for an
         explanation of error termination contingencies.

         If you execute the @SETC,I control statement before run termination, the @SETC,I
         makes the run termination process act as if the run were terminating without errors.
         The C option causes the files to be cataloged; the D option causes the files to be
         deleted. See Section 7.57 for more information on @SETC.


                                                 Caution
                If a system stop occurs before run termination, the run does not terminate
                either normally or abnormally. Files in a to-be-cataloged state (created with
                @ASG,C or @ASG,U) are not cataloged.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   5–17
Getting On and Off the System




5.4.2. Termination Task Scheduling
        A site can configure the Exec to schedule a task (in other words, a program) that
        executes in a batch or demand run just prior to the termination of the run.

        The scheduling of the termination task overrides forced run terminations. For example,
        if an X keyin terminates a batch run prior to the scheduling of the termination task, the
        termination task is still scheduled. Once the task begins execution, the run can again
        be subject to forced termination.

        The termination task can be thought of as a FIN processor. It does not replace any of
        the standard run termination process performed by the Exec, but rather executes and
        terminates the task, and then the Exec begins its regular final termination actions.

        No control statements are processed after the termination task is done (including
        PMD, PADS, @ASG, @XQT, processor calls, and so on).

        The same task is scheduled for all batch and demand runs. The first of two
        configuration parameters (run_termination_task) is a program name. The program
        must reside in SYS$*RUN$ or SYS$LIB$*RUN$. When the program is scheduled, the
        Exec searches SYS$LIB$*RUN$ first. The Exec executes the program as a program
        rather than a processor.

        The second configuration parameter (sys_termination_task_schedule) allows a site to
        configure whether or not the task must be scheduled for the SYS run. This provides a
        way to avoid system hangs caused by SYS accessing files on removable packs that
        cannot be registered until after SYS FIN.

        The configuration of a termination task affects which part of a breakpoint (BRKPT)
        PRINT$ file contains the tailsheet. In the default condition, when a termination task is
        not configured, the BRKPT file is closed and the tailsheet is printed in the standard
        PRINT$ file.

        But if a termination task is configured, then the tailsheet (and all other PRINT$ output
        from the termination task) is printed in the BRKPT file, and then the BRKPT file is
        closed. The final part of the PRINT$ file is not queued and is deleted because it always
        be empty. The termination task never receives images from the primary READ$ file.

        Facility control statements can be included in a termination task, but not in an
        addstream (because no control statements are processed after the termination task
        ends). A demand user might submit transparent facility ECL statements.

        The termination status of the termination task does not affect the C or D conditional
        cataloging options on the @ASG control statement. The cataloguing and dropping of
        files still occur after the termination tasks ends, but the options are enforced using the
        value of the run status just prior to the scheduling of the termination task. This applies
        even to files that are named on transparent facility control statements entered after
        the termination task is scheduled.




5–18                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                           Getting On and Off the System




         Accounting for system resource usage continues while the termination task is
         executing. (QUOTA limits also continue to be enforced.) Thus the system accounting
         file, written after the termination task ends, includes charges accumulated throughout
         the execution of the termination task.

         Because SUP accumulations continue during the execution of a termination task, it is
         possible for the termination task to receive a "max time" contingency.


5.5. Closing a Session ($$CLOSE)
         To close the application session you opened with the $$OPEN communications
         network statement (see Section 5.1), enter
           $$CLOSE

         When your session is closed, you receive this message:
           *SESSION PATH CLOSED*

         It is not necessary to issue a $$CLOSE statement when you want to change sessions.
         To establish a session with another application, enter another $$OPEN statement. This
         closes the current session and opens a new one. Use this procedure even when your
         system administrator specifies automatic session establishment for your terminal.

Using Processors

         This section covers processor calls and other statements that are used with
         processors. It describes how to generate, correct, and execute basic and extended
         mode programs.


6.1. Calling a Processor (@processor)
         A processor is a system program that performs a function. A processor call statement
         is the instruction to execute a processor. An example is a language processor that
         translates a source program into machine-readable form.

         Format
         The general format of the processor call statement is
           @[label:]processor[,options] field-1,field-2,field-3,..., field-n

         label
             Can be used to name the processor field, but is not required.

         processor
             Identifies the processor to be called.
             The processor call is actually an instruction to execute the absolute element
             specified in the processor field. For processors supplied by Unisys, such elements
             are contained in the system library files.
             To locate the absolute element on a processor call, the system uses these rules:
                   If you specify a file name (for example, @UTL.PROOFER), that file is searched
                    for the absolute element.
                   If you do not specify a file name but do use a leading period (for example,
                    @.PROOFER), the Exec searches the default file, TPF$, for the element.
                   If you do not specify a file name and there is no leading period (for example,
                    @SPELL), the Exec searches the system library files first; if the element is not
                    found, TPF$ is searched.
                 The abbreviations for the standard processors (for example, SSG for Symbolic
                 Stream Generator) are the names of the respective absolute elements.




7830 7949–031                                                                                     6–1
Using Processors




        options
             Provide specific instructions about how the processor is to be used.
             In general, the options field has meaning only for a particular processor, although
             some options have the same meaning for most processors supplied by Unisys.
             Refer to the reference manual of a particular processor for a list and explanation
             of options for that processor.

        field-n
             The fields (field-1,field-2...field-n) provide information to a processor; they are
             placed in an internal table and are supplied to the processor when the processor
             executes the first read instruction. These fields are numbered from 1 through 63.
             Note: Although you can use more than 63 fields on the call line, you must not
             do so. The fields after 63 are put in the internal table following the first 63
             fields and are numbered from 1 to n again (up to 63), giving some fields
             duplicate numbers.
             Use a semicolon (;) at the end of a line to continue the fields on the processor
             call.
             The fields are assumed to be in the system standard file name or element name
             notation, although they do not have to be names of elements. For example, since
             the DATA processor works only with system data format (SDF) files, it assumes
             file names rather than element names. The meaning of the fields depends upon
             the processor.
             The section discusses the rules about fields and the processors that are supplied
             by Unisys:
                 If a processor call has a field for the name of a program file and the program
                  file is not specified, the Exec uses file TPF$, unless the file name is taken
                  from a previous field in that call statement.
                 If a field must contain an element name and you specify an element name
                  without the file name and the leading period, the Exec uses TPF$ as the file.
                 If a field must contain an element name and you specify an element name
                  without the file name but with the leading period, either of the following
                  happens:
                     The file name is taken from the previous field (if the field exists and is
                      intended to name an element or a program file)
                     The file TPF$ is used.
        Examples
          @SPELL,AHPUV PROG-DOC.SEC3

            Calls Spelling Checker to check the spelling of the text within element SEC3 of
            program file PROG-DOC.




6–2                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                              Using Processors




           @UFTN FILE26.TEST,,,,OPTIONS

             Calls UCS FORTRAN to compile a FORTRAN element called TEST in file FILE26.
             This statement produces an object module of the same name in the same file.
             Compiler options are printed due to the OPTIONS keyword.

           @FTN ICARUS.CALC

             In this example, the ASCII FORTRAN language processor compiles symbolic
             element CALC in file ICARUS. Since the processor-output field is not used, the
             resulting element has the same name as the element in the symbolic-input field
             (ICARUS.CALC). In other words, program file ICARUS has two elements named
             CALC, one symbolic and one relocatable, after execution of the FTN processor.

         Processor Load Error

6.2. Unformatted Processor Call Statements
         The unformatted processor call statement is used to load a processor and then to
         pass the complete unformatted text of the image verbatim to the processor. It is
         identified by the character sequence @’ in the first two columns of the image. Not all
         processors can be called with an unformatted processor call statement. Only those
         processors that explicitly document its usage (for example, CIFS utility @’ZIPUT) can
         be called with an unformatted processor call statement.

         Format
           @’[label:]processor[,options] [arbitrary-char-string]

         label
             Can be used to name the processor field, but is not required.

         processor
             Identifies the processor to be called.
             The processor call is actually an instruction to execute the absolute element
             specified in the processor field. For processors supplied by Unisys, such elements
             are contained in the system library files.
             To locate the absolute element on a processor call, the system uses these rules:
                 If you specify a file name (for example, @UTL.PROOFER), that file is searched
                  for the absolute element.
                 If you do not specify a file name but do use a leading period (for example,
                  @.PROOFER), the Exec searches the default file, TPF$, for the element.
                 If you do not specify a file name and there is no leading period (for example,
                  @SPELL), the Exec searches the system library files first; if the element is not
                  found, TPF$ is searched.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   6–3
Using Processors




            The abbreviations for the standard processors (for example, SSG for Symbolic
            Stream Generator) are the names of the respective absolute elements.

        options
                Provide specific instructions about how the processor is to be used.
                In general, the options field has meaning only for a particular processor, although
                some options have the same meaning for most processors supplied by Unisys.
                Refer to the reference manual of a particular processor for a list and explanation
                of options for that processor.

        The following text discusses the rules about fields and the processors that are
        supplied by Unisys:
           If a processor call has a field for the name of a program file and the program file is
            not specified, the Exec uses file TPF$, unless the file name is taken from a
            previous field in that call statement.
           If a field must contain an element name and you specify an element name without
            the file name and the leading period, the Exec uses TPF$ as the file.
           If a field must contain an element name and you specify an element name without
            the file name but with the leading period, either of the following happens:
                 The file name is taken from the previous field (if the field exists and is
                  intended to name an element or a program file)
                 The file TPF$ is used.

        Additional Unformatted Processor Control Statement Syntax
        Throughout this discussion, the @’[label:]processor[,options] portion of the
        unformatted processor control statement is referred to as the first part of the image.
        The following are key discussion points that are unique to the unformatted processor
        control statement syntax:
           The first part of the image can be up to 80 characters long. It is scanned according
            to the standard control statement syntax rules.
           When the end of the first part of the image is detected, no further scanning of the
            image is done.
           Traditional continuations of an unformatted processor control statement are not
            allowed, so a semicolon encountered as part of this initial scan is treated as a
            space and ends the scan.
           The maximum length of unformatted processor control statements is not
            restricted to the 80-character maximum of other control statements. The
            maximum length is the same as for data images such as traditional noncontrol
            statements and varies by run type (demand, batch, or demand batch) and file type
            (@ADD file, @@INQ, or demand interactive).




6–4                                                                                  7830 7949–031
                                                                             Using Processors




            For batch runs, the Exec normally prints the entire control statement. For
             unformatted process control statements, the Exec prints only the portion of the
             image scanned to produce the INFOR. This is done because of the potentially
             larger size of the image. The remainder of the image could also contain sensitive
             security information such as read or write keys.
            An INFOR table is created for the first part of the image and is used by the Exec
             to load the appropriate program or processor. The INFOR is then released and no
             INFOR is returned to the program. Once loaded, the program is expected to issue
             the appropriate ER SYMB$ to read the unformatted processor control statement.
             The complete text of the image is passed verbatim including the @’ identifier and
             any semicolons. See the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for
             more information on ER SYMB$.
            In addition to ASCII and Fieldata, unformatted processor calls in the Unicode
             character set are accepted by the Exec. Characters in the first part of the image
             (used to load the appropriate processor) must be in the ASCII/ISO range 000
             through 0177. The first character not in this range terminates the Exec scan for the
             processor and options information.


6.3. Basic Mode Programs
         Generating and executing a basic mode program is a four-step process
         (see Figure 6–1):

6.3.1. Step 1. Writing the Program
         The first step in generating a program is to write a source program in a programming
         language supported on the system.

         To enter the lines of the program into the system, you can use a text editor, such as
         EDIT 1100. Once entered, your program is stored as a symbolic element in a program
         file and is ready to be compiled.

         Note: Do not choose a processor name such as DATA or ELT as the name for your
         program. The Exec recognizes these names in a processor call (@DATA or @ELT,D).
         If you use a processor name, the results are unpredictable.

6.3.2. Step 2. Compiling the Program
         Before the computer can read and interpret your program, it must be translated into a
         form the computer can understand. This form is known as machine language, and a
         compiler performs the translation. To start a compiler, you use a compiler call
         statement, such as @ACOB for ASCII COBOL or @FTN for ASCII FORTRAN.

         The compiler produces a machine-readable element called a relocatable element,
         which is stored in a program file. However, this relocatable element is still not ready to
         be executed; first it must undergo a process called collection.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  6–5
Using Processors




6.3.3. Step 3. Collecting the Program (Collection)
        A processor called the Collector finishes the job of preparing a program so that it can
        be executed. The main function of the Collector is to join your relocatable elements
        with relocatable elements from user and system relocatable subroutine libraries.

        The Collector joins these relocatable elements to form a single new element called an
        absolute element, which is ready to be executed. You call the Collector with the
        @MAP statement. Refer to the Collector Programming Reference Manual
        (7830 9887) for instructions on how to use the Collector.

6.3.4. Step 4. Executing the Program
        Once you have produced an absolute element, execute it using the @XQT statement
        (see Section 7.70).




          Figure 6–1. Generating and Executing a Basic Mode Program




6–6                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                              Using Processors




6.4. Extended Mode Programs
         Figure 6–2 shows the process of generating and executing an extended mode
         program. It involves four steps, eliminating the intermediate step of using the
         Collector, although you can optionally use a process called static linking, which is
         similar to using the Collector.

6.4.1. Step 1. Writing the Program
         Just as you would for a basic mode program, you first write a source program in a
         programming language supported on the system. The four UCS language products
         supported are UCS COBOL (@UCOB), UCS FORTRAN (@UFTN), UCS Pascal (@UPAS),
         and UCS C (@UC).

         Refer to these reference manuals for detailed information on each UCS product:
            COBOL Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 1 (7831 0448)
            COBOL Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 2 (7831 0455)
            FORTRAN Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 1 (7831 0489)
            FORTRAN Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 2 (7830 7477)
            C Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 1 (7831 0422)
            C Compiler Programming Reference Manual, Volume 2 (7831 0430)

         Enter the lines of the program into the system by using a text editor. Once entered,
         your program is stored as a symbolic element in a program file and is ready to be
         compiled.

6.4.2. Step 2. Compiling the Program
         Use the Universal Compiling System (UCS) compiler for your programming language.
         A UCS compiler produces a type of compiled element called an object module. This
         object module can be executed immediately after compilation; you do not have to
         explicitly combine a program’s separately compiled object modules before execution,
         as with collection.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   6–7
Using Processors




6.4.3. Step 3. Static Linking (Optional)
        Although object modules can be executed immediately after compilation, this can be
        inefficient for some programs. If one object module of a program calls another,
        execution is interrupted while the Linking System searches the file system for the
        called object module. This process is called dynamic (execution time) linking.

        To avoid this interruption of execution (and for other reasons, see the Linking System
        Programming Reference Manual (7831 0505)), you can choose to link a program’s
        object modules together before execution. This process is called static (preload)
        linking and is similar to collection. Static linking creates another object module, which
        is the same as an object module produced by compilation. This object module has all
        external references removed, thus removing interruptions of execution.

        You can link some or all of a program’s object modules together during static linking.
        Object modules not linked during static linking are linked during execution.

        Static linking also lets you create special kinds of object modules called bound object
        modules and zero overhead object modules (ZOOM). A ZOOM is a type of object
        module that does not contain unresolved external references and cannot be called by
        other object modules. Object modules for a transaction environment must be ZOOMs.
        Bound object modules and ZOOMs execute more efficiently than standard object
        modules but lose the ability to link with other object modules. (Bound object modules
        can still call other object modules.)

        See the Linking System Programming Reference Manual (7831 0505) for details on
        the Linking System.




6–8                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                                       Using Processors




6.4.4. Step 4. Executing the Program
         Use the @XQT statement to execute an object module, bound object module, or
         ZOOM, just as you do with an absolute element produced by the Collector (see
         Section 7.70).

         Figure 6–2 displays how to generate and execute an extended mode program.

6.5. Calling a Compiler
        A language processor, often referred to as a compiler, is used to translate a source
        program from a programming language, such as ASCII FORTRAN or ASCII COBOL,
        into machine-readable form.

6.5.1. Calling a Basic Mode Compiler
        Language processors for basic mode programs have a common interpretation of
        several options, as well as the first three fields.

        Format
        The typical language processor call statement is
          @processor[,options] [symbolic-input,processor-output,symbolic-output ]

        processor
           Identifies the processor to be called. See the description and rules for the general
           processor call statement in Section 6.1.

        options
           Provide specific instructions about how the compiler is to be used.
           The two major options are
           I
                  Indicates that you are providing the source program to be compiled in the
                  runstream, immediately after the compiler call statement.

           U
                  Indicates that you are updating a source program that already exists in a
                  symbolic element on mass storage. The resulting updated source program is
                  stored as the next S-cycle of the original symbolic element.

           If neither the I nor the U option is used on a compiler call statement, it indicates
           that you are updating a source program that already exists, but without S-cycling.
           The updated program is saved only if the symbolic-output field is used.
           These are other options that are common to the standard compiler call
           statements:

           A
                  Allows the runstream to continue in spite of errors detected in the
                  compilation.

           L
                  Provides a long listing. The exact meaning of this option varies from compiler
                  to compiler, but it usually includes a listing of the object program generated.
                  This option can be used instead of the S option.



6–10                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                               Using Processors




            N
                   Provides the shortest possible listing of the compilation. This option can be
                   used in place of the S option.

            P
                   Indicates that the symbolic element produced by the compiler must be in
                   Fieldata format.

            Q
                   Indicates that the symbolic element produced by the compiler must be in
                   ASCII format.

            P and Q
                   Indicates that the symbolic element produced by the compiler can be a
                   combination of Fieldata format and ASCII format.

            neither P nor Q
                   Indicates that the symbolic element produced by the compiler can be a
                   combination of Fieldata format and ASCII format. When the I option is
                   included, the format is determined by the format of the runstream images.
                   When the I option is not included, the format is determined by the format of
                   the symbolic input element images.

            S
                   Provides a summary listing of the compilation. The resulting listing gives the
                   average user the information needed.

                Note: If you do not specify the L, N, or S option, the compiler produces a
                listing that is less than the S option listing, but slightly more than the N option
                listing.

            W
                   Lists the correction images entered. This option can be used when correction
                   images are used with the U option. It can also be used with neither the I nor
                   the U option.

            X
                   Terminates the run, if errors are detected in the compilation.

         Symbolic-input
            This can be
                  The name of the file.element where the source program given in the
                   runstream is to be saved as a symbolic element (I option).




7830 7949–031                                                                                   6–11
Using Processors




              The name of the symbolic element to be updated and then compiled (U
               option, or neither I nor U). If the U option is used without the symbolic-output
               field, the updated element is saved as an S-cycle of the symbolic-input
               element.
               The I and U options, (along with the symbolic-input field) determine how the
               compiler call statement is interpreted. Table 6–1 and Table 6–2 describe the
               valid possibilities. You receive an error message if you deviate from these
               rules.
               Table 6–1 is valid for the language processors that use the symbolic-input,
               processor-output, and symbolic-output fields (FTN, for example). Table 6–2 is
               valid for the processors that use only the symbolic input and symbolic output
               fields (for example, ELT).

        processor-output
           Specifies the name of the file.element into which the processor output is to be
           placed. There is no restriction on the type of element produced. For example,
           most of the processors produce relocatable binary elements; the Collector
           produces either absolute or relocatable binary elements.

        symbolic-output
           Is the name of the file.element to be used for the updated symbolic element, if
           any. Table 6–1 and Table 6–2 describe the use of the symbolic output field, along
           with the I and U options, and the symbolic-input and processor output fields.
           The compiler automatically assigns to your run those files that are specified in the
           output fields. This requires exclusive use of the output files. If another run has any
           of the files exclusively assigned, you receive an error message and the
           compilation terminates. You can prevent a compiler termination by placing
           @ASG,AX statements for the cataloged files named in the runstream before you
           execute the compiler call statement.

           Compilers do not check the input and output field to determine whether the
           names are unique or duplicated. If an element name in an output field matches an
           already existing element in name, version, and type, the old element is replaced
           with the new element.

        Examples
        @FTN ICARUS.CALC
        @EOF

           In this example, the ASCII FORTRAN compiler compiles symbolic element CALC in
           file ICARUS. Since the processor-output field is not used, the resulting element
           has the same name as the element in the symbolic-input field (ICARUS.CALC). In
           other words, program file ICARUS has two elements named CALC, one symbolic
           and one relocatable.

6.5.2. Calling an Extended Mode Compiler
         Format
         The standard processor call format for a UCS compiler is as follows.

           @processor[,letter-options] [source-element][,[object-element]
           [,,[keyword-options-element][,keyword-options]...]]

         letter-options
            The options are as specified for each UCS compiler. See the documentation on the
            compiler.
            If the effect of a letter option conflicts with the effect of a keyword option
            specified on the processor call, the keyword option takes precedence. If the
            effect of a letter option conflicts with the effect of a keyword option specified in
            the keyword-options-element, the letter option takes precedence.

         source-element
            Specifies the name of the program file symbolic source element that contains the
            program to compile. If you do not specify the source element name, the compiler
            source program must directly follow the processor call in the runstream, and you
            must use letter option I.
            If only the I option is used, the @EOF statement (or another control statement)
            must follow the source program to signal termination of the source.

         object-element
            Specifies the name of the program file object module that receives the compiled
            program. If you do not specify the object element name, the file and element
            name of the source program is used. If you do not specify either name, temporary
            file TPF$ and element name NAME$ are used.

         keyword-options-element
            Specifies a source element that contains compiler keyword options.




7830 7949–031                                                                                6–13
Using Processors




        keyword-options
            Specifies the keyword options as described in the compiler documentation.
            Separate keyword-options with commas.

        General Rules
        These general rules apply to UCS compilers:
           Correction lines are not accepted. You must apply correction lines before
            compiling the source program. Use the ELT processor or a text editor to do this.
           In most cases, UCS compilers do not produce symbolic-output. Therefore, field 3
            of the processor call line is normally blank. Some special processing, such as the
            UFTN CONVERT routine, accepts a value in field 3. See the UCS FORTRAN
            Programming Reference Manual Volume 1 (7831 0489) and Volume 2 (7830 7477).
        Examples
        @UCOB PEGASUS.FRONT-END3,.FRONT-END

            In this example, the UCS COBOL compiler compiles source element FRONT-END3
            in program file PEGASUS. The resulting object element is named FRONT-END.
            Since a file is not specified, the object element is placed in PEGASUS, which is the
            file given in the source element field.

        @UFTN,S PROGFILE.SYM,TPF$.OM,,SITE*SITE.UCS-OPTS,NO-WARNING

            In this example, the UCS FORTRAN compiler compiles FORTRAN element SYM
            from program file PROGFILE. During compilation, the compiler uses keyword
            option NO-WARNING to suppress warning messages. Keyword options in
            element SITE*SITE.UCS-OPTS are also used. In addition, a listing of the source
            program is printed as a result of the S option letter. Object module OM is
            produced in TPF$.

6.6. Correcting Symbolic Elements
        To correct a symbolic element in batch mode, you can use statements called
        correction images. You can change source basic mode programs by inserting
        correction images immediately following a processor call statement.

        Correction images can be used only to update symbolic elements and cannot be used
        with processor call statements that use the I option.

        To either create or update symbolic elements, you can use correction images with the
        ELT processor. See the ClearPath OS 2200 ELT Processor Operations Reference
        Manual (8206 2365) for more information on ELT.

        Note: Correction images are not supported for extended mode programs. You can
        use ELT before compilation by a UCS compiler as an alternative.

        You can use correction images to do the following:
           Delete one or more lines
           Insert one or more lines
           Replace old lines with new lines
           Replace one character string with another
           Replace all characters in certain columns with a character string
           Replace partial lines

        The correction images are applied to the element identified in the symbolic–input field
        of the processor call statement. A symbolic element consists of a sequence of
        implicitly numbered lines or images. The lines or images are sequentially numbered,
        beginning with line 1, and increment by 1 for each successive line. The numbers used
        in correction images refer to the line numbers within the element you are correcting.

        Images from the symbolic-input element and from the runstream have traditionally
        been in the Fieldata and ASCII coded character sets (CCS). For international use there
        are now available an additional 39 ASCII-like CCSs. The alphabetic, numeric, and most
        special characters in the ASCII-like CCSs are identical to the traditional ASCII CCS. Each
        ASCII-like CCS has additional characters that are unique for a country or language.
        Both basic mode and extended mode programs can be written with any desired
        combination of Fieldata, ASCII, and ASCII-like CCSs for the symbolic-input element
        images and for the runstream correction images.

        There are an additional 22 CCSs defined that are not Fieldata, ASCII, or ASCII-like.
        Programs cannot be written using images in these CCSs. However, elements
        containing images in these CCSs could be used as data to be read by your programs.
        You can use the ELT processor to either create or update symbolic elements
        containing images in these 22 “other” CCSs. Note the documented restrictions on the
        use of images in these CCSs as runstream correction images.




6–18                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                               Using Processors




6.6.1. Correction Image Format Rules
         Follow these rules when using correction images:
            A change indicator must appear in the first column. This is normally a minus sign
             ( - ). If you need to use minus signs within the correction images, you must
             redefine the change indicator. To do so, enter
                -=x

             where x is the new change indicator, which can be from 1 to 3 characters in
             length. If you do not define x, the statement is ignored. You can redefine the
             change indicator as often as you like, but only one change indicator is recognized
             at any one time.

            All correction images must be arranged in numerical order according to line
             number.

            When one correction image follows another, the line numbers specified in the
             second correction image must be greater than the line numbers specified in the
             first correction image; they cannot overlap. The only exception is when you are
             inserting new lines after replacing lines or changing partial lines. In this case, you
             can insert lines at the last line replaced or changed.

            Any lines inserted between the processor call statement and a correction image
             are placed before the first line of the element being updated.

            All correction images must be Fieldata, ASCII, or ASCII-like.

         Use the W or V option on the processor call statement to see a listing of the
         corrections that were made by using the correction image format.

         The following subsections give the format and explain how to use correction images
         to perform these tasks:
            Deleting lines

            Replacing old lines with new lines

            Inserting new lines

            Replacing partial lines




7830 7949–031                                                                                   6–19
Using Processors




6.6.2. Deleting Lines
        Format
          -n,m

        Deletes specified lines from the symbolic element you are updating, where -n,m
        indicates the range of lines to be deleted. m must be greater-than-or-equal-to n. If you
        use an exclamation point (!) for m (-n,!), everything is deleted between n and the end
        of the symbolic element.

        Example
          @ACOB,US ACCT-SUMM.MAIN,ACCT-SUMM.MAIN
          -240,!
          @EOF

        The compiler deletes line 240 through the end of symbolic element MAIN of file
        ACCT-SUMM. The U option causes the updated element to be stored as the next
        S-cycle of element MAIN. The S option generates a summary listing.

6.6.3. Replacing Old Lines with New Lines
        Format
          -n,m
          new line
          new line
          new line
          .
          .
          .

        Deletes lines n through m from a symbolic element and replaces them with new lines.
        If you use an exclamation point (!) for m (-n,!), everything is deleted between n and the
        end of the symbolic element.

        All lines between the correction image (-n,m) and the next correction image or control
        statement are considered replacement lines.

        Any number of lines can follow the correction image. You can replace the deleted
        lines with fewer or more new lines. The symbolic element is implicitly renumbered to
        number the lines consecutively, beginning with 1.

        The new lines can be Fieldata, ASCII or ASCII-like images, or images in any of the 22
        "other" CCSs.




6–20                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                                               Using Processors




         Example
           @ACOB,SW LEDGER.SUB1,LEDGER.SUB1R,LEDGER.SUB1/NEW
           -62,65
           DATA DIVISION.
           FILE SECTION.
           -138,138
           MOVE A TO B.
           PERFORM LOOK-UP.
           @EOF

         The S option generates a summary listing; the W option causes the six correction
         images to be listed (everything between the @ACOB and @EOF statements). Lines 62
         through 65 are deleted and replaced with two lines, DATA DIVISION and FILE
         SECTION. Line 138 is also deleted and replaced with two lines, MOVE A TO B. and
         PERFORM LOOK-UP.

         The changes shown are applied to symbolic element SUB1 of file LEDGER. The
         updated element is saved as symbolic element SUB1/NEW. The updated element
         SUB1/NEW is compiled to produce relocatable element SUB1R.

6.6.4. Inserting New Lines
         Format
           -n
           new line
           new line
           new line
           .
           .
           .

         Inserts new lines in a symbolic element following the line number that you specify,
         where n is the line number after which the new lines are inserted, and new line
         represents a line to be inserted.

         The new lines can be Fieldata, ASCII or ASCII-like images, or images in any of the 22
         "other" CCSs.

         To insert new lines before line 1, place the new lines immediately after the processor
         call statement without specifying any insertion line numbers, or use zero (0) as the line
         number.

         To insert new lines after the last line, use an exclamation point ( ! ) as the line number.

         The compiler inserts all lines between the preceding correction image (-n) and the
         next correction image or control statement.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   6–21
Using Processors




        After the element has been completely updated, it is implicitly renumbered to number
        the lines consecutively, beginning with 1.

        Example
          @FTN,UL FILEX.SYM,FILEY.REL
          -31
          WRITE(6,10)
          FORMAT(1X,'HI,I')
          -56
          CALL PLOTER (XXX,100,500,INTRVL)
          @EOF

        The changes shown are applied to symbolic element SYM of file FILEX. Because the
        U option is used, the updated element is saved as the next S-cycle of element SYM.
        The L option generates a complete listing. Two new lines, WRITE(6,10) and
        FORMAT(1X,‘HI,I’), are inserted between lines 31 and 32 of element SYM. One new
        line, CALL PLOTER (XXX,100,500,INTRVL), is inserted after line 56 in element SYM
        (after the line that was 56th before the compiler was called).

6.6.5. Editing Lines
        Format
          -n,m-
          editing statement
          editing statement
          editing statement
          .
          .
          .

           or

          -n-
          editing statement
          editing statement
          editing statement
          .
          .
          .

        Replaces portions of the specified lines in the symbolic element you are updating,
        where n,m indicates the range of lines to be partially replaced. The line number
        specified by n must be greater than the number specified on any previous correction
        image. The line number specified by m must be greater than or equal to n. All lines n
        through m must be in Fieldata, ASCII, or an ASCII-like CCS.

        The minus sign (-) immediately following the m is an editing indicator. You must
        always use a minus sign to designate the editing indicator. You must follow the -n,m-
        with one or more editing statements, with the number of editing statements
        corresponding to the number in the -n,m- range.



6–22                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                                                                Using Processors




         For example, if
           -2,7-

         is the correction image, you must follow it with six editing statements corresponding
         to lines 2 through 7. If the number of editing statements is greater than the number in
         the -n,m- range, the excess statements are ignored and an error message is issued.

         The -n- indicates that the following editing statements are applied successively to line
         n. The changes are applied until another correction image appears or an error occurs.
         If an error occurs, the remaining editing statements are ignored.

         Note: Replacement of partial lines is possible, but avoid doing so because it is
         difficult to apply changes later.

         Editing statements must be in Fieldata, ASCII, or an ASCII-like CCS.

         Editing statements can take one of the following forms:
         c/new-data
             Replaces characters from column c to the end of the line. The new-data field
             contains the replacement characters.

         c,d/new-data/
             Replaces a specified number of characters on a line. The columns specified by c,d
             indicate the range of characters to be replaced; the new-data field contains the
             replacement characters. If the number of replacement characters is greater than
             the specified range, all characters on the line are shifted to the right. If the number
             of characters is fewer than the range, all characters are shifted to the left to adjust
             the spacing.

         /old-data/new-data
             Replaces the character string indicated by the old-data field with the characters in
             the new-data field to the end of the specified line. The old-data field recognizes
             both uppercase and lowercase letters.

         /old-data/new-data/
             Replaces one or more characters specified by the old-data field with the
             characters in the new-data field. If the fields are not of equal length, the line is
             shifted to the right to accommodate extra characters, or to the left to eliminate
             extra spaces. The old-data field recognizes both uppercase and lowercase
             characters.

         For each of the editing statement formats, the slash (/) is commonly used as a
         separator character. You can change the separator character to any character other
         than a digit or a blank space in any of the editing statement formats. In the c/new-data
         format, the separator also cannot be a comma. In either of the old-data/new-data
         formats, the character cannot be the same character that you use as a change
         indicator.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  6–23
Using Processors




        Regardless of the separator character you choose, you must never use the same
        character within the old-data or new-data fields in any of the formats.

        Example
          @FTN,LU FILEX.ABC
          -1-
          /ABC/abc/
          /GHI/ghi/
          /MNO/mno/
          -2,5-
          9/ccccdddd
          5,8/ffff/
          /KKKK/kkkkllll/
          /NNNN/nnnn/

        Updates element ABC in FILEX and creates a new cycle of element ABC. The following
        corrections are made to the element:
        Line 1
            Uppercase characters ABC, GHI, and MNO are replaced with their lowercase
            counterparts.

        Line 2
            Starting at column 9, characters ccccdddd replace the original characters. Any
            remaining characters are cleared to the end of the line.

        Line 3
            Between columns 5 and 8, characters ffff replace the original characters.

        Line 4
            Lowercase characters kkkkllll replace uppercase characters KKKK. Any remaining
            characters are cleared to the end of the line.

        Line 5
            Lowercase characters nnnn replace uppercase characters NNNN.

6.6.6. EDIT 1100
        To correct a symbolic element, you can also use EDIT 1100, the IPF full screen editor
        for manipulating text, source code, or other data. The editor provides an easy way to
        move, copy, reformat, insert, and delete (among many other editing functions) data
        within files and elements.

        You can use EDIT 1100 to correct any symbolic element, whether it contains a source
        program, a canned runstream, general text, or other symbolic images. You can also
        use it to correct data files.

        To learn more about EDIT 1100, refer to the IPF 1100 EDIT 1100 User's Guide (7833
        3812).

 7.1. @ADD—Add Partial Canned Runstreams and
       Data
          The @ADD statement lets you include canned runstreams or data for repetitive
          functions. Control statements or data are entered only once, but can be used in many
          subsequent runs.

          When the system processes an @ADD statement, the contents of the added file or
          element replace the @ADD statement. Control then returns to the run that contained
          the @ADD statement.

          If the file that contains the added runstream is assigned to the run when the Exec
          reads the @ADD statement, the file is still assigned when control returns to the main
          runstream. If the file is not assigned to the run when the Exec reads the @ADD
          statement, the file’s condition when control returns to the main runstream depends
          on whether the file has an internal file name attached to it. An added file that is not
          assigned, but has an internal file name, is assigned. An added file that is not currently
          assigned and does not have internal file name is not assigned, even if the added
          runstream contains an @ASG statement to assign the file. The F option can be used
          to explicitly free the file upon completion of @ADD processing.

          Format
            @ADD[,options] name

          options

                D
                    Allows the insertion of files or elements when operating under the DATA or
                    the ELT,D processors.

                E
                    Provides an implied @EOF statement at the end of the added file or
                    element. If the DATA or the ELT,D processors are executed at the time of
                    the @ADD with the E option, the EOF return is ignored.

                F
                    Frees the file containing the added runstream upon completion of @ADD
                    processing. All @USE names attached to the file are retained, with the
                    exception of any @USE names attached by @ADD processing.

                L
                    Lists all control statements in an added file or element at the demand
                    terminal until the runstream returns control to the demand terminal input.
                    Also lists control statements from other files or elements added by any
                    @ADD statements nested within the overall addstream. This option is
                    ignored in batch mode. Control statements in an addstream are always
                    listed in batch.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–5
@ADD—Add Partial Canned Runstreams and Data




           P
                Prints the @ADD statement in the program listing.

           R
                Gives the control statements in the @ADD file execution priority over the
                top entry of the deferred control statement execution (DCSE) stack.
                If ER QECL$ is used with @ADD files and the @ADD files are to be
                interpreted first, the R option must be used. The following restrictions apply
                when ER QECL$ and @ADD are used together:
                   If something is on the DCSE stack and you submit an @ADD statement
                    with the R option, all subsequent @ADD files must have the R option to
                    maintain priority.
                   You must not execute @IPF from an @ADD,R file if something is on the
                    DCSE stack. Execution of these statements might result in IPF reload
                    errors.
                See the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for a description
                of ER QECL$.
        name
           Identifies the file or element to be added, which must be stored in either an SDF
           file or a symbolic element of a program file. The symbolic element cannot reside
           in a Large Element Program File (LEPF). The file or element can be created by any
           of the following:
              The SSG processor
               This is a method to generate runstreams to be added with @ADD. The SSG
               processor can add (@ADD) them automatically. See the SSG Programming
               Reference Manual (7831 1784).

              The EDIT 1100 processor
               See the IPF 1100 EDIT 1100 User's Guide (7833 3812).

              The @FILE statement
               See Section 7.27.

              The DATA processor
               See the ClearPath OS 2200 ELT Processor Operations Reference Manual
               (8206 2365).

              The ELT processor
               See the ClearPath OS 2200 ELT Processor Operations Reference Manual
               (8206 2365).

              Symbiont output (for example, alternate print or @BRKPT)

              A user program



7–6                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                      @ADD—Add Partial Canned Runstreams and Data




          A file name must be followed by a period; otherwise, it is interpreted as an element
          name. If a file name is not specified, TPF$ is assumed. If an element name is
          specified without a version name, the system uses the symbolic element with a
          blank version name, if one exists. If one does not exist, the system uses the first
          nondeleted version of the symbolic element in the program file.

          Notes:
               Do not include statements such as @FREE, @PACK, or @ERS that could change
                the structure of the file that contains the statements.
               Do not use the @PASSWD statement within an added file. It compromises the
                secrecy of your password, and the system ignores the @PASSWD statement
                anyway.

          You can correct the prestored, partial runstreams before they are added by using the
          EDIT 1100 processor. Do not type directly into batch-type processors such as ASCII
          COBOL, MASM, or MAP. Instead, introduce your line corrections with the @ADD,E
          statement or use EDIT 1100 to make source corrections.

          Example 1
          Suppose you have several files that you always use together. Instead of assigning
          them individually, you can store @ASG statements for the files in an element.
          Whenever you want to assign the files to your run, you can add the element with an
          @ADD statement.

          To illustrate this, suppose you create an element called PJT*UTL.STD-ASGS and
          insert the following statements into it:
              @ASG,A PJT*WORKFILE.
              @ASG,A PJT*ACCT-PROGS.
              @ASG,A PJT*ACCT-DATA.

          You can assign all three files at once using the following statement:
              @ADD PJT*UTL.STD-ASGS

          Example 2
              @ADD,P PROFITS.

          The statements in file PROFITS replace the @ADD statement. Because of the P
          option, the @ADD statement appears in the program listing.

@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




 7.2. @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and
       Peripheral Devices
         The @ASG statement is used to name a file, state its I/O facility requirements, and
         assign it to the requesting run under the given external file name. If the file is
         cataloged, the facility requirements are known and need not be specified when
         assigning the file.

         You can use the @ASG statement for the following device types:
            Sector-addressable mass storage
            Word-addressable mass storage
            Magnetic tape
            Absolute devices

         You must assign files to your run before you can reference them for I/O operations.

         The only time you can reference a file without first assigning it with an @ASG
         statement is when you specify the file on some control statements or processor call
         statements (the Collector, for example). The actual assignment is made when the
         program handles the given statement. Information concerning the assignment is
         taken from the master file directory (MFD).

         The @FREE statement releases files and peripheral devices from your run. After you
         release a file or device, you can no longer reference it without reassigning it with
         another @ASG statement.

         You can place the @ASG and @FREE statements anywhere in the runstream.
         Dynamic @ASG and @FREE statements can appear anywhere in the user program.
         These features let you assign and free files as required, without tying up the files and
         facilities from the beginning of the run until its completion.

         However, you might have to wait until the facility or file is available. Examples of
         when this can happen are as follows:
            A magnetic-tape unit is being used by another run.
            An arbitrary device is being used by another run.
            A cataloged magnetic-tape file is being used by another run.
            A cataloged file is being used exclusively by another run.
            A magnetic-tape reel is being used by another run, except when the reel number
             is for a scratch tape.
            Insufficient mass storage is available.
            A reel number is currently in use for another file.
            A cataloged file is rolled out to tape.




7–8                                                                               7830 7949–031
                               @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




          When you assign a file to your run, you are adding an entry for the file to your run’s
          program control table (PCT). The PCT contains information about the files assigned to
          your run. If a file is not listed in your run’s PCT, you cannot read from it, write to it,
          or execute it.

          Similarly, when you release a file from your run (using an @FREE or @@FREE
          statement), you are actually removing the file from your run’s PCT (see Section 7.30).

          You can examine the files assigned to your run using @PRT,I (see Section 7.48).

          Figure 7–1 shows you how to assign files.




                                Figure 7–1. Assigning Files

 7.2.1. Assigning Mass Storage Files
          The @ASG statement assigns a random-access, mass storage file to your run.

          Note: When you assign a previously created file, you must pass security validation
          in order to gain access to the file. See the discussion in 4.3 on security access
          validation.

          Format
            @ASG[,options] filename[,type/reserve/granule/maximum
            /placement][,pack-id-1/.../pack-id-n,,,ACR-name/encrypt-option]




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–9
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         options

         General Options
         I
             Automatically frees the file at the next task termination regardless of how the
             task terminates. (A task is a discrete processing step in a run, involving the
             execution of an absolute element; for example, a system processor or user
             program.)

         Z
             Specifies that this statement is not to cause a hold condition. Control is returned
             to the user, indicating whether a hold state would have resulted from the
             assignment. Also, this option requests that this file be reloaded if it is unloaded.

         Options for Assigning Files to Be Cataloged
         B
             Indicates that when this file is cataloged and subsequently assigned, it is saved
             and reloaded as part of any full checkpoint or restart.

         C
             Catalogs the file at run termination if the run terminates normally. (See Section
             5.4 for a description of run termination.) If the file is freed before termination, it is
             cataloged at that time. If a file by this file name already exists in the master file
             directory, the request is rejected. Use @CAT instead of @ASG,C to catalog a file if
             you want the file cataloged without having it assigned to your run.
         G
             The meaning of this option depends on how security and Quota are configured at
             your site. Only the unconditional delete file system privilege overrides the G
             option.
                  Unowned files
                   If your site has fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the file is
                   unowned, the following applies:
                      When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its read
                       key, write key, privacy mode, or all three overridden by privileged runs.
                      If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read keys or
                       write keys for the file set are obscured by ‘////////////’ from all users. If a
                       particular F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the privacy
                       mode and either the project-ID or account number under which the file
                       was created are also guarded.
                      The G option means the file cannot be backed up.




7–10                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                 @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                    Owned files
                     If your site has Security Level 1, 2, or 3, the file is owned, and the dynamic
                     configuration parameter (owned_file_read_write_keys) is FALSE:
                         G-option files are no longer protected from privileged runs.
                         The G option means the file cannot be backed up by FAS. When you
                          need to back up a file, you must use another product such as FURPUR
                          or IRU.
                     If your site has Security Level 1, 2,or 3 and the file is owned and the
                     dynamic configuration parameter (owned_file_read_write_keys) is TRUE, the
                     following applies:
                         When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its read
                          key, write key, privacy mode, or all three overridden by privileged runs.
                         If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read keys
                          or write keys for the file set are obscured by ‘////////////’ from all users. If
                          a particular F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the
                          privacy mode and either the project-ID or account number under which
                          the file was created are also guarded.
                         The G option means the file cannot be backed up.
                    Quota system
                     The use of the G option is also controlled by the Quota system on an
                     account basis, as follows:
                         If the Exec is configured to maintain quota limits for each account, this
                          option can be used only if it is allowed in the quota limits for the run.
                         If the Exec is not maintaining quota limits, this option can be used by all
                          runs.
          P
                Catalogs the file as a public file. If you create unowned files (only for sites with
                Fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and you omit the P option
                (default), the file is cataloged as a private file and can be accessed only by runs
                that have the same project-ID or account number as your run.
                If you create an owned file and you omit the P option, the file can be private (only
                you can access it) or ACR-controlled (if you attach an ACR to it).
                For owned files, a file is cataloged as public when the P option is specified on the
                @ASG statement and an access control record (ACR) is not specified.
                The file is cataloged as private if the P option and ACR are not specified on the
                @CAT statement (default).

          R
                Indicates that it is a read-only file. You cannot write to a read-only file; you can
                only read or delete it.
                If your site has Security Level 1 or higher, you can assign a cataloged file as
                read-only, regardless of how the file was cataloged.



7830 7949–031                                                                                        7–11
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         S
             Indicates store-through file. Data written to this file is stored directly on a
             nonvolatile mass storage medium. Absence of this option indicates data can be
             stored on volatile areas of mass storage, such as cache storage. Using this
             option does not prevent the storage of data on solid-state disk. (Although this
             option no longer has any effect, it is allowed since it might still be in user
             runstreams.)

         U
             Indicates the same conditions as the C option, except that the file is cataloged
             unconditionally when the run terminates (excluding a system stop) or when you
             release the file from your run with an @FREE statement.

         V
             Indicates that, when the file is cataloged, its text is not to be unloaded to tape at
             any time. If the Exec is configured to maintain quota limits for each account, this
             option can be used only if it is specifically allowed in the quota limits for the run.
             If the Exec is not maintaining quota limits, this option can be used by all runs.

         W
             Indicates write-only file. No user can read a file cataloged with the W option.
             Anyone who tries to read the file receives an error message.

         Options for Assigning Previously Cataloged Files

         A
             Indicates that the file is already cataloged and ensures that it is not treated as a
             temporary file. The request is rejected if the name cannot be found in the master
             file directory.
             If the file is owned, the following applies:
                An ACR cannot be specified with this option.
                If this option is combined with the R option, read-only access is given.
                The user must have access privileges specified in the file’s ACR.

             If the file is application private, you must be running in the application-private
             common name section. Refer to the MHFS Planning, Installation, and
             Operations Overview (7830 7469).
             If the file is unowned, you cannot use the A and R options together. The
             combination of these options results in an error.

         D

             Deletes a cataloged file from the master file directory if the run terminates
             normally (excluding a system stop), or when you release the file from your run
             with the @FREE statement. (See Section 5.4 for a description of run termination.)
             If the file is owned, you must have delete access to the file in order to delete it.

                If your site has Fundamental Security, you must include any read or write keys
                that are attached to the file in order to delete the file.
                If your site has Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the dynamic configuration parameter
                owned_file_read_write_keys is TRUE, then you must include read or write keys

          E
                Assigns this file with only the directory information accessible. The file is
