          K
                Indicates the same conditions as the D option, but the file is deleted from a

                If the file is owned, you must have delete access to the file in order to delete it.
                If your site has Fundamental Security, you must include any read or write keys

                If your site has Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the dynamic configuration parameter

          Q
                Assigns the file even if the system has disabled it; does not inhibit read/write

          T
                Specifies that the file is temporary. The file can have any name, as long as the

@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         X
              Specifies that this run is to have exclusive use of the file until the run terminates,
              the file is released by an @FREE statement, or exclusive use is released through

         Y
              Indicates the same conditions as the E option, except disks are not selected. If

         If you are creating a new cycle for an existing file cycle set, and you omit the type,
         the type is taken from the latest existing cycle of the file. If all cycles of the file are in
         a to-be-cataloged or to-be-dropped state, then the type from the highest cycle of this
         type is used.

         Options for Assigning Temporary Files
         Do not use a processor name (ELT or DATA, for example) as a file name. The results
         can be unpredictable.

         You cannot use the shared directory-ID (for MHFS).

         The options field, if left blank, defaults to the A option unless the file is already
         assigned, in which case the options on the previous assign are used. If the file
         specified is not cataloged, the blank options field defaults to a T option, thus creating
         a temporary file. Any option not allowed on a statement causes the statement to be
         rejected.

         If your site has Fundamental Security, the cataloging options B, C, G, P, S, R, U, V, and
         W are valid only when you are assigning a file to be cataloged. The C and U options
         indicate that a file is to be cataloged. The G, P, R, S, V, and W options place
         restrictions on the file after it is cataloged.

         If you are assigning a file that was previously cataloged, be sure to use the A option.
         If you assign a file without the A, C, T, or U option, the Exec must search the master
         file directory for it. If it finds the file, the Exec assigns the file and honors any other
         options. If it cannot find the file, the Exec assigns the file as a temporary file and
         might ignore some of the options.

         If you are assigning an owned file, you can assign a cataloged file as read only,
         regardless of how the file was cataloged, using

             @ASG,AR filename

         Do not attempt to do this if the file is unowned.

         To delete a cataloged file by using the D, K, E, or Y option, you must include any read
         or write keys for the file on the @ASG statement if your site has Fundamental
         Security. If your site has Security Level 1 or higher, you must have delete access to
         the file.




7–14                                                                                  7830 7949–031
                                 @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




          filename
                Identifies the file being assigned to the run.

          type
                Specifies a combination of letters and numbers that identify the addressing mode
                of the file (sector- or word-addressable) and the equipment type required for the
                file. The type field is also called the assign mnemonic.
                Most types supplied by Unisys start with D or F, but sites can configure any
                mnemonics they wish. D represents word-addressable and F represents
                sector-addressable mass storage. If you omit type, the Exec uses
                sector-addressable mass storage. You cannot use the shared directory-ID for
                memory files (FMEM and DMEM) assign types. Appendix D, Table D-1 shows the
                standard type supplied by Unisys entries.
                Refer to Appendix D, Table D-1 for a list of the available mass storage assign
                mnemonics and Table D-2 for the selection sequences supplied by Unisys.
                Local fixed files can be placed in memory rather than on channel. FMEM
                (sector-addressable) and DMEM (word-addressable) can be used for this
                purpose; your site can configure additional assign mnemonics. Placing files in
                memory reduces access time, but consumes memory space that might
                otherwise be available for programs. Also, data in memory files is lost when the
                system is rebooted. Use of memory files assign mnemonics on systems that are
                not or cannot be configured to support memory files results in the request being
                satisfied on channel-connected mass storage.
                Most removable disk files can be assigned using any assign mnemonic.
                However, for physically - the pack is mounted on a device that does not support
                physically removable packs, the following error message appears:
                  E:200633 pack xxxxxx cannot be mounted -- equipment type does not
                  permit interchanging of packs.

                If you attempt to assign a file using a physically removable assign mnemonic and
                there are no units configured, the following error message appears:
                  E:256033 requested unit(s) not available

          reserve
                Gives an estimate of the space needed to create or update the file. The reserve
                can be 1 to 12 numbers. If you omit reserve, the Exec uses 0.
                For sector- and word-addressable files, the initial reserve is an integer specifying
                the number of granules required by the file. See Section 3.2. You must provide a
                reasonable estimate of the space needed to create or update the file. The value
                used for a file update must include those granules already in use. Specifying a
                reserve reduces system overhead, as the space is allocated in contiguous
                granules, if possible. Omission causes the Exec to dynamically allocate the
                granules as they are required by the file.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–15
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




            The system places the first reserve value you specify for a cataloged file in the
            master file directory. Subsequent changes to the reserve subfield value are then
            treated according to the type of access established for a particular file. For
            cataloged files that are write enabled, the system overrides and replaces the
            recorded value with the new value you specify in your @ASG statement.
            You cannot assign a new reserve value greater than a file’s maximum. For files
            cataloged as read-only or assigned without an existing write key, the reserve
            subfield value must be the same as the master file directory value; otherwise,
            the request is rejected.
            The facility that enables a user to expand an initial reserve (on a cataloged or
            temporary file) following its first specification is referred to as static expansion.
            With this facility, an initial reserve can be expanded, both on the device that was
            specified on the first @ASG statement and on other units or device types.
            Expansion of a file assignment across a set of units is accomplished by changing
            the initial reserve and the type or placement fields. Changing the initial reserve
            field initiates allocation if the specification is an amount greater than the current
            initial reserve or the highest granule assigned. The extent of allocation
            corresponds to the increment above the mass storage currently allocated to the
            file. For files created with absolute placement, the allocation occurs on the
            device originally specified if the placement field is empty. If the mass storage is
            unavailable to do this, the request is rejected.
            The maximum number of words allowed for the initial reserve is 262,143 times
            the number of words-per-granule, based on the granularity (track or position) of
            the file. Word-addressable files are allocated on a granule basis, and the relative
            sizes of reserve and maximum subfields are compared on a granule basis, not on
            a word basis.
            Your system can be configured so that the unused portion of the initial reserve
            area allocated to cataloged files is released when the file is freed. This area is
            reallocated when the file is reassigned.

         granule
            Specifies the granule size. It can be as follows:
            TRK
               One software track (64 software sectors).

            POS
               One software position (64 software tracks). File space is allocated and
               released in 64-track increments or file-relative 64-track boundaries. The
               64-track increments are not guaranteed to be contiguous on the physical
               medium.

            If you omit granule, the Exec uses TRK. Once a file is created, the granularity can
            never be changed. The granularity is recorded in the master file directory.




7–16                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                   @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




          maximum
                Is the maximum allowable length of the file, in granules (for sector-addressable
                files) or words (for word-addressable files), given in 12 characters or less. Values
                for maximum are the same as for reserve. The maximum overrides the system
                default. If you did not specify maximum when you created the file, the reserve or
                system default is used, whichever is larger.
                If a maximum was supplied when the file was cataloged, its value and the
                number of granules currently in use are recorded in the master file directory and
                used whenever the file is assigned. If a maximum is specified on a subsequent
                @ASG of a cataloged file, it replaces the previous maximum in the master file
                directory only if the file is assigned write-enabled. If the file is not assigned
                write-enabled and a new maximum is specified, the request is rejected. If you
                specify a maximum that is less than the highest granule assigned, the request is
                rejected.
                This field is used to give the run an I/O error if the length of the I/O request
                exceeds the number of granules specified. It is used primarily to ensure that a
                runaway-file situation does not occur during debugging. However, you can also
                use this field to override the system default for all files.

          placement
                Specifies the placement of the file on a controller or device. The specification can
                be a logical or absolute request.
                The placement can be any of the following:
                *cu
                     Is a controller name (absolute request).

                *device
                     Is a device name (absolute request).

                i
                     Is a letter, A to Z, representing logical subsystems A through Z.

                in
                     n is a number, 1 to 15, representing a logical device on controller i.

          If an absolute placement cannot be done as specified, it is rejected. The Exec
          attempts the following file assignments:
               Files with the same logical specifications (that is, the same controller and device
                number) are assigned to the same physical device.
               Files with the same logical controller but different device numbers are assigned
                to different physical devices on the same control unit.
               Files with different logical controllers and device numbers are assigned to
                physical devices that are reachable by completely different CUs within the CONV
                selection string for the assign type specified.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–17
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         Since logical placement is driven off of logical CU selections, specifying logical
         placement causes the Exec to avoid placing this file into memory space, even if
         MEMFL is specified for the assign type. Consequently, do not use the logical
         placement field if you want a file placed in memory on systems with MEMFLSZ
         configured. If a logical specification cannot be honored on a device within the CONV
         selection string, processing of the assign request ignores the placement field.
         Placement on removable disk is not supported. The pack-ID enables you to specify
         allocation on a removable disk.
         When the file is cataloged, placement information is placed in the directory to
         indicate the type of selection (logical or absolute, controller or device) and the device
         chosen for initial allocation. The directory cell containing this information is not
         affected by subsequent assignment of the file.
         On reassignment, a placement specification is taken as a placement change
         overriding the last device used for allocation. A maximum of six characters, seven in
         the case of absolute placement, is allowed for specification of this subfield.
         Logical placement specifications have meaning only within the current run. For
         example, logical controller "A" can represent two different physical controllers in two
         different runs.
         Logical placement applies only to the reserve specified. If the file dynamically
         expands beyond the initial reserve, the Exec attempts to allocate on the same device
         as the last placement specified. If this is not possible, the expansion occurs on
         devices other than those specified in the placement field.
         If the file is expanded through static expansion (reserve specified) and the file was
         created with absolute placement, the Exec allocates mass storage only on the device
         originally specified, unless a different device is specified in the placement field on the
         assignment. If there is not enough room on the specified (either implicitly or
         explicitly) device to satisfy the request, the request is rejected.

         pack-ID

             Specifies the removable disk packs required for the file. Pack-IDs consist of from
             one to six characters of the set A through Z, 0 through 9. The pack-IDs for
             cataloged files are recorded in the master file directory and need not be specified
             on reassignments.

             A pack's master file directory must have sufficient space available to record the
             file otherwise a generation request is rejected with the following message:

               E:207433 File cannot be created due to lack of removable directory
               space on pack pack-id.




7–18                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                 @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                A pack-ID cannot be specified unless the type subfield is also specified. If
                pack-ID is omitted on requests for noncataloged file space, fixed disk is assumed
                if disk equipment is requested. For cataloged removable disk files, specification
                of a pack-ID causes the pack to be mounted and registered. If already registered,
                the pack information is compared with the image for compatibility.
                All cycles of a removable disk file must be on the same set of packs.
                The maximum number of pack-IDs that can be specified on an @ASG statement
                is 510.

                Many jobs can specify the same set of removable disk packs for unique files.
                Pack-IDs can be added to unassigned single file cycle files by specifying the
                original pack-ID list with the new pack-ID s appended on an @ASG,A request.
                Packs can only be added if the A option is specified (but not the Y option).
                Packs cannot be added to currently assigned files or to files that have more than
                one file cycle.
                If packs are being added, you must have delete access to the file.
                For important information about using removable pack files, see the removable
                disk packs section in the Exec System Software Administration Reference
                Manual (7831 0323).

          ACR-name
                Specifies the access control record (ACR) for the cataloged file (if your system
                has Security Level 1 or higher). This must be an ACR that you have previously
                created with your security management product. See Section 4.3 for more
                information on creating and attaching ACRs.

          encrypt-option
                This subfield is used to specify encryption actions. For @ASG options C and U,
                DOENCR specifies that the file must be catalogued as encrypted, and DNENCR
                specifies that it must not be catalogued as encrypted. When these mnemonics
                are omitted, the default flag setting in the file owner’s userid record is used to
                determine encryption state.
                For @ASG with the A and X options, the MTENCR (maintain encryption) option
                can be specified when assigning encrypted files. This option allows the file to be
                written to and read from without encrypting or decrypting the data. This option is
                required by FAS (the File Administration System) to successfully save and restore
                encrypted files. ***Warning***This option is not recommended for general use.

 7.2.2. Security Access Validation
          When you assign a previously created file, you must pass security validation in order
          to gain access to the file. You receive access according to the validation rules for
          mandatory access control and discretionary access control. See Section 4 for more
          information.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–19
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




 7.2.3. Assigning Files on Shared Devices
         If your system has Multi-Host File Sharing (MHFS), the following applies:
            You can assign cataloged files to shared devices. When you assign the file, it is
             allocated to either shared or local devices, but not both.
            You cannot assign a temporary file to a shared device.
            You cannot assign a shared device absolutely.
            You might not be able to assign a shared mass storage file if its assignment is
             restricted by the application-private feature. Refer to the MHFS Planning,
             Installation, and Operations Overview (7830 7469) for further information.

         Examples
         Assume that the following examples are all in the same run:

         @ASG NEWBASE1.

             The system initially assumes that NEWBASE1 is a cataloged file. If it cannot find
             the file, the system assigns the file as a temporary file.

         @ASG,A NEWBASE2.

             This statement assigns the file NEWBASE2 to the run. The A option means the
             file has been previously cataloged. The characteristics of the file were
             determined when the file was created.

         @ASG,AZ NEWBASE3/NEON.

             This statement requests that file NEWBASE3 be assigned to the run. NEON is the
             read key for the file. The A option means the file was previously cataloged.
             Because of the Z option, the system cannot assign the file if this would cause the
             run to be held.
             The Z option is useful when you suspect a file has been rolled out to tape and
             you do not want to wait for it to be rolled back in.

         @ASG,AX NEWBASE4.

             File NEWBASE4 was previously cataloged (A option). The X option indicates that
             the file must be assigned exclusively to this run.

         @ASG,T NEWBASE5.,F///400

             This statement creates temporary file NEWBASE5. It is a sector-addressable
             file (F) with a maximum size of 400 tracks.




7–20                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                 @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         @ASG,T NEWBASE5.,F94/100//300

                NEWBASE5 refers to the same file as the one in the previous example. This
                shows how you can use the @ASG statement to change the equipment type (F
                to F94) and initial reserve (10 to 100 tracks) from what you specified previously. If
                the file had already been cataloged, you would have used the A option.

          @ASG,C NEWBASE6.,F/10//300

                This statement assigns file NEWBASE6 to the run. The C option means the file
                must be cataloged if the run terminates normally, or if you release the file
                (@FREE) before the run terminates. NEWBASE6 is a sector-addressable file (F)
                with an initial reserve of 10 tracks and a maximum size of 300 tracks. It is a
                private file (no P option).

          @ASG,UPR NEWBASE7.,F///3000/A1

                This statement assigns file NEWBASE7 to the run. The U option means the file is
                cataloged when the file is released from the run (@FREE) or when the run
                terminates, even if the run terminates in error. When the file is cataloged, it is
                public (P option) and read only (R option). NEWBASE7 is given logical control unit
                placement A1. The file is on sector-addressable mass storage (F) and has a
                maximum size of 3000 tracks.

          @ASG,CP NEWBASE8.,F///100/A2

                This statement assigns the file NEWBASE8 to the run. The file is cataloged as a
                public file (P option) if the run terminates normally or if the file is released
                (@FREE) before the run terminates. NEWBASE8 is on sector-addressable mass
                storage (F) and has a maximum size of 100 tracks. NEWBASE8 is given the logical
                unit placement A2. Since NEWBASE7 was given the logical unit placement A1 in
                the previous example, the system tries to place the two files on disk drives that
                are connected on the same subsystem.

          @ASG,AD NEWBASE9//ARGON.

                This statement assigns file NEWBASE9 to the run. ARGON is the file’s write key
                (ignored if the site has Security Level 1 or higher and the file is owned). The
                A option means the file has been previously cataloged.

                If the site has Fundamental Security, the D option deletes the file if the run
                terminates normally, or when you release the file from the run (@FREE).

                If the site has Security Level 1 or higher, you must have delete access to the file.

          @ASG,CP SHARED#FILEM.

                FILEM is cataloged in the shared master file directory. If the system does not
                have the file-sharing feature configured, the request is rejected. If the
                assignment is successful, then all hosts in the file-sharing system are able to
                assign the file after the file is freed.

 7.2.4. Changing Assignment Fields for Mass Storage Files
         You can change the type, reserve, maximum, or placement fields for a file with an
         @ASG statement when the following applies:
             You have already assigned the file with the A option. Change by adding the X and
              I options. You can assign the file again with the same options and specify a new
              type, reserve, maximum, or placement.
             You have already assigned the file with a C or U option. You can assign the file
              again with the same option and specify a new type, reserve, maximum, or
              placement.
             You have already cataloged the file but not assigned it. You can assign the file
              with an @ASG,A statement and give new specifications for the type, reserve,
              maximum, or placement.

         To change the subfields that can be changed, the file must be write enabled. You
         cannot change the granule subfield.

         The format for changing assignment fields is
             @ASG[,options] filename[,type/reserve//maximum/placement]

         options

              A
                   Indicates that the changes apply to an already cataloged file. This option is
                   required.

              C
                   Indicates that the file is to be cataloged if the run terminates normally or if
                   the file is released from the run. Use this option if the file was initially
                   assigned with the C option.

              I
                   Automatically releases the file from the run the next time a task terminates,
                   regardless of the type of termination.

              U
                   Indicates that the file is to be cataloged unconditionally when the run
                   terminates (excluding a system stop) or when the file is released from the
                   run. Use this option if the file was initially assigned with the U option.

              X
                   Specifies that this run is to have exclusive use of the file until the run
                   terminates, the file is released from the run, or the exclusive use of the file
                   is released.




7–22                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                 @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                Z
                    Specifies that this statement is not to cause a hold condition. Control is
                    returned to the user, indicating whether a hold state would have resulted
                    from the assignment.
                    This option also requests that this file be reloaded if it is unloaded.

          filename
                Identifies the file on which you are changing fields. See Section 3.3 for a
                complete description of the filename field.

          type
                Specifies the addressing mode of the file (sector- or word-addressable) and the
                equipment type requested for the file. For more information about the type field,
                refer to the explanation of the @CAT statement.
                You can use type to spread a file across different equipment types. However,
                the new type must be compatible with the old type. For example, if the old type
                is mass storage, the new type cannot be tape.

          reserve
                The number that you specify here changes the value of your initial reserve. This
                lets you increase the space for your file. For more information about the reserve,
                refer to the explanation of the @CAT and @ASG statements. The reserve cannot
                be expanded beyond the size given in the maximum subfield.

          maximum
                The number you specify changes the previous maximum allowable length of the
                file in granules (sector-addressable files) or words (word-addressable files). For
                more information about the maximum subfield, refer to the explanation of the
                @CAT and @ASG statements. The maximum can be expanded or reduced, but
                not below the highest granule assigned.

          placement
                Specifies the placement of the file on a controller or device. For more information
                about the placement field, refer to the explanation of the @ASG statement.
                You can change the placement for the current assignment of the file. However,
                placement is not changed in the master file directory unless the placement is an
                absolute placement request.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 7–23
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




 7.2.5. Assigning Tape Files to Your Run
         The @ASG statement lets you assign a tape file and one or two tape drives to a run.
         Using the subfields and letter options, you specify the type of hardware required and
         the mode in which it is to be used. The information recorded in the master file
         directory (MFD) and the specifications from the @ASG statement are used to select a
         tape unit for the file.

         You must be aware of the following terms that are used in this section.
            The Half-Inch Cartridge (HIC) tape that can be used to record 18-track or 36-track
             formatted data.
            The Digital Linear Tape (DLT)

            Linear Tape Open (LTO): This device is released as different generations of the
             Ultrium technology. To denote the different generations, the generation number
             is appended to LTO. Therefore, a third generation LTO device is referred to as
             LTO3.
         If the file is a shared file, then the file’s MFD items are in the shared MFD, but only
         tape drives on the host on which the assign is done can be allocated.

         You can specify all subfields of the @ASG statement when you are assigning a tape
         file that was previously cataloged, and the subfields are honored for the duration of
         the run. However, the values stored in the MFD are not changed.

         A tape file or tape unit can be assigned to only one user at a time. Subsequent
         requests for the assigned file or unit are held until the file or unit is released from its
         current assignment, so you must free them as soon as possible.

         If you enter an @ASG statement for a tape file that is already assigned to your run,
         the statement is ignored. You are warned that the file is already assigned; fields or
         options are not changed.

         A temporary tape file is a file that exists only during the duration of a run and is
         accessible only by the run that created the temporary file. A temporary file can have
         the same file name as an unassigned cataloged file.

         You might have to wait until a tape unit or file becomes available if your request is
         for one of the following:

          A tape unit that is being used by another run
          A cataloged tape file that is being used by another run
          A tape that is being used by another run except when the tape identifier is for a
            scratch tape (This is true only if the Tape Automatic Volume Recognition (TAVR)
            feature is on.)
          A tape currently in use for another file (only if TAVR is on)
         Note: If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, you must pass security validation
         to access a tape with a security label.




7–24                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




          Format
            @ASG,options filename,type[/units/log/noise/processor/tape/
            format/data-converter/block-numbering/data-compression/
            buffered-write/expanded-buffer/,reel-1/reel-2/.../
            reel-n,expiration/mmspec,ring-indicator,ACR-name,CTL-pool ]

       options

                 General Options

                 B
                         Specifies that the tape identifiers associated with the file being
                         assigned must be considered nonunique on a system and run basis.

                 I
                         Automatically releases the file from the run the next time a task
                         terminates, regardless of the type of termination. (A task is a discrete
                         processing step in a run, involving the execution of an absolute
                         element, such as a system processor or user program.)

                 E
                         Indicates even parity. Available only on 7-track tape units. This option is
                         not allowed for any other tape types.

                     N
                         Specifies that a tape unit is to be assigned to the user, but no volume is
                         assigned to the unit, and load messages to the operator are inhibited. In
                         a program that uses the N option, you must issue ER TINTL$ or ER
                         TSWAP$ before the tape file can be accessed for requests requiring
                         that a tape be mounted (ER IOW$, ER TLBL$, and so forth). If you do
                         not, the request is not processed and it hangs, waiting for a tape to be
                         mounted.

                         If you use the N option for a cartridge tape within a cartridge tape
                         library (CTL), the Exec searches the CTL for the cartridge-ID (or the
                         BLANK identifier if a cartridge-ID is not specified). If the cartridge is
                         found or if the CTL allocates a blank tape for this @ASG statement, a
                         CTL-controlled tape drive is selected. When you issue ER TSWAP$, a
                         request is issued to the CTL to mount the tape indicated on ER
                         TSWAP$. Therefore, you need to ensure that the tape drive allocated on
                         an N option assignment is the correct one to handle ER TSWAP$.

                         No general statement can be made about the result of a processor call
                         that accesses a tape file assigned with the N option because of the
                         various ways tape files are handled. See the ER Programming
                         Reference Manual (7830 7899) for information on Executive requests.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–25
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




             R
                 Indicates a read-only file. A file assigned with the R option cannot be
                 overwritten. The file can only be read or deleted. Any activity requesting to
                 write in the file is put in error mode. If your system has Security Level 1 or
                 higher, you can assign a previously cataloged file as read only, regardless of
                 how the file was originally cataloged.

             W
                 Indicates a write-only file. The file can be only written into and extended in
                 the process. Files created on labeled volumes are labeled as write-only.

             Z
                 Specifies that the run must not be held, waiting for a tape unit or tape. If the
                 required type of tape unit is configured in the system but is not currently
                 available for assignment to the requesting run, a reject status is returned to
                 the user.
                 In a CTL system, the Z option bypasses the database cartridge-ID search if
                 the CTL is unavailable and no CTL pool name is specified. The system then
                 attempts to allocate a freestanding tape drive. If the Z option is specified on
                 an @ASG when requesting a blank tape and the CTL is unavailable when a
                 CTL pool name is specified, the @ASG fails.

                 For owned files, a file is cataloged as public when the P option is specified
                 on the @ASG statement and no access control record (ACR) is specified.

                 Indicates the same conditions as the C option, except that the file is

             Options for Assigning Previously Cataloged Tape Files

             A
                 Indicates that the file is already cataloged and ensures that it is not treated

                    An ACR cannot be specified with this option.

             D
                 Deletes a cataloged file, in addition to releasing it from the run. If it is a

                 For systems with Fundamental Security, to delete cataloged files assigned
                 with the C or U option, you must have included the correct read and write
                 keys (if any) when you assigned the file to the run.
                 If the file is owned, you must have delete access to the file in order to
                 delete it.

                    If your site has Fundamental Security, you must include any read or write

                    Requests that this file assignment be honored even if the system has

                    the file being disabled.

                    For tape assignments, the X-option can be used when the open reel block
                    count checking feature is enabled by configuration tag block_count_check
                    (BLOKCK). The X-option has no effect for cartridge tapes. The X-option
                    ensures that I/O is not inhibited after the following two errors have

                       Volume has no EOF label.

                Y
                    Assigns the file only for the purpose of examining the master file directory
                    entry for the file. A PCT file item is created. Exclusive use, disabled, rolled
                    out, and private mode are ignored. The file is read- and write-inhibited and
                    the inhibit can never be overridden. No tape units are selected.


                Options for Assigning Temporary Tape Files

                R
                    Specifies that files written to labeled volumes are labeled as read-only files.
                    They cannot be written to or deleted. If your system has Security Level 1 or
                    higher, you can assign a previously cataloged file as read only, regardless of
                    how the file was originally cataloged.

                T
                    Specifies that the file is a temporary file. If one of the options from the
                    group A, C, T, or U is not specified and the file name is not found in the
                    master file directory, the system defaults to this option. The shared
                    directory-ID cannot be used.

                    You cannot use the T option with the A, C, or U option; it is considered an

             Tape Labeling Options

             F
                 Writes information on a labeled output tape to indicate that any
                 reassignment of the tape for input requires only verification of the tape
                 identifier unless security for tapes is configured. If you omit this option
                 when you create a labeled output tape, the qualifier and file name are
                 written into the label blocks. This forces all later assigns to use the same
                 qualifier and file name that were used to create the tape and pass any
                 security checks enforced at your site.
                 The F option has meaning only at file creation, not at file input time.
                 Specifying the F option for an unlabeled tape does not cause a reject.
                 For systems with autolabeling configured, an unlabeled tape assigned with
                 the F option is labeled automatically. For systems without autolabeling, the
                 F option for an unlabeled tape is ignored.
                 Note: The F-option is implied for J-option tape assigns when the tape
                 volume security level equals 2 (TVSL = 2). See the following table for tape
                 volume security level descriptions.

             J
                 Your system is configured at one of four tape volume security levels (0-3);
                 the J option meaning depends on which level your system has:

                    Level                                    Meaning

                      0      Indicates the tape volume is to be unlabeled. Read and write accesses
                             are allowed.
                      1      Indicates the tape volume is to be unlabeled. Read and write accesses
                             are allowed.
                      2      For non-privileged users, all tapes written with the J option are
                             automatically given security labels and those labels are created as if
                             the user had also specified to F-option. Read of unlabeled tapes is
                             permitted.
                             For privileged users, write of unlabeled tapes requires executing with
                             the system compartment set and clearance level 63 (system high) and
                             possession of the bypass volume check privilege (which requires that
                             the file SYS$*DLOC$ be assigned to the run).
                      3      To read or write to an unlabeled tape, you must be executing with the
                             system compartment set and clearance level 63 (system high) and
                             possess the bypass volume check privilege. If you are not executing
                             under these conditions you receive an error message and the J option
                             is ignored.

                F and J
                    When the Media manager is loaded, F and J assign options are allowed
                    together. If you use the F option along with the J option, the Media
                    Manager does not enforce Qual*filename matching, but does provide all
                    other access controls. However, these options are not allowed together
                    when the Media Manager BYPASS, is used.
                    Subsequent tape accesses must use the matching Qual*filename with the
                    Media Manager when J is used without the F.

                If you do not specify an option, the master file directory is searched for a
                cataloged file with this name. If the file cannot be found, it is assigned as a
                temporary file.

                The @ASG statement options for tape files affect either the creation of a new
                tape file or the assignment of an existing tape file. If you use an option that is
                not allowed, the statement is rejected.

                The options for assigning a file to be cataloged cause the name and
                characteristics of the file to be placed in a master file directory, and the file to
                be assigned to your run. The C and U options cause the file to be cataloged; the
                G, P, R, and W options place restrictions on the file when it is cataloged. If your
                system has Security Level 1 or higher, the G, P, R, and W options work as listed
                in the mass storage assign.

                For cataloged tape files, the J option is recorded in the master file directory;
                however, the F option cannot be used when cataloging tapes.

                The hardware options are used with the temporary, cataloging, or cataloged
                options. All hardware options specified on the assignment of a tape file are
                recorded in the master file directory upon cataloging of the file.

                If you specify more than one density option (H, L, M, S, and V), the @ASG
                statement is rejected. When you use a density option (E, H, S, or V), make sure
                it is compatible with the type. If a density option and the type conflict, the
                @ASG statement is rejected.

                For 18-track tape assignments, the E, H, M, S, and V options are invalid. For
                HICL, the L option is assumed. These assumed options are used in the absence
                of overriding mode options.

          General Mnemonics
          The assign mnemonic used is the one supplied by the user, unless it is one that is
          flagged as a general mnemonic. Assign mnemonics are designated as general
          mnemonics by the site at system generation time. General mnemonics are refined to
          a more specific assign mnemonic by the Exec before cataloging the file. The Exec, as
          supplied by Unisys, has U9, HIC, and T flagged as general mnemonics.

          You must use the most general assign mnemonic for your requirements in order to
          give the system more freedom in assigning units. To ensure that the options are
          compatible with all tape types accessible with that assign mnemonic, be careful



7830 7949–031                                                                                     7–33
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         when you use options with the type field. For example, when using assign mnemonic
         T, you must specify only those options compatible with all types of units.

         Selection Sequences
         All assign mnemonics have a selection sequence associated with them. In some
         instances, only one choice is defined for an assign mnemonic. In those cases where
         more than one equipment type is associated with an assign mnemonic, the selection
         sequence supplied by Unisys always starts with the fastest equipment and then
         moves to slower equipment. This selection sequence can be changed by a site at
         system generation time. See Table D-4 for the selection sequences supplied by
         Unisys.

         Assign Mnemonics and the CTL
         The assign mnemonics associated with a CTL are determined at your site. The Exec,
         as supplied by Unisys, recognizes HICL, HICM, HIC, HIC40, HIC51, HICSL, LTO, LTO3,
         LTO4, and T as CTL-related assign mnemonics. When you use an assign mnemonic
         that is associated with a CTL, the Exec searches the CTL for the specified
         cartridge-ID (reel-ID).

         If that cartridge is found in the CTL, a tape drive controlled by the CTL is allocated for
         the @ASG statement. If not found in the CTL, the Exec attempts to allocate a
         freestanding tape drive. If not found and if no freestanding devices are configured,
         the assignment is rejected. (The CTL is not searched if NONCTL is specified on the
         CTL-pool field.)

         See your site administrator for CTL information specific to your site.

         Assign Mnemonics and the ACS
         When a system has a StorageTek Automatic Cartridge System (ACS) installed, there
         are special considerations to take into account when using certain assign
         mnemonics. Mnemonics such as U47, U47M, HICL, HICM, HIC, T, HIC51, HIC52,
         DLT70, HIS98, HIS99B, LTO, LTO3, and LTO4 select the type of device to assign, but
         do not determine whether the device should be selected from an ACS or a
         freestanding device.

         For specific reel-ID assignments, an ACS-query determines the location of the
         cartridge. Once the location of the specific reel-ID is known, the Exec can select an
         appropriate device. An assignment requesting a specific cartridge that is found in the
         ACS results in a tape drive controlled by the ACS being allocated for the @ASG
         statement. An assignment requesting a specific cartridge that does not reside in an
         ACS results in a freestanding device selected.

         For BLANK tape assignments, two CSC configuration tags (with the names
         prefer_scratch_in_acs and query_for_scratch) control whether a freestanding drive or
         a drive in the ACS library is assigned. See your system administrator for information
         about your site configuration. Also, see the CSC Site Administrator’s Guide for more
         information on the ACS.

         Mnemonics like U47L, U47NL, U47M, U47LM, NLCART, or LCART not only select the
         type of device, but also determine the location of the device—in other words,



7–34                                                                               7830 7949–031
                              @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




          whether it must be inside an ACS or outside an ACS. The mnemonics U47NL, U47M,
          and NLCART always select a freestanding device. The mnemonics U47L, U47LM, and
          LCART always select an ACS device.

          Notes:
           Assign mnemonics that can select an ACS drive are T, HIC, HICL, HICM, HIC51,
             HIC52, HIS98, U47, U47L, U47LM, LCART, DLT70, LTO, LTO3, and LTO4. Assign
             mnemonics HICL, U47, DLT70, HICM, HIC, LTO, LTO3, and LTO4 result in either
             an ACS query or cartridge tape library (CTL) poll. If the Automated Cartridge
             System (ACS) query is positive, an ACS drive is assigned. If the CTL poll is
             positive, a CTL drive is allocated. If the ACS query and CTL poll are negative, a
             free standing drive is allocated. NONCTL can be used on ACS or CTL
             assignments.
           In any configuration, absolute device assignment selects the requested device.
           For an ACS, the pool has no bearing on device assignment. The pool has bearing
             only during BLANK tape allocation and mounting.
          ACS names can also be supplied in place of the assigned mnemonic field. See your
          system administrator for these names.

          Tape Density
          Unless otherwise specified by assign mnemonic or mode option, the highest
          possible density for a tape is assumed. For example, 6250 bpi is the assumed density
          for a UNISERVO 36 tape unit.

          Note: In some cases, you are not able to append data to a tape (write past
          loadpoint).

          Compatibility Between Devices
          Half-inch Serpentine(HIS) tape devices and LTO tape devices cannot read U9 (9-track)
          or DLT formatted tapes. HIC, U9( 9-track), HIS, DLT, and LTO device types can only
          read tapes created for those specific types of drives. Tapes for one device type are
          not compatible with any other device type. Also, a two-unit assign cannot be mixed
          between HIC, DLT, HIS, LTO and U9 type devices.

          Tape Automatic Volume Recognition (TAVR)
          When the TAVR feature is installed, the assign request can be satisfied by a unit that
          is premounted with the requested tape and is compatible with the request.

          If there is no premounted unit compatible with the request, the assignment is
          satisfied by a unit that is selected according to the selection sequence dictated by
          the type field. This unit can be overridden by an aftermount of the tape by the
          operator, if the aftermount unit is compatible with the request.

          If the requested tape is being used by another run, the request is held except when
          the tape identifier is for a scratch tape. If the requested tape is being used by the
          requestor’s run and if the run has only one activity, the request is rejected.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–35
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




         If this is a multiactivity run, the request is held except for scratch. However, if this file
         is assigned with a B option (subject to security check), the request overrides the
         tape-ID conflict.

         When all available units are in a premount-only status, the Exec cannot select a unit
         except when the request is for an absolute device/control unit or the requested tape
         is premounted on one of the units. For more information on TAVR, refer to the
         Exec Administration Reference Manual (7831 0323).

         units
               Specifies the number of tape units required; it can be integers 1 or 2. If omitted,
               the Exec assumes that one unit is required. A nonnumeric character or a numeric
               value greater than 2 causes the statement to be rejected. The number of units
               assigned is not retained in the master file directory upon cataloging. When two
               units are specified, the Exec guarantees that both units are compatible.
               Prior to SB4R6, the two cartridges specified on a two-unit @ASG could not reside
               in different cartridge library units (CLU), nor could one of the cartridges be in a
               CLU while the other was nonresident. Now (with TAVR), a two-unit tape @ASG
               completes successfully even if the two cartridges specified reside within
               different CLUs, or if one cartridge resides in a CLU and one cartridge is not
               resident in any CLU. The nonresident cartridge is assigned to a freestanding
               drive.
               With absolute device specification, a two-unit @ASG can explicitly allocate
               cartridge tape drives in different CLUs, or mix freestanding and CLU-controlled
               drives. In addition, the specified cartridge-IDs might reside in any CLU or outside
               the CLUs. The cartridges must be available to the explicitly specified drives for a
               successful @ASG.
               You cannot request a BLANK tape on both a CTL-drive and a freestanding drive
               on the same two-unit @ASG request.
               If the system cannot immediately grant the user’s request but has the potential
               to do so, the user can be put on hold and sent an appropriate message. If the
               user’s request cannot be granted now or later, the request is rejected. For
               example, a request for two tape servos is rejected if the user’s quota limit is set
               to one servo, regardless of how many servos are currently available. But if a user
               with a quota limit of two servos makes the same request with one servo
               currently available, that request is put on hold.

         log
               Assigns a single letter indicating a logical control unit. The Exec attempts to
               assign all files with the same letter to the same physical control unit, and those
               with different letters to different control units. The letter specified is not placed
               in the master file directory. This subfield permits more efficient I/O operation
               because of the separate control units.
               Logical control unit specification has meaning only within the current run.

         noise
               Specifies an integer from 1 to 63 that overrides the standard system noise
               constant. If you omit noise, either the standard system noise constant is used or


7–36                                                                                 7830 7949–031

                the value is stored in the master file directory, in the event of the assignment of
                a cataloged file (@ASG,A). Any 9-track tapes written in a density of 1600 bpi and
                6250 bpi have 0 as the system standard value. The noise value is recorded in the
                master file directory upon cataloging. Do not specify a noise subfield if you are
                assigning a cartridge tape.

          processor/tape
                Specifies the type of translation required. Processor defines the format of the
                data in the processor, and tape defines the format of the data on tape. You must
                specify both processor and tape or omit both. If you omit them, no translation
                occurs.
                Data translation is file independent and the translation mode remains in effect for
                the duration of the reading or writing of the tape. You can change data translation
                from file to file, but you must track this information yourself.
                The supported processor/tape mnemonics are


                       Processor Code             Tape Code

                    ASCII                     EBCDIC
                    ASCII                     FLDATA
                    EBCDIC                    ASCII
                    EBCDIC                    BCD
                    FLDATA                    ASCII
                    FLDATA                    BCD
                    FLDATA                    EBCDIC


                Your site can define additional processor/tape mnemonics, provided neither code
                exceeds 6 characters. When the file is cataloged, the values given in
                processor/tape are stored in the master file directory.
                All translation takes place in the hardware.

          Note: If you are using the data compression feature to read and write to half-inch
          cartridge tape, you cannot use the data translation feature.

          format
                Specifies the data transfer format for the word-to-byte conversion.
                Permissible format entries are as follows:
                Q
                      Quarter word

                8
                      8-bit packed (default on 9-track, 1/2-inch cartridge tape)




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–37
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




             The data transfer format is recorded in the master file directory upon cataloging,
             to be used on subsequent assigns unless specifically overridden.

         data-converter
         This field only applied to 7-track tape and now must be left blank. (Although this
         option no longer has any effect, it is allowed since it might still be in user
         runstreams.)

             Its allowable value is as follows:
             OFF
                   Turns off the data-converter if assign is made from the master file directory
                   (@ASG,A) and the file was cataloged with data conversion. In all other cases,
                   OFF is ignored.
             If you do not specify data-converter, no action is taken in relation to the data
             converter. Furthermore, the OFF mnemonic is not recorded in the master file
             directory, except as implied by the absence of data-converter.

         block-numbering
                   Determines whether block numbering is on. Block numbering is available on
                   HIC, HIS, DLT, and LTO tape subsystems. For the HIC, HIS, DLT, and LTO
                   cartridge tape subsystems, the user cannot turn on block numbering with
                   this subfield because it is performed by the hardware and is transparent to
                   the user.

              Specify one of the following values:
             BLKON
                   Turns block numbering on (invalid for HIC ,DLT, and LTO cartridge tape
                   subsystems).

             BLKOFF
                   Indicates that blocks must not be numbered. (This does not actually turn off
                   block numbering.)

             BLKOPT
                   Gives the user the option to turn block numbering on at a later date (invalid
                   for HIC, DLT, and LTO cartridge tape subsystems).

         data-compression
                   Reduces the amount of physical tape required to record data by removing
                   repetitive data before recording it (available for HIC, HIS, DLT, and LTO
                   cartridge tape subsystems only). Data compression is generally performed
                   on a file basis.

             For half-inch cartridge tape subsystems, these are the valid data-compression
             values and their meanings:




7–38                                                                               7830 7949–031
                              @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                CMPON
                  Enables 8- or 9-bit data compression depending on the format parameter.
                  When Q is specified on the format subfield, enables 9-bit data compression;
                  when either 8 or nothing is specified on the format subfield, enables 8-bit
                  data compression. Enables LTO-DC for an LTO cartridge tape device.

                CMPOFF
                  Disable data compression.

                CMP8ON
                  Enables 8-bit mode of data compression.

                CMP9ON
                  Enables 9-bit mode of data compression.

                CMPOPT
                  Capable of LTO-DC data compression. Gives you the option to enable data
                  compression at a later date; must be used if there is any possibility that the
                  cartridge tape contains an LTO-DC compressed file.

                CMPEON
                  Enables enhanced data recording capability (EDRC) mode of data
                  compression.

                CMEOPT
                  Capable of EDRC data compression. Gives you the option to enable EDRC
                  data compression at a later date; must be used if there is any possibility that
                  the cartridge tape contains an EDRC compressed file.

                  For DLT, HIS98, and HIS99B tape subsystems, these are the valid
                  data-compression values and their meaning:

                CMPLON
                  Enables LZ1 data-compression. DLT and HIS98 cartridge tapes are not
                  compatible with each other or with future Unisys tape products that can use
                  this compression value.

                CMPOFF
                  Disable data compression.
          Examples
                @ASG,TF TAPE.,HICL/////////CMPEON/BUFON,111C,,RING

                    The half inch cartridge tape is assigned as labeled with EDRC data
                    compression explicitly requested and buffered-write capability.

                @ASG,TJ TAPE.,HICL/////////CMEOPT,111C,,RING



7830 7949–031                                                                                7–39
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                   The half-inch cartridge tape is assigned as unlabeled, requesting a tape
                   device that has the hardware capability of supporting EDRC data
                   compression.

            Support for 4780 18- and 36-track tapes is provided by standard Exec.
            Compression on the 4780 subsystems is called improved cartridge recording
            capability (ICRC) and is totally compatible with the 5073 enhanced data recording
            capability (EDRC). It is selected by using the CMPEON value.

            Device characteristics for compressed tape readability are

          Unisys proprietary compressed cartridge tapes cannot be read on 4780 drives, but
            EDRC compressed cartridges from 5073 drives can be successfully read.

          A cartridge drive on a 4780 that does not have compression hardware can read
            only uncompressed cartridge tapes.

          The 4780 drives that have compression hardware can read EDRC compressed
            tapes without having to explicitly request CMPEON.
            Also, 36-track tapes have more capacity on current cartridges because data is
            written in both directions on the tape, and more capacity with longer tapes can
            hold up to four times more data than current cartridges (1,100 feet [E-carts]).

         The following tape assign and catalog modes are available for 4780 drives:
           @ASG,TJ T.,HICM/////////CMPEON/BUFON/EBCOPT,REELID

         The following tape assign and catalog modes are available for 5136 devices:
           @ASG,TJ T.,HIC51/////////CMPEON/BUFON/EBCOPT,REELID

         Notes:
          Although you can explicitly specify 8- or 9-bit data compression with CMP8ON
            and CMP9ON, you can allow the system to select the best compression ratio
            by specifying the format of the data.
          You might experience a loss in performance if you use the read backwards
            function (the RB$ function of the ER IOW$) of the 8- or 9-bit data compression
            feature on a half-inch cartridge tape subsystem.
          Tapes created by using 8- or 9-bit data compression cannot be used with Exec
            levels lower than 41R6/41R6M.
          An I/O error status of 024 (012 for MR$ operation) results if you use the read
            backward function on an EDRC compressed data block.
          When you are using EDRC data compression on a half-inch cartridge tape, user
            data block sizes are limited to 128K bytes or smaller. An I/O error status
            results if user data block sizes are greater than 128K bytes when writing with
            EDRC data compression used.
          When you are reading a tape with EDRC compressed data, EDRC mode need not
            be enabled, as long as an EDRC capable device has been assigned (for example,
            CMEOPT was used on the assignment).



7–40                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




           When you are reading a tape with LZ1 compressed data, LZ1 mode need not be
             enabled, as long as an LZ1 capable device has been assigned (such as a DLT70
             assign mnemonic was used on the assignment).
           Tapes created using EDRC data compression cannot be used with Exec levels
             lower than SB4R7.
           Tape devices that support EDRC or LZ1 data compression do not support data
             translation (ASCII/EBCDIC) or 8- or 9-bit data compression.
           If you write data that is not highly compressible to USR5073, a compression
              error occurs in the subsystem and is reported to the Exec. This compression
              error is logged in the 1252 log entry by the Exec and your I/O is reissued as
              part of recovery action. The USR5073 then writes the data uncompressed into
              the tape. If, however, the compression error occurs too often, you might
              experience a loss in performance. A solution would be to turn compression
              off.
           CMPEON, CMEOPT, and EBCOPT are valid values for the USR5073 device when
             using HICSL.
           When using the HICL mnemonic in combination with CMPEON, CMEOPT, and
             EBCOPT, a SCSI USR5073 or a BMC 5073 device might be selected.
          buffered-write
                Specifies whether buffered writes are to be used when a tape is mounted on a
                device controlled by a control unit that has buffering capability.
                These are the values:
           BUFTAP

                Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks and file marks for the entire
                tape.
           BUFFIL

                Enables the buffering of write data including label blocks and tape marks for a file
                written to labeled tapes. The system ensures that writing of the data and file
                marks occurs at the close of a file.
           BUFON

                Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks.
           BUFOFF

                Disables any buffered write mode.
          The @ASG statement is rejected if it contains the BUFTAP or BUFFIL value and there
          are no tape units up and available that support tape mark buffering (TMB). Even
          though TMB is supported on the CTS5236, the BUFTAP value is not. The rejection
          message is:

            E:256033 requested unit(s) not available.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–41
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




        The following rules apply when using BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, and BUFON:
           When the user switches modes from BUFFIL to BUFON or BUFOFF, writing the
            buffer to tape is postponed until the next I/O to the tape subsystem. This also
            applies when switching modes from BUFTAP to other modes.
           If BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, or BUFON is not specified, and the configuration tag
            TAPBUF (dynamic nametape_buffering) is zero, the system uses the default value
            BUFON.
           If BUFFIL is specified for an unlabeled tape, the data blocks for writes are buffered
            and one synchronization per file is done by a WEF$ function just as it is without
            the BUFFIL specification.
           When using buffering, it is the user’s responsibility to retain the original data for
            possibly performing error recovery, if that is the user’s requirement. The Exec
            provides no means for the user to recover this data. With the use of the BUFTAP
            option, it is possible for the user to have received good status on previous writes
            of thousands of files, when in fact none of the files has made it to tape, and if an
            error occurs while they are being written to tape, the remaining blocks in the tape
            subsystem’s buffer might never get written to tape.
                The Block ID SAFE (BSAFE$) I/O function provides a means for the user to
                determine what block has been actually written to tape by the tape
                subsystem.
                    When using BUFTAP, a FSAFE$ can be performed at any point if a user
                     wants to insure that buffered data/tape marks have been written to tape.
                     It is highly recommended that an FSAFE$ be performed and its status
                     checked after all user data/tape marks have been written to the tape
                     device, but before releasing the tape. This insures that the user is notified
                     of any errors in writing any remaining buffered data/tape marks to the
                     tape. This also allows the user to know that an error on a @FREE, TSWAP$,
                     TINTL$, or TLBL$ was not the result of writing any user buffered data/tape
                     marks to the tape.

            expanded buffer
                The expanded buffer lets you explicitly select a tape unit that has the
                hardware capability of supporting the data block sizes up to 256K bytes. If the
                tape unit supporting the selection is not available, then the request is rejected
                with the error message, "Requested unit(s) not available." If EBCOPT is not
                specified in the expanded buffer subfield, then any one of the first available
                units is selected.

            Notes:
               An I/O error status of 06 results if user data block sizes are greater than
                128K bytes when writing with EDRC data compression.
               The CTS5136, CTS5236, CTS9840, DLT7000, CTS9940B, LTO3, and LTO4
                devices always have expanded buffering, so the EBCOPT is not needed to
                get a CTS5136, CTS5236, CTS9840 DLT7000, CTS9940B, LTO3, or LTO4
                which supports expanded buffering.




7–42                                                                              7830 7949–031
                               @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




            Examples

                @ASG,TF TAPE.,HICL///////////EBCOPT,111C,,RING

                  The half-inch cartridge tape is assigned as labeled, requesting a tape device
                  that has the hardware capability of supporting block sizes of up to 256K
                  bytes.

                @ASG,TJ TAPE.,HICL/////////BUFON,111C,,RING

                  The half-inch cartridge tape is assigned as unlabeled with buffered-write
                  capability. The selected drive can be capable of supporting block sizes of up
                  to 256K bytes.

            reel-n
                 The reel-n specifies the identifier for each tape reel or cartridge required. Each
                 tape identifier is limited to 6 characters from set A through Z and 0 through 9.
                 Do not specify an identifier with a single A, E, Y, or N. These characters
                 correspond to valid responses to tape labeling messages. Using them as
                 identification could cause tape assign problems.
                 When an assignment uses a specific reel-ID, its location is determined by an
                 ACS query or a CTL poll. The reel-ID’s location, together with the assign
                 mnemonic, determines the resultant device assigned. When a BLANK is
                 assigned, no ACS query is done. However, BLANK assignments result in a CTL
                 poll.
                 The special mnemonics BLANK and SCRTCH have these meanings:

            BLANK
                 Designates a tape volume that can be overwritten. In a CTL system, blank
                 tapes can be allocated automatically from a named pool (CTL-pool). A tape
                 with the BLANK identifier can be retained after the assign for the duration of
                 the label’s expiration period, or until you release the tape.
                 Obtain the tape reel number from the system operator or from operator
                 messages logged in your run’s tailsheet. Your site must have procedures
                 established for allocating blank tapes.

            SCRTCH
                 Designates a tape volume for temporary use during this assignment. The tape
                 can be used by anyone else after it is freed (@FREE). The label might be
                 written, but if you use the SCRTCH reel-ID, anyone is allowed access.
                 If you want a BLANK tape request to be satisfied by the CTL, specify a
                 CTL-pool name on the CTL-pool field. If you do not want a BLANK tape request
                 to be satisfied by the CTL, specify NONCTL on the CTL-pool field.
                 Note: Your system can be configured to allocate BLANK cartridge tapes
                 from the CTL even if you do not specify a CTL-pool name (for example, the
                 default CTL pool can be used).




7830 7949–031                                                                                 7–43
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




           A maximum of 2,047 reels or cartridges can be specified with the @ASG
           statement, although only two can be accessed at any one time.

           If the file is to be cataloged, all tape identifiers are recorded in the master file
           directory. Tapes are used and cataloged in the order specified.

           If you omit this field, the Exec directs the operator to mount blank tapes on the
           appropriate tape units and to provide identifiers for each tape that is unlabeled.
           (Omitting this field is the same as entering BLANK.)

           If additional tapes are requested by ER TSWAP$, the operator is asked to load the
           required blank tapes and provide identifiers for each unlabeled tape. On a tape file
           with SCRTCH for an identifier, ER TSWAP$ cannot swap tapes beyond the total
           units count (1 for one-unit assignment and 2 for two-unit assignment). On an
           attempt to swap tapes beyond the total units count, the first scratch tape is
           rewound and used again.

           For currently cataloged files, the reel field is normally void, indicating that the reels
           or cartridges listed in the master file directory are used in the order created.

           If you supply tape identifiers, they must be of the set listed in the master file
           directory, but can be a subset and listed in any order, allowing the user to omit or
           access them in any order. If you enter an invalid tape identifier, the @ASG
           statement is rejected. The Exec does not detect the case of a legal identifier for a
           tape that does not exist.

           In either case, when the known tapes are exhausted and additional ones are
           requested, blank tapes are used, and their numbers are added to the master file
           directory. (This is not allowed if the file is cataloged in the read-only state.)

           When an unlabeled tape is being mounted, the following prompt is displayed on
           the system console to ask for the tape’s reel number:

             n ANSWER WITH REEL NO ON unit E,REEL

           When this tape is @FREE and the next one assigned, the same scenario is
           repeated.

           However, a special case occurs when an autoloader is installed and the S option is
           used on the @FREE statement: For the first tape, the operator is prompted for the
           reel number as described above. If this tape is released using @FREE,S, the next
           unlabeled tape in the autoloader is not prompted for the reel number.

           This is a useful feature that can significantly improve efficiency, especially when a
           bunch of unlabeled tapes are to be processed.




7–44                                                                                7830 7949–031
