            expiration-period
                  This field has meaning only for labeled tape volumes and is ignored in all other
                  cases. It specifies the number of days that this file is to be retained.
                  The maximum number allowed is a site configuration field that can never
                  exceed 4,095 days. Specification of a value greater than the maximum causes
                  the @ASG statement to be rejected. The system standard value, which is also
                  site configurable, is used if no expiration period is specified.
                  In addition, you can use the F option to determine whether the tape can be
                  overwritten prior to the expiration date.
                  The Exec guarantees that the expiration period on all files beyond the first file
                  on a volume can be less than or equal to the first file. If a subsequent assign
                  has an expiration period greater than that remaining on the first file, the Exec
                  automatically changes the expiration period of the newly added file to the
                  remaining expiration period of the first file. The expiration period is stored on
                  the tape and not in the master file directory.


                     Assign Tape              File name match             File names do not match

                BLANK tape requested     read - > error                 read - > error
                                         write - > only if expired      write - > only if expired
                BLANK tape not           expired - read or write is     expired write - > OK
                requested                allowed. (Access code no       not expired if ‘F’ set
                                         longer has meaning.)           read/write inhibits based on
                                         not expired - set read/write   access code. Not ‘F’ error.
                                         inhibits based on HDR1
                                         access code


                  The expiration period also specifies how long a file is protected by

                 File name verification (F option on the @ASG statement)
                 Restricted read access (R option on the @ASG statement)
                 Restricted write access (W option on the @ASG statement)
            mmspec
                  A Media Manager specification subfield of mmspec is relevant when the
                  Media Manager is being used. The subfield must be 6 characters or less, and
                  the variable portion must be less than 100 for xx, yy, and zz for specifications,
                  USEDxx, DCYCyy, and YEARzz. mmspec can be one of the following:
                  BYPASS
                      Bypass the Media Manager, subject to site restrictions.

                  USEDxx
                      Expire if not used for xx days.




7830 7949–031                                                                                       7–45
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




               MFD
                   Expire if not cataloged in the MFD.

               DCYCyy
                   Retain yy copies with unique create dates.

               FCYCyy
                   Retain yy copies regardless of create dates.

               READ
                   Do not expire and do not allow to be written.

               NOSCR
                   Do not expire but allow write by owner.

               YEARzz
                   Retain zz years.

               DAYS
                   Interpret expiration as a number of days regardless of the Media Manager
                   parameter STRXCODE.

               You can code any legal value for the expiration field when you use it with the
               Media Manager specification for the HDR1 label. The expiration of the tape by
               the Media Manager is subject to the following rules:

              READ, NOSR, and YEAR take precedent over the expiration value
              USED, MFD, DCYC, and FCYC are considered in addition to the expiration.
               You cannot use mmspec on an @CAT statement, but you can enter it on the
               @ASG,A statement for a cataloged tape file.

               You can overwrite the files on the tape before the end of the expiration period
               (assuming you pass the security checks) only if one of the following sets of
               conditions is true:
               Condition 1:

              You created the tape with the F option and without the R option.
              You specified the reel-ID on the @ASG call or ER TSWAP$ function 2 request
               that matches the reel-ID in the tape volume label that you want to overwrite.
               If additional tapes are requested by ER TSWAP$, the operator is asked to load
               the required blank tapes and provide identifiers for each unlabeled tape. On a
               tape file with SCRTCH for an identifier, ER TSWAP$ cannot swap tapes
               beyond the total units count (1 for one-unit assignment and 2 for two-unit
               assignment). On an attempt to swap tapes beyond the total units count, the
               first scratch tape is rewound and used again.



7–46                                                                           7830 7949–031
                               @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                Condition 2:

               You created the tape without either the F or R options.

               You access the file with the same qualifier and file name.

               The reel-ID matches the one in the tape volume label.
                If you used both the F and R options when you created the tape, you cannot
                overwrite the files until the end of the expiration period.

            ring-indicator
                This field specifies whether the media for this file (open reel or cartridge) is
                write protected or write enabled. For 10-1/2 inch open reels, a write ring
                allows/disallows write operations. For cartridge tapes, a file-protect switch on
                the cartridge itself allows/disallows write operations.
                The allowable values (independent of tape equipment used) are as follows:
                WRITEPROTECT or NORING
                    Specifies that write operations (cartridge or open reel media) are not
                    allowed.

                WRITEENABLE or RING
                    Specifies that write operations (cartridge or open reel media) are allowed.

                If you do not specify a value for ring-indicator, the operating system ensures
                that the tape is write enabled if the first I/O to the tape at load point is a write
                function.

                Note: You must always specify an allowable value in this field to ensure
                that the tape is properly protected.

                Enforcement of the ring-indicator values in a CTL is accomplished in a different
                manner. The CTL sets the tape drive allocated for the assignment in a
                write-protect or write-enable mode. The cartridge is not required to have the
                write-protect switch set when the tape drive is set to write-protect mode.
                However, if the cartridge has write-protect set, no write is possible without
                changing the physical cartridge switch.

            ACR-name
                Specifies the access control record (ACR) for the cataloged file if your site has
                Security Level 1 or higher. The ACR-name is 1 to 6 characters in any
                combination of letters (A through Z), numbers (0 through 9), $, and - (dash). The
                ACR must already exist and must be owned by the user doing the assign.
                To attach an ACR to a temporary tape, you must use @TLABEL.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–47
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




           CTL-pool
              Can be one of the following:
              CTL-pool-name
                  Directs the Exec to allocate BLANK tapes from the designated
                  CTL pool of cartridge tapes. CTL-pool-name can be 1 to 12 characters,
                  consisting of the alphanumeric characters, $, and - (hyphen). Using a CTL
                  pool name might place your assignment in a hold condition while the Exec
                  waits for an available tape drive (except when you specify the Z option,
                  which returns a reject status). You can remove the wait status with an
                  @@X T statement.

              NONCTL
                  Directs the Exec to use freestanding cartridge tape drives. The Exec
                  cannot search the CTL for a cartridge-ID because the cartridge cannot be
                  inserted into the CTL.
              Your site might have a default CTL pool for assignments that specify BLANK
              tapes but do not specify a CTL pool.
              You can override a previously specified CTL pool name for a cataloged tape
              file by specifying a different CTL pool name on an @ASG,A statement. If you
              do not specify a CTL pool name on an @ASG,A statement, the CTL pool name
              is taken from the master file directory. You cannot change the CTL pool name
              for a cataloged file in the master file directory.
              If the CTL-pool field is blank, the Exec searches the CTL for the cartridge
              (reel-ID) and uses the CTL if the cartridge is found there; otherwise, it allocates
              a freestanding cartridge tape drive and issues the LOAD message. If the
              cartridge is not found in the CTL or if no freestanding drives are configured,
              the assignment is rejected.
              If you specify the Z option when the CTL is not available, and you do not
              specify a CTL pool name, the Exec attempts to use freestanding tape drives; if
              you do specify a CTL pool name, the request is rejected. If you specify
              NONCTL on the CTL-pool field, the assignment request is not impacted when
              the CTL is unavailable. See your site administrator for CTL information specific
              to your site.

             @ASG,A FREMONT1.

                was cataloged. The project-ID of the current run is used as a qualifier.

             @ASG,ADS FREMONT2.,28N//A/////////,N212,,,ACR5

                This statement assigns file FREMONT2 to the run. The file is currently
                cataloged but is deleted if the run terminates normally. The UNISERVO 28
                nine-track tape unit is to be on logical channel A and reel N212 is to be used.
                The density is 6250 bpi (S option).

                @ASG,T FREMONT4.,T///36

   7.2.6. Assigning VTH Files to Your Run
            Virtual tape handler (VTH) simulates tape by using mass storage. The @ASG
            statement lets you assign virtual tape files to a run. You assign them in the same
            manner as a standard tape file, using an assign statement. Your access and
            manipulation of virtual tape files is the same as standard tape files. Your control
            statements remain identical for a virtual tape as for a standard tape. Programs
            cannot tell the difference between a virtual tape and a real tape. Virtual tapes have
            the characteristics of most open reel types and therefore do not support fast tape
            access (FTA), block numbering, data compression, buffered writes, or expanded
            buffer.

            The options and parameters on the assign statement for a virtual tape are
            generally the same as for a standard file.

            Format
                @ASG,options filename,type[/units/log/noise/processor/tape/
                format/data-converter/,reel-1/reel-2/.../reel-n,expiration/
                mmspec,ring-indicator,ACR-name,CTL-pool]




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–51
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




           options
               Because there is no physical reel to mount and no way to identify to the
               handler a different file to assign, the B option is illegal for virtual tape
               assignments.

           type
               Installation of the virtual tape feature adds two new type mnemonics (VT and
               VTH) to the standard set used for assigning tape files.

           reel-n
               The reel number specifies the identifier for each virtual tape assignment. Each
               reel identifier is limited to 6 characters from the set A through Z and 0 through
               9.

   7.2.7. Assigning DVD Tape
           The DVD tape simulates tape by using DVDs as the recorded media. You assign
           them the same way as a standard tape file, using a tape assign statement.

           Your access and manipulation of DVD tape files is the same as standard tape files
           except that you only have read capability. DVD tapes have the same
           characteristics of most open reel types, and therefore do not support fast tape
           access (FTA), block numbering, data compression, buffered writes, or expanded
           buffer. DVD tapes do not support ACS or CTL; therefore assignments with
           CTL-pool are rejected.

           Because the DVD tape is read-only, use of the W option, use of RING or
           WRITEENABLE in the ring field, and use of BLANK or SCRTCH in the reel-ID field
           are all rejected.

           The options and parameters on the assign statement for DVD tape are generally
           the same as for a standard tape file but are restricted to the functionality
           described above.

           Format
             @ASG,options filename,type[/units/log/noise/processor/tape/format/
             data-converter/,reel-1/reel-2/.../reel-n,expiration/mmspec,ring-indicator,
             ACR-name,CTL-pool]

           where:

           options
               Because the DVD tape is read-only, the W option is rejected for DVD tape
               assignments.

           type
               The DVD tape feature adds the type mnemonic "DVDTP" to the tape
               assignment set.



7–52                                                                              7830 7949–031
                               @ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




            reel-n
                 The reel number specifies the identifier for each DVD tape assignment. Each
                 reel identifier is limited to 6 characters from the set A through Z and 0 through
                 9. Because the DVD tape is read-only, a reel-ID of BLANK or SCRTCH is
                 rejected.

            ring-indicator
                 Because the DVD tape is read-only, the values RING or WRITEENABLE are
                 rejected.

   7.2.8. Assigning Absolute Devices
            Use an absolute device assign to assign special I/O devices and symbiont devices,
            and for online maintenance of all system peripherals. If the device is configured as
            a mass storage device or a symbiont device, then it must be put in reserved state
            by the system operator before you assign it.

            You cannot catalog (@CAT) a file as an absolute device except in the case of tape
            files.

            Note: You must have the privilege to assign arbitrary devices in order to
            assign absolute devices.

   Absolute Device Assign for Mass Storage
            The format is
                @ASG[,options] filename,*name,pack-id

            options
                 The only allowed options are H, I ,T, and Z in any combination. The H option
                 assigns cache mode capability on the mass storage subsystem where the
                 device is connected. Successful assignment of cache mode lets you use
                 cache mode hardware commands through the arbitrary device interface. See
                 the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for more information on
                 the arbitrary device interface.

            filename
                 Specifies the external name of the file.

            name
                 The asterisk preceding the name field is mandatory for an absolute device
                 assign. The name field can be one of the following:
                 *device-name
                      Must be reserved by the operator (RV keyin). The Exec considers only the
                      specified device for allocation to the run.




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–53
@ASG and @@ASG—Assign Files and Peripheral Devices




                 *controller-name
                     The Exec considers only devices that are attached to the specified
                     controller and allocates one device to the run. There must be at least one
                     device on the control unit that is reserved.

           pack-ID
                 Specifies that the disk pack is required for the file. A pack-ID consists of from
                 1 to 6 characters from set A through Z and 0 through 9. This field is required.

   Absolute Device Assign for Tape
           The Exec normally controls the units for tape file assignment. However, you can
           direct the tape assignment to a particular control unit or device by specifying that
           control unit or device. Unisys does not recommend an absolute control unit or
           device specification for assigning tapes used in normal operations. However,
           maintenance routines, real-time programs, or special hardware requirements
           might make it necessary for you to use these specifications.

           When a tape device is put in reserved state by an RV unsolicited console keyin, it
           can be assigned only by specifying one of the following on the @ASG statement:

                The absolute control unit name

                The tape device name itself
           However, it is not necessary to have a tape device in a reserve state for an
           absolute assign.

           The format is
                @ASG[,options] filename[,*type/*units/noise/processor/
                format,data-converter/block-numbering/data-compression
                /buffered-write,reel-1/.../reel-n,expiration-period,
                ring-indicator,ACR-name,CTL-pool]

           All fields except type and units have the same meaning as the fields described in
           7.2.5. The ACR-name field is valid only if you specify the C or U option.

           Specify one of these combinations of values for *type/*units:
               *dev1/*dev2

           Use this combination to explicitly choose two devices on the assignment.
               *cuname/units

           Use this combination to select one or two units on the control unit cuname. The
           integers 1 and 2 are the allowed values for units. If you do not specify a value, the
           system uses the default value of 1.




7–54                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                 @BRKPT and @@BRKPT—Breakpoint Primary Print Files




   Devices Other Than Mass Storage or Tape
             The format is
                @ASG[,options] filename,*type

             options
                 The only options allowed are I, T, and Z in any combination.

             filename
                 Specifies the external name of the file.

             type
                 The asterisk (*) preceding the type field is mandatory for an absolute device
                 assign. The type can be either of these:

             *device-name
                 The Exec considers only the specified device for allocation to the run.

             *controller-name
                 The Exec considers only devices that are attached to the specified controller
                 and allocates one device to the run.

             The devices can be in a reserved state or in an UP state. However, you can assign
             symbionts only if they are reserved. Input/output to these devices must be
             through the arbitrary device interface (ER IOAID$).


7.3. @BRKPT and @@BRKPT—Breakpoint Primary
      Print Files
         For demand runs, the @BRKPT statement diverts output to a user-defined print file
         instead of to the terminal.

         For batch runs, it can divert several print files to the same tape file.

         This statement also diverts output back to the terminal (demand) or the PRINT$ (batch)
         file.

         Note: The @BRKPT statement also diverts output from PUNCH$, the primary
         output file for 80-column card images, to a user-defined file. The description of
         @BRKPT PRINT$ also applied to @BRKPT PUNCH$.

         Format 1
             @BRKPT,L PRINT$[/part-name]




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–55
@BRKPT and @@BRKPT—Breakpoint Primary Print Files




        L
             Provides a method of stacking multiple files on a single magnetic tape file and
             provides a label for each file by which the file can be referenced on a subsequent
             @SYM statement. The label is the part-name from the @BRKPT,L statements.

        PRINT$
             Is the primary print file being breakpointed.

        part-name
             Is an internal file name identifying a new user-defined file to which subsequent
             primary output is to be written. If you omit the part-name field, subsequent
             output is directed back to the PRINT$ file. If the L option is used, part-name is
             required; part-name provides a label, which identifies a new part to be written on
             a previously breakpointed magnetic tape file. This subfield is applicable only with
             Format 1 of the @BRKPT statement.

        A slash ( / ) is the only legal punctuation mark for Format 1. You cannot use a period
        after symbiont-name or part-name. The @BRKPT statement closes the previous file
        part.

        If you do not specify part-name in a batch run, the Exec creates a new part for the
        PRINT$ file. The previous part is queued for printing.

        If the part name or file name is a user-defined file, the file is closed by writing an EOF
        mark. In the case of a magnetic tape file, the tape is positioned so that a new file can
        be started.

        If part-name is not assigned to your run, the Exec assigns the file for you with an
        implied @ASG,AZ statement and performs the breakpoint. When the user-defined file
        is breakpointed back to PRINT$, the file's assignment condition depends on whether
        the file had an internal file name attached to it. A breakpoint file that was not assigned,
        but had an internal file name, is assigned. A breakpoint file that was not assigned and
        did not have an internal file name is not assigned. If the Exec cannot assign the file,
        the @BRKPT statement is not executed and a warning message is displayed.

        You must use a user-defined mass storage file as a part-name only once, unless you
        save the contents of the file. If you attempt to write multiple parts into a mass
        storage file, the previous parts are overwritten.

        User-defined breakpoint files are not automatically printed. You must use the @SYM
        statement to queue such files for printing.

        Format 2
            @BRKPT PRINT$[,filename]

        PRINT$
             Is the primary symbiont output file being breakpointed.




7–56                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                 @BRKPT and @@BRKPT—Breakpoint Primary Print Files




         filename
                Specifies the user-defined internal or external file to which subsequent primary
                output is to be written. If you omit filename, output is again directed to the
                terminal or PRINT$ file.

         The comma and any file-name punctuation are allowed on Format 2. You cannot use a
         period after symbiont-name.

         If the file name is a user-defined file, the file is closed by writing an EOF mark. In the
         case of a magnetic tape file, the tape is positioned so a new file can be started. You
         can have a maximum of 511 @BRKPT or @@BRKPT statements in each demand run.

         If you do not specify the file name in a batch run, the Exec creates a new part number
         for the PRINT$ file. The file name created with the previous part number is queued for
         printing. A run can breakpoint to a maximum of 511 print files using part numbers. For
         a batch run, this includes user-defined print files and Exec-defined print file parts.

         If the file name is not assigned to your run, the Exec assigns the file for you with an
         implied @ASG,AZ statement and performs the breakpoint. When the user-defined file
         is breakpointed back to PRINT$, the Exec releases the file from the run (@FREE),
         assuming the Exec assigned the file implicitly. If the Exec cannot assign the file, the
         @BRKPT statement is not executed and a warning message is displayed.

         User-defined breakpoint files are not automatically printed. You must use the @SYM
         statement to queue such files for printing.

         You can use the @BRKPT statement within a batch run or a demand run. After you
         breakpoint to a user-defined file within a demand run, all interactive responses are
         written to the file until output is redirected back to the terminal with another @BRKPT
         statement.

         Example
             @BRKPT PRINT$,POUT.
             @PRT,S WORKFILE.NBR-CRUNCH
             @BRKPT PRINT$

         After the first @BRKPT statement, output is diverted from the terminal (assuming it is
         a demand run) to the user-defined print file POUT. The @PRT statement lists the
         contents of the symbolic element NBR-CRUNCH in program file WORKFILE. Since
         output has been breakpointed, this listing is written to print file POUT instead of being
         displayed at the terminal. After the second @BRKPT statement, output is again
         directed to the terminal.

 7.3.1. Breakpointing Alternate Symbiont Files
            The @BRKPT statement closes or partitions alternate print and read files that you
            define.

            An @FREE of the alternate file must not be done before an @BRKPT. An @FREE does
            not close the alternate file, and a successive @BRKPT or alternate Executive request
            to the freed file results in an I/O error.

            Format 1
                @BRKPT[,E] internal-fname

            E
                 Inhibits EOF positioning for alternate read files on magnetic tape.

            internal-fname
                 Identifies the alternate read or print file being breakpointed. Alternate symbiont
                 files assigned as temporary must use this field. The internal-filename
                 corresponds to the internal-filename used in the ER packet for the alternate read
                 and print requests.

            Format 2
                @BRKPT[,E] ,fname

            E
                 Inhibits EOF positioning for alternate read files on magnetic tape.

        fname
                 Is an optional field that specifies an external or internal file name identifying the
                 alternate read or print file being breakpointed. If you are using Format 2, the
                 comma preceding the file name is required.

        Do not use Format 2 for temporary assigned alternate files.

        The discussion on primary file breakpointing generally applies to alternate file
        breakpoints. The differences are as follows:

               The alternate file is closed and is no longer known to the symbionts.

               In the case of input tape files, breakpoint is normally used to prematurely
                terminate reading of the file. In the absence of the E option, the input tape is
                positioned forward to the next EOF mark so that a subsequent file on the tape can
                be initiated as a new alternate read file. Using the E option avoids needless tape
                movement when you are finished with the tape.

               Stacking of output on tape is possible, but you must provide the part labeling by
                varying the internal-filename for each alternate file written to a tape.




7–58                                                                                    7830 7949–031
                                 @BRKPT and @@BRKPT—Breakpoint Primary Print Files




 7.3.2. Using @BRKPT and @SYM Together
          The following example illustrates how you can use the @BRKPT and @SYM
          statements together. This run partitions its primary print output into five parts. The
          example shows line numbers from 1 to 13, which are reference points for the
          description that follows.

                1. @RUN
                2. @ASG,CP MTAPE,T,1234
                3. @ASG,CP SYMFILE,F
                4. @BRKPT PRINT$/MTAPE
                    .
                    .
                    .
                5. @BRKPT,L PRINT$/LABEL1
                    .
                    .
                    .
                6. @BRKPT PRINT$/SYMFILE
                7. @FREE MTAPE
                8. @SYM MTAPE,,PR1,MTAPE/LABEL1
                    .
                    .
                    .
                9. @BRKPT PRINT$

                10. @FREE SYMFILE
                11. @SYM,U SYMFILE
                12. @SYM,U SYMFILE,3,RMSITE
                13. @FIN

         The first print part (all output generated up to line 4) is stored in primary print file
         PRINT$ and is printed on the default printer for the input device used for the run.

         The second print part (output generated between lines 4 and 5) and the third print part
         (output generated between lines 5 and 6) are stacked on magnetic tape file MTAPE.
         The second print part is given the label (part-name) MTAPE, and the third print part is
         given label LABEL1.

         Line 7 releases print file MTAPE from the run, causing the file to be cataloged. (The
         C option is in line 2.) A user-defined print file must be cataloged before you can queue
         it to a printer.

         Line 8 queues the second and third print parts to the printer PR1. Labels (part-names)
         MTAPE and LABEL1 are specified. After being printed, file MTAPE is deleted.

         The fourth print part (all output generated between lines 6 and 9) is stored in mass
         storage file SYMFILE.

         Line 10 releases SYMFILE from the run, causing it to be cataloged (because the C
         option was used in line 3).



7830 7949–031                                                                                       7–59
@CAT and @@CAT—Create Permanent Files




       Line 11 queues SYMFILE to the default printer for the input device used for the run.

       Line 12 queues the same print file (SYMFILE) to the printer at remote site RMSITE;
       three copies are printed. The U option is used to prevent SYMFILE from being deleted
       after either @SYM statement (line 11 or 12) is processed

       The last print part (all output generated after line 9) is again stored in primary print file
       PRINT$ and printed at the default printer.


7.4. @CAT and @@CAT—Create Permanent Files
       The @CAT statement catalogs a file in a master file directory without having it
       assigned to the run.


7.5. Cataloging Mass Storage Files
           Format
               @CAT[,options] filename[,type/reserve/granule/maximum,pack-id-1/...
               /pack-id-n,,,ACR-name/encrypt-option]

           instead of one. (For more information about transparent statements, see Section
           2.2)

           options
           B
                Saves and reloads the file as part of any full checkpoint or restart.

           G
                The meaning of this option depends on how security and Quota are configured
                at your site.

               Unowned files
                     If your site has Fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2,or 3 and the file
                     is unowned, the following applies:
                        When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its read
                         key, write key, privacy mode, or all three overridden by privileged runs.
                        If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read keys
                         or write keys for the file set are obscured by ’////////////’ from all users.
                         If a particular F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the
                         privacy mode and either the project-ID or account number under which
                         the file was created are also guarded.
                        The G option means the file cannot be backed up.

               Owned files

                        The G option means the file cannot be backed up by FAS. When you

                     If your site has Security Level 1, 2,or 3, the file is owned, and the dynamic
                     configuration parameter (owned_file_read_write_keys) is TRUE, the
                     following applies:
                        When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its
                         read key, write key, privacy mode, or all three overridden by
                         privileged runs.
                        If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read
                         keys or write keys for the file set are obscured by ’////////////’ from all
                         users. If a particular F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G
                         option, the privacy mode and either the project-ID or account number
                         under which the file was created are also guarded.
                        The G option means the file cannot be backed up.

               Quota system
                     The use of the G option is also controlled by the Quota system on an
                     account basis, as follows:
                      If the Exec is configured to maintain quota limits for each account, this
                        option can be used only if it is allowed in the quota limits for the run.
                      If the Exec is not maintaining quota limits, this option can be used by
                        all runs.
            P
                Catalogs the file as a public file. For systems with Fundamental Security, if you
                omit the P option (default), the file is cataloged as a private file and can be
                accessed only by runs that have the same project-ID or account number as the
                run that created the file.
                For systems with Security Level 1 or higher, the file is cataloged as public if the
                P option is specified on the @ASG statement and an ACR is specified. The file
                is cataloged private when the P option and ACR are omitted from the @CAT
                statement (default). You can even be given the option to create unowned files
                with Security Level 1, 2, or 3.

            R
                Catalogs a file as a read-only file. A file cataloged with the R option cannot be
                overwritten. The file can be only read or deleted. Any nonprivileged activity
                requesting to write in the file is placed in error mode.

Cataloging Mass Storage Files




           S
               This option only applied to 7-track tape and now must be left blank (although
               this option no longer has any effect, it is allowed since it can still be in user
               runstreams.) It indicated that this file is a store-through file. Any writes done to
               this file result in the data being stored directly on a nonvolatile mass storage
               medium. Absence of this option indicates that data can be stored on volatile
               areas of mass storage such as cache storage. Presence of the option does not
               prevent the storage of data on solid-state disk. If the file is XPC cached, this S
               option is ignored because the data for the file is kept in the XPC.

           V
               Indicates that this file is never unloaded to tape at any time. If the Exec is
               configured to maintain quota limits for each account, you can use this option
               only if it is specifically allowed in the quota limits for the run. If the Exec is not
               maintaining quota limits, all runs can use this option.

           W
               Catalogs a file as a write-only file. A file cataloged with the W option cannot be
               read. Any nonprivileged activity requesting to read the file is placed in error
               mode.

           Z
               Indicates that the Exec must not hold the run if it cannot process this
               statement right away. The Exec must process the next statement instead.
               If the Exec goes into a hold situation, the statement is rejected and the
               appropriate message is displayed on the screen.

           filename
               Identifies the file being assigned to the run.

           type
               Specifies a combination of letters and numbers that identify the addressing
               mode of the file (sector- or word-addressable) and the equipment type
               required for the file. The type field is also called the assign mnemonic. When a
               system is configured, assign mnemonics are defined to correspond to a
               prioritized list of specific equipment types.
               Most type field entries supplied by Unisys start with either D or F, but sites
               can configure any mnemonics they wish. Typically, D represents word-
               addressable and F represents sector-addressable mass storage. If you omit
               type, the Exec uses sector-addressable mass storage. Appendix D, Table D-1
               shows the standard type entries supplied by Unisys.
               If you are creating a new cycle for an existing file cycle set, and you omit the
               type, the type is taken from the latest existing cycle of the file. If all cycles of
               the file are in a to-be-cataloged or to-be-dropped state, then the type from the
               highest cycle of this type is used.




7–62                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                            Cataloging Mass Storage Files




                When space is not available for the specified device type, or if the specified
                device type is no longer available on your system, another device type is
                substituted that satisfies the request. The order in which device requests are
                satisfied is configured by your site addressable or word addressable, and if
                necessary, what type of equipment must be administrator. Requests are
                satisfied from fastest to slowest device. See Appendix D, Table D-2 for
                selection sequences supplied by Unisys.
                The selection sequences pertain only to fixed mass storage. For removable
                disk file assignments, only the first equipment type is searched or selected.
                Local fixed files can be placed in memory rather than on channel-connected
                mass storage. The standard mnemonics FMEM (sector-addressable) and
                DMEM (word-addressable) can be used for this purpose; however your site
                can configure additional assign mnemonics. Placing files in memory reduces
                access time, but consumes memory space that might otherwise be available
                for programs. Also, data in memory files is lost when the system is rebooted.
                Use of memory file assign mnemonics on systems that are not or cannot be
                configured to support memory files results in the request being satisfied on
                channel connected-mass storage.
                For physically removable disk file assignments, you must use the assign
                mnemonic that corresponds to the pack type that is in use.
                 F30      selects equipment type 8430
                 F33      selects equipment type 8433
                 D30      selects equipment type 8430
                 D33      selects equipment type 8433

                If any other mnemonic is used to catalog and assign removable disks, the file
                cannot be assignable after changes to equipment configurations.
                When specifying a physically removable assign mnemonic, the first equipment
                specified in the configuration statement CONV’s selection sequence must be
                for a physically removable device. If the first equipment specified in the CONV
                statement is not a physically removable device, the following error message
                appears:
                  E:200633 pack xxxxxx cannot be mounted -- equipment type does not permit
                  interchanging of packs.

                If you specify a physically removable assign mnemonic but no units are
                configured, the following error message appears:
                  E:256033 requested unit(s) not available

            reserve
                Specifies the amount of space you want to reserve. The reserve consists of 1
                to 12 numbers. For most files, you do not need to use reserve.




7830 7949–031                                                                              7–63
Cataloging Mass Storage Files




               When you specify a reserve, you must provide a reasonable estimate of the
               space needed to create the file. When you specify a reserve, you reduce
               system overhead by allowing the Exec to find and allocate space in contiguous
               granules, if possible. When you do not specify a reserve, the Exec must find
               and allocate the space dynamically, as it is needed by the file. The amount of
               space given as the initial reserve is not actually allocated until you assign the
               file, and even then, only if the file can be written to, as follows:

                    For sector-addressable files, the initial reserve is the number of granules
                     (tracks or positions) required by the file. Refer to 2.2 for file size
                     information.
                    For word-addressable files, the initial reserve is the number of words
                     required by the file. The maximum number of words allowed for the
                     reserve is 262,143 times the number of words-per-granule, based on the
                     granularity (track or position) of the file. Word-addressable files are
                     allocated on a granule basis.
           granule
               Specifies granule size. A granule is the increment by which storage space is
               allocated to your file (initially and when more space is needed).
               The granule can be either of these:
               TRK
                     One software track (64 software sectors)

               POS
                     One software position (64 software tracks)

               If you omit granule, the Exec uses TRK. The granularity is recorded in the
               master file directory.

           maximum
               Specifies the maximum allowable length of the file. Permissible values are the
               same as the reserve subfield.
                    For sector-addressable files, this maximum is given in granules (tracks or
                     positions).
                    For word-addressable files, the maximum is specified in words.
               If an I/O request exceeds the number of granules specified, the run is given an
               I/O error.

               When you specify maximum, it overrides the system default. If you omit
               maximum, the reserve subfield value or system default is used, whichever is
               larger. The maximum must be at least as large as the reserve. This lets your
               file dynamically expand to the maximum length when it is needed.




7–64                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                              Cataloging Mass Storage Files




            pack-ID
                 Specifies the removable disk packs required for the file. A pack-ID consists of
                 from 1 to 6 characters in any combination of letters and numbers. The pack-ID
                 s for cataloged files are recorded in the master file directory and need not be
                 specified on reassignments.
                 A pack's master file directory must have sufficient space available to record
                 the file otherwise a generation request is rejected with the following
                 message:
                   E:207433 File cannot be created due to lack of removable directory space
                   on pack pack-id.

                 A pack-ID is applicable only to removable disks. You cannot specify a pack-ID
                 unless you specify the equipment type. If you omit the pack-ID on requests
                 for noncataloged file space, fixed disk is assumed if you request disk
                 equipment. For cataloged removable disk files, specification of a pack-ID
                 causes the pack to be registered. If the pack is already registered, its
                 information is compared with the image for compatibility.
                 All cycles of a removable disk file must be on the same set of packs. The
                 maximum number of pack-IDs that you can specify on an @ASG statement is
                 510.
                 For important information about using removable pack files, see the
                 removable disk packs section in the Exec System Software Administration
                 Reference Manual (7831 0323).

            ACR-name
                 Specifies the ACR for the cataloged file (for Security Level 1 or higher). It must
                 be an ACR that was previously created using your security management
                 product.

            encrypt-option
                 This subfield is used to specify encryption actions. For @CAT, DOENCR
                 specifies that a file must be catalogued as encrypted. DNENCR specifies that a
                 file must not be catalogued as encrypted. When these mnemonics are
                 omitted, the default flag setting in the file owner’s userid record is used to
                 determine encryption state.

            Examples
                @CAT PISCES1.

                   Since only the file name is given (PISCES1), all of the default values are used.
                   It is private, sector-addressable mass storage file, with a maximum track
                   size configured by the system. A default qualifier is used as the qualifier for
                   the file name.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 7–65
Cataloging Mass Storage Files




              @CAT,P FRS*PISCES2.,FMD///500,PK12

                 This statement catalogs a public file (P option) named FRS*PISCES2. It
                 requests sector-addressable mass storage on a 9720 or 9494 disk (FMD),
                 with a maximum size of 500 tracks. The removable disk pack requested is
                 PK12.

              @CAT,W FRS*PISCES3.,D/10//300,,,,ACR1

                 This statement creates a ACR-controlled file named FRS*PISCES3. It has an
                 ACR attached to it called ACR1.
                 This file is word addressable (D), with an initial reserve of 10 words and a
                 maximum size of 300 words.

              @CAT,PR PISCES4/RK54.,F

                 This statement catalogs a file that is public (P option) and read only (R
                 option).
                 If your site has Fundamental Security, anyone who wants to read from the
                 file must know the read key, RK54. If your site has Security Level 1 or higher,
                 the read key is ignored.
                 The F means that the file is sector addressable. Since no maximum size is
                 specified, the file cannot exceed the maximum track size configured by the
                 system. The run project-ID is used as the qualifier for the file name, since
                 none is specified.

              @CAT,W FRS*PISCES5.,F//POS/20

                 This statement catalogs a file named FRS*PISCES5 that is private (no P
                 option) and write only (W option). The F indicates that the file must be
                 sector addressable. Space is allocated to the file in positions (POS) instead
                 of tracks. The maximum size of the file is 20 positions, which is equal to
                 1280 tracks.

   7.5.1. Cataloging Tape Files
           The @CAT statement catalogs a tape file without allocating tape facilities to your
           run. You can even catalog a tape file on equipment that is down, provided that you
           designate a specific equipment type (if equipment is down, you cannot use T or
           U9 on the type field).

           Note: If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, your security officer chooses
           one of four levels of protection for tape volumes (TVSL). If TVSL is set to 1, 2,
           or 3, you can give a tape an access list. Please see the discussion on tape
           security in Section 7.3 for more information.

            You must be aware of the following two tape terms that are most important when
            cataloging tape files:

                The half-inch cartridge (HIC) tape that can be used to record 18-track or
                 36-track formatted data.

                The digital linear tape (DLT)

                @CAT,options filename,type[/units/log/noise/processor/tape/

                         When the file is cataloged, the G option guards against having its read

                         If any F-cycle of a file set is cataloged with the G option, the read
                          keys or write keys for the file set are obscured by ’////////////’ from all

                          option, the privacy mode and either the project-ID or account number

            filename
                Specifies the external name of the file.

            type
                A combination of letters and numbers that specifies what type of magnetic
                tape equipment must be used for the file. If you do not specify type and the
                file is not already cataloged, the Exec catalogs the file as a mass storage file.
                The type field is also called the assign mnemonic. The assign mnemonic is
                stored in the MFD upon cataloging the file. See Table D-3 for the allowable
                assign mnemonics.
                When a system is configured, assign mnemonics are defined to correspond to
                a set of specific equipment types. Table D-3 shows the permissible type
                entries.
                If you use a density option (H, S, or V), make sure that it is compatible with the
                assign you use. For example, when you use the assign mnemonic T, specify
                only those options compatible with all types of units.
                Based on the assign mnemonic you specify, the system selects an equipment
                type for your file. If the assign mnemonic corresponds to a particular
                equipment type, that type is used. If you use a more general type, however,
                the Exec selects an equipment type before cataloging the file, based on a
                standard selection sequence. The selection sequence supplied by Unisys is
                from the fastest equipment to the slowest, but this can be changed when the
                system is configured. See Table D-4 for the selection sequences supplied by
                Unisys.

               Note: Use the most general assign mnemonic that still meets your
               requirements, because it gives the system more freedom in assigning units.
               Unless otherwise specified by an assign mnemonic or mode option, the

           noise
               Specifies an integer from 1 to 63 that overrides the standard system noise
               constant. If you omit noise, the Exec uses the system standard noise constant.
               The system standard value is 3 for all 9-track tapes written in a density of 800
               bpi. For 9-track tapes written in a density of 1600 bpi or 6250 bpi, the system
               standard value is 0. The noise value is recorded in the master file directory
               when the file is cataloged. The value for noise must be zero for all cartridge
               type tape assigns.

           processor/tape
               Specifies the type of translation required. Processor defines the format of the
               data in processor, and tape defines the format of the data on tape. You must
               specify both processor and tape or omit both. If you omit them, no translation
               occurs.
               Data translation is file independent and the translation mode remains in effect
               for the duration of the reading or writing of the tape. You can change data
               translation from file to file, but you must track this information yourself.
               The supported processor/tape mnemonics are


                      Processor          Tape
                        Code             Code

                       ASCII            EBCDIC
                       ASCII            FLDATA
                       EBCDIC           ASCII
                       EBCDIC           BCD
                       FLDATA           ASCII
                       FLDATA           BCD
                       FLDATA           EBCDIC


               Additional processor/tape mnemonics can be defined by your site, provided
               neither code exceeds six characters. When the file is cataloged, the values
               given in processor/tape are stored in the master file directory.
               All translation takes place in the hardware.

               Note: If you are using the data compression feature to read and write to a
               5073 cartridge tape, you cannot use the data translation feature.

            format
                Specifies the data transfer format for the word-to-byte conversion.
                The format subfield is also used in determining the data compression mode
                for write operations for the 5073 tape subsystem.
                Permissible format entries are as follows:
                Q
                     Quarter word

                8
                     8-bit packed (default on 9-track and 1/4-inch tape cartridge)

                The data transfer format is recorded in the master file directory upon
                cataloging, to be used on subsequent assigns unless specifically overridden.

            data-converter
                This option only applied to 7-track tape and now must be left blank (although
                this option no longer has any effect, it is allowed since it can still be in user
                runstreams.) The allowable data-converter values were as follows:
                DC
                      Three 8-bit bytes are converted to or from four 6-bit tape characters. The
                      data-converter (DC) status is recorded in the master file directory upon
                      cataloging.

                OFF
                      Turns off the data-converter if an assign is made from the master file
                      directory (@ASG,A) and the file was cataloged with data conversion. In all
                      other cases, OFF is ignored.
                      If you do not specify data-converter, no action is taken in relation to the
                      data converter. Furthermore, the OFF is not recorded in the master file
                      directory, except as implied by the absence of data-converter.

                      block-numbering

                     This field must be left blank (although it no longer has any effect, it is
                     allowed since it can still be in user runstreams). It determines whether
                     block numbering is on. Block numbering is available only on 5061, HIC, DLT,
                     and LTO tape subsystems. For the HIC, DLT, and LTO tape subsystems,
                     you cannot turn on block numbering with this subfield because it is
                     performed by the hardware and is transparent to the user. Specify one of
                     the following:

                     BLKON

                     Turns block numbering on (invalid for HIC, DLT, and LTO tape subsystems).




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–73
Cataloging Mass Storage Files




                  BLKOFF

                  Indicates that blocks must not be numbered.

                  BLKOPT

                  Gives you the option to turn block numbering on at a later date (invalid for
                  HIC, DLT, and LTO tape subsystems).

                  data-compression

                  Reduces the amount of physical tape required to record data by removing
                  repetitive data before recording it (available for 5061, HIC, DLT and LTO
                  and tape subsystems only). Data compression is generally performed on a
                  file basis.

               For half-inch cartridge tape subsystems, these are the data-compression
               values:
               CMPON
                  Enables 8-bit data compression when Q is specified on the format
                  subfield; enables 9-bit data compression when either "8" or nothing is
                  specified on the format subfield. Enables LTO-DC for an LTO cartridge tape
                  device.

               CMPOFF
                  Indicates no data compression.

               CMPOPT
                  Capable of 8- or 9-bit data compression. Gives you the option to enable 8-
                  or 9-bit data compression at a later date must be used if there is any
                  possibility that the cartridge tape contains an 8- or 9-bit compressed file.
                  Capable of LTO-DC data compression. Gives you an option to enable data
                  compression at a later date; must be used if there is any possibility that
                  the cartridge tape contains an LTO-DC compressed file.

               CMPEON
                  Enables Enhanced data recording capability (EDRC) mode of data
                  compression.

               CMEOPT
                  Capable of EDRC data compression. Gives you the option to enable EDRC
                  data compression at a later date; must be used if there is any possibility
                  that the cartridge tape contains an EDRC compressed file.

                For DLT and HIS98 tape subsystems, these are the valid data-compression

                     Enables LZ1 data-compression. DLT and HIS98 cartridge tapes are not

               Although you can explicitly specify 8- or 9-bit data compression with

               When using the HICL mnemonic in combination with CMPEON, CMEOPT,

               The CTS9840, DLT7000,U9840C, CTS9940B, LTO3, and LTO4 devices

                CTS9840, DLT7000, U9840C, CTS9940B, LTO3, or LTO4 which supports

               The CTS9840, DLT7000, U9840C, CTS9940B, U9840D, and UT10KA tapes
                always have expanded buffering, so the EBCOPT is not needed to get a
                CTS9840, DLT7000, U9840C, or CTS9940B.
               Assign mnemonics that can select an ACS drive are T, HIC, HICL, HICM,
                HIC51, HIC52, HIS98, U47, U47L, U47LM, LCART, DLT70,LTO,LTO3, and
                LTO4. Assign mnemonics HICL, U47, HICM, HIC, DLT70,LTO,LTO3,and LTO4
                result in either an ACS query or cartridge tape library (CTL) poll. If the
                Automated Cartridge System (ACS) query is positive, and ACS drive is
                assigned. If the CTL poll is positive, a CTL drive is allocated. If the ACS
                query and CTL poll are negative, a free standing drive is allocated. NONCTL
                can be used on ACS assignments.

                @CAT,P TAPE.,HICL/////////CMPEON,111C

                   The tape is cataloged as a public file with EDRC data compression
                   requested.

                @CAT,P T.,HICM,REELID

7830 7949–031                                                                             7–75
Cataloging Mass Storage Files




               @CAT,J TAPE.,HICL/////////CMEOPT,111C

                     The tape is cataloged as a private file requesting a tape device that has the
                     hardware capability of supporting EDRC data compression.

               Support for 4780 18- and 36-track tapes is provided by the standard Exec.
               Compression on the 4780 subsystems is called improved cartridge recording
               capability (ICRC) and is totally compatible with the 5073 enhanced data
               recording capability (EDRC). Compression can be selected by using the
               CMPEON value.

               Device characteristics for compressed tape readability are:

                    Unisys proprietary compressed cartridge tapes cannot be read on 4780
                     drives, but EDRC compressed cartridges from 5073 drives can be
                     successfully read.

                    A cartridge drive on a 4780 that does not have compression hardware can
                     read only uncompressed cartridge tapes.

                    The 4780 drives that have compression hardware can read EDRC
                     compressed tapes without having to explicitly request CMPEON.
               Note: In some cases, you are not able to append data to a tape (write past
               loadpoint). Appending is not allowed on 18-track half-inch cartridge, U9840C,
               and UT10KA tape subsystems.

        buffered-write
           Specifies whether to use buffered writes when a tape is mounted on a device
           controlled by a control unit that has buffering capability.
           These are the values.

           BUFTAP
                   Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks and file marks for the
                   entire tape.

           BUFFIL
                   Enables buffering of write data including label blocks and tape marks for a file
                   written to labeled tapes. The system ensures that writing of the data and file
                   marks occurs at the close of a file.

           BUFON
                   Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks.

           BUFOFF
                   Disables any buffered write mode.

           The @CAT statement is rejected if it contains the BUFTAP or BUFFIL value and
           there are no tape units up and available that support tape mark buffering (TMB).



7–76                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                             Cataloging Mass Storage Files




            Even though TMB is supported on the CTS5236 the BUFTAP value is not. The
            rejecting message is:
                E:256033 requested unit(s) not available.

            The following rules apply when using BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, and BUFON:

               When the user switches modes from BUFFIL to BUFON or BUFOFF, writing
                the buffer to tape is postponed until the next I/O to the tape subsystem. This
                also applies when switching modes from BUFTAP to other modes.

               If BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, or BUFON is not specified, and the configuration
                tag TAPBUF (dynamic name_tape_buffering) is zero, the system uses the
                default value BUFON.

               If BUFFIL is specified for an unlabeled tape, the data blocks for writes are
                buffered and one synchronization per file is done by a WEF$ function just as it
                is without the BUFFIL specification.

               When using buffering, it is the user’s responsibility to retain the original data
                for possibly performing error recovery if that is a requirement. The Exec
                provides no means for the user to recover this data. With the use of the
                BUFTAP option, it is possible to have good status on previous writes of
                thousands of files, when in fact none of the files has made it to tape. If an
                error occurs while they are being written to tape, the remaining blocks in the
                tape subsystems buffer can never get written to tape. The Block ID SAFE
                (BSAFE$) I/O function provides a means for the user to determine what block
                has been actually written to tape by the tape subsystem.

               When using BUFTAP, a FSAFE$ can be performed at any point if a user wants
                to ensure that buffered data/tape marks have been written to tape. It is highly
                recommended that the FSAFE$ be performed and its status checked after all
                user data/tape marks have been written to the tape device, but before
                releasing the tape. This ensures that the user is notified of any errors in
                writing any remaining buffered data/tape marks to the tape. This also allows
                the user to know that an error on a @FREE, TSWAP$, TINTL$, or TLBL$ was
                not the result of writing any user buffered data/tape marks on the tape

         .Examples
            @CAT,P TAPE.,HICL///////////EBCOPT,111C

                The tape is cataloged as a public file, requesting a tape device that has the
                hardware capability of supporting block sizes of up to 256K bytes.

            @CAT,J TAPE.,HICL//////////BUFON,111C

                The tape is cataloged as a private file with buffered-write capability requested.
                The requested drive cannot be capable of expanded buffer operation.

        reel-n
            Specifies the identifier for each tape reel or cartridge required. Each tape identifier
            is limited to six characters from set A to Z and 0 to 9. Do not specify an identifier
            with a single A, E, Y, or N character. These characters correspond to valid
            responses to tape labeling messages. Using them as identification could cause
            tape assign problems.
            Tapes are used in the order specified, and all reel or cartridge identifiers are
            recorded in the MFD. A maximum of 2047 reels or cartridges can be specified with
            the @CAT statement.
            Also, 36-track tapes have more capacity on current cartridges because data is
            written in both directions on the tape, and more capacity with longer tapes can
            hold four times more data than current cartridges (1,100 feet [E-carts]).
            The @CAT statement accepts the mnemonic. For example:
                 @CAT,P T.,U47L/////////CMPEON/BUFON/EBCOPT,REELID

            This statement can use the mode values.
            When an assignment uses a specific reel-ID, its location is determined by an ACS
            or a CTL poll. The reel-ID’s location, together with the assign mnemonic,
            determines the resultant device assigned. When a BLANK is assigned, no ACS
            query is done. However, BLANK assignments result in a CTL poll.

        ACR-name
             Specifies the access control record (ACR) for the cataloged file (for sites with
             Security Level 1 or higher). It must be an ACR that you have previously created by
             using your security management product.

        CTL-pool
             Can be one of the following:
             CTL-pool name
                    Allocates a BLANK tape from the CTL pool of BLANK cartridge tapes.
                    CTL-pool-name can be 1 to 12 characters, consisting of the alphanumeric
                    characters, $, and -.

             NONCTL
                    Associates the file with freestanding cartridge tape drives. The Exec does
                    not use the CTL for this file.

        See your site administrator for CTL information specific to your site.

        Examples
        @CAT TAPE-STORE1.,T

            This statement catalogs tape file TAPE-STORE1 as a private file (no P option).
            The T means the file can be on any type of tape unit that is available. Default
            values are used for all other fields. The project-ID is used as the qualifier for the
            file name.


7–78                                                                                7830 7949–031
                                                            Cataloging Mass Storage Files




         @CAT,PJ GCH*TAPE-STORE2.,U9

            This statement catalogs tape file GCH*TAPE-STORE2 as a public file (P option) on
            an unlabeled tape (J option). The U9 means that the file can be on any 9-track tape
            unit that is available.

         @CAT,PR TAPE-STORE3/KIWI.,U9V//////6

            This statement catalogs file TAPE-STORE3 as a public (P option) and read-only
            (R option) tape file.
            If your site has Fundamental Security, or Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the file is
            unowned, anyone who wants to read from the file must know the read key (KIWI).
            If your site has Security Level 1 or higher and the file is owned, the read key is
            ignored.
            U9V means that the file must be on a 9-track tape unit, and that very high tape
            density (1600 bpi) must be used. The 6 indicates that 6-bit packed format must be
            used for the word-to-byte conversion.

         @CAT,S TAPE-STORE4//FRITZ.,28N,NC18

            This statement catalogs the file TAPE-STORE4 as a private file (no P option).
            If your site has Fundamental Security or Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the file is
            unowned, anyone who wants to write to the file must know the write key (FRITZ).
            If your site has Security Level 1 or higher and the file is owned, the write key is
            ignored.
            28N means that the file must be on a UNISERVO 28 tape unit. The S option means
            that the file must be written with super high density (6250 bpi). Reel number NC18
            is used for the file.

         @CAT,PRV TAPE-STORE5.,45N///////////,,,,ACR2

            This statement catalogs file TAPE-STORE5 as a read-only public file on a 9-track
            tape in the 2145 tape subsystem, using the required density mode of 1600 bpi. The
            O option indicates odd parity. Access control record ACR2 is attached to the file.
            Because the data-converter, block-numbering, and data-compression subfields are
            not specified, they take on the system default values, which are required by the
            2145 tape subsystem.

            This statement catalogs file TAPE-STORE6 as a public file on 18-track cartridge
            tape. The BLANK tape is allocated from the CTL pool named CTL-AUDIT1.

         @CAT,P T.,HIC51/////////CMPEON/BUFON,EBCOPT,REELID

            This statement specifies data compression, buffering, and expanded block

@CHG—Change File or Element Attributes




7.6. @CHG—Change File or Element Attributes
        In a single @CHG statement, you can change either file attributes or program file
        element attributes.

        File attributes changes are described in Section 7.6.1 and Section 7.6.2. Section 7.6.3
        contains examples of each kind of file attribute change. File attributes that can be
        changed using @CHG are as follows:

           Keys
               Read
               Write
           Modes
               Read-only
               Write-only
               V-OPTION FLAG
           File Names
               Qualifier
               Filename
           Security
               public
               private
               ACR-controlled
           Caching attributes
           File type
               Program file
               Large Program file

7.6.1. Changing Keys, Modes, and Names of Cataloged Files
         You can use the @CHG statement to change the following cataloged file attributes:

             Change the privacy state to public (P option) or private (Q option). Change the
              privacy state to ACR-controlled (K option) for systems with Security Level 1, 2 or 3.
              Refer to Section 7.6.2 , “@CHG and File Security”, for information on whether the
              change applies to one or all members of an F-cycle set. Include the M option to
              change the privacy state for all members of an F-cycle set for all security
              configurations and file types.
             Change the read key and write key for all members of an F-cycle set.
             Change the read-only mode and write-only mode (V, W, and Z options) for one
              member of an F-cycle set. Include the M option to change the modes for all
              members of an F-cycle set. The change does not take effect until the file is freed
              by all runs that currently have it assigned.
             Change the file caching attributes (F option) for one member of an F-cycle set.
             Change the qualifier and filename (N option) for all members of an F-cycle set.
             Change an empty, sector-addressable, temporary or cataloged mass storage file
              to a program file (E and T options) for one member of an F-cycle set. For a
              description of program file types and attributes, refer to Section 3.8.4 through
              3.8.7. This is the only type of file @CHG that applies to temporary files.
             Change the V-option flag mode (I and U options) for one member of an F-cycle set.
              Include the M option to change the modes for all members of an F-cycle set. I
              option requires user to have SSDNK and SSDBACK privileges while U option can
              be used by all users.
         You can use a single @CHG statement to change the first three change types (privacy
         state, read and write keys, and read-only and write-only modes). There is one
         exception: You cannot change the privacy state to ACR-controlled and the read and
         write keys on the same @CHG statement. The three change types have different rules
         on which members of an F-cycle set are changed. Include the M option if you want all
         the change types to apply to all members of an F-cycle set.

         Format
             @CHG[,options] filename-1[,name-1]

         options
              C
                  Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.

                  Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
                  ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
                  should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
                  command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.

                  The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.

               sectors of text. Specify the E option by itself to create a standard LEPF that has
