7.15. @@CQUE—Queue Input in a Main Storage
       Buffer
         The @@CQUE statement lets you enter lines of statements and data into a buffer in
         the computer’s main storage. The images in the resulting input queue are processed
         in the order they were entered. This lets you continue entering input without waiting
         for the next SOE character.

         Format
           @@CQUE soe-parameter
           input-image
           input-image
           input-image
            .
            .
            .
           @@END CQUE

         Valid values for the soe-parameter field are
             N
                  No SOE characters are issued by the system when in this input queuing
                  mode. The system resumes issuing appropriate SOE characters when the
                  corresponding @@END control statement is received to return the terminal
                  to interactive mode.

             S
                  SOE characters are issued by the system when in this input queuing mode
                  after each input image is transferred to a system main storage buffer. The
                  system continues to issue appropriate SOE characters when the
                  corresponding @@END control statement is received, allowing the terminal
                  to return to interactive mode.

         The soe-parameter field is a 1-character field. If more than one character or anything
         other than an N or S is specified, the statement is ignored and the following error is
         displayed at the terminal:
           @@ERROR - SYNTAX

         input-image represents the statements and data you want to enter into the buffer in
         main storage.



7830 7949–031                                                                               7–131
@CYCLE—Alter Cycle Retention Limit




        You must provide your own SOE character once you enter CQUE mode if the N is
        specified or no soe-parameter is specified.


7.16. @CYCLE—Alter Cycle Retention Limit
        Sets the maximum range of absolute F-cycle numbers to be retained for a cataloged
        file, or the maximum number of element cycles for a program file symbolic element.
        When number is omitted, cycle information regarding the current F-cycle series is
        displayed. See Section 3.4 for a detailed discussion of F-cycle sets.

        The filename or element-name parameter of the @CYCLE statement is required.

7.16.1. Set File Cycle Range
        Format for Files
          @CYCLE filename[,number]

        filename
            Specifies the F-cycle set.

        number
            A decimal value from 0 to 32 that specifies the maximum range of F-cycles for the
            set. If number is omitted, information about the F-cycle set is output.

        The specified filename must be a member of a cataloged F-cycle set. The filename
        can include an absolute or relative F-cycle number or can be an internal file name. If
        number is specified and if the file has read and write keys, either the file must be
        assigned with the keys or the keys must be specified on the @CYCLE statement, in
        any combination. For example, the file can be assigned with the read key and the write
        key can be specified on @CYCLE.

        FURPUR reads the MFD entry for the specified file name, which contains a description
        of the F-cycle set and all of its members, including their absolute F-cycle numbers and
        file statuses (currently cataloged, to be cataloged, to be deleted, or not cataloged).

        When you omit number, information about the entire F-cycle set is displayed in the
        following format:
            MAX-RANGE= a         CUR-RANGE= b
            NO. OF F CYCLES= c: d-1, d-2, ... d-b

        Where a is the maximum number of members of the F-cycle set (1 to 32), b is the
        current number of members of the F-cycle set (1 to 32), c is the number of members
        of the F-cycle set that are currently cataloged (1 to 32), and d-1 through d-b are the
        absolute F-cycle numbers (1 to 999) and file statuses for each of the b files in the
        current range. There are four possible file statuses for members of the F-cycle set.




7–132                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                                     @CYCLE—Alter Cycle Retention Limit




         The following are the displayed formats for absolute F-cycle number d for each status:

            d       Absolute F-cycle d is currently cataloged.
            *d*     Absolute F-cycle d is deleted or was not cataloged.
            +d+     Absolute F-cycle d is to be cataloged. It changes to currently
                    cataloged when freed by the run that created it with @ASG,C or
                    @ASG,U.
            -d-     Absolute F-cycle d is to be deleted. It changes to deleted when
                    freed by all of the runs that currently have it assigned.

         Note: The b files in CUR-RANGE can have any of the above four file statuses while
         the c files in NO. OF F CYCLES are only the F-cycle members that are currently
         cataloged.

         If number is nonzero, it specifies the new maximum F-cycle range. Only the F-cycle
         members in the new range are retained. If there are any F-cycle members outside the
         new range they are deleted.

         If the highest absolute F-cycle number is highest, then the new range includes F-cycle
         numbers from highest through highest - number + 1, in decreasing order. For example,
         if the highest absolute F-cycle number is 49 and number is 16, the new range is
         absolute F-cycles 49 through 34 (49-16+1). If the formula yields 0 or a negative
         number, this indicates that the F-cycle set range wraps around from F-cycle 1 back to
         F-cycle 999. In this case the new range includes F-cycle numbers from highest
         through 1 and 999 through 1000 + highest - number, in decreasing order. For example,
         if the highest absolute F-cycle number is 7 and number is 12, the new range is
         absolute F-cycles 7 through 1 and 999 through 995 (1000+7-12). Note that whenever
         the F-cycle range wraps around, the F-cycle numbers highest through 1 are considered
         to be "higher" than 999 through 1000 + highest - number. In the second example,
         F-cycles 7 through 1 are considered to be higher than 999 through 995.

         If number is nonzero, there must be at least one F-cycle member in the new range
         that can be assigned to the run. If filename is a retained F-cycle member, it is the
         F-cycle that is used. If filename is an F-cycle member that is to be deleted, then
         beginning with the highest absolute F-cycle the new retained F-cycle range is
         searched for an F-cycle member that can be assigned. The F-cycle member can be
         currently cataloged or be marked as cataloged or as deleted, as long as it can be
         assigned to the run. If no retained F-cycle can be assigned to the run, @CYCLE is
         terminated in error. See Appendix B.7 for a complete list of error messages
         associated with @CYCLE.

         F-cycle members are deleted when number is 0 or when there are F-cycle
         members outside the new maximum F-cycle range specified by number. FURPUR
         begins by checking that each F-cycle member to be deleted can be assigned to the
         run (exclusively when number is nonzero) and that each is not currently on a
         symbiont queue. This includes F-cycle members that are currently cataloged, to be
         cataloged and to be deleted.




7830 7949–031                                                                              7–133
@CYCLE—Alter Cycle Retention Limit




        If this check fails, no F-cycle members are deleted. Error messages are output to
        list all of the F-cycle members that cannot be assigned and all of the F-cycle
        members that are on symbiont queues. @CYCLE is terminated in error.

        When all of the F-cycle members to be deleted are assigned to the run and it has been
        determined that none are on symbiont queues, then FURPUR begins deleting them.
        The deletion begins with the lowest absolute F-cycle and continues in increasing
        F-cycle order.

        If number is 0, then after all F-cycles have been successfully deleted the following
        message is output and @CYCLE is complete:

            DROP FLAG SET ON ALL CYCLES

        If number is nonzero, then after the F-cycles outside of the new range have
        been successfully deleted, the MFD entry for the F-cycle set is updated. The
        maximum F-cycle range is set to number, the following messages are output,
        and @CYCLE is complete:

              NUMBER-CYCLE CYCLE-LIMIT
            OLD    c      a
            NEW    c      a

        Where c is the current number of members of the F-cycle set and a is the maximum
        number of members for the F-cycle set. The OLD row shows the values at the
        beginning of @CYCLE and the NEW row shows the values at the end of @CYCLE. The c
        values in the NUMBER-CYCLE column correspond to the NO. OF F CYCLES= c value
        output when number is omitted. The a values in the CYCLE-LIMIT column correspond
        to the MAX-RANGE= a value output when number is omitted.

        The following is a summary of @CYCLE file assignment information:
            The specified filename can be any member of the F-cycle set that is or can be
             assigned to the run.
            The specified filename can include an absolute F-cycle number, a relative F-cycle
             number, or can be an internal file name.
            The read and write keys for the F-cycle set must be supplied by assigning
             filename with the keys or by specifying the keys on @CYCLE, in any combination.
            If number is nonzero, there must be at least one currently cataloged, to be
             cataloged or to be deleted F-cycle member in the new range that is or can be
             assigned to the run.
            No F-cycle members to be deleted can be on a symbiont queue.
            All F-cycle members to be deleted must be assigned to the run by you or by
             FURPUR.
            Fixed mass storage files and cataloged tape files are assigned with the Y option;
             removable mass storage files are assigned with the E option.
            When number is nonzero, the F-cycle members to be deleted are assigned
             exclusively (X option).



7–134                                                                            7830 7949–031
                                                          @CYCLE—Alter Cycle Retention Limit




             Files currently assigned to the run are freed and reassigned under the following
              conditions:
                 A removable mass storage file assigned with the Y option is freed and
                  reassigned with the E option.
                 A file assigned without required read and write keys is freed and reassigned
                  with the keys, when they are available.
              In both cases the file is not restored to its original assignment state when @CYCLE
              is complete.
             In the following exception cases, files that would otherwise be freed and
              reassigned are instead marked as not assignable:
                 If the file status is to be cataloged
                 If the file status is to be deleted
                 If the file is assigned with the D option or K option

         Notes:

             @CYCLE operations use the MFD entry initially read, which describes the F-
              cycle set at the instant that the read is done. If multiple runs are working with
              the same F-cycle set and particularly if F-cycle members are being cataloged or
              deleted by other runs, then @CYCLE operations that delete F-cycle members or
              change the maximum F-cycle range might error or yield unexpected results.
              Having runs assign files exclusively (X option) might not overcome this problem,
              since @CYCLE uses the Y or E option on file assignments, which causes
              exclusive use to be ignored.
             Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
              ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
              should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
              command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.

7.16.2. Set Element Cycle Limit
         Format for Elements
             @CYCLE element-name,number

         element-name
              Specifies a program file symbolic element whose cycle limit is to be changed.

         number
              Specifies the maximum number of element cycles to be retained.

         The A, O, R, S, and Y options are not appropriate for this statement.

         When a program file element is named, the @CYCLE statement sets the maximum
         number of element cycles. If number specifies a new maximum less than the current
         number of element cycles being retained, a new element with the same name is




7830 7949–031                                                                              7–135
@@DCT—Change DCT Terminal Characteristics




        created and some data image control words can be changed and some images cannot
        be transferred at all.

        Any image deleted in a cycle number less than the lowest cycle number being
        retained, because of the new lower maximum number of cycles, is not transferred to
        the new element. Any images added but not deleted in a cycle number less than the
        lowest cycle number being retained are transferred, but S6 of each data image control
        word is changed to reflect the new lowest cycle number retained. All other
        nondeleted and deleted images are transferred to the new element.

        Examples
        The following examples illustrate the use of the @CYCLE statement:
          @CYCLE Q*A.B,2

               Assume that symbolic element B in program file Q*A consists of element cycles
               5, 6, 7, and 8. Since the new limit is two cycles, a new element B is created
               consisting of cycles 7 and 8.

          @CYCLE Q*D.,2

               Assume that the master file directory entry for file Q*D indicates that four
               absolute F-cycles 18, 15, 14, and 12 of the file exist. Since the new limit is two,
               absolute F-cycles 15, 14, and 12 are deleted. The limit is considered to be the
               range starting from the highest current absolute F-cycle number.

          @CYCLE Q*D.

               Assuming this statement follows the second example, the following F-cycle
               information is displayed:
                     MAX-RANGE= 2              CUR-RANGE=                1
                     NO. OF F CYCLES= 1:        18



7.17. @@DCT—Change DCT Terminal Characteristics
        The @@DCT statement changes characteristics associated with the DCT 500 terminal.
        The @@DCT and @@TTY statements are interchangeable. You can submit the
        statements from either device (see Section 7.68).

        Format
          @@DCT function-1,value-1[,...,function-n,value-n]

        function-n
           Indicates which characteristics to change. They are as follows:

           C
                  Changes character delete.




7–136                                                                                7830 7949–031
                                                      @DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




            I
                   Changes input image length.

            L
                   Changes line delete.

            P
                   Changes page length.

            S
                   Changes solicit character.

            T
                   Changes image terminator.

            W
                   Changes page width.
         value-n
            Is the new value you are setting for the field (character) just specified. Most fields
            can take a character, octal, or decimal value. However, the I, P, and W functions
            can take only an octal or decimal value. You can indicate character values by
            specifying the octal value for ASCII characters. You cannot assign the following as
            values: T for termination character, L for line delete, or C for character delete.

         Examples
           @@DCT W,96,T,010,S:

            The page width is changed to 96. The image terminator is octal 10, which is the
            octal representation for the ASCII backspace character. The solicit character is the
            colon (:).

           @@DCT I,40

            The input image length is 40.


7.18. @DELETE—Delete Files and Elements
         The Delete command deletes cataloged files, deletes program file elements (changes
         elements from current to deleted), or undeletes program file elements (changes
         elements from deleted to current).

         All parameters in the @DELETE statement are optional except name-1.

         Format
           @DELETE[,options] name-1 [,name-2,...,name-n,subtype-list]

         options
            When you delete cataloged files, the N option can be used. See Section 7.18.1.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–137
@DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




            When you delete elements, the A, O, R, S, V, and Y options can be used. See
            Section 7.18.2.
            When you undelete elements, the U option must be specified and the A, O, R, S, V,
            and Y options can be used. See Section 7.18.3.

            Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$
            on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be
            used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be
            input to a process later on in the runstream.

        name-n
            Specifies the cataloged file to be deleted or the program file element to be
            deleted or undeleted.

        subtype-list
            When elements are deleted or undeleted, this field can be used to select
            executable element subtypes. You must specify the A and Y options in order for
            this field to be interpreted as a subtype list. When you specify the A and Y
            options, you must specify a subtype list as the last field.

7.18.1. Deleting Files
        When you delete a cataloged file, only the N option applies.

        When you specify an external file name, you must specify the F-cycle if it is not the
        latest F-cycle. If read and write keys exist, you must either specify them or must have
        assigned the file to the run with the read and write keys.

        The file is not actually deleted until all other runs that have the file assigned to them
        have freed the file. When the file is deleted, the master file directory items are
        updated. The older F-cycles have their relative F-cycle number increased.

        The N option is available for the file DELETE command. The N option deletes the file
        entry from the master file directory (MFD), but retain any internal file names that were
        attached to the file before it was deleted.

        When a removable pack is in the DN state (brought down by a DN,PACK keyin), the
        operator can be able to make the pack available so that the delete can be performed.
        See the Exec Operations Reference Manual (7831 0281) for more information on the
        Down Pack feature.

        You can also use the @FREE,D statement to delete files.

        To delete all members of an F-cycle set, you can use the @CYCLE command. See
        Section 7.16 of this manual for more information.




7–138                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                     @DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




7.18.2. Deleting Elements
         One or more elements can be deleted in a program file, based on element name,
         version name and element type. When a symbolic procedure element is deleted, all
         procedure table entries associated with the element are deleted. When a relocatable
         element is deleted, the relocatable entry point table is removed. However, when an
         object module executable element is deleted, the object module entry point table is
         not affected.

         Until the @PACK command (see Section 7.43) is used, deleted elements can be
         undeleted (changed from deleted to current) with the @DELETE,U command. See
         Section 7.18.3 for a detailed description. Once the @PACK command is used, the
         deleted elements, their associated element text, and their associated procedure table
         entries, if any, are permanently removed from the program file and can no longer be
         undeleted.

         When the V option is not specified, any combination of the element type options A, O,
         R, and S can be specified, but at least one must be specified. If the A option is
         specified the Y option can be included to select only the executable element subtypes
         specified in the subtype-list field. The element name must be specified. If the version
         name is not specified, it is assumed to be spaces. If a version name is specified, it
         cannot include asterisk (*) mask characters. The element cycle cannot be specified.
         For each element type specified for which an element could not be found and deleted,
         the following message is output:
           q*f(c).e/v type NOT FOUND

         When the V option is specified, any combination of the element type options A, O, R,
         and S can be specified. If the A option is specified, the Y option can be included to
         select only the executable element subtypes specified in the subtype-list field. If you
         do not specify any element type options, then all element types are selected. If the
         element name is not specified, then elements are selected without regard to element
         name. If a version name is not specified, it is assumed to be spaces. If version name is
         specified it can include asterisk (*) mask characters. The element cycle cannot be
         specified. See Section 7.14.3 for a detailed description of the V option and version
         name mask characters.

         Either with or without the V option, one of following messages summarizes the
         results of the @DELETE for name-n:
           [a SYM] [b REL] [c ABS] [d OMN]
           NOTHING DELETED

         In the first message, a, b, c, and d are the number of elements of each type that were
         deleted. If no elements were deleted for an element type, then the corresponding part
         of the message does not appear. If no elements of any element type were deleted,
         the second message is output.




7830 7949–031                                                                              7–139
@DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




        Examples
        The following examples illustrate the use of the @DELETE statement:
          @DELETE FLAP.,TARE5.,ZEBRA4.,BAKER.

             Relative F-cycle 0 of cataloged files FLAP, TARE5, ZEBRA4, and BAKER is
             dropped from the master file directory (the files are decataloged).

          @DELETE,S F.ELT1/VERS,F1.ELTY

             The symbolic elements ELT1/VERS in program file F and ELTY in program file F1
             are marked as deleted. Any associated procedure names are also marked as
             deleted.

          @DELETE,OV F1./************

             All omnibus elements in program file F1 are marked as deleted.

          @DELETE,UOV F1./************

               Undelete the highest relative sequence number for each omnibus
               element/version/type set in program file F1. If file F1 did not have any deleted
               omnibus elements before the previous example, then this example "undo" the
               @DELETE,OV and restore file F1 to its previous state.

          @DELETE,RSV F2./VERS

             All relocatable and symbolic elements that have a version name of VERS in
             program file F2 are marked as deleted. If any relocatable elements are deleted,
             the relocatable entry point table is removed. If any symbolic procedure
             elements are deleted, the associated procedure table entries are also deleted.

          @DELETE,RSVU F2./VERS

             Undelete the highest relative sequence number for each relocatable and
             symbolic element/version/type set with a version name of VERS in program file
             F2. If any relocatable elements are undeleted, the relocatable entry point table is
             removed. If any symbolic procedure elements are undeleted, the associated
             procedure table entries are also undeleted. If file F2 did not have any deleted
             relocatable or symbolic elements before the previous example, then this
             example "undoes" the @DELETE,RSV and restores file F2 to its previous state,
             with the exception of the relocatable entry point table. An @PREP (see Section
             7.46) is needed to restore the relocatable entry point table.

          @DELETE,V FAST./V***********

             All elements having a version name that begins with V in program file FAST are
             marked as deleted.

7.18.3. Undeleting Elements
         One or more elements can be undeleted (changed from deleted to current) in a
         program file. The U option must be specified to undelete elements. Undeletion of an
         element can cause the deletion of an element with the same element name, version
         name, and element type.

         When a symbolic procedure element is undeleted, all procedure table entries
         associated with the element are undeleted. When a symbolic procedure element is
         deleted, all procedure table entries associated with the element are deleted. When a
         relocatable element is undeleted or deleted, the relocatable entry point table is
         removed. When an object module is undeleted, the object module entry point table is
         removed.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–141
@DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




         If a program file initially has no deleted elements, an element @DELETE can be
         followed by an @DELETE,U with the same options and specifications to restore the
         program file elements and procedure table entries to their original state. Note that an
         @PREP (see Section 7.46) might be needed to restore the relocatable entry point table
         if relocatable elements were undeleted or deleted.

         Once the @PACK command (see Section 7.43) is used, the deleted elements, their
         associated element text, and their associated procedure table entries, if any, are
         permanently removed from the program file and can no longer be undeleted.

         Element/Version/Type Sets
         All elements with the same element name, version name, and element type make up
         an element/version/type set. At most, one of the elements in the set can be
         undeleted. The rest of the elements in the set are deleted. @DELETE,U allows any
         deleted member of the element/version/type set to be undeleted. If the set contains
         an undeleted element, that element is deleted before another member of the set is
         undeleted.

         The members of the element/version/type set can be uniquely identified by either
         their absolute sequence number or their relative sequence number. This dual
         identification is unique to element undeletion. The following illustrates the use of
         @PRT,TL (see Section 7.49.3) to display the complete element/version/type set for
         element name UTILABS, version name 3R2A, and element type absolute (A option).
        @PRT,TLA WORKFILE.UTILABS/3R2A
        STD#QUAL*WORKFILE(1) PF, 2153/5000 elements, 2765/9999 tracks
                      ELEMENT TABLE                              SEQUENCE PREAMBLE   TEXT   CYCLE WORD FLAG        SECTOR
        D NAME        VERSION    TYPE        DATE      TIME        NUMBER   SIZE     SIZE   MAX CUR NUM BITS     LOCATION
        * UTILABS     3R2A     ABSOLUTE     2014-01-18 10:43:44     1712             1340              QTR,CLR     153550
        * UTILABS     3R2A     ABSOLUTE     2014-02-03 14:09:49     1733             1344              QTR,CLR     155600
        * UTILABS     3R2A     ABSOLUTE     2014-02-08 09:31:45     1740             1344              QTR,CLR     156990
        * UTILABS     3R2A     ABSOLUTE     2014-02-16 13:59:24     1748             1347              QTR,CLR     159119
           UTILABS    3R2A     ABSOLUTE     2014-05-05 12:24:52     1917             1351              QTR,CLR     173687
        NEXT AVAILABLE LOCATION-                                                                                   176916
        *File contains 97 deleted elements and 1423 tracks of deleted text
        *PLEASE PACK FILE


         There are five members in this element/version/type set. The first four members are
         deleted ("*" in D column) and the fifth member is undeleted. The members can be
         identified by their absolute sequence numbers (SEQ #) 1712, 1733, 1740, 1748, and 1917.
         The members can also be identified by their relative sequence numbers -4, -3,
         -2, -1, and 0, respectively. The element with the highest absolute sequence number is
         always relative sequence number 0. The element with the next highest absolute
         sequence number is relative sequence number -1, and so on.

         Element Selection Methods
         There are two methods that can be used to select elements for undeletion.
             An element can be selected by its relative sequence number in an
              element/version/type set. The A, O, R, or S option selects the element type,
              element name and version name specified, and the relative sequence number is
              specified in the element cycle subfield. If the element cycle subfield is not
              specified, then relative sequence number 0 is assumed. The V and Y options can
              also be specified.




7–142                                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                     @DELETE—Delete Files and Elements




             An element can be selected by its absolute sequence number in a program file.
              Element type (A, O, R, and S options), element name, and version name cannot be
              specified, and the absolute sequence number is specified in the element cycle
              subfield. The V and Y options also cannot be specified.
         Examples
         The following examples use the element/version/type set shown with the preceding
         @PRT,TL.
             @DELETE,UA WORKFILE.UTILABS/3R2A(-2)

              This example uses method 1 and specifies relative sequence number -2 of the
              UTILABS/3R2A absolute element set. It would delete element number 1917 and
              undelete element number 1740.

             @DELETE,UA WORKFILE.UTILABS/3R2A

              This example uses method 1 and specifies relative sequence number 0 (assumed)
              of the UTILABS/3R2A absolute element set. Following the previous example, it
              would delete element number 1740 and undelete element number 1917.

             @DELETE,U WORKFILE.(1733)

              This example uses method 2 and specifies absolute sequence number 1733.
              Following the previous example, it would delete element number 1917 and
              undelete element number 1733.

         Undelete Specifications and Operation
         The following additional information applies to element selection method 1.

         When the V option is not specified, any combination of the element type options A, O,
         R, and S can be specified, but at least one must be specified. If the A option is
         specified, the Y option can be included to select only the executable element
         subtypes specified in the subtype-list field. The element name must be specified. If
         the version name is not specified it is assumed to be spaces. If a version name is
         specified, it cannot include asterisk (*) mask characters. If the element cycle is not
         specified, the relative sequence number is assumed to be 0. If the element cycle is
         specified, it identifies the relative sequence number and must be in the range of -9999
         to 0. The same relative sequence number is used for each element/version type set
         selected by the A, O, R, and S options. For each element type option specified for
         which an element could not be found and undeleted, the following message is output:
             q*f(c).e/v type NOT FOUND




7830 7949–031                                                                             7–143
@ENABLE—Enable Disabled Files




        When the V option is specified, any combination of the element type options A, O, R,
        and S can be specified. If the A option is specified, the Y option can be included to
        select only the executable element subtypes specified in the subtype-list field. If you
        do not specify any element type options, then all element types are selected. If the
        element name is not specified, then elements are selected without regard to element
        name. If the version name is not specified, it is assumed to be spaces. If the version
        name is specified, it can include asterisk (*) mask characters. If the element cycle is
        not specified, the relative sequence number is assumed to be 0. If element cycle is
        specified, it identifies the relative sequence number and must be in the range of
        -9999 to 0. The same relative sequence number is used for each element/version type
        set selected. See Section 7.14.3 for a detailed description of the V option and version
        name mask characters.

        The A and Y options select only the executable element subtypes specified in the
        subtype-list field. Note that it is possible for members of an executable
        element/version/type set to have different subtypes. If this is the case, then the
        subtype-list must include all of the subtypes in the set for a member to be selected
        for undeletion.

        The following additional information applies to element selection method 2.

        No options other than U can be specified. Element name and version name cannot be
        specified. Element cycle must be specified. It identifies the absolute sequence number
        and must be in the range of 1 to 26,146. If the specified sequence number does not
        exist in the file, the following message is output:
          *ERROR PRA002663: The sequence number specified does not exist in the program file.
          The largest sequence number in the file is n.


        Since method 1 requires at least one of the A, O, R, S, V, and Y options and since
        method 2 does not allow any of these options, methods 1 and 2 cannot be specified
        on the same @DELETE,U command.

        For all element selection methods, one of the following messages summarizes the
        results of the @DELETE,U for this name-n:
          [a SYM] [b REL] [c ABS] [d OMN]
          NOTHING UNDELETED

        In the first message, a, b, c, and d are the number of elements of each type that were
        undeleted. If no elements were undeleted for an element type, then the
        corresponding part of the message does not appear. If no elements of any element
        type were undeleted, the second message is output.


7.19. @ENABLE—Enable Disabled Files
        The Enable command removes the disable flag for cataloged files.

        All parameters in the @ENABLE statement are optional.

        Format
          @ENABLE[,options] [filename-1,filename-2,...,filename-n]



7–144                                                                           7830 7949–031

         options
             C
                 Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.

                 Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
                 ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
                 should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
                 command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.

                 The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.

         filename-n
             Specifies the cataloged files to be enabled.

         The A, O, R, S, and Y options are not appropriate for this statement.

         If the file you specified is not disabled, a message to this effect is printed on the listing
         (normal exit is taken). If there are any keys, you must specify them.


7.20. @END—End of Input for @DATA and @ELT
         The @END statement terminates the @DATA and @ELT processors. Refer to the
         ClearPath OS 2200 ELT Processor Operations Reference Manual (8206 2365), UP
         13402 for more information.

         If encountered in a runstream by anything other than the @DATA or @ELT processors,
         this statement is ignored. If a READ$-type request encounters the statement, it is
         treated in the same manner as any other control statement. In that situation an
         end-of-file status is given.


7.21. @@END—Terminate Special Modes
         The @@END statement terminates special modes. After the special mode is
         terminated, the terminal is returned to normal input mode.

         Format
           @@END [mode]

         mode indicates which special mode to terminate. You can process in more than one
         mode at a time. If you enter @@END without specifying a mode, all the modes in
         which you are processing terminate.

         The special modes are
         CQUE
             Input queue in main storage

@ENDF—Terminate the @FILE Card File




        INQ
              Input queue on mass storage

        FUL
              Full screen mode

        CONS
              Console mode

        ESC
              Escape mode

        PTI
              Paper tape input

        CDI
              DCT 1000 card read input mode

        HOLD/PR/TM
              Hold conditions as specified

        Note: To initiate a special mode, enter the mode you want preceded by @@.
        For example, @@FUL initiates full screen mode.


7.22. @ENDF—Terminate the @FILE Card File
        The @ENDF statement marks the end of the images for a file created by the @FILE
        statement.

        Format
            @ENDF

        The @ENDF statement cannot have a label and cannot be continued.

        The @FILE and @ENDF statements can be disabled on your system because they do
        not have proper security protection. If you use either statement in your runstream
        when they are disabled, the system removes your run.

        These are the security problems:
             Any cataloged file can be deleted by the use of @FILE,AD or @FILE,KD.
             Read/write key validation is bypassed with @FILE.
             On systems with Security Level 1 or higher, the user-ID is not validated for @FILE,
              and the ACR validation is bypassed. Also, a private file created with @FILE is given
              the user-ID of EXEC8.




7–146                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                                 @ENDX—Terminate CLIST Mode




7.23. @ENDX—Terminate CLIST Mode
         The @ENDX statement gives a program or processor an end-of-file return and
         terminates CLIST mode.

         It marks the end of the images for a file created by the @FILE statement.

         Format
           @ENDX

         If you enter @ENDX when your run stream is not in CLIST mode, the Exec returns the
         message:
           @ENDX IGNORED - NOT IN CLIST MODE

         Refer to the Exec System Software Executive Requests Programming Reference
         Manual (7830 7899) for more information about CLIST mode.


7.24. @EOF—Indicate the End of Input
         The @EOF statement indicates the end of input from the runstream to the program
         being executed, which can be a compiler, user application, or any OS 2200 system
         processor.

         Format
           @EOF [s]

         Note: Label is not allowed on this control statement.

           s    is an optional, 1-character, user-defined sentinel that, if specified, must be in
                column 6 of the @EOF statement.

         When an @EOF statement is detected on a read request (READ$, AREAD$, READA$,
         AREADA$, ATREAD$, TREAD$ or SYMB$), any user-defined sentinel is returned either
         in the SYMB$ packet or for non-SYMB$ requests, right-justified in the activity’s A0
         register. For non-SYMB$ requests, control is transferred to the end-of-file return
         address specified in the packet. Once an @EOF statement is encountered, it is
         possible to continue reading from the runstream. Attempting to read a control
         statement other than @EOF inhibits further reading by the program and an abnormal
         return to the end-of-file return address is given. In this way, the @EOF statement can
         be used to divide datasets.




7830 7949–031                                                                                       7–147
@ERS—Empty (Erase) a File




        Examples:
          @ACOB,IS FILEZ.SYM,FILEZ.REL
          program lines
          program lines
          program lines
           .
           .
           .
          @EOF

        The @EOF indicates the end of input to the ASCII COBOL compiler and causes the
        compiler to commence generation of the output relocatable element.

          @XQT    PROGX
          ..
          @XQT    PROGX
          ..
          data for part 1
          ..
          @EOF A
          ..
          data for part 2
          ..
          @XQT    PROGY

        All data between the two @XQT statements are to be read by PROGX. The @EOF
        control statement serves as a separator between the two logical datasets.


7.25. @ERS—Empty (Erase) a File
        The @ERS statement releases mass storage from cataloged or temporary,
        sector-addressable or word-addressable files. The @ERS statement exclusively
        assigns the files to be processed. Options are available to zero-fill mass storage
        before it is released and to zero-fill mass storage that is retained.

        If the first track of the file is retained and if the first track was previously written, the
        first 28 words of the file are zeroed. If this is a sector-addressable file, this makes the
        file available as an initially empty program file (PF). After an @ERS, the @CHG
        statement T and E options (see Section 7.6) can be used to create an empty large
        program file (LPF) or an empty large-element program file (LEPF), respectively.

        All @ERS parameters are optional.

        Format
          @ERS[,options] [filename-1,filename-2, . . . ,filename-n]




7–148                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                                                     @ERS—Empty (Erase) a File




         options

           Options for releasing mass storage

           None
                 For sector-addressable files, release all mass storage past the initial reserve.
                 If the file does not have an initial reserve, release all mass storage. For
                 word-addressable files, release all mass storage, including the initial reserve.

           C
                 Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.

                 Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
                 ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
                 should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
                 command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.

                 The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.

           I
                 Release all mass storage, including the initial reserve.

           N
                 Do not release any mass storage.

           Options for zeroing mass storage

           None
                 Zero the first sector (28 words) of the file, if the first track (1,792 words) of mass
                 storage is retained and if the first track was previously written.

           G
                 Zero mass storage that is retained.

           Z
                 Zero mass storage before it is released.

         filename-i
               Specifies the name of the file to process.

         If the N option is specified, it overrides both the I and Z options. The following
         informational message is displayed if the I and/or Z options are included with the N
         option:
           N OPTION SPECIFIED – [I][Z] OPTION[S] IGNORED




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–149
@@ESC—Pass Unaltered Input to a Program or Unaltered Output to a Terminal




        If the I option is specified, it overrides the G option. The following informational
        message is displayed if the G option is included with the I option:
            I OPTION SPECIFIED – G OPTION IGNORED

        When the G option is specified for sector-addressable files, retained mass storage is
        zeroed from the beginning of the first track to the lesser of the highest track written
        and the highest track retained. When the G option is specified for word-addressable
        files, retained mass storage is zeroed from the beginning of the first track to the
        greater of the highest track written and the initial reserve. Note that the G option can
        actually cause additional mass storage to be allocated for files that contain unallocated
        areas (holes).

        If the Z option is specified and if file is XPC cached, it must be changed to not cached
        with an @CHG,F filename-i.,DNC (see Section 7.6) before the @ERS. This assures that
        the mass storage granules are actually zeroed before they are returned to the
        available pool.

        If no filename-i are specified, TPF$ is processed.


7.26. @@ESC—Pass Unaltered Input to a Program or
       Unaltered Output to a Terminal
        The @@ESC statement lets input to a program or output to a terminal pass in the
        format in which it was entered.

        Format
            @@ESC [function]

        function can be one of the following:
        I
             Escape mode for input. The cursor positions are not stripped from the input data
             while in escape mode.

        O
             Escape mode for output.

        Example
            @@ESC I


7.27. @FILE—Create a Mass Storage Card File
        The @FILE statement creates a mass storage file at input time, while the images are
        being read, and assigns it to the run.

        Creating a file with the @FILE statement, rather than by means of the ELT or DATA
        processors, reduces overhead since it is accomplished at input time rather than at
        execution time. The data is handled only once when creating the file, rather than being



7–150                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                   @FILE—Create a Mass Storage Card File




         read again from auxiliary storage with the runstream and then transferred to the file by
         the DATA or ELT processors at execution time.

         The @FILE statement is valid only within a batch run and cannot have been initiated
         with the @START statement.

         Note: The @FILE statement can be disabled on your system because it does not
         have proper security protection. See your security officer for information about the
         availability of this statement.

         Format
             @FILE[,options] filename[,type/reserve/granule/maximum/
             placement,pack-id-1/.../packid-n,,,ACR-name]

         The format is identical to the @ASG statement for mass storage devices (except the
         label field is not allowed). The options are the same as the @ASG statement. If you do
         not specify an option, the default is U. Use the T option only for removable disk files.
         Use the X option for previously cataloged mass storage files.

         If you do not supply a qualifier on the file name, Q$Q$Q$ is assumed. For private files,
         the project-ID is picked up from the @RUN statement.

         Pack-IDs are used only if the type field specifies removable disk. Sector-formatted
         files cannot be temporary files, except for removable disks.

         An @FILE statement must not be more than 80 columns in length. You cannot
         continue an @FILE statement to another line.

7.27.1. Security Considerations
         The @FILE and @ENDF statements can be disabled on your system because they do
         not have proper security protection. If you use either statement in your runstream
         when they are disabled, the system removes your run. These are the security
         problems:
             Any cataloged file can be deleted by the use of @FILE,AD or @FILE,KD.
             Read/write key validation is bypassed with @FILE.
             On systems with Security Level 1 or higher, the user-ID is not validated for @FILE,
              and the ACR validation is bypassed. A private file created with @FILE is given the
              user-ID of EXEC8.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–151
@FILE—Create a Mass Storage Card File




7.27.2. Terminating @FILE
        To terminate the @FILE statement, use one of the following statements:
            @ENDF
            @FIN
            Another @FILE statement

        Data images and all control statements, except @COL and its accompanying end
        sentinel, are placed into the created file. The @COL statement and sentinel are
        processed immediately, and the file is marked when the mode switch is made.

        Do not nest @FILE statements for mass storage files. It causes @FILE mode to
        terminate with an error message.

        Example
            @FILE,T FILE1.

7.27.3. Creating a Tape File from Card Images
        The @FILE statement creates a tape file at input time, while the images are being read,
        and assigns it to the run.

        Do not nest @FILE statements unless they use the same file name and are for tape
        files.

        Note: The @FILE statement can be disabled on your system because it does not
        have proper security protection. See your security officer for information about the
        availability of this statement.

        Format
            @FILE,[options] filename,[type/units/log/noise/processor/tape/
            format/data-converter/block-numbering/data-compression/
            buffered-write,reel-1/reel-2/.../reel-n,expiration-period,
            ring-indicator,ACR-name]

        The format is identical to the @ASG statement for tape files (label field is not allowed).

        The options are the same as the @ASG statement. If you do not specify an option, the
        default is U. Use the T option for tape files.

        An @FILE statement must not be more than 80 columns in length. You cannot
        continue an @FILE statement to another line.




7–152                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                               @FIN—Identify the End of a Run




         The @FILE and @ENDF statements can be disabled on your system because they do
         not have proper security protection. If you use either statement in your runstream
         when they are disabled, the system removes your run. These are the security
         problems:
             Any cataloged file can be deleted by the use of @FILE,AD or @FILE,KD.
             Read/write key validation is bypassed with @FILE.
             On systems with Security Level 1 or higher, the user-ID is not validated for @FILE,
              and the ACR validation is bypassed. Also, a private file created with @FILE is given
              the user-ID of EXEC8.

         Example
             @FILE,TJ FILE2,U9V//////109A


7.28. @FIN—Identify the End of a Run
         The @FIN statement identifies the end of a run. The @FIN statement must be the last
         statement in all runs, whether demand or batch.

         The @FIN statement must be coded exactly as shown (entered in the first four
         columns):
             @FIN

         The @FIN statement is never treated as data by any processors, including the DATA
         and ELT processors. If the Exec reads an @FIN statement in an @ADD stream, it does
         not terminate the run, and it displays the following message:
             @FIN IN ADD FILE - IGNORED

         After you enter the @FIN statement, the run terminates. You can start another run by
         pressing the XMIT key. If you enter anything other than @@TERM or a $$ statement
         (except for @@SEND), you see this message:
             Enter userid/password and clearance level:

         If you want to start another run, respond to this and the subsequent prompts.

         If you do not want to start another run, sign off from the system. Refer to @@TERM.

         See Section 5.4 for information on executing a run termination task.

         See Appendix E for a description of the tail sheet.




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–153
@FIND—Position Tape Within Element Files




7.29. @FIND—Position Tape Within Element Files
        Locates an element on a magnetic tape file (file must be in element file format) and
        positions the tape immediately preceding the element’s label block.

        All parameters in the @FIND statement are required except options.

        Format
          @FIND[,options] element-name

        options
           Can be one of the A, C, O, R, or S options.

           Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$
           on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be
           used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be
           input to a process later on in the runstream.

        element-name
           Specifies the file and the element to be located

        The search is made forward until either the element is found or a hardware EOF mark
        is encountered. When the EOF mark is encountered, the tape is backspaced to the
        previous EOF mark (or load point, whichever is encountered first) and the search is
        repeated. If no find is made, the error exit is taken when the EOF mark is encountered.

        Normally, the @FIND statement is used just before an @COPIN statement (see Section
        7.12) requesting that the element just located (or all elements up to the EOF mark) be
        inserted into a program file located on sector-formatted mass storage. It is also
        required before calling a language or systems processor that uses the source
        input/output routine (SIR$) to read the element from tape (specified as the SI field).

        Note: Be careful when you do an @FIND operation on other than the first reel of a
        multireel file. If an EOF is encountered before locating the desired element, the reel
        is backspaced only to the load point, not to the EOF, which can be located on a
        previous reel.




7–154                                                                           7830 7949–031
                              @FREE and @@FREE—Release Files and Peripheral Devices




7.30.@FREE and @@FREE—Release Files and
      Peripheral Devices
         The @FREE statement releases files, reels, internal file names, and the exclusive use
         of files from your run.

         When used for mass storage files, the @FREE statement can cause a file to be
         deleted, cataloged, or just released from your run. What action is taken depends upon
         what option was used when the file was assigned and what option is used on the
         @FREE statement.

         After you release a file with an @FREE statement, you can no longer reference the file
         without reassigning it with another @ASG statement. You must free tape drives as
         soon as possible so that other people can use them.

         When you release a temporary file with @FREE, the file is deleted. Temporary files are
         automatically deleted by run termination. All files are automatically released at run
         termination. Therefore, it is not necessary to do an @FREE before entering @FIN.

         Notes:

             If a shared mass storage file is application-private, its application-private state
              is not cleared when the file is freed. Refer to the MHFS Planning, Installation, and
              Operations Overview (7830 7469).
             An @FREE of an alternate print file must not be done before an @BRKPT. An
              @FREE does not close the print alternate file, and a successive @BRKPT to the
              free file results in an I/O error.

         Format
             @FREE[,options] filename

         options
              These are the options:
              A
                   Releases only the specified internal file name given to the file with an @USE
                   statement.

              B
                   Releases only the specified internal file name associated with the file, unless
                   it is the only internal name for the file, in which case the entire file is released
                   from the run.

              D
                   Deletes a cataloged file, in addition to releasing it from the run. If it is a
                   temporary file, it is just released from the run. If the file was assigned (@ASG)
                   with the C or U option, it is not cataloged as it normally would be.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–155
@FREE and @@FREE—Release Files and Peripheral Devices




               For systems with Fundamental Security, to delete cataloged files assigned
               with the C or U option, you must have included the correct read and write
               keys (if any) when you assigned the file to the run.
               If the file is owned, you must have delete access to the file in order to delete
               it.
               If your site has Fundamental Security, you must include any read or write
               keys that are attached to the file in order to delete the file.
               If your site has Security Level 1, 2, or 3 and the dynamic configuration
               parameter owned_file_read_write_keys is TRUE, then you must include read
               or write keys to delete the file.

           I
               Inhibits the cataloging of a file that was assigned (@ASG) with a C or U
               option. You can accomplish the same thing with the D option.

           R
               Releases the specified file from the run, but retains all internal names
               associated with the file. If the file was assigned (@ASG) with the C or U
               option, it is also cataloged.

           S
               Releases the file from the run, but keeps the physical tape unit assigned to
               the run.
               When an unlabeled tape is being mounted, the following prompt is displayed
               on the system console to ask for the tape’s reel number:
                n ANSWER WITH REEL NO ON unit E,REEL

               When this tape is freed (@FREE) and the next one assigned, the same
               scenario is repeated.
               However, a special case occurs when an autoloader is installed and the
               S option is used on the @FREE statement: For the first tape, the operator is
               prompted for the reel number as described above. If this tape is released
               using @FREE,S, the next unlabeled tape in the autoloader is not prompted for
               the reel number.
               This is a useful feature that can significantly help improve efficiency,
               especially when a large number of unlabeled tapes are to be processed.
               You can reassign the unit to your run by using a normal @ASG statement.
               Just be sure the type you specified corresponds to the unit reserved for your
               run. Since a pooled unit can be used only by your run, your request for a tape
               file can be satisfied immediately.




7–156                                                                          7830 7949–031
                                @FREE and @@FREE—Release Files and Peripheral Devices




             X
                    Releases exclusive use of the file when the file was assigned with the X
                    option. The file is not released from the run. This lets other runs use the file.
                    If you do not specify the A or X option, the file or device is released from
                    your run. If the file was assigned (@ASG) with the C or U option, it is also
                    cataloged. If it is a temporary file, the file no longer exists.

         When you are releasing tape files from your run, the S option lets you release just the
         file and not the physical unit. The physical unit is reserved exclusively for your run.
         Other users cannot use the unit until your run terminates, or until you reassign the
         unit, and then release it completely.

         The Exec issues I/O to write two tape marks. If tape-mark buffering is enabled, the
         Exec then issues an FSAFE$ request. The TMB feature increases the importance of
         checking for an FSAFE$ failure, because the feature introduces the potential of leaving
         a tape in an incomplete state, with missing file marks or data. Currently no status is
         returned to the user for any closing tape operation, including @FREE.
         Table 7-3 shows options allowed for releasing different types of files and devices.
         An asterisk (*) indicates the option is allowed but has no effect.


                  Table 7–3. FREE Options for Releasing Files and Devices


                         Item Being Released                        Valid Options

                 Mass storage files to be cataloged        Blank, A, B, D, I, R, and X*
                 Already cataloged mass storage files      Blank, A, B, D, R, and X
                 Temporary mass storage files              Blank, A, B, D, R, and X*
                 Tape files to be cataloged                Blank, A, B, D, I, R, and S
                 Already cataloged tape files              Blank, A, B, D, R, and S
                 Temporary tape files                      Blank, A, B, D, R, and S
                 Tape devices                              Blank, A, B, D, R, and X*
                 Internal file name                        Blank, A, B, R, S, and X*


         If you assigned the cataloged file with the D or K option on the @ASG statement,
         any @FREE statement that releases the file from the run deletes the file.

         filename
             Identifies the file or device to be released from your run. This can be either the
             name given to the file when it was created or an internal file name given to the file
             with an @USE statement.

         Example
           @FREE,D FREMONT1.

             This statement frees file FREMONT1 from the run and also deletes the file.


7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–157
@@FUL—Enter Input a Full Screen at a Time




7.31. @@FUL—Enter Input a Full Screen at a Time
        The @@FUL transparent statement initiates full-screen mode, which lets you enter
        data and statements a full screen at a time. The screens of information are stored on
        mass storage until you terminate full-screen mode with an @@END FUL statement
        (See Section 7.21).

        You must provide your own SOE character for the first line of your input; the other
        lines do not require an SOE character. You must also provide your own SOE character
        on the @@END FUL statement.

        It is a good idea to leave the first line on the screen blank, in case the system gives
        you a timeout warning. Otherwise, the first line of your input is lost.

        If the input lines entered produce any output, it is held until full-screen mode is
        terminated.

        Format
           @@FUL

        Example
           @@FUL (xmit)*FULL SCREEN INPUT MODE*
           line of input (cr)
           line of input (cr)
           line of input (cr)
           line of input (cr)
           .
           .
           . (xmit)
           @@END FUL (xmit)

        line of input
               Represents the lines of data and statements you want to enter. Each line on the
               screen is considered a separate input image.

        (cr)
               Indicates that you must press the carriage return key after each line of input.

        (xmit)
               Indicates that you must press the XMIT key after each screen of input, before the
               @@END FUL statement. If you do not press the XMIT key before you enter the
               @@END FUL statement, you lose your last screen of data.

               Note: The carriage return key only moves the cursor to the next line, but the
               XMIT key transmits the data on the screen to the system.




7–158                                                                               7830 7949–031
                               @HDG and @@HDG—Provide a Heading for Printer Output




7.32. @HDG and @@HDG—Provide a Heading for
       Printer Output
         The @HDG statement lets you specify a heading to be printed on every page of the
         printout, as well as page numbers and the date when the file was created. Use @HDG
         with the @BRKPT statement when you are directing output into a user-defined file.

         Any number of @HDG statements can appear in the runstream.

         Note: If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, printouts can be labeled with the
         clearance level and compartment set associated with your print file. See Section 7.3
         for more information.

         Format
           @HDG[,options heading.printcontrol]

         options
            N
                    Suppresses printing of heading, date, and page number.

            P
                    Starts page numbering with page 1 instead of current page number.

            X
                    Suppresses printing of date and page number.

         heading
                Contains the heading that is to appear within the top margin of each page (two
                print lines before the main body of text printed on the page). This heading can be
                any length up to a maximum of 96 characters (including embedded blanks); any
                additional characters are ignored.
                The heading starts with the second character after the options field. Leading
                blanks are permitted in the heading. The end of the heading text is signified by
                the end of the statement, a period, or the 96-character limit, whichever occurs
                first. The text can be followed by print control fields.
                If the top margin is less than two lines (including the heading line), the heading is
                not printed. Unless suppressed (N or X options), the date and page number are
                printed to the right of the heading. Page numbering begins with the page count
                current to the print file unless the P option is specified, in which case page
                numbering begins with page 1.
                The continuation character (;) and the period character are not permitted as part
                of the heading text.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–159
@HDG and @@HDG—Provide a Heading for Printer Output




        printcontrol
             This field consists of a period immediately followed by a print control function.
             This field can be repeated up to a maximum of 96 characters including the
             heading.
             Some types of printers do not support all print control functions.

        These are the print control function formats:
        A
            Allows error recovery. The I and A functions control the automatic recovery of
            errors for individual output files. These functions can be used in pairs more than
            once in an individual file to control automatic recovery over specific areas of
            output. If autorecovery is inhibited, a console message asks the onsite operator
            whether recovery must be attempted on the file.

        B,lpi ctid,eltname
            Specifies print cartridge (band) ctid or change lines-per-inch to lpi, or both.
            Nonstandard cartridge-ID code buffer can be found in eltname in the file
            SYS$*PRINTER$. Except for lpi, this is for 0776 printers only.
            lpi
                   Lines-per-inch; lpi must be 8, 6, or * (an asterisk indicates device default) as
                   desired; no leading spaces between the comma and lpi are allowed. Lpi can
                   be the only field in this print control function; however, a change in lpi
                   implicitly changes the page size. Therefore, unless special forms are desired,
                   use an M function on the same statement as the B function to keep the page
                   size the same.
            ctid
                   Cartridge identification code. This is the hexadecimal cartridge code that
                   appears on the cartridge case. Print data following this image is printed after
                   the operator has replaced the print cartridge currently loaded with the one
                   specified here (if necessary). This field is ignored at print time if the printer is
                   not a type 0776 printer.
            eltname
                   If a special cartridge to be used is not known to the Exec, eltname is the
                   name of the element in the SYS$*PRINTER file, in which this load code buffer
                   can be found. Coding eltname with no ctid is an error. ctid can be the only
                   field supplied if the cartridge is known to the Exec and lpi is not needed.




7–160                                                                                  7830 7949–031
                               @HDG and @@HDG—Provide a Heading for Printer Output




         H,options,page,text
            Provides a page heading for the printout, where:
            options
                   N    Do not print heading.

                   X    Suppress printing page number and date.


            page
                   Is the page number to be used for the first page on which this heading
                   appears. If no page number is given and there is no X or N option, the page
                   numbering is not affected; it continues in its normal sequence.
                   Note: The Exec symbiont handlers do not print page numbers greater than
                   262,144.

            text
                   Is the text of the heading you want to appear within the top margin of each
                   page (up to 96 characters long). This text cannot contain periods. The heading
                   is printed at the top of each succeeding page, where the page size is
                   determined by the margin function (M), described later. If the top margin is
                   less than two lines (including the heading line), the heading is not printed.

            I
                   Inhibits error recovery.

            L,nn
                   Spaces the printer to logical line number nn-1. The first logical line number is
                   0, (1 = 0); that is, both L,0 and L,1 position the printer to position 1 before the
                   first printable line. This statement causes the printer to be logically
                   positioned so that a print statement with a space count of 1 is printed on
                   printable line nn.

         M,length,top,bottom,lpi
            Provides margin setting information for readjusting page length, top and bottom
            margins, and the number of lines per inch. Hardware limitations require that the
            page length for a 0776 printer be no more than 192 lines. Other printers can also
            have limitations on page length.
            length
                   Is the number of lines per page. This field can be a decimal value (maximum
                   of three digits), an asterisk ( * ), blank, or X.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–161
@HDG and @@HDG—Provide a Heading for Printer Output




                  An asterisk specifies the system standard value; a blank specifies no change
                  from the value currently in effect. An X specifies absolute line spacing; it
                  changes the method of calculating spacing, and all subsequent fields (top,
                  bottom, and lpi) are invalid. After an M,X function, spacing is not truncated by
                  an end-of-page condition, and top and bottom margins are zero. Any lpi
                  change must have been set up by a previous print control function. Any M or
                  B statement causes absolute line spacing mode to be exited.

            top
                  Is the number of blank lines used for the top margin (must be less than 63).
                  This field can be a decimal value (maximum of two digits), an asterisk (*),
                  or blank.
                  An asterisk specifies the system standard value; a blank specifies no change
                  from the value currently in effect.

            bottom
                  Is the number of blank lines used for the bottom margin (must be less than
                  63). This field can be a decimal value (maximum of two digits), an asterisk (*),
                  or blank.
                  An asterisk specifies the system standard value; a blank specifies no change
                  from the value currently in effect.

            lpi
                  Is the number of lines per inch. This field can be a decimal value, an asterisk
                  (*), or blank.
                  A decimal value can be only one digit (either 6 or 8). An asterisk specifies the
                  system standard value; a blank specifies no change from the value currently
                  in effect.

        R
            Inserts a logical break into print output files; used by the print symbionts when
            skipping forward through a print file. When the symbiont encounters the R
            function, it stops skipping. It then asks the operator to indicate whether a reprint is
            desired.

        S,text
            Requests special forms for processing the print file. The text can be up to 48
            characters long. When this control function is encountered for onsite printers, the
            text is displayed on the operator’s console. For remote batch devices, the text is
            displayed on a remote printer. The text cannot contain any periods.

        U
            Ignores any following print control functions. This option is reserved for users. It is

         W,line width
              Changes the maximum print width allowed. The standard line width value is 22,

          @HDG,N
