7.33. @@HOLD—Hold Terminal Messages and Print
       Output
        The @@HOLD statement places a hold on terminal messages and print output.

        Format
          @@HOLD [type/type]

        type can be the following values:
        TM
             Holds all terminal messages. Terminal messages are generated by @@TM,
             TM keyins, and TB keyins. Immediate TB keyins (TB /I) are displayed.
        PR
             Holds print output.

        The system standard (default) is both TM and PR.

        Examples
          @@HOLD TM

               Holds all terminal messages.

          @@HOLD

               Holds all terminal messages and print output. Same as @@HOLD TM/PR.




7–164                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                          @@INQ—Queue Input in a Mass Storage Buffer




7.34.@@INQ—Queue Input in a Mass Storage Buffer
         The @@INQ statement lets you enter lines of statements and data into a buffer on
         mass storage. This statement is similar to the @@CQUE statement. The major
         difference is that statements entered in @@CQUE mode are processed immediately.
         Statements entered in @@INQ mode are not processed until you enter the @@END
         INQ or @@END statement.

         Format
           @@INQ soe-parameter
           input-image
           input-image
           input-image
            .
            .
            .
           @@END INQ or @@END

         Valid values for the soe-parameter field are

             N
                  No SOE characters are issued by the system when in this input queuing
                  mode. The system resumes issuing appropriate SOE characters when the
                  corresponding @@END control statement is received to return the terminal
                  to interactive mode.

             S
                  SOE characters are issued by the system when in this input queuing mode
                  after each input image is transferred to a system mass storage buffer. The
                  system continues to issue appropriate SOE characters when the
                  corresponding @@END control statement is received allowing the terminal to
                  return to interactive mode.

         The soe-parameter field is a 1-character field. If more than 1 character or anything
         other than an N or S is specified, the statement is ignored and the following error is
         displayed at the terminal:
           @@ERROR - SYNTAX

         input-image represents the statements and data you want to enter into the buffer on
         mass storage.

         You must provide your own SOE character once you enter INQ mode if the N is
         specified or no soe-parameter is specified.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–165
@@INS—Change the Insert Point on the Display




        If you use @@INQ mode outside of an active run, the input images are discarded until
        you begin a run with an @RUN statement.

        If you enter @RUN statements while in @@INQ mode without a demand run active,
        the resulting runs are considered remote batch runs. If a demand run is already active,
        the @RUN statements in the INQ are ignored.


7.35. @@INS—Change the Insert Point on the Display
        The @@INS statement lets you change the insert point on the screen display. The
        insert point is the line on the display where new lines first appear.

        Format
          @@INS [n]

        n indicates the line on the display to be used as the insert point. The lines are counted
        down from the top.

        For standard 24-line displays, the normal insert point is at line 23 and the @@INS
        statement with no fields gives the default of line 23.

        Examples
          @@INS 22

              The insert point is the 22nd line down from the top. This saves any text on the
              23rd line.

          @@INS

              This gives the default insert point at line 23. This is the same as @@INS 23.


7.36.@JUMP—Branch from Within the Runstream to
      Another Point
        The @JUMP statement advances control to the specified labeled statement in the
        runstream.

        Format
          @JUMP label

        label specifies the label or name attached to a subsequent statement to which control
        is passed. This field can be a decimal value (from 1 to 999999), indicating how many
        statements are to be skipped. Those statements that cannot have labels must not be
        included in the count. A numeric value of 0 as a field is not permitted.

        The @JUMP statement must refer to a statement not yet processed.




7–166                                                                             7830 7949–031
                               @LOG and @@LOG—Place Information in the System Log




         Examples
           @JUMP TAG

                Control is advanced to the control statement containing label TAG.

           @JUMP 4

                After execution of the @JUMP statement, control is advanced to the fourth
                control statement. The fourth control statement can have a label field.


7.37. @LOG and @@LOG—Place Information in the
       System Log
         The @LOG and @@LOG statements are used to insert user-specified information in the
         system log. The system log is a file maintained by the Exec as a historical record of
         the activity in the system.

         Format
           @LOG message

         message is a user-specified message to be placed in the system log.

         The message can be up to 132 characters long, including embedded blanks. The first
         nonblank character is considered the beginning of the message. The end of the
         message is the last character before the end of a line, before a comment ( . ), or within
         the 132-character limit. The message cannot begin with a comma ( , ) or a slash ( / ),
         and cannot include the continuation character ( ; ). The blank-period-blank ( . ), which
         introduces a comment, also cannot be used.

         When the Exec encounters the @LOG statement, it prefixes the message with your
         run-ID and the date and time, and enters it in the system log.

         Examples
           @LOG TRANSPORT PROBLEM NO. 12 . Revised 5-1

                In this example, the message consists of 26 characters (the blank preceding the
                period is considered part of the message) and is terminated by blank-period-

7.38.@MARK—Mark an EOF on Tape
         The @MARK statement writes an EOF mark on a tape. If the tape is unlabeled,
         FURPUR writes a second EOF mark and positions the tape between the two EOF
         marks.

         All parameters except filename-1 are optional.



7830 7949–031                                                                                7–167
@MARK—Mark an EOF on Tape




        Format
                @MARK[,options] filename-1[,filename-2,...,filename-n]

        options
            C
                 Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.

                 Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$
                 on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be
                 used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be
                 input to a process later on in the runstream.

                 The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.

            E
                 Used for unlabeled tapes to improve write performance. Write a single EOF mark
                 instead of writing two EOF marks and backspacing over one of them. Before
                 finishing with the tape (for example @FREE, @MOVE,B or @REWIND), you must
                 close the output tape with @CLOSE (see Section 7.8) or with another @MARK. The
                 E option is ignored for labeled tapes, which always write a single EOF mark.

            W
                 Used when the buffered-write mode BUFTAP is enabled on the tape to assure that
                 all buffered data has successfully been written to tape. After the write of the EOF
                 mark, a synchronize (F$SAFE) I/O function is used, if necessary. Note that the
                 synchronize increases the time to write this file, as if the buffered-write mode
                 BUFFIL was enabled. To maximize performance, the W option must be used only
                 periodically, to establish error recovery "checkpoints." The W option is ignored for
                 unlabeled tapes when the E option is not specified. In these cases the tape is
                 implicitly synchronized by the Exec or by the tape unit.

        filename-i
                 Specifies the tape files on which to write the EOF marks.

        @MARK is typically used under the following conditions:
                After output tape functions that do not write EOF marks, such as @COPOUT with
                 any of the AORSVX options (see Section 7.13) and @COPY with neither the G nor
                 the M options (see Section 7.14.1)
                To close an unlabeled output tape when the E option has been specified on
                 @COPOUT or @COPY to improve the tape write performance. In this case an
                 @MARK,E can be used to write a second EOF mark to close the unlabeled output
                 tape.




7–168                                                                                7830 7949–031
                      @MODE and @@MODE—Change the Mode Settings for a Tape File




         Notes:
             If you use the @MARK statement on an unlabeled tape immediately after
              @COPOUT, @COPY, or @MARK have written an EOF mark, you are creating a
              logical end-of-file on the tape. Even though additional data can be written to the
              tape, the data cannot be accessible once the tape is rewound or released.
             If you use the @MARK statement on a labeled tape immediately after
              @COPOUT, @COPY, or @MARK have written an EOF mark, you are creating a
              null file on the tape. A null file is a file that has Exec tape labeling system label
              blocks and EOF marks but does not have any user data blocks. A null file does
              not usually serve a useful purpose on a labeled tape.

7.39.@MODE and @@MODE—Change the Mode
      Settings for a Tape File
         The @MODE statement lets you change the hardware mode settings that were initially
         specified when a tape file was assigned. To change the mode settings, the file must
         be currently assigned to your run.

         You must be aware of the following two terms that are most important in this
         subsection:
             The Half-Inch Cartridge (HIC) tape that can be used to record 18-track or 36-track
              formatted data.
             The Digital Linear Tape (DLT)

             Linear Tape Open (LTO): This device is released as different generations of the
              Ultrium technology. To denote the different generations, the generation number is
              appended to LTO. Therefore, a sixth generation LTO device is referred to as LTO6.

         The only other way to change the mode settings for a file is to release the file from
         your run (@FREE) and then reassign it (@ASG).

         Format
             @MODE,options filename [,noise/processor/tape/format/
             data-converter/block-numbering/data-compression/
             buffered-write]

         All fields on the @MODE statement are optional except filename.

         options
              The system does not default to a particular option if none is specified. The
              specified options are not placed in the master file directory because they apply
              only to the current run.
              If you enter an invalid option, the statement is rejected. These are the options:

              E
                   Indicates even parity. This option is only allowed for 7-track tapes.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–169
@MODE and @@MODE—Change the Mode Settings for a Tape File




            H
                This option is available on 9-track and U9840D tape subsystems. If the density
                option "H" is specified with the general assign mnemonic "T", then one of the
                devices supporting the highest density that allows "H" density option is
                assumed by the Exec. This option is not available for other tape subsystems.
                With the "H" density option now allowed for two different tape types, such as
                9-track and U9840D; and these tapes selectable through the general assign
                mnemonic "T", the Exec’s selection sequence criteria remains basically the
                same except that either 9-track or U9840D would get assigned.

                The selection sequence is dependent on what is configured, available,
                premounted, and what is in the CONV default list for tape assignment
                mnemonics and how it is ordered.

                Note: The potential for a run stream compatibility issue, for files assigned
                using the general assign mnemonic T option and the H density option, exists
                if the CONV default has both U9840D and U9H devices on the system.

        The following variable error message is returned if an invalid density option is used:

          Assign mnemonic [asg_mnemonic] does not support density option [n].

            L

           Q

                Tapes created using 8- or 9-bit data compression cannot be used with Exec

                When you are reading a tape with EDRC compressed data, EDRC mode need

                Tapes created using EDRC data compression cannot be used with Exec

           device controlled by a control unit that has buffering capability.
           These are the allowable values:
           BUFTAP
                 Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks and file marks for the entire
                 tape.

           BUFFIL
                 Enables buffering of write data including label blocks and tape marks for a file
                 written to labeled tapes. The system ensures that writing of the data and file
                 marks occurs at the close of a file.

           BUFON
                 Enables buffered write mode for user data blocks.

           BUFOFF
                 Disables any buffered write mode.

           The @MODE statement is rejected if BUFTAP or BUFFIL is used and the device
           does not support tape mark buffering (TMB). Even though TMB is supported on
           the CTS5236, the BUFTAP value is not. The rejection message is
               E:256233 unit is not compatible with request.




7–174                                                                             7830 7949–031
                     @MODE and @@MODE—Change the Mode Settings for a Tape File




            The following rules apply when using BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, and BUFON:
                 When the user switches modes from BUFFIL to BUFON or BUFOFF, writing
                  the buffer to tape is postponed until the next I/O to the tape subsystem. This
                  also applies when switching modes from BUFTAP to other modes.
                 If BUFTAP, BUFFIL, BUFOFF, or BUFON is not specified, and the configuration
                  tag TAPBUF (dynamic name_tape_buffering) is zero, the system uses the
                  default value BUFON.
                 If BUFFIL is specified for an unlabeled tape, the data blocks for writes are
                  buffered and one synchronization per file is done by a WEF$ function, just as it
                  is without the BUFFIL specification.
                 When using TMB, it is the user’s responsibility to retain the original data for
                  possibly performing error recovery, if that is the user’s requirement. The Exec
                  provides no means for the user to recover this data. With the use of the
                  BUFTAP option, it is possible for the user to have received good status on
                  previous writes of thousands of files, when in fact none of the files has made
                  it to tape, and if an error occurs while they are being written to tape, the
                  remaining blocks in the tape subsystem’s buffer can never get written to tape.
                  The Block ID SAFE (BSAFE$) I/O function provides a means for the user to
                  determine what block has been actually written to tape by the tape
                  subsystem.
                 When using BUFTAP, an FSAFE$ can be performed at any point if a user wants
                  to ensure that buffered data/tape marks have been written to tape. It is highly
                  recommended that an FSAFE$ be performed and its status checked after all
                  user data/tape marks have been written to the tape device, but before
                  releasing the tape. This ensures that the user is notified of any errors in
                  writing any remaining buffered data/tape marks to the tape. This also allows
                  the user to know that an error on an @FREE, TSWAP$, TINTL$, or TLBL$ was
                  not the result of writing any user buffered data/tape marks to the tape.

         Example 1
           @MODE TAPE.,//////CMPEON

                The tape, assigned by a previous @ASG ECL statement as the file TAPE, explicitly
                requests EDRC data compression.

         Example 2
           @MODE,EL FILEY,30

                The E and L options override the mode settings initially assigned to FILEY. A new
                noise level of 30 is also specified for the file.

         Support for 4780 18- and 36-track tapes is provided by standard Exec. Compression on
         the 4780 subsystems is called improved cartridge recording capability (ICRC) and is
         totally compatible with the 5073 enhanced data recording capability (EDRC).

        Device characteristics for compressed tape readability are
            Unisys proprietary compressed cartridge tapes cannot be read on 4780 drives,

             only uncompressed cartridge tapes.
            The 4780 drives that have compression hardware can read EDRC compressed
             tapes without having to explicitly request CMPEON.

        Also, 36-track tapes have more capacity on current cartridges because data is written

7.40.@MOVE—Position Tape Files
        This command moves a magnetic tape file forward or backward over a specified
        number of hardware EOF marks.

        The filename parameter is required for the @MOVE statement. All other parameters in
        the @MOVE statement are optional.

        Format
            @MOVE[,options] filename[,number]

        options
             Specifying B moves the tape backward. Omitting B moves the tape forward.

             Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$
             on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be
             used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be
             input to a process later on in the runstream.

        filename
             Specifies the name of the tape file. This parameter is required.

        number
             Specifies the number of EOF marks to be skipped. If you do not specify number,
             FURPUR specifies 1.


7–176                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                                                           @MOVE—Position Tape Files




         When you direct FURPUR to move a tape forward, the move stops either at the
         beginning of a file or between the two EOF marks comprising an end-of-recorded area
         sentinel. FURPUR never moves the tape beyond the first EOF mark of a pair of EOF
         marks that constitute an ERA sentinel. If you attempt to move beyond an ERA sentinel,
         FURPUR positions the tape to this sentinel and informs you that the tape is positioned
         at the ERA sentinel.

         If FURPUR encounters a swap indicator during a forward move, it swaps to the next
         reel and continues the move forward on the next reel.

         Exercise care when moving tape in the backward direction. Assume that tape file BOB
         is positioned at file 6:

                        tape position                                          tape position


Tape            E            E               E            E            E            E            E
 file           O   File 1   O      File 2   O   File 3   O   File 4   O   File 5   O   File 6   O   File 7
BOB             F            F               F            F            F            F            F


                       Position A


                                 Figure 7–2. Positioning Tape Files

         To position the tape to the start of file 2, execute the following sequence:
           @MOVE,B BOB,5
           @MOVE BOB,1

         The first statement moves the tape to position A, and the second statement moves
         the tape to the start of file 2.

         If an @MOVE,B statement for a multireel tape file encounters the load point of the reel
         it is currently on, a diagnostic message is given and the ERR$ exit is taken.

         When you use a 1/4-inch cartridge tape subsystem, you cannot use an @MOVE,B
         statement. If you do, the operation is not performed and an appropriate error message
         is displayed.

7.41. @MSG and @@MSG—Send a Message to
      Various Console Types
        The @MSG statement sends a message to an I/O, communications,
        hardware-confidence, or system console from a run.

        Format
          @MSG[,options] message

        options

           C
                  Sends a message to a communications console.

           H
                  Sends a message to a hardware-confidence console.

           I
                  Sends a message to an I/O console.

           N
                  Suppresses message display. The message appears only in the user’s print
                  file. N option overrides W option and is used to place a comment in the print
                  file.

           S
                  Sends a message to the operator’s (system) console.

           W
                  Holds your run until the operator responds to your message. Your message
                  remains displayed on the operator’s console until the operator responds. For
                  all demand runs where the print file has not been breakpointed (BRKPT), the
                  response appears on your terminal. If the print file has been breakpointed,
                  the response appears in the breakpointed (BRKPT) file. If the @MSG,W is
                  from a batch run and the operator replies with an ’X’, then the run is aborted.
                  The message can be directed to one console category only. The order of
                  precedence is I, C, H, and S. If none of these options is present, the message
                  is displayed on the operator’s console.




7–178                                                                             7830 7949–031
                       @MSG and @@MSG—Send a Message to Various Console Types




         message
            Contains the message to be sent. The message can be up to 60 characters long,
            including embedded blanks. The first nonblank character is considered the
            beginning of the message. The end of the message is the last character before the
            end of a line, before a comment (.), or within the 60-character limit.
            The message cannot begin with a comma ( , ) or a slash ( / ). The @MSG can
            include the continuation character ( ; ) or blank-period-blank ( . ) which introduces a
            comment, but the @@MSG cannot include either character. Keep your messages
            as concise as possible.

         When the message is displayed, it is prefixed with your run-ID and is entirely in
         uppercase letters, regardless of whether you used uppercase or lowercase letters
         when you entered it.

         Examples
           @MSG,I EXPECT 2 REELS OF OUTPUT FOR FILE XYZ

                Illustrates a 37-character message to be displayed at the I/O console (I option).
                The message is strictly informational, and no operator response is expected.

           @MSG,W IS REMOTE HOOKUP READY? . Answer required

                This 23-character message requires a reply from the operator (W option). Since
                no particular console has been specified, the message is displayed on the
                operator’s console. Run processing does not continue until the operator replies

7.42. @@NOPR—Terminate a Local Printer
         The @@NOPR statement terminates output to a local printer.

         Use this statement after an @@PRNT statement. The @@NOPR statement causes
         subsequent output to be sent only to the terminal.

         Format
           @@NOPR

         Example
           @@PRNT
           This list of filenames ...
            .
            .
            .
           @@NOPR

         An @@PRNT statement is terminated with the @@NOPR statement. The text following
         the @@NOPR statement is sent only to the terminal.


7.43.@PACK—Remove Deleted Elements
         The Pack command rewrites an entire program file, removing specified types of
         elements (depending on the options specified) and all elements marked as deleted.
         The @COPOUT and @COPY,P statements (see Sections 7.13 and 7.14.1) have the same
         effect on output files since they do not copy deleted elements. Mass storage space
         that is no longer needed is returned to the system.

         The FURPUR @PACK command is used with large program files to remove elements in
         the file which have previously been marked as deleted. The D, L, and M options on the
         @PACK statement are not supported for large program files. If entered, these options
         are allowed, but are ignored.

         FURPUR calls the PACK function in Program-Callable FURPUR (PCFP) to perform the
         pack operation on large program files. For this reason, updated levels of both products
         must be installed concurrently to pack large program files.

         The FURPUR @PACK command can also be used with large element program files
         (LEPFs). See Section 3.7 for more information on LEPFs.

         All parameters in the @PACK statement are optional.

         Format
           @PACK[,options] [filename-1,filename-2,...,filename-n, subtype-list]

         filename-n
            Specifies the program files to be packed.




7830 7949–031                                                                             7–181
@PACK—Remove Deleted Elements




        subtype-list
           Use the last specification to specify the subtype mnemonics of executable
           elements when you specify the AY option combination.

        options
           None
               Used to remove all deleted elements and release all unused granules except
               those granules initially reserved. If granule zero remains allocated (see N option)
               and there are no nondeleted elements, the first sector is zero-filled.
           A
               Used to remove all elements except nondeleted executable elements.
           C
               Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.
               Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
               ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
               should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
               command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.
               The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.
           D
               Used in conjunction with the M option to inhibit creation of entry-point tables.
               This option is ignored if no M option is specified
           I
               Used to release all unused granules including initial reserve.

           L
               Used to print diagnostic messages if any duplicate relocatable entry points are
               found. (Used only when a prep is done as part of the @PACK command. Also
               see D, M, and P options.)

           M
               Used to create a minimum-size table of contents by starting each program file
               table in the sector following the previous nonempty program file table. The
               element text is started in the first track not used for the table of contents. Both
               a relocatable and an object module entry-point table are created unless the D
               option is specified.
               After an @PACK,M statement, the room to add new elements to the program
               file is highly restricted. If any procedure tables exist or an entry point table was
               created, you can be able to add one or two elements, if any at all, because the
               next table starts at the next available sector. If no procedures or relocatable
               entry points exist, the space available to add new elements varies up to a track,
               which allows up to 179 entries in the element table. This is due to the starting
               element text address being forced to a track boundary.




7–182                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                        @PACK—Remove Deleted Elements




                 If you want to expand the table of contents, you must transfer the elements to
                 another file. You can use @COPY,P or @COPOUT statements for this transfer.
                 Alternatively, you can delete existing elements followed by an @PACK
                 statement without the M option.

             N
                 Used to prevent the release of any granules.
             O
                 Used to remove all elements except nondeleted omnibus elements.
             P
                 Used to create both entry-point tables. The prep is done before FURPUR
                 releases unused space. The P option is assumed if the M option is specified and
                 the D option is not specified.
             R
                 Used to remove all elements except nondeleted relocatable elements.
             S
                 Used to remove all elements except nondeleted symbolic elements.
             Y
                 Used in conjunction with the A option to cause FURPUR to save all executable
                 elements with a subtype that matches one of the subtypes specified in the
                 subtype list.
             Z
                 Used to zero out granules released during the @PACK process.

         Note: The D, L, and M options are not supported for large program files. If
         entered, these options are allowed, but are ignored.

         You can specify any combination of A, O, R, and S options; or, if you want to select
         executable subtypes, you can select the AY option combination. If you specify no
         options, FURPUR removes only all deleted elements.

         Thus, FURPUR stops the pack process to prevent destroying your file.

         Normal Termination
         If the file has position granularity, the term "FILE SIZE" in the completion message is
         the number of positions required to contain the program file.

         If the file has track granularity, the term "TEXT" in the completion message is the
         number of tracks required to contain the element text, and TOC is the number of
         tracks required to contain the table of contents.

         The number of elements of each element type is printed at termination.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–183
@PASSWD and @@PASSWD—Use and Change Passwords




        Abnormal Termination
        The @@X T or @@TERM operator commands or system stops cause abnormal
        termination resulting in possible loss of data. You must examine the file to verify that
        all elements are complete.

        Packing a Large Program File
        When the file that you specify on the @PACK statement is a large program file (LPF),
        FURPUR calls PCFP to pack the file. During this operation, PCFP utilizes a temporary
        file, whose size is equal to the length of the file being packed, as a temporary storage
        for all of the elements to be retained. B.7 describes the error messages for all of the
        possible errors that can be encountered during the pack of an LPF.


7.44.@PASSWD and @@PASSWD—Use and Change
      Passwords
        In batch mode, you supply your user-ID on the @RUN statement, and your password
        and executing clearance level on the @PASSWD statement. You can place the
        @PASSWD statement anywhere in the runstream between the @RUN statement and
        the @FIN statement. For batch runstreams initiated with a @START statement, the
        @PASSWD statement is not required and if it is found, it is ignored.

        Long passwords, both case-sensitive and case-insensitive, are accepted on
        @PASSWD and @@PASSWD statements.

        The current state of password case sensitivity is maintained when an @@PASSWD is
        performed. For example, if the user’s password is case-sensitive at the time of
        @@PASSWD, the new password is also case-sensitive.

        You can include several @PASSWD statements in the same runstream. However, if
        any of the passwords are illegal, the system terminates your run. If more than one
        @PASSWD statement is in error, the error associated with the first incorrect
        @PASSWD statement is placed in your run’s print file.

        Do not place the @PASSWD statement within an @ADD file. This compromises the
        secrecy of your password, and the system ignores the @PASSWD statement anyway.

        When you use the @START statement to execute a batch run, do not include an
        @PASSWD statement in the created runstream. If you do, security is compromised
        because the password is made visible. In addition, the @PASSWD statement is always
        ignored when this situation occurs.

        Notes:

           You cannot use the @PASSWD statement to change passwords if the
            machine-generated passwords feature is implemented at your site. The
            @PASSWD statement is still valid for password validation in batch mode.
           If your system has Fundamental Security, this subsection can or cannot be
            applicable, depending on how your system is configured.




7–184                                                                             7830 7949–031
                              @PASSWD and @@PASSWD—Use and Change Passwords




             If your site has Security Level 1 or higher, this subsection is applicable. Check
              with your security officer if you are not sure of your security level.
         Format
         The format of the @PASSWD statement is

             @PASSWD[,N] old-password[/new-password] [clearance level,comp-1/comp2.../comp-n]


         N
              Indicates the old-password/new-password field is not present. The N option can
              only be specified in @RUN,/B or @@INQ runstreams.
         old password
              Is the current password for your user-ID.
         new password
              Is your new password, if you are changing your password. Do not include any
              blank character spaces between the slash (/) and the old and new passwords (old
              password/new password).
         clearance-level
              If your site has Security Level 1 or higher, you can specify an executing clearance
              level. The clearance level you specify must be in your clearance level range. If you
              do not specify a clearance level, it is set to the minimum clearance level in your
              range.
              If you enter more than one @PASSWD statement, the system uses the clearance
              level specified or assumed on the last @PASSWD statement in the runstream as
              the clearance level for the entire run.

         comp-n
              If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, you can use this field to supply
              compartment information on the @PASSWD statement. If you cannot fit all the
              compartment names on one line, use a semicolon (;) as the continuation character.
              The continuation character cannot appear before the first compartment name.

         If you enter more than one @PASSWD statement in the batch runstream, the
         compartment set associated with the last @PASSWD statement processed is the set
         associated with your run.

         You can specify the null compartment set by entering "NULL," or you can specify your
         maximum compartment set by entering "MAX." If you enter the @PASSWD statement
         with no compartments listed, your default compartment set is given to your run. The
         maximum or default compartment sets are given to your run at the time it is put into
         backlog.

         If your system has the compartment feature, and your user compartment set changes
         while your run is in backlog, the run terminates in error when it comes out of backlog.
         This happens because the READ$ file cannot be assigned by the run. You receive this
         message:
             READ$FILE REJECT STATUS 264733


7830 7949–031                                                                                7–185
@PASSWD and @@PASSWD—Use and Change Passwords




        For example, you are executing with compartments A, B, and C. While a run you
        entered is in backlog, the security officer removes compartment C from your user
        compartment set. The run comes out of backlog and terminates in error because the
        READ$ file has compartments A, B, and C associated with it and you are no longer
        executing with compartment C.

        If you make any errors in the password or clearance level fields of the @PASSWD
        statement, you do not receive any messages on the compartments field, whether or
        not you enter the compartment information correctly.

        The clearance level and compartment set security attributes are displayed in the print
        file following the @RUN statement. Messages regarding password replacement or
        compartment set validation follow the display of the mandatory attributes.

        Examples
        Here is an example of using an @PASSWD statement with a remote batch run:
          @RUN,/B BCD,802910,CAPRICORN
           .
           .
           .
           .
          @PASSWD OMNI/RUXMEN 10,PAYROLL
           .
           .

        These are examples of using compartments with the @PASSWD statement:
          @PASSWD RQZ ,PAYROLL/ACCOUNTING/INVENTORY

          @PASSWD RQZ 63,PAYROLL/;
          ACCOUNTING/;
          INVENTORY

          @PASSWD RQZ HIGHCL,PAYROLL/TOPSECRET

        Changing Your Password Using @@PASSWD
        The @@PASSWD statement lets you change your password in demand on systems
        where it is allowed. The system administrator may disallow it because of the risk that
        an unauthorized person might see the password on the screen as it is being entered.
        Unlike the response to the initial user-id/password solicitation, which can be blanked
        out to protect its confidentiality, the system is unable to prevent the display of the
        characters you enter in the @@PASSWD statement. The administrator might also
        disallow the use of @@PASSWD because it conflicts with the user of Configured
        Password Profiles. @@PASSWD is never allowed in Security Level 3. Attempts to
        change your password on a system where it is not allowed returns the error
          System configuration disallows password changes by @@PASSWD.

        Format
          @@PASSWD old-password/new-password




7–186                                                                           7830 7949–031
                              @PASSWD and @@PASSWD—Use and Change Passwords




         For example, the following statement changes your password from QMKE to PAX01.
           @@PASSWD QMKE/PAX01


                                                Caution
                The password specified in an @@PASSWD statement is visible to
                observers. Security can be compromised if you execute this statement.
                The most secure way to change your password is during sign-on.



         A demand terminal is user authenticated before the user is allowed to enter a batch
         runstream by using the @RUN,/B statement. The same user-ID is required on the
         @RUN,/B image or the run is removed. To allow a user-ID with a nonzero
         authentication type access to the @RUN,/B interface, an N option exists for the
         @PASSWD statement to indicate that the password/newpassword field is not
         present. An @PASSWD,N statement with no parameters indicates the defaults for
         clearance level and compartment sets must be used. The user can optionally specify
         other than default clearance level or compartment sets.

         The N option is available to all @RUN,/B users regardless of authentication type. If the
         @RUN,/B runstream contains an @PASSWD image without the N option, the
         verification for password still takes place. If the user-ID is not an Exec authentication
         type (AT=0), the run is removed with the following error message:
           @PASSWD ERROR: Userid's authentication type is not valid for batch.

7.45. @PCH—Punch Program File Elements
        The @PCH command creates 80-column card images from program file elements.

        All parameters in the @PCH statement are optional except element-name.

        Format
          @PCH[,options] element-name[,sequence-character]

        options

           Can be one or more of the following options:
           A,O,R,S
                  Specify the type of element to be processed. Any combination of A, O, R, or
                  S can be used, but at least one must be given. See Section 6.4 for additional
                  information on these options.
           C
                  Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.
                  Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
                  ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
                  should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
                  command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.
           Q
                  Set punch control to create ASCII card images.


           You can use the following options only in conjunction with the S option:
           D
                  Set data mode to allow statement images to be read by the ELT processor.
                  FURPUR generates an @ELT,ID statement with F$S in the parameter field 3
                  as the end sentinel. The last card image created contains the corresponding
                  end sentinel (@END F$S).
           G
                  Produce output containing compressed symbolic images. Compressed
                  symbolic output is produced only in Fieldata code. ASCII code images are
                  first converted to Fieldata code.
           H
                  Place sequence number into columns 73 to 80 of each image. The
                  sequence-character must contain an alphabetic sequence from 1 to 3
                  characters. The characters are left-justified and overlay columns 73 to 80.




7–188                                                                            7830 7949–031
                                                     @PCH—Punch Program File Elements




            J
                   Compress input images and sequence output card images in columns 73 to
                   80.

                   Note: Do not specify the G and J options in the same statement.

         element-name
            Specifies the element to be processed.

         sequence-character
            Specifies the alphabetic sequencing characters when you choose the H option.

         Description
         Card readers and card punches are no longer supported. @PCH is supported for
         compatibility with existing runstreams. @PCH output can be directed to a file by
         @BRKPT PUNCH$/filename ... @PCH command ... @BRKPT PUNCH$, but its use is
         discouraged. The FURPUR processor ensures that the input elements contain the
         control statements needed to reinsert the elements a program file with the same
         name in a later run. The first image of the procedure element is an @PDP,I control
         statement. For all other elements, it is an @ELT,I statement. The file name on the
         @PDP or @ELT control statement is the name of the file from which the element was
         created.

         Relocatable and executable elements are automatically (without special option)
         sequenced in columns 79 to 80. Sequencing starts with AA and ends with ZZ, starting
         over with AA if necessary. If you specify the H option, FURPUR sequences symbolic
         images in columns 76 to 80. The card sequence is 100 apart and is preceded by the
         designated alphabetic string given in the sequence-character field on the @PCH
         statement.

         The output is either preceded by a properly formatted @ELT,I statement or an @PDP,I
         statement. The command statement images produced by @PCH have the same
         element name as the @PCH statement. Thus, if you assign the file containing the
         element that was created by @PCH to a subsequent run, all that is necessary to
         reintroduce the element is to include the images produced by the @PCH statement in
         the runstream.

         Examples
         The following examples illustrate the use of the @PCH statement:

           @PCH,S UPDATE.RUNPROG

                Symbolic element RUNPROG in program file UPDATE is copied and transformed
                onto 80-column card images.

           @PCH,SRJH A.B,XYZ

                Symbolic element B of program file A is transformed into 80-column card
                images. The input images are sequenced in columns 76 to 80. The identification



7830 7949–031                                                                            7–189
@@PMOD—Control Output Sent to a Printer Connected to Your Terminal




               sequence, XYZ, is placed into columns 73 to 75. The input images are also
               compressed.
               Relocatable element B of program file A is also transformed and output. The
               text has been previously sequenced, and the FURPUR processor sequences the
               preamble.


7.46.@@PMOD—Control Output Sent to a Printer
      Connected to Your Terminal
        By defining the peripheral mode operations, the @@PMOD statement lets you control
        the way in which data is sent from a UTS 400 terminal in demand mode to a printer.
        To return to print transparent mode (normal mode), enter @@NOPR.

        Format
          @@PMOD [function]

        function
           Can be one or more of the following:
           F
               Prints form; the terminal handler uses the print form function to send data to
               the printer.

           P
               Prints all; the terminal handler uses the print function to send data to the printer.

           X
               Prints transparent; the terminal handler uses the print transparent function to
               send data to the printer (default).

        Example
          @@PMOD P

        Sends all characters between the SOE (or home position) and the cursor to the printer
        (except FCC sequences).


7.47. @PREP—Create Entry-Point Tables
        Using the PREP command creates relocatable and object module entry-point tables
        from the preambles of relocatable elements and from the control information in object
        modules.

        All parameters in the @PREP statement are optional.

        Format
          @PREP[,options] [filename-1,filename-2,...,filename-n]




7–190                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                              @@PRNT—Start a Local Printer




         options

             C
                   Used to direct FURPUR not to exit through ERR$ if an error is encountered.

                   Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER
                   ERR$ on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option
                   should be used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR
                   command could be input to a process later on in the runstream.

                   The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands.

             F
                   Forces a prep of a file. Without the F option, FURPUR does not perform a
                   prep if an entry-point table already exists.

             L
                   Prints duplicate relocatable entry points found with the sequence numbers of
                   the corresponding elements.

         filename-n specifies the program files for which entry-point tables are to be created.

         The addition of a relocatable element into a program file or the deletion of a
         relocatable element from a program file destroys any existing relocatable entry-point
         table in that file. The object module entry-point table is unaffected by the addition of
         an object module to a program file, and the deletion of an object module only causes
         the entry points of that element to be lost from the object module entry-point table.

         If the @PREP operation is unsuccessful because there are too many relocatable entry
         points for the space allocated to the relocatable entry-point table, use the @PACK,M
         statement on the file (see Section 7.43). Note that because the object module entry-
         point table exists in the text area of a program file, it is essentially open-ended and is
         bounded only by the "MAX" size of the file. Because of this, the object module
         entry-point table is never too small for object module entry points on which an @PREP
         statement has been used.

         The visibility of entry points not contained in an entry point table depends on the type
         of entry point. A relocatable entry point is not visible unless it exists within the
         relocatable entry-point table. In contrast, an object module entry point need not be in
         the object module entry-point table for it to be visible to the Linking System. The only
         advantage in performing a prep (@PREP statement) of object module entry points is
         that the Linking System can resolve link faults and external references faster when the
         associated entry points are contained in the object module entry-point table.


7.48.@@PRNT—Start a Local Printer
         The @@PRNT statement directs output to both the terminal and a local printer (a
         printer connected directly to a terminal). All output following the @@PRNT statement
         is sent to both the terminal and the local printer.

         Terminate @@PRNT with an @@NOPR statement.


7830 7949–031                                                                                7–191
@PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




        Format
          @@PRNT

        Example
          @@PRNT
          output from statements here goes to both the printer and the terminal

        The text following the @@PRNT statement is sent to the printer and to the terminal.


7.49.@PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File
      Directory
        Obtains a listing of the text of a symbolic element, the table of contents of a program
        file, information regarding temporary files, or the master file directory items of
        cataloged files. The statement does not list executable, omnibus, or relocatable
        elements. You can list these elements with the LIST processor.

        All parameters in the @PRT statement are optional.

        Format
          @PRT[,options] [name-1,name-2,...,name-n]

        options

        name-n

                 The name of a cataloged file in any format
                 The name of a program file
                 The name of an element
                 The name of a temporary file
                 An account number
                 A project-ID
                 A removable disk pack-ID and disk equipment type
                 The number of elements to print
                 A subtype list

           When name-n is a subtype list or the number of elements to print, it must be the
           last specification on the statement.

            You also see displayed all owned cataloged files with the account number of the
            requesting run, if the user-ID of the requesting run is the owner of these files.
            They are sorted alphanumerically by project-ID. (Read/write keys are not
            displayed.) If the M option is specified and if this is either a batch run or if the L
            option is specified, then the output format is the same as for @PRT,F.

            If the shared subsystem is not available when you perform the @PRT,N statement,
            FURPUR displays the following message:

              FILES WITH SPECIFIED PROJECTS ON SHARED SUBSYSTEM ARE NOT AVAILABLE.

        P
            Used to display by project-ID. When the requesting run is privileged, the lack of a
            name field causes the entire master file directory to be displayed and sorted
            alphanumerically by project-ID. When name fields are specified, only the files
            cataloged with the specified project-ID are displayed. They are sorted in the order
            specified in the name fields.
            When you are in nonprivileged mode, you do not need to specify a name field. If
            you do, FURPUR ignores it. In this mode, you see all unowned cataloged files with
            the project-ID of the requesting run displayed. You also see all owned cataloged
            files with the project-ID of the requesting run, if the user-ID of the requesting run
            is the owner of these files. (Read/write keys are not displayed.) If the M option is
            specified and if this is a batch run or if the L option is specified, then the output
            format is the same as for @PRT,F.
            If the shared subsystem is not available when you perform the @PRT,P statement,
            FURPUR displays the following message:
              FILES WITH SPECIFIED PROJECTS ON SHARED SUBSYSTEM ARE NOT AVAILABLE.

        T
            Used to display the table of contents for each specified program file or program
            file element.




7–196                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                  @PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




         U
             Used to display the current usage of the removable disk pack specified. The name
             fields are the same as the @PRT,D statement. The output consists of the first line
             of the @PRT,D output, which displays pack-ID, tracks available, and current
             number of assigns. If file sharing is configured, the output consists of the first two
             lines of the @PRT,D output, the second line displaying the DIRECTORY keyword,
             and the name of the directory associated with the pack.

         V
             Used in conjunction with the T option to list the table of contents for elements
             with the same version name as specified in the name field. When the version
             name is omitted from the name field, only those elements having a blank version
             name are listed. The V option can be used with any combination of A, B, O, R, and
             S options, but must be accompanied by the T option.

         Y
             When you specify this option, you must also specify the A option and, at the end
             of the statement, the subtype list. You use the AY option combination to limit the
             display of elements in a program file to executable elements that have a subtype
             matching one of the subtypes specified in the subtype list.

7.49.1. @PRT,F Output Format
         You can use @PRT,F to output information about cataloged and temporary mass
         storage and tape files. FURPUR uses a number of information sources to gather the
         information presented. Different information is presented for each file type, as
         described in detail under the topics below. Each bullet describes the information on
         one output line.

         Date and Time reporting
         @PRT,F reports date and time information related to files using the Unisys standard
         time display format yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss [zone]. The zone mnemonic is left blank
         when the time zone mnemonic is not available. This occurs when the source
         timestamp is in TDATE$ format.

         Cataloged Mass Storage Files
         For cataloged mass storage files most of the information comes from the MFD entry
         for the file. Some file assignment and file caching information is gathered from other
         sources. The following information is output:

            STD or SHARED, the directory for the file if file sharing is configured.

            The project-ID and account number for the file.

            The complete name of the file, including qualifier, filename, F-cycle, optional read
             key and optional write key. The assign mnemonic, initial reserve, granularity and
             maximum size. If this is a removable disk file, the pack-IDs for the file.




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–197
@PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




           The ‘MODES:’ line containing a list of the following file modes, separated by
            commas:

            o    PUBLIC, PRIVATE or SEMI-PRIVATE, the file privacy,

            o    WRITE if the file is write-only.

            o    READ if the file is read-only.

            o    X-USE if the file is assigned exclusively.

            o    a-OPT for each of the options C, D, G, K, S, U, and V with which the file is
                 cataloged or assigned.

            o    DROP if the file is marked as to-be-deleted.

            o    UNLOD if the mass storage has been unloaded to tape.

            o    DATA-DSABLD if the file is data disabled because of a cache destage failure
                 on an XPC.

            o    DSABL if the file is hardware disabled, software disabled, or FAS disabled.

            o    ASG-D if the file is assigned to any run.

            o    SYM if the file is on a symbiont queue.

            o    ENCRYPT if the file is encrypted.

           The file owner user-ID if the file is owned. The file ACR if the file is semi-private.
            The ACR owner user-ID or UNOWNED, if the file is semi-private and if either the
            file is unowned or the ACR is unowned.

           One of the following file caching statuses if XPC file caching is configured:

                CACHED-ON: xpc-name,SPEC=spec
                NOT-CACHED DUE TO reason,SPEC=spec
                CACHING STATE AND DEVICE NAME NOT AVAILABLE,SPEC=D
                FILECACHING INFORMATION NOT AVAILABLE-FILECACHE$ ERROR: status OCCURRED.

           The number of granules assigned. The number of granules assigned to each of the
            eight groups (GP1 through GP8) if the file is loaded. The number of granules
            backed up to tape by FAS if the file is unloaded.

           The highest granule assigned and the total number of file assignments.

           The highest track written.

           The file catalog date and time and the last reference date and time.

           The backup date and time if the file has been backed up by FAS. NOT-CURRENT if
            the file has been updated since it was backed up.


7–198                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                   @PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




             A descriptive line for each file disable if the file is software disabled, hardware
              disabled, FAS disabled or data disabled.

             * * PROJ: DEV                ACCNT: 298631       * *
             DEV*TESTFILE(1),FSCSI/100/TRK/999,SPAR02/SPAR03

         Cataloged Tape Files
         For cataloged tape files many of the tape specifications in the MFD entry for the file
         can be dynamically changed with the @ASG and @MODE statements. FURPUR gathers
         the information that currently applies when a tape file is assigned to the run. The
         following information is output:

             STD or SHARED, the directory for the file if file sharing is configured.

             The project-ID and account number for the file.

             The complete name of the file, including qualifier, filename, F-cycle, optional read
              key and optional write key. The assign mnemonic. The volume-IDs for the file.
              ‘(LTOn)’ immediately follows a volume-ID if this is an LTO tape file and if the
              volume is currently mounted. It identifies the type of LTO cartridge that is
              mounted.

             The ‘MODES:’ line containing the same list of file modes as shown for cataloged
              mass storage files. The UNLOD and DATA-DSABLD modes do not apply to
              cataloged tape files.

            The file owner user-ID if the file is owned. The file ACR if the file is semi-private.

            The ‘TAPEMODES:’ line containing a list of the following tape modes:

             o   The density and parity if this is an open reel tape, VTH virtual tape, or DVD.

             o   The buffered-write mode if this is a half-inch cartridge tape. In addition to the

                 cataloged tape file is not assigned to the run and the buffered-write mode is

             o   Q-WORD or 8-BIT, the data transfer format.

             o   The processor/tape translation, if specified.

             o   DC if data converter is specified.

             o   BLKON if block numbering is specified.

             o   CMPON, CMPEON, or CMPLON if data compression is specified.

             o   EBCOPT if expanded buffer is specified.

             o   CTL=name if a cartridge tape library pool name is specified.

            The file catalog date and time and the last reference date and time.

            The backup date and time if the file has been backed up by FAS.

        For temporary sector-addressable mass storage files, the following information is

         For temporary tape files, the following information is output:

              ‘(LTOn)’ immediately follows if this is an LTO tape file and if the volume is

7.49.2. Listing the Master File Directory
         The @PRT statement reports the files from the local MFD and from the shared MFD, if
         a shared directory is available. For @PRT, the @QUAL,D statement does not affect the
         selection of directories.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–201
@PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




        You can select a subset of MFD files by using the N or P options. You can also limit
        the selected files to specified removable pack(s) by using the D option. See Section
        7.48 “Description of Options” topic.

        The long report (using the L option or in batch mode) formats each selected file in a
        format similar to @PRT,F. Otherwise, the short format provides a one line summary for
        each selected file.

        If the requesting run is nonprivileged, slashes replace all read and write keys, as well
        as all project-IDs and account numbers not matching the run to protect exposure of
        sensitive data.

7.49.3. Listing the Table of Contents
        The @PRT,T statement is used to output information from the table of contents of
        program files. Refer to Sections 3.8.4 through 3.8.7 for additional information about
        program files. The @PRT,T statement provides the following three levels of
        information detail.

           Long format (@PRT,TL)
           Short format (@PRT,T)
           Summary format (@PRT,TN)

        If both the L option and the N option are specified, long format is selected and the N
        option is ignored.

        The following describes, in order, the @PRT,T output and indicates for which formats
        the information is produced:

               File and element summary information–all formats
               Element Table information–long and short formats; the elements selected for
                output depends on the format, the presence of an element name, and the
                presence of the A, B, O, R, S, V, and Y options.
               Procedure Table information–long format; when element name and the A, B,
                O, R, S, V, and Y options are not included.
               Relocatable Entry Point Table information–long format; when element name
                and the A, B, O, R, S, V, and Y options are not included.
               Object Module Entry Point Table information–long format; when the table is
                present, when element name, and the A, B, O, R, S, V, and Y options are not
                included.
               Invalid Element Table Entry Count –long format only; this is only produced if
                the long format element table validation finds invalid values in element table
                entry fields.
               Deleted element summary information–all formats when the file contains at
                least one deleted element.




7–202                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                @PRT—List Files, Elements, and Master File Directory




File and Element Summary Information
            The summary information output for all formats is as follows:

                filename type, a/b elements, c/d tracks

            where:

            filename

                The name of the file in format: directory-id#qualifier*filename(F-cycle)

            type

                The program file type that can have a value of “PF”, “LPF”, “Standard LEPF”, or
                “Large LEPF”. Refer to Section 3.8.4 for additional information about program
                file types.

            a

                The number of elements in the program file, including deleted elements.

            b

                The maximum number of elements that could possibly be contained in the
                program file based on the current allocation.

            c

                The number of tracks occupied by program file tables and text.

            d

                The maximum number of tracks for the file.

            You can use the @PACK statement when the current number of elements or
            tracks approach their respective maximum values. Refer to the Section 7.43 for a
            detailed description of @PACK.

Element Table information (Long Format)
            For long format, a column header line is output to identify the element information.
            One element is output for each line. The following is a description of the column
            headers and contents:

            D

                The deleted element flag. An asterisk ( * ) appears in this column if the
                element has been replaced by another element with the same element name,
                version name, and element type. Refer to the Section 7.18.3 for information on
                undeleting elements.

        NAME and VERSION

            The element name and version name, respectively. Version name can be spaces.

        TYPE

            The element type. The basic element types are executable, omnibus, relocatable,
            and symbolic. Executable, omnibus, and symbolic types can also have subtypes.
            The element type and, if available, subtype appear in this column. For symbolic
            elements, “-Q” is appended to the type and subtype, if the element is marked as
            being in the ASCII character set.

        DATE and TIME

            The date and time in the format yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss [zone]. The zone is blank
            when the time zone mnemonic is not available. This occurs when the source
            timestamp is in TDATE$ format. Usually denotes the date and time when the
            element was originally created.

        SEQUENCE NUMBER

            The sequence number of the element in the file. Elements are numbered
            sequentially beginning with 1.

        PREAMBLE SIZE

            This field applies only to relocatable elements. The number of sectors of
            relocatable preamble text in the element.

        TEXT SIZE

            The number of sectors of element text.

        CYCLE WORD

            The element cycle information is present only for symbolic elements. Three
            columnar fields for the cycle information are shown.

               MAX Maximum number of element cycles
               CUR Current absolute cycle number
               NUM Number of element cycles present

         FLAG BITS

                  BOTH If the element is both quarter-word and third-word sensitive.

             The arithmetic fault mode values can be:

Element Table Information (Short Format)

             The (s-cycle) field is present only for symbolic elements and is the current

Procedure Table Information
        Procedure Table information is produced only for long format when element name and
        the A, B, O, R, S, V, and Y options are not included.

        A program file can have, in order, an Assembler Procedure Table, a COBOL Procedure
        Table, and a FORTRAN/PLUS Procedure Table. If a table does not have any entries, the
        following is output:

            table-name EMPTY

        If a table has entries, a column header line is output to identify the procedure
        information. The entries are sorted by procedure name before they are output.
        FURPUR sorts blocks of 1,680 Assembler Procedure Table entries, 839 COBOL
        Procedure Table entries, and 1,680 FORTRAN/PLUS Procedure Table entries. If a table
        exceeds this number of entries, then a separator line with 12 asterisks ( * ) is output,
        followed by the next block of procedure table entries. Each block is sorted separately.
        For the Assembler Procedure Table and the FORTRAN/PLUS Procedure Table, three
        procedure entries are output per line. For the COBOL Procedure Table, two procedure
        entries are output per line.

        Procedure entries in these tables are associated with symbolic procedure elements.
        Assembler Procedure Table entries are associated with element type ASM PROC.
        COBOL Procedure Table entries are associated with element type COB PROC.
        FORTRAN/PLUS Procedure Table entries are associated with element types FOR
        PROC and PSP SYMB.

        The following is description of the column headers and contents:

        D

             The deleted entry flag. An asterisk ( * ) appears in this column if the procedure
             entry and the element associated with it are marked as deleted.

        NAME

             The procedure name. Assembler and FORTRAN/PLUS procedures names can be
             up to 12 characters and COBOL procedure names can be up to 30 characters.

        LOCATION

             The word location of the start of the symbolic procedure text, relative to the start
             of the file. This location is always within the element text of the associated
             procedure element.

        LINK

             The sequence number of the associated procedure element.

         If the table does not have any entries, the following is output:

             RELOCATABLE ENTRY POINT TABLE EMPTY

         If the table has entries, a column header line is output to identify the entry point
         information. The entries are sorted by entry point name before they are output.
         FURPUR sorts blocks of 1,680 Relocatable Entry Point Table entries. If the table

         followed by the next block of Relocatable Entry Point Table entries. Each block is

         Object Module Entry Point Table information is produced only for long format when
         the table is present and when element name and the A, B, O, R, S, V, and Y options are

                 The non-prepped Object Module Entry Point Table lists entry points for object
                  modules added to the file after the last @PREP or @PACK,P or all entry points
                  if neither @PREP nor @PACK,P is performed.
                 The duplicate Object Module Entry Point Table lists entry points that are

        Additional verification of each selected element table entry is performed when the
        long format is requested. Errors are reported for each element and are summarized
        when the program file has been completely processed.

        Fields that are verified are listed in the following table.


        Validated Field                How error conditions are indicated

         TYPE               Illegal element types are reported as type *UNDEFINED*
         DATE and TIME      The DATE and TIME fields contain the text:
                               *ERR* e1, e2
                            Where:
                                e1 is the AEDIT$ error code.
                                   See the SYSLIB Programming Reference Manual (7833 1733).
                                e2 is the timestamp that is in error.
                            Both errors are reported in octal.
         TEXT SIZE          If the element size is illegal, then asterisks indicate the condition.

            *File contains 1 invalid element table entry
            *File contains n invalid element table entries
