7.50. @QUAL and @@QUAL—Specify a Qualifier or
       Directory for File Names
         The @QUAL statement lets you use implied directory-IDs or qualifier names for
         subsequent control statements involving references to external file names.

         You can change the following with the @QUAL statement:
             The default directory-ID
             The implied directory-ID
             The default qualifier
             The implied qualifier

         The default directory-ID and default qualifier are the directory-ID and qualifier given on
         the last @QUAL,D statement performed in a run. The implied directory-ID and implied
         qualifier are the directory-ID and qualifier given on the last @QUAL (with no options)
         performed in a run.

         Any number of @QUAL statements can appear throughout the runstream. Each time
         an @QUAL (with no options) statement is encountered, the new directory-ID or
         qualifier overrides the implied directory-ID or qualifier specified on a previous @QUAL
         (with no options) statement. Each time an @QUAL,D statement is encountered, the
         new directory-ID or qualifier overrides the default directory-ID or qualifier specified on
         a previous @QUAL,D statement.

         Format
             @QUAL[,options] [directory-id#][qualifier]




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–215
@QUAL and @@QUAL—Specify a Qualifier or Directory for File Names




        options

            D
                    Specifies the default directory-ID or qualifier. When you specify the
                    directory-ID, your run’s default directory is set to it. When you specify the
                    qualifier, your run’s default qualifier is set to it.

            R
                    Reverts your run’s default and implied directory-ID and qualifier back to the
                    values they had when your run started. When you use this option, you cannot
                    specify a directory-ID or qualifier.

            You can use only one option.

            If you do not specify an option, you must include a directory-ID, qualifier, or both.
            If you give the directory-ID, your run’s implied directory-ID is set to it. If you give
            the qualifier, your run’s implied qualifier is set to it.

        directory-id
            Specifies the master file directory used on subsequent file names that do not
            specify a directory-ID.


                                                  Caution
                If you change the default directory-ID to SHARED, it affects all file name
                references (except for the references that explicitly specify a directory-ID),
                including assign requests issued by the Exec. This can cause errors on
                subsequent control statements, processor calls, and alternate library
                references.



        qualifier
            Specifies the name extension used to qualify subsequent file names.
            The qualifier must follow the rules given in the explanation of naming files.
                     @ASG,A STD#PROJECTID*FILEA(2).




7–216                                                                                7830 7949–031
                @QUAL and @@QUAL—Specify a Qualifier or Directory for File Names




7.50.1. Initial and Default Values
         Before a run opens, the implied and default qualifiers are initialized to a run’s
         project-ID. The initial values for the default and implied directory-IDs depend on the
         system’s configuration. On systems without the Multi-Host File Sharing (MHFS)
         feature, before a run begins, the default and implied directory-IDs are initialized to
         STD. For MHFS systems, the initial values depend on whether the system is a single
         master file directory search or a double master file directory search.

         Whenever you specify a file name without the qualifier or directory-ID or both, the
         Exec assumes default values for them. Whenever you omit the qualifier, but you
         specify an asterisk, the implied qualifier is used. If you omit both the asterisk and the
         qualifier, then the default qualifier is used. The selection of the default directory-ID
         depends on the system configuration.

7.50.2. Single MFD Search
         For single search, the default and implied directory-IDs are initialized to STD.

         Systems with MHFS that have single master file directory search and systems without
         MHFS both respond as follows:
             If you omit the directory-ID, but specify the #, the system uses the implied
              directory-ID.
             If you omit both the # and the directory-ID, then the default directory-ID is used.

         When you specify the file name as filename, the implied qualifier is assumed.

         When you specify the file name as #qual*filename, the implied directory-ID is
         assumed.

         When you specify the file name as filename, the default directory-ID and qualifier are
         assumed.

         As an example of a single MFD search, assume the following statements are in the
         same run and the system has the file sharing feature with single master file directory
         search:
             @RUN RUNID,ACCT,PROJECTID
             @QUAL STD#1STQUAL
             @USE M,FILEX
             @FTN FILEA.DO/ABC
             @QUAL 2NDQUAL
             @ASG,AX FILEJ(5).
             @FREE #*FILEA
             @QUAL,D SHARED#DEFAULTQUAL
             @ASG,A FILEB(-4).




7830 7949–031                                                                                 7–217
@QUAL and @@QUAL—Specify a Qualifier or Directory for File Names




        The first @QUAL statement specifies that all subsequent file name references having
        a preceding asterisk are interpreted as having qualifier 1STQUAL. File name references
        that have a preceding pound sign are interpreted as having directory-ID STD. The
        @USE statement is interpreted as
            @USE M,STD#PROJECTID*FILEX(-0)

        but the file name specified on the @FTN statement shown in the example is
        interpreted as
            STD#PROJECTID*FILEA(-0).DO/ABC

        The qualifier on the second @QUAL statement supersedes the implied qualifier given
        on the first @QUAL statement. Therefore, subsequent file name references that have
        a preceding asterisk have implied qualifier 2NDQUAL. The @ASG statement is
        interpreted as
            @ASG,AX STD#PROJECTID*FILEJ(5).

        but the file name specified on the @FREE statement is interpreted as
            STD#2NDQUAL*FILEA(-0).

        With the third @QUAL statement, the default directory-ID is changed to SHARED and
        the default qualifier is changed to DEFAULTQUAL. Therefore, subsequent file name
        references that do not specify a directory-ID or a pound sign and do not specify a
        qualifier or an asterisk have a directory-ID of SHARED and a qualifier of
        DEFAULTQUAL. The file name specified on the @ASG,A statement is interpreted as
            SHARED#DEFAULTQUAL*FILEB(-4).

7.50.3. Double MFD Search
        On systems with MHFS with the double MFD search, the default and implied
        directory-IDs are not initialized to anything before a run opens.

        Whenever you omit the directory-ID, these rules apply:
            When you perform an @ASG or @FREE, the section for the name of the user is
             searched first to see if the qualifier*filename(cycle) is known to the run. This
             section is found either by the USE name or by being assigned to the run.
            If the file is assigned to the run, then the directory-ID of the known file is
             assumed. If the file exists in both master file directories, and both files are known
             to the run, then the standard master file directory is assumed.
            If the file is not known to the run, then the following apply:
                ASG,C; @ASG,U; or @CAT), the standard master file directory is searched for
                 the qualifier*filename. If any cycle of the file is found, then STD is the assumed
                 directory-ID. If no cycle is found, then the shared master directory is searched
                 for the qualifier*filename. If any cycle of the file is found, then SHARED is used
                 as a directory-ID.




7–218                                                                              7830 7949–031
                 @QUAL and @@QUAL—Specify a Qualifier or Directory for File Names




                 Cataloging requests that do not specify a cycle (or use relative cycle -0) are
                  rejected if any cycles of the file exist (both master file directories are
                  searched); otherwise, STD is the assumed directory-ID.
                 When a cataloged file is assigned (for example, @ASG,A), the standard master
                  file directory is searched for the file. If any cycle of the file is found, then STD
                  is assumed as the directory-ID. If no cycle is found, then the shared master file
                  directory is searched. If the file is found, then SHARED is assumed and that file
                  is assigned; otherwise, the request is rejected.
                  Note: The same qualifier*filename can appear in both the STD and
                  SHARED master file directories. Be careful, when assigning a file without a
                  directory-ID, to make sure that the correct file is assigned when duplicate
                  qualifier*filename cycle sets exist.
                 Once you enter @QUAL,D, the default directory has a value and the assumed
                  defaults are the same as on a system that does not have the double MFD
                  search configured. Similarly, once an @QUAL (with no options) is entered with
                  a directory-ID specified, the implied directory-ID has a value and is used as on
                  a system that does not have the double MFD search configured.
         The following examples show double MFD search.

         Assume the following statements are in the same run, and the system has file sharing
         with double master file directory search:
           @RUN RUNID,ACCT,PROJECTID
           @CAT FILEA(2).
           @CAT SHARED#FILEA(2).
           @ASG,A FILEA(2).
           @USE XX,FILEB
           @ASG,C XX.
           @ASG,A #FILEA(2).
           @QUAL,D STD#DEFAULTQUAL
           @QUAL STD#
           @ASG,A FILEC(-3).

         The three statements in sequence following the @RUN statement show that an assign
         statement assigns the file in the standard master file directory if the file exists in both
         the master file directories. The images are interpreted as
           @CAT STD#PROJECTID*FILEA(2).
           @CAT SHARED#PROJECTID*FILEA(2).
           @ASG,A STD#PROJECTID*FILEA(2).

         The next two statements show that cataloging assumes STD. In addition, the @USE
         statement does not select a default directory-ID. This is not determined until the file is
         assigned. The images are interpreted as
           @USE XX,PROJECTID*FILEB
           @ASG,C STD#PROJECTID*FILEB.

         The @ASG,A #FILEA(2). statement shows that the assignment is for a file that is
         already assigned.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–219
@REWIND—Rewind Tape Files




        After the two @QUAL statements are done, the default and implied directory-ID s both
        have valid values. Hence, any file name that does not specify a directory-ID or that has
        only a # specified always has a default directory. The Exec now supplies defaults that
        are exactly the same as on a system that does not have the double MFD search
        configured.

        The @ASG is interpreted as
          @ASG,A STD#DEFAULTQUAL*FILEC(-3).


7.51. @REWIND—Rewind Tape Files
        Rewinds magnetic tape files back to the load point of the first reel.

        All parameters in the @REWIND statement are optional.

        Format
          @REWIND[,options] [filename-1,filename-2,...,filename-n]

        options
            Are the C and I options.

            If the I option is specified, the tape file is rewound with interlock; if omitted, the
            tape file is rewound without interlock.

            Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$
            on error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be
            used with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be
            input to a process later on in the runstream.

            The C option is valid for all FURPUR commands

        filename-n
            Specifies the tape files to be rewound.


7.52. @@RLD—Cause Screen Images to Scroll Down
        The @@RLD statement causes the lines of the display to scroll down instead of up, as
        they normally do.

        This statement could be used, for example, when there is something important in the
        top part of the screen and you do not want it to scroll off the screen.

        Format
          @@RLD n

        n indicates the line on the display from which output is to scroll down. The lines are
        counted down from the top.




7–220                                                                                7830 7949–031
                                               @@RLU—Cause Screen Images to Scroll Up




         You can restore the display to its normal setting with an @@RLU 23 statement if your
         terminal has a standard 24-line display.

         Examples
           @@RLD 1

                All the images on the screen scroll down starting at line 1.

           @@RLD 5

                All the images on the screen scroll down starting at line 5. The images
                preceding line 5 are saved.


7.53. @@RLU—Cause Screen Images to Scroll Up
         The @@RLU statement causes the images displayed to scroll up from a specified line
         on the screen. This statement can be used to reverse the action taken by the @@RLD
         statement.

         Format
           @@RLU n

         n indicates the line on the display from which output is to scroll up. The lines are
         counted down from the top.

         Examples
           @@RLU 22

             The images scroll up starting at line 22. The images after line 22 are saved.

           @@RLU 23

             This is the normal scrolling.


7.54. @@RQUE—Stop an Output File and Place It in a
       Queue
         The @@RQUE statement stops printing the present batch output file, requeues it for
         later printing (@@SEND statement), and returns the terminal to inactive mode. You can
         issue this statement from any terminal in remote batch mode.

         Format
           @@RQUE

7.55. @RSTRT—Restart a Run
        The @RSTRT statement lets you restore information from the check pointed data and
        resume processing. See the CKRS Programming Reference Manual (7830 7360) for
        more information.

        Format
          @RSTRT[,scheduling-priority/options/processor-dispatching-priority]
           run-id,[acct-id/user-id,project-id, filename.element,ckpt-number,
           eqpmnt-type,reel-1/... reel-n]

        scheduling-priority
           Indicates what preference the run must be given in relation to all other runs that
           are available for execution. The scheduling priority can be any letter from A
           through Z, where A is the highest priority and Z is the lowest. If you specify a
           scheduling priority that is higher than is permitted for the account number (acct-ID)
           you specify, the Exec changes the priority to the highest priority allowed for that
           account.
        processor-dispatching-priority
           Indicates the processor dispatching priority that is used to place the run’s
           activities into a switching group once the run is opened. The processor
           dispatching priority can be any letter from A through Z, where Z is the lowest.

        options

           A
                  Does not terminate the run for certain nonfatal errors.

           B
                  Uses the saved (checkpointed) absolute element if the absolute element
                  cannot be found in the original program file. Restart always restores the
                  current state of the program.

           J
                  Assigns an unlabeled checkpoint tape. This must agree with the @CKPT
                  statement.

           M
                  Prints full diagnostic messages without diagnostic snapshots while
                  processing the full checkpoint data.

           N
                  Does not print error message or diagnostics in the run’s print file.




7–222                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                                          @RSTRT—Restart a Run




             P
                   Displays error message on the console.

             Q
                   Prints diagnostic snapshots while processing full restart data.

             R
                   Restores the saved mass storage symbiont files. (Tape symbiont files are
                   always restored.)

             S
                   Performs only a partial restart.

             U
                   Prevents verification of files. Use this option to bypass file verification if the
                   CKRS_FILE_VERIFY parameter is set to true.

             V
                   Forces verification of files. Use this option to force file verification if the
                   CKRS_FILE_VERIFY parameter is set to false.

                   Note: If both the U and V options are specified on a restart request, the
                   U option overrides the V option.

             Y
                   Lets the restart initialization processor print diagnostic snapshots in the run’s
                   print file.

             Z
                   Prints diagnostic snapshots while processing partial restart data.

         run-id
             Identifies the run-ID for the restarted run. The original run-ID or the system
             generated run-ID of the restarted run must match the generated run-ID of the run
             that took the checkpoint.

         acct-id
             Specifies the account number. This is optional. However, the account number
             must match the account number of the checkpointed run. This ensures that all
             private files assigned to the checkpointed run is assigned to the restarted run.

         user-id
             Identifies the user-ID of the checkpointed run. This ensures that the restarted run
             is able to assign all of the owned files that were assigned to the checkpointed run.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–223
@RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




        project-id
            Specifies the project name for the restarted run. If you do not specify one, the
            project-ID is Q$Q$Q$.

        filename
            Identifies the external file name of the checkpoint data. The file name is optional if
            you specify reel-number-n and the tape is unlabeled. A file name without a period
            is treated as an element in TPF$. A file name can include the directory-ID.

        element
            Specifies the element from which the checkpoint data can be retrieved. This
            element cannot reside in a Large Element Program File (LEPF).

        ckpt-number
            Specifies the checkpoint number; you must include the ckpt-number if the
            checkpoint is on tape. The ckpt-number is a sequence number that specifies
            which checkpoint on the tape to use.

        eqpmnt-type
            Specifies the equipment type.

        reel-n
            Identifies the reel number of the tape containing the checkpoint.

        Examples
        See the CKRS Programming Reference Manual (7830 7360) for examples of @RSTRT.


7.56. @RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec
        A run is a sequence of tasks linked to form a self-contained unit of work. A run is
        controlled by a series of control statements, which tell the system what to do.

        Start a run with an @RUN statement and end it with an @FIN statement. Between the
        two, you can include the following:
           Other control statements to create or manipulate files or run a program
           Lines of a source program to be compiled and executed
           Instructions to a system processor
           Data for an executing program to process

        If your user-ID is configured to generate the @RUN statement for you, you do not
        have to enter an @RUN statement; the system does it for you, based on the
        information you provide when you sign on. However, if your user-ID is configured for
        the @RUN statement to be user-entered, you must enter an @RUN statement.

        There are two basic types of runs: batch and demand.



7–224                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                                         @RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




7.56.1. Batch Run
         A batch run is a run you submit as a complete job. It is designed to run independently,
         from start to finish, without further instructions from you. Use batch runs for routine
         and repetitive applications that process large volumes of data or require a lot of
         processing time.

         When you submit a batch run for processing, the Exec stores the runstream in a file
         (READ$) until the system has enough resources to open the run. Even after the Exec
         opens a run, the run does not have exclusive use of the system resources; it must
         share them with other active runs.

         As the run is processed, the system reads the images from READ$ and processes
         them in order. Any output produced during the run is stored in a file (PRINT$). When
         the run terminates, this output is printed.

         There are two kinds of batch runs: canned runs and remote batch runs.

         Canned Runs
         Canned runs are batch runstreams that you prepare in advance, by using a text editor
         such as EDIT 1100 (the IPF 1100 editor). You store the canned runstream in an SDF file
         or symbolic element for later use.

         Using canned runs is a timesaving technique you can use for repetitive functions and
         for runstreams that you want to use more than once.

         There are two kinds of canned runstreams: full and partial. The main difference is that
         full canned runstreams include @RUN and @FIN statements, while partial canned
         runstreams do not.

         Full canned runstreams are complete batch runs that you start by using the @START
         statement. Partial canned runstreams are a sequence of control statements (and other
         input, if desired) that you add to an active run by using the @ADD statement.

         The following are examples of canned runstreams that can be initiated with @START:

           @RUN R231,03412,CAPER,10/100 . last run

             Run R231 of project CAPER is assigned standard system scheduling and
             processor-dispatching priorities by the Exec. Expenses incurred by the run are
             changed to account 03412. Run time is estimated at 10 minutes; results are
             required an hour after the run is submitted. The run cannot terminate automatically
             when run time or page estimates are exceeded unless automatic termination was
             provided for when the system was configured. The Exec uses the system’s
             standard page-output estimate because that field is omitted. The run is scheduled
             by the Exec for execution according to its priority (start-time is omitted). This run
             statement includes a comment (.last run).




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–225
@RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




            @RUN,C/P 716,03412,CAPER,,300

             Run 716 of project CAPER has a scheduling priority of C. The P option indicates
             that the run must be terminated automatically if more than 300 pages of output
             are produced. Expenses incurred by the run are charged to account 03412. The
             Exec uses the system’s standard value for estimated run time, since none is
             specified in the statement, and assumes that there is no deadline, since none is
             provided. The Exec considers the run immediately (because start-time is omitted)
             and schedules the run according to its priority.

            @RUN,A 201,90431010,EXODUS1,S50,50,D830

             Run 201 of project EXODUS1 has a scheduling priority of A. Run expenses are
             charged to account 90431010. Run-time is estimated at 50 seconds with an
             expected output of less than 50 pages. The start-time field specifies that the run
             not be considered for execution before 8:30 a.m. Unless provided for at system
             generation, automatic run termination does not occur if running time or output
             estimates are exceeded, since these options are not specified.

        Remote Batch Run
        You enter a remote batch run at a terminal without saving the runstream in a file or
        element. You enter the entire runstream at a terminal, much as you would for a
        demand run. To indicate that you want to start a remote batch run and not a demand
        run from a demand terminal, use the B option on the @RUN statement (see Section
        7.56). As you enter the runstream, it is stored in a READ$ file and then queued for
        processing like other batch runs after the @FIN statement is entered. Responses to
        statements do not appear on your terminal, as they would if you were entering a
        demand run; responses and all other output are stored in a PRINT$ file and printed
        when your run terminates.

        Starting a Batch Run
        You must include the @PASSWD statement in a batch run. For more information on
        the @PASSWD statement (see Section 7.44).

        Notes:
            You cannot start a remote batch job if your user-ID is configured for the @RUN
             statement to be always system generated.
            Do not initiate long-running, computing-intensive programs. Use the B option
             with the @RUN statement to improve system scheduling and to free the
             terminal for further use.
            When you enter the @RUN statement from a remote terminal, use the N option.
             This inhibits postmortem dumping and dynamic diagnostic dumping.

         Format
           @RUN[,scheduling-priority/options/processor-dispatching-priority run-id,acct-
           id/user-id,project-id,run-time/deadline,pages/cards,start-time]

         scheduling-priority
            Indicates what preference the run must be given in relation to all other runs that
            are available for execution. The scheduling priority can be any letter from A
            through Z, where A is the highest priority and Z is the lowest. If you specify a
            scheduling priority that is higher than is permitted for the account number (acct-id)
            you specify, the Exec changes the priority to the highest priority allowed for that
            account.
            Examples:
            @run,B//A runid…. (scheduling priority B, processor dispatching priority A)
            @run,//A  runid …. (scheduling priority from default, processor dispatching priority A)

            Notes:
               Normally, when the Exec is holding a run in backlog because resources are
                not available (such as a file), other lower-priority runs are not allowed to
                start. To avoid holding up the start of runs, start as many runs as possible at
                the same priority. However, if the dynamic configuration tag
                bypass_facility_held_runs is set, lower priority runs can open.
               When a batch run is initiated and its required resources are unavailable, the
                run is placed on the hold queue. The status of such runs can be viewed in the
                backlog queue using the BL D console command, which provides detailed
                information about held runs.
                The hold queue is monitored to evaluate the currently queued actives.
                Periodically all runs held on the hold queue are removed and reevaluated.
                The run is then either allowed to proceed, or it is requeued to the hold
                queue.
                For runs waiting on the exclusive use of a local file, the Exec issues a
                console message indicating how long the run has been waiting. This
                message is generated approximately every 20 minutes, based on the time
                the run was queued to the hold queue.
                If a run is waiting for local resources, the run is removed from (and
                potentially requeued to) the hold queue every 60 minutes. If a run is waiting
                on shared resources, the run is removed from (and potentially requeued to)
                the hold queues every 5 seconds. Hence these console messages never
                appear for runs held for shared files.

         General Options
            B
                Treats the run input from a demand terminal as batch input and schedules the
                run as a batch run.

            D
                Allows more files to be assigned to the run. For each file assigned to a run,
                several data structures are needed to manage that assignment. This option
                causes the device area descriptor (DAD) tables to be moved to a separate
                run-level bank, thus freeing up PCT space for additional file assignments.
                See the Exec Administration Reference Manual (7831 0323) for further
                information on this option.
                This option is ignored if the configuration parameter User_DAD_Bank is zero.

            O
                Allocates DAD tables for assigned files in the run’s PCT when the
                configuration parameter User_DAD_Bank is set to 2. This option is provided to
                maintain compatibility regarding the location of the DAD tables.
                If both the D option and O option are used, then the D option is ignored.
                Note: Options E through M, which control the minimum size of the PCT, are
                not meaningful on XPA hardware because PCTs are given the maximum
                configured PCT size allowable by your site (see configuration tag PCTMAX).

            P
                Terminates the run if the page estimate is exceeded.
            R
                Reschedules the run if a recoverable system failure occurs. If the R option is
                specified and the associated run is open at the time of system failure, the run
                is reinstated in the schedule queue during system recovery. When the run is
                selected for reopening, bit 4 is set in the run’s condition word.
                The following actions and restrictions govern the use of the R option:
                   All queued print and punch files generated by the open run being
                    rescheduled are removed from the print and punch queues and
                    decataloged during the recovery, with the exception of user-defined files
                    that have been sent to a printer by using @SYM with the U option. These
                    files are not decataloged; however, they are removed from the
                    appropriate print or punch queue.
                   The R option is ignored on all demand runs and these runs are never
                    rescheduled.
                   The user is responsible for handling facility assignments in the run to
                    resolve potential conflicts during the restart of the run. The condition word
                    can be examined by the run to determine whether the run has been
                    restarted.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–229
@RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




           S
               Processes this run in sequence with the previous run submitted from the
               same site-ID; holds this run until the previous run completes. The S option is
               used for runs entered with @RUN,/B or from RSI$ remote batch terminals. It is
               ignored for demand runs and for batch runs started with the ST keyin or the
               @START control statement.

           T
               Terminates the run if the standard unit of processing (SUP) usage estimate is
               exceeded.

           X
               Disregards system holds when opening run (requires a security privilege).
               The name of the new dynamic configuration parameter is
               batch_run_x_option_modes. On Security Level 1 or higher systems, the
               security privilege SSRUNXOPT is required for runs specifying the X option on
               @RUN or @START control statements and the ST keyin.

        Options for Postmortem and Dynamic Dumping
           N
               Does not write the program or processor to the diagnostic file. The PMD
               statements are not honored, but are printed along with the message PMD
               NOT ALLOWED. Diagnostic dumps are not printed. This option overrides the
               W and Y options.

           Y
               Always writes the program or processor to the diagnostic file, regardless of
               the source of the program (even for system processors from SYS$*LIB$ or
               SYS$LIB$ files). Appropriate PMD statements are honored, and diagnostic
               dumps are printed. Use this option only when a program in the SYS$*LIB$ or
               SYS$LIB$ files is being debugged.

               Note: System processors are not currently allowed to be zero overhead
               object modules (ZOOM) or object modules.

           W
               Specifies that only user programs that error are to be written to the diagnostic
               file. In addition, for batch programs, the appropriate PMD processor is loaded
               to dump the program in error. An automatic @PMD call assumes the L and P
               options; an automatic @PADS call assumes the DIAG$ standard procedure;
               and an automatic @DAP call assumes the NPE$PMD function. Diagnostic
               dumps are automatically printed only if the program taking a diagnostic dump
               terminates in error. The W option saves overhead.




7–230                                                                          7830 7949–031
                                                             @RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




                   The time at which dumps are taken is different for basic mode and extended
                   mode programs. For basic mode programs, dumps are performed at program
                   termination time. For extended mode programs (object modules or ZOOMs),
                   dumps are performed for each activity when a contingency occurs
                   (contingencies include both error conditions and normal activity termination).
                   Note: The diagnostic file formats for basic mode programs and extended
                   programs are completely different.
                   When you specify both the W and Y options, all user programs and LIB$
                   processors are written to DIAG$. In addition, an automatic postmortem dump
                   of error user programs and LIB$ processors is received.
                   When you omit the N, Y, and W options, the program, unless it is a processor
                   loaded from the system library (LIB$) or an alternate library, is dumped to the
                   diagnostic file (DIAG$), and normal postmortem dump action occurs. See the
                   PMD Programming Reference Manual (7862 7288) for information concerning
                   normal PMD action. PMD statements encountered after a LIB$ processor call
                   statement are not honored and appear on the printout, along with the
                   message
                          PMD NOT ALLOWED

                   Absolute programs collected with the TYPE NPEDIAG directive only has
                   activities that terminate in error written to the diagnostic file, regardless of the
                   W option or no-option specification. An automatic PMD is only performed
                   according to the W and Y options.
                   The rules governing postmortem dumping also apply to the printout for
                   diagnostic dumping. The no-option mode must be used whenever one or
                   more programs other than those in library LIB$ are being debugged. This is the
                   normal mode for debugging runs.
                   If you use an @@CONS E,N run-id command, the N option (no postmortem
                   dump) on the @@CONS E command overrides the Y and W options.

         run-id
             Identifies the run to the Exec. The run-ID consists of 1 to 6 characters in any
             combination of letters and numbers. If you omit run-ID, the Exec uses RUN000.
             If you specify a run-ID that duplicates a run-ID already in the system, the Exec
             modifies your newly submitted run-ID to make it unique. Both the original and the
             modified run-IDs appear on the operator’s console, in the system log, and in the
             printer listing.

         acct-id
             Specifies an account number used for billing purposes. The account number
             consists of 1 to 12 characters in any combination of letters, numbers, periods (.),
             and hyphens (-).
             If your site has Fundamental Security, a file can be private by account number
             (depending on how security is configured at your site). This means files can be
             assigned only by runs whose account number is the same as the account number
             of the run that created the file.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–231
@RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




           If your system has Security Level 1 or higher and user-IDs in your security
           management product are set up to create owned files (this is the default), files are
           private by the user-ID that created the file.
           If you omit acct-ID, the Exec uses 000000.
           A system is configured as either restrictive or nonrestrictive.
           If the system is restrictive, all runs using an account number that is not registered
           with the Exec are rejected.
           If the system is nonrestrictive and the account number submitted is not registered
           with the Exec, the system operator is notified and can accept or reject the run.

        user-id
           Identifies the user of the account specified (acct-ID). The user-ID consists of 1 to
           12 characters in any combination of letters, numbers, periods (.), and hyphens (-). If
           your site requires a user-ID and you do not enter one, the system uses the user-ID
           you entered at sign-on time. If you do enter a user-ID on the @RUN statement, it
           must match the one you entered when you signed on or the system rejects the
           run.

        project-id
           Classifies the run for file access and accounting purposes. The project-ID is also
           used as the qualifier for file names when you do not provide one. Project-IDs can
           be up to 12 characters and can include any combination of letters, numbers,
           hyphens (-), and dollar signs ($).
           Unowned files can be private by project-ID (depending on how security is
           configured at your site). This means files can be assigned only by runs whose
           project-ID is the same as the project-ID of the run that created the file.
           Owned files are private by the user-ID that created the file.
           If you omit project-ID, the Exec uses Q$Q$Q$.

        run-time
           Estimates run time in standard units of processing (SUP). This is roughly the same
           as minutes, but you can use a leading S to specify seconds. When your run
           exceeds the estimated run time, the Exec does the following:
                 Notifies the operator, allowing the operator to manually terminate the run
                 Terminates the run if the T option is specified or if automatic run termination
                  was specified when the system was configured

           The Exec can be configured to maintain a quota limit on run time for each account.
           If the Exec is maintaining a quota limit and you specify a run time that exceeds the
           quota limit, the quota limit is used. In addition, if you do not specify a run time at
           all, the Exec uses the quota limit.
           When the Exec is not maintaining a quota limit and you do not specify a run time,
           the Exec uses the system standard value of 2,184 minutes. If you specify a run
           time greater than 2,184 minutes, the Exec replaces it with 2,184.

                                                          @RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




            In all cases, when you specify a run time of 0, the Exec uses a run time of
            1 minute.

         deadline
            Is a request that a batch run be completed by a specific deadline. The deadline is
            ignored if no estimated run time and the run is started as a normal batch run. As
            the deadline approaches and the batch run has not been started yet, the system
            raises the run’s priority to complete processing by the requested deadline and at
            that time the run becomes a deadline batch run.
            Deadline time can be specified as either elapsed time since run submission or
            time of day. Time of day is based on a 24-hour clock using the local time base.
            The format is hhmm for elapsed time and Dhhmm for time of day. Both are
            limited to maximum of 2400, that is 24 hours. If the specified time of day is earlier
            than the current time, the system considers it as the time of the next day.


                                                 Caution
                Be careful if you decide to use deadline runs. System performance can be
                severely hampered as the deadline time approaches and your run priority
                increases. Also, depending on how your site has set Quota limits, deadline
                processing can require privileges that you do not have. If you want to use
                deadline runs, check with your site administrator first.



            Indicate deadline as either elapsed time since run submission or the time of day.
            Enter the deadline in the following format:
                     [D]hhmm

            D
                  Indicates that the deadline is a time of day (within the next 24 hours). If you
                  omit the D prefix, the deadline is the elapsed time since the start time (the
                  deadline is then the length of time during which the run must be completed).

            hh
                  Specifies hours.

            mm
                  Specifies minutes.

            You do not need to use leading zeros for hhmm.

            Here are some examples of deadlines:
            D910
                  Run must be done by 9:10 a.m. (on the day of run submission if submitted at or
                  before 9:10 a.m.; on the next day if submitted after 9:10 a.m.)




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–233
@RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




           D2110
                 Run must be done by 9:10 p.m. (on the day of run submission if submitted at
                 or before 9:10 p.m.; on the next day if submitted after 9:10 p.m.)

           100
                 Run must be done 1 hour after submission.

           230
                 Run must be done 2.5 hours after submission.
                 If the run is not completed by the specified deadline, the Exec raises the
                 priority of the run so that it completes as soon after the specified deadline as
                 possible. This action, however, can degrade system operation since other
                 runs, including demand runs, can be given relatively fewer resources.
                 A system can be configured to prevent the use of deadlines. If you specify a
                 deadline when it is not allowed, the deadline is ignored.

           quota limit.
           When the Exec is not maintaining quota limits and you do not specify pages, the
           Exec uses a system standard value. If the page estimate is exceeded, the Exec
           does one of the following:
                Notifies the operator and gives the operator the option of terminating the run
                Terminates the run if the P option is specified or if automatic run termination
                 was specified when the system was configured
           When the Exec is not maintaining quota limits and you specify pages,

           When the Exec is not maintaining quota limits and you do not specify cards,
           the Exec uses a system standard value. If the cards estimate is exceeded, the

                Terminates the run if the C option or automatic run termination was specified

            When the Exec is not maintaining quota limits and you specify cards, the

         start-time
            Specifies the earliest time when a run can be processed.

            Start-time is a request to delay the start of a batch run until a specified time.
            Before that time is reached, the Exec places the run in a hold state. Once the
            start-time has been reached, the Exec releases the run from the hold state and
            schedules it under normal priority rules. The Exec does not interpret other @RUN
            statement fields such as deadline and priority until the start-time has been
            reached. The start-time is considered the time of run submission when
            considering the deadline.

            Start-time time can be specified as either elapsed time since run submission or
            time of day. Time of day is based on a 24-hour clock using the local time base. The
            format is hhmm for elapsed time and Dhhmm for time of day. Both are limited to
            maximum of 2400, that is 24 hours. If the specified time of day is earlier than the
            current time, the system considers it as the time of the next day.

                      [D]hhmm

            D
                   Indicates that the start-time is a time of day (within the next 24 hours). If you
                   omit the D prefix, the start-time is elapsed time from when the Exec reads
                   this @RUN statement to when the Exec starts the run.

            hh
                   Specifies hours.

            mm
                   Specifies minutes.

         You do not need to use leading zeros for hhmm, but if you specify a start-time greater
         than 24 hours, your run is flagged for error termination.

7.56.2. Demand Run
        A demand run is an interactive run. You enter ECL and other types of statements one
        at a time at a terminal and generally wait for each statement to be processed before
        entering another. Demand runs let you correct errors right away and get answers
        more quickly than you could by using batch runs.

        To start a demand run after signing on the system, you can have to enter an @RUN
        statement, or the system can automatically generate one for you, depending on how
        your user-ID is configured. The system can prompt you for certain kinds of information
        after you sign on.

        Demand runs do not use READ$ and PRINT$ files for input and output. All input is
        taken directly from your keyboard. All output is displayed directly on the screen of
        your terminal.

        To terminate a demand run, use the @FIN statement.

        You can still add statements and data from files and send output to printers, but you
        must use special statements to do so. @ADD lets you add data files or symbolic
        elements to your run (see Section 7.1). @BRKPT and @SYM let you save and direct
        output to a file or a printer (see Section 7.3 and Section 0).

        Note: Do not execute long-running, computing-intensive programs while in
        demand mode; use batch runs instead. This improves system scheduling and frees
        the terminal for other uses.

        Starting a Demand Run
        Format
          @RUN[,scheduling-priority/options processor-dispatching-priority
          run-id,acct-id/user-id,project-id]

        scheduling-priority
            Specifies printing priority of A through Z in the print queue.

        processor-dispatching-priority
            Indicates the processor dispatching priority that is used to place the run’s
            activities into a switching group once the run is opened. The processor
            dispatching priority can be any letter from A through Z, where Z is the lowest.

        options
            Your site can be configured to use the terminations specified by the P and T
            options whether or not the options are specified.

            private by the user-ID that created the file.
            If you omit acct-id, the Exec displays
                   *MISSING ACCOUNT*

            A system is configured as either restrictive or nonrestrictive.
            If the system is restrictive, any run using an account number that is not registered
            with the Exec is rejected.
            If the system is nonrestrictive and the account number submitted is not registered
            with the Exec, the operator is notified and can accept or reject the run.




7–238                                                                               7830 7949–031
                                                         @RUN—Identify a Run to the Exec




         user-id
            The user-ID subfield is optional. If your site requires a user-ID and you do not enter
            one, the system uses the user-ID you entered at sign-on time. If you do enter a
            user-ID, it must be the same as the one you used to sign on, or the system rejects
            the run. If user-IDs are required by your site, a user-ID must be specified on batch
            jobs.

         project-id
            Classifies the run for file access and accounting purposes. The project-ID is also
            used as the qualifier for file names when you have not provided one. The
            project-ID can be up to 12 characters and can include any combination of letters,
            numbers, hyphens (-), and dollar signs ($).
            Unowned files can be private by project-ID (depending on how security is
            configured at your site). This means files can be assigned only by runs whose
            project-ID is the same as the project-ID of the run that created the file.
            Owned files are private by the user-ID that created the file.
            If you omit project-ID, the Exec uses Q$Q$Q$ as the project-ID.

            Example
                @RUN LMN,766120,PROD-SCHED

                      This is an example of how your @RUN statement might look if your user-ID
                      is configured to either require you or allow you to enter your own @RUN
                      statement. LMN is the run-ID, 766120 is the account number, and
                      PROD-SCHED is the project-ID.

7.57. @@SEND—Receive a Print File Queued to Your
       User ID
         The @@SEND statement tells the system to send you the print files queued to your
         user-ID or your terminal’s site-ID.

         You cannot use the @@SEND statement during an active run. The best time to use
         @@SEND is immediately after you have terminated a run (@FIN), but before you have
         logged off the system (@@TERM) or the network ($$SOFF).

         Normally, the output is just displayed at your terminal. If a local printer is connected to
         your terminal, you can also receive a printout of the queued output by entering the
         @@PRNT statement before you use the @@SEND statement.

         Note: You cannot be allowed to use @@SEND, depending on your system’s
         security configuration. Check with your site administrator or security officer.

         Format
             @@SEND[,U] [filename]

         U
              Sends you the files queued to your user-ID. If you do not specify this option, the
              files queued to your terminal’s site-ID are sent. You can queue files to a site-ID or
              user-ID with the @SYM statement.

         filename
              Identifies a specific file you want sent to your terminal. If you do not specify a file
              name, you receive all files queued to your user-ID or site-ID.

         The following are examples of the @SEND statement that lets you print files queued
         to your user-ID or your terminal’s site-ID:
             @@SEND

                This statement sends you all print files queued to your terminal’s site-ID.

             @@SEND,U

                This statement sends you all print files queued to your user-ID.

             @@SEND URSA*TEST1.

                This statement sends you print file URSA*TEST1, which is queued to your
                terminal’s site-ID.

             @@SEND,U URSA*TEST2.

                This statement sends you print file URSA*TEST2, which is queued to your
                user-ID.



7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–241
@@SETC—Store a Value in a Condition Word




7.58. @@SETC—Store a Value in a Condition Word
        The @SETC statement stores values in the condition word.

        Format
          @SETC[,options] [f/]value[/j]

        options

           A
                  Clears bit 5 of the condition word. This allows a normal termination of this
                  run.

           I
                  Sets bit 5 of the condition word. This inhibits run termination after a program
                  error terminates. The I option permits runs with independent tasks or tasks
                  with nonfatal errors to continue with normal processing after any error
                  terminations occur. It also permits tests, during which error conditions are
                  expected to be encountered, to continue. When an error condition is
                  encountered, console messages and log entries inform the run. See the ER
                  Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for information on error
                  termination contingencies.
                  This option is overridden by the E keyin. Refer to the Exec Operations
                  Reference Manual (7831 0281) for more information on the E keyin.
                  If you specify the I option, standard units of processing (SUP) accumulate
                  beyond the time an error is detected.

           N
                  Sets bit 3 of the condition word. This inhibits page ejects between processor
                  calls.

           P
                  Clears bit 3 of the condition word. This enables page ejects between
                  processor calls.
                  If the configuration parameter control-image-spacing is nonzero, there is a
                  line spacing equal to the value of control-image-spacing instead of a page
                  eject.

           f
                  Specifies the type of operation used to alter the part of the condition word
                  designated by j. The operation can be AND, OR, or XOR. This field is optional.
                  If the f field is specified, the result of the logical operation between the
                  designated part of the condition word and the value specified in the control
                  word statement is stored in the designated part of the condition word. If you
                  do not specify the f field, the designated bits are replaced in the condition
                  word.



7–242                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                  @@SETC—Store a Value in a Condition Word




              value
                      Specifies a positive octal value not exceeding four digits in length. The value
                      is used in the logical operation specified by f or is entered into the
                      designated portion of the condition word. The value is right-justified,
                      zero-filled prior to a partial word store into the designated portion. If the
                      magnitude of value exceeds the capacity of the designated portion,
                      truncation occurs.

              j
                      Designates the portion of the condition word to change. The portion can be
                      T1, T2, S2, S3, or S4. If you omit j, the default is T2. Within T1 and S2, only bits
                      7 and 8 are modified. Entries T2, S3, and S4 designate the corresponding
                      word parts. Tn and Sn are partial word designators. They refer to a third or
                      sixth of a word, respectively. The following diagram shows the partial word
                      designators in relation to a word of storage:

                            T1                            T2                            T3
                     S1            S2             S3             S4             S5              S6
             0                6              12             18             24             30          35


         You can examine the condition word in either a runstream or an executing task. You
         can alter only bits 7 and 8, T2, or T3. You can modify bits 7 and 8 with either a control
         statement or an Executive request (ER SETC$). You can modify T2 with a control
         statement and T3 with an Executive request (ER SETC$).
         The condition word is set to all zeros at the start of a run, unless one of the following
         occurred:
             The run was started by an @START statement with a set field, in which case T2
              initially contains the value of that field.
                The run has been rescheduled across a recovery boot through use of the R option
                 on the @RUN statement, in which case bit 4 is set.

         Notes:

             @SETC,A and @SETC,I do not affect the ABORT$ and EABT$ Executive requests
              or E–keyin unsolicited keyin.
                @SETC,I alters the ER ERR$ processing and other error processing, such as
                 guard mode and illegal operations.

         Examples
             @SETC 6

                   Loads octal 6 into T2 of the condition word. (T2 is assumed since the j field is
                   omitted.)




7830 7949–031                                                                                        7–243
@@SKIP—Skip Lines of Output




            @SETC 10/S3

               Loads octal 10 into S3 of the condition word. The value is treated as octal even
               when the leading zero is omitted.

            @SETC,I 4/S4

               Loads octal 4 into S4 of the condition word. Sets bit 5 of the condition word.

            @SETC 7777/T1

               Sets bit 7 and 8 of the condition word.


7.59. @@SKIP—Skip Lines of Output
        The @@SKIP statement is used to skip a specified number of lines of output. It is
        usually used after an output interrupt (MSG WAIT key).

        Format
            @@SKIP n

        n
             Indicates the number of lines of output that must be skipped. You can skip up to
             63 lines.

        If you specify that a certain number of lines must be skipped and fewer lines than that
        are output by a program, the system continues to skip lines of output, even if they are
        responses to statements you enter.

        If you make a mistake with the @@SKIP statement, you can reset it by entering
        @@SKIP 0 after an output interrupt (MSG WAIT key).

        Examples
            @@SKIP 5

               This skips five lines of output.

            @@SKIP 0

               No lines are skipped. This is the default.


7.60.@@SOLI—Solicit for User-ID/Password
        The @@SOLI statement generates a traditional user-ID/password solicit for demand
        users while the Authentication and Session Initiation Subsystem (ASIS) is temporarily
        not available or draining.




7–244                                                                            7830 7949–031
                                      @START and @@START—Start Canned Runstreams




         Normally, if the ASIS is not available or draining and demand terminal users try to sign
         on, they receive an error message:
             The Authentication Subsystem is not available. This sign-on is
             rejected. Contact the Site Administrator.

         The user can then enter an @@SOLI command to force a traditional Exec solicit for a
         user-ID/password.

         Format
             @@SOLI


7.61. @START and @@START—Start Canned
       Runstreams
         The @START statement starts canned runstreams that were previously entered into
         the system. The statements and data that make up such a runstream must be stored
         in either a data file or a symbolic element within a program file. The symbolic element
         cannot reside within a large element program file (LEPF). Such a file or element can be
         created by
             An editor
             A user program that writes system data format (SDF) files (data files) or symbolic
              elements to a program file

         The first statement in the stored runstream must be an @RUN statement that
         complies with the rules detailed in 7.56. At the end of the file or element, the run is
         automatically terminated (the system provides an implied @FIN statement).

         If you currently have an active run on a demand terminal, and you are not in control
         mode (such as during program execution), you can start a canned run from that
         terminal by using the @@START statement.

         You can use the @START statement to
             Submit runs for execution at a time or time interval of your choosing (for example,
              on a daily basis).
             Start a run that generates data for input to another run.
             Start a run that builds a cataloged file containing an entire runstream and then calls
              for the runstream to be scheduled. (Thus, you can use the @START statement to
              initiate parallel processing, since tasks from different runs can be executed
              concurrently.)
             Start batch runs from demand terminals. The run-control statements for the batch
              run must have been previously stored in files or elements. The run is scheduled as
              a batch run, and its output is sent to onsite peripherals.




7830 7949–031                                                                                7–245
@START and @@START—Start Canned Runstreams




        The @START statement has two formats.

        Format 1
        Use this format when you want to use all fields from the stored @RUN statement
        except for the account number (acct-ID), which is the same as the run in which the
        @START statement is used:
          @START runstream-name

        where runstream-name identifies the file or element that contains the stored
        runstream. The runstream-name field must include the name of a file. If the runstream
        name is a file name only, the file must be a data file.

        If the runstream name is an element name without a version name, the system uses
        the symbolic element with a blank version name, if one exists. If one does not exist,
        the system uses the first (not necessarily the oldest) nondeleted symbolic element in
        the named file, regardless of its version name. The specified element cannot reside in
        a Large Element Program File (LEPF).

        Format 2
        Use this format when you want to change all or part of the @RUN statement in the
        stored run:
          @START[,scheduling-priority/options/processor-dispatching-priority]
          runstream-name[,setc,run-id,acct-id/user-id,project-id,runtime/
          deadline,pages/cards,start-time]

        scheduling-priority
           Indicates what preference the run must be given in relation to all other runs that
           are available for execution. The scheduling priority can be any letter from A
           through Z, where A is the highest priority and Z is the lowest. If you specify a
           scheduling priority that is higher than is permitted for the account number (acct-ID)
           you specify, the Exec changes the priority to the highest priority allowed for that
           account.
        processor-dispatching-priority
           Indicates the processor dispatching priority that is used to place the run’s
           activities into a switching group once the run is opened. The processor
           dispatching priority can be any letter from A through Z, where Z is the lowest.
        Any fields included on the @START statement replace the corresponding fields in the
        stored @RUN statement. The fields on the @RUN statement are replaced for a
        particular run but not deleted.

        Note: At the time a runstream is submitted to the Exec for execution, the Exec
        makes a copy of the runstream in an Exec file to execute. Therefore, if you make
        any changes to a runstream after the @START statement is finished and before the
        run is opened, these changes cannot be reflected in the copy of the runstream that
        the Exec executes.




7–246                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                        @START and @@START—Start Canned Runstreams




         priority
             Indicates what preference the run must be given in relation to all other runs that
             are available for execution. The priority can be any letter from A through Z, where
             A is the highest priority and Z is the lowest. When the Exec is holding a run in
             backlog because resources are not available (such as a file), other lower-priority
             runs are not allowed to start. To avoid holding up the start of runs, start as many
             runs as possible at the same priority.
             Note: Normally, when the Exec is holding a run in backlog because resources
             are not available (such as a file), other lower-priority runs are not allowed to
             start. To avoid holding up the start of runs, start as many runs as possible at the
             same priority. However, if the dynamic configuration tag
             bypass_facility_held_runs is set, lower priority runs can open.

         options
             If specified, options replace those on the @RUN statement for the stored
             runstream. Following is a list and abbreviated description of the @RUN options and
             the two special @START options, U and Z.

         B
             Treats the run input from a demand terminal as batch input and schedules the run
             as a batch run.

             Note: Options E through M, which control the minimum size of the PCT, are not
             meaningful on XPA hardware because PCTs are given the maximum configured
             PCT size allowable by your site (see configuration tag PCTMAX).

             N
                    Does not write the program or processor to the diagnostic file. PMD
                    statements are not honored, but are printed along with the message PMD
                    NOT ALLOWED. Diagnostic dumps are not printed. This option overrides the
                    W and Y options.

             P
                    Terminates the run if the page estimate is exceeded. Your site can be
                    configured to use this termination, whether or not the option is specified.

             R
                    Reschedules the run if a recoverable system failure occurs.

             T
                    Terminates the run if the standard unit of processing (SUP) usage estimate is
                    exceeded. Your site can be configured to use this termination, whether or not
                    the option is specified.




7830 7949–031                                                                                 7–247
@START and @@START—Start Canned Runstreams




            U
                Lets you start a runstream under a user-ID other than your own. With this
                option, the run executes under the user-ID specified on the @RUN statement
                in the runstream. The MAC and DAC attributes associated with the user-ID on
                the @RUN statement must be the same or dominate those of the runstream’s
                starter. See Section 4.3 for more information on MAC and DAC. Also, see the
                ClearPath OS 2200 Apex Help (8207 4154).

            V
                The V option can be used on an @START statement to start a run at the
                minimum clearance level and default compartment set of the user-ID under
                which the started run executes (the target user-ID). Without the V or Z option,
                the started run assumes the starter’s executing mandatory attributes. That
                user-ID depends on how the V option is used, as follows:

           @START with V option used alone—The starting run’s user-ID (the run from which
            @START was executed).

           @START with both the U and V options—The user-ID specified by the @RUN
            statement in the runstream being started.
                The V option allows trusted user-IDs to start runstreams that have more
                privilege. Without the V option, the started run assumes the starter’s
                executing mandatory attributes (clearance level 0 and default compartment
                set of NULL). The V option is ignored for systems with fundamental security.
                See Table 7-5 for references to the various @START statement formats when
                using the V option.

            W
                Specifies that only user programs and processors in the system files that
                encounter an error are written to the diagnostic file. Diagnostic dumps are
                printed only if the program producing the diagnostic dumps terminates in
                error.

            X
                Disregards system holds when opening a run; requires a security privilege.

            Y
                Always writes the program or processor to the diagnostic file, regardless of
                the source of the program. All PMD statements are honored, and diagnostic
                dumps are printed.

            Z
                Lets you start a runstream with mandatory security attributes at system high.
                Without the Z option or the U option, the started run assumes your executing
                mandatory attributes. If you specify the U option but not the Z option, the
                started run assumes the mandatory attributes of the user-ID on the @RUN
                statement in the runstream.



7–248                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                    @START and @@START—Start Canned Runstreams




                The Z option exists so that a started run can execute with system high
                attributes. Executing at system high means that the run has all compartments
                and the highest clearance level. See Section 5.2 for more information on
                compartment sets and clearance levels.

                To use the Z option, the following conditions apply:
                   You must have the privilege to start runs at system high.
                   You must have system-high capability, or if you specify the U option, the
                    user-ID on the @RUN statement in the started runstream must be able to
                    run at system high.
                The Z option is not useful unless your system has Security Level 1 or higher.

        runtime/deadline,pages/cards,start-time
           Here is an example of this option:
           If you have an inventory system that includes the following two data files
                File INV*MASTER (current inventory information)
                File INV*DTRANS (the day’s transactions)

           Then each day, you execute the same three absolute elements, as follows:
                INV*PROG.D-UPDATE (updates the inventory file using the day transactions)
                INV*PROG.STATUS-RPT (generates a stock status report based on the
                 inventory file)
                INV*PROG.TRANS-LIST (generates a list of the transactions posted against the
                 inventory file)

           Instead of executing these three programs individually, you could create a canned
           run to execute all of them at the same time. You then use the @START statement
           to initiate the canned run whenever you need to.

           To illustrate this, suppose you put the following statements into an element called
           INV*RUNS.DAILY:
               @RUN R231,03412,INV84,10,150
               @ASG,A INV*PROG.
               @ASG,A INV*MASTER.
               @ASG,A INV*DTRANS.
               @XQT INV*PROG.D-UPDATE
               @XQT INV*PROG.STATUS-RPT
               @XQT INV*PROG.TRANS-LIST
               @FIN

           To execute this entire sequence of statements, just enter the following
           statement:
                @START INV*RUNS.DAILY

           Or, here is another example for this option:
                @START FILEC.ELTB,,R231,03414,,,50

           The run in element ELTB of file FILEC is scheduled for execution. The system uses
           the run-ID (R231), account number (03414), and page estimate (50) on the @START
           statement instead of those on the @RUN statement in the stored runstream.
