7.62. @SYM and @@SYM—Queue Print Files and
       @SYMCN Control Statement
         The @SYM statement queues previously created print files to a printer, group of
         printers, or user-ID, for printing. It also directs the PRINT$ file (the primary print file) to
         an alternate device.

         Request output with the @SYM statement rather than using SITE from a text editor,
         which ties up your terminal. To protect classified data, your security officer cannot let
         you use @SYM to queue print files to another terminal or user-ID. For information on
         using @SYM and @BRKPT together, see Section 7.3.

         Format
         Use this format to queue any data file (you cannot specify program files with the
         @SYM statement) to a printer; you can also use this format to queue a file to any
         terminal that is configured in the system generation:
           @SYM,options filename,[number,device,pname-1/pname-2/pname-3
           /.../pname-n,banner]

         Use this format to queue print files to a user-ID instead of to a printer:
           @SYM,options filename,[number,user-id/U,pname-1/pname/pname-3
           /.../pname-n,banner]

         options

             A
                   Specifies that all files on the tape are to be printed in the order that they
                   appear on the tape; therefore, the file name given on the @SYM statement
                   must be a tape file.

             D
                   Deletes the current part of the file when the file part is closed, and produces
                   no output. The file name must be PRINT$.
                   The device field is ignored when this option is used.

             F
                   Directs this part and all future parts of the PRINT$ file to the device specified,
                   until the Exec finds another @SYM statement, with or without the F option,
                   for a primary PRINT$ part. When the Exec processes the second @SYM
                   statement, the device specification from the original @SYM,F statement is
                   lost. You can reinstate it with another @SYM,F statement.

             J
                   Print the top and bottom separator page regardless of the three system
                   generation parameter values: demand_batch_top_separator,
                   rsi_remote_top_separator, and rsi_bottom_separator.



7830 7949–031                                                                                     7–255
@SYM and @@SYM—Queue Print Files and @SYMCN Control Statement




           K
                   Do not print the top and bottom separator page.

           L
                   If security labeling is configured, prints the label on all pages of the printout.

           N
                   If security labeling is configured, only the banner and trailer pages are
                   labeled.

           U
                   Inhibits deletion of the file when processing is completed. This option is
                   applicable only to user-defined files. Do not use this option unless it is
                   necessary. Overuse of the U option loads the system with unnecessary files.
                   Also, modifying the file can result in unpredictable output.

               Note: If both the J and K options are specified, the J option is used. The J and
               K options are meaningful only for print files. The options are ignored on an
               @SYM of a punch file.

        filename
           Identifies the file to be queued. If the file name is a user-defined file, it must be a
           cataloged file. It cannot be in a to-be-cataloged state. The file name must be an
           internal or external file name or PRINT$ (the primary print file). If an internal name
           is specified, the associated file must be assigned to the run.
           When file name is PRINT$, the @SYM statement applies only to the current part of
           the PRINT$ file. In this case, you must not have breakpointed the PRINT$ file to a
           user-defined file with the @BRKPT statement.

        number
           Indicates how many copies of the file are to be printed. If omitted, one copy is
           assumed. You can specify up to 63 copies.

        device
           Identifies the device on which the file is to be printed. This can identify a specific
           onsite device, a specific remote site, or a group of onsite devices (that is, the
           group might be all onsite printers). Device group and remote site identifiers are
           defined when the system is configured. If omitted, the output file is printed at the
           default printer for the terminal used for the run.
           For RSI$ terminals with configured site-IDs, the default is the site-if of the
           terminal. For RSI$ terminals with nonconfigured nongeneric site-IDs, the default is
           the system default print queue. For RSI$ terminals with generic site-IDs, the
           default is the user-ID of that user.
           You can queue a file to any terminal that is configured in the system generation
           (instead of to a printer) by using the terminal’s site-ID in the device field. To
           receive a file that has been queued to your terminal, use the @@SEND statement.



7–256                                                                                 7830 7949–031
             @SYM and @@SYM—Queue Print Files and @SYMCN Control Statement




         user-id/U
             Is any valid user-ID within the system. The /U indicates that you want the print file
             queued to a user-ID instead of a device. A slash ( / ) must precede the U.
             If the given user-ID is invalid, the Exec issues the message:
                     ILLEGAL USERID SPECIFIED.

             You can queue the print file to your own user-ID or to some other valid user-id.
             The print file is then either printed at the printer connected to the specified user’s
             terminal (if there is one) or displayed at the user’s terminal (the @@PRNT
             statement directs output to the printer). The file is printed or displayed when you
             enter @@SEND,U.

         pname-n
             Are the labels of the symbiont file parts of a multifile tape to be printed. If omitted,
             only the first part on the tape is processed. This field is not applicable to mass
             storage files.
             The order in which the part names are specified on the @SYM statement must
             correspond to the order in which the parts are located on tape. However, not all
             parts on the tape need be processed. Any parts not named on the @SYM
             statement are bypassed.

         banner
             Specifies the banner to appear on the first page of the printout. The banner must
             be a maximum of 12 characters. If this option is omitted, the run-ID is used.
             Note: The banner field is ignored for a nonstandard file if the file is saved and
             restored with the SV and SR operator keyins. The run-ID of the @SYM
             statement is used for the banner in this case.

         Once the print file has been printed, it is deleted, unless you include the U option. If
         you intend to queue the same print file with more than one @SYM statement, you
         must use the U option. If you do not, the print file ceases to exist when all copies of
         the file are printed.

         After you have queued a print file to a printer, you can check where your file is in the
         print queue by using the @@CONS SQ statement.

         You cannot delete a file that is listed in a print queue unless you first remove it from
         the queue with the @@CONS SX statement.

         After queuing a file to a printer, avoid using the print file until after the file has been
         printed.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    7–257
@SYM and @@SYM—Queue Print Files and @SYMCN Control Statement




        @SYMCN Control Statement
        A user program can dynamically specify line advancement before control statement
        images are printed. The options on this control statement override dynamic
        configuration parameter control-image-spacing. The @SYMCN control statement is
        available in the runstream as well as through ER CSF$ and ER ACSF$.

        Options on @SYMCN statements are
        L
            The standard line spacing for processor call statements is used.
            If configuration parameter page-eject-on-processor calls is TRUE, or if the run has
            done @SETC,P, a page eject occurs before processor control statements are
            printed. Line spacing is 3 lines for all other control statements.
            If dynamic configuration parameter page-eject-on-processor-calls is FALSE, or if
            the run has done @SETC,N , line spacing is 3 lines for all control statements.

        N
            Advance n lines before any control statement image is printed where n is the
            number specified for dynamic configuration parameter control-image-spacing.
            The value n is used for all control statements including processor statements.
            If n is zero, a value of 3 is used.
            Continuation images of a control statement advance n lines or 4 lines, whichever
            is less.

        Security Labels on Printouts
        If your site has Security Level 2 or higher, printouts can be labeled with the clearance
        level and compartment set associated with your file and with a sequence number.
        Check with your security officer or site administrator to determine whether you have
        this feature.

        If you have print labeling configured, the security label always appears on the first
        (banner) and last (trailer) pages of your printout. To print the label on all the pages,
        specify the L option on the @SYM statement. Use the N option to print the label on
        only the banner and trailer pages. If you do not specify either option, the label can or
        cannot appear on all pages, depending on how your system is configured.

        If your site labels every page, remember that a printed page holds fewer lines of text
        than if your site did not label printouts. Check with your security officer to find out the
        allowable maximum width of your printouts. Printout width must be the same as or
        larger than the configured width for labels.

        The security label appears on the top and bottom of each page, except the banner
        page, where it appears below the banner. Labels are one to four lines long (up to 225
        characters) and they are preceded and followed by a single blank line.




7–258                                                                              7830 7949–031
              @SYM and @@SYM—Queue Print Files and @SYMCN Control Statement




         The symbolic clearance level of the file appears first in the label, followed by the
         compartment set. A space separates each word in the label. For example,
         Figure 7–5 shows a security label for a user with executing clearance level SECRET
         and executing compartment set PAYROLL, PERSONNEL, and PLANNING.




                             Figure 7–5. Sample Printout Label

         The following four special cases change the label appearance:
             If your file has the system compartment set associated with it, the label says
                 clearance level ALL

             If compartments are not installed on your system, the label contains only the
              clearance level.

             If no compartments are associated with the file, the label says
                 clearance level NULL

             If the label is longer than 225 characters, it says
                 clearance level ALL (The security label is too long to be printed.)

         Examples
             @SYM LPRNT,2,PR6

                This @SYM statement queues user-defined print file LPRNT to print queue PR6.
                Two copies of the printout are generated. After the file is printed, it is deleted.

             @SYM,L LPRNT,,REMPR1

                This @SYM statement queues user-defined print file LPRNT to printer REMPR1.
                If security labeling is configured, the security label appears on all pages of the
                printout.

@@TERM—Sign Off from the System




7.63.@@TERM—Sign Off from the System
        The @@TERM statement terminates your terminal at the end of a run. Enter this
        statement as follows after an @FIN statement when you do not want to start a new
        run:
            @@TERM

        Although you could enter an @@TERM statement before an @FIN statement to
        terminate the run and the terminal simultaneously, you must use it only as a last
        resort. If you enter the @@TERM statement without first entering an @FIN, the
        following happens:
            Files that were supposed to be deleted at the end of the run due to an @ASG,D
             statement are not deleted.
            Files that were supposed to be cataloged at the end of the run due to an @ASG,C
             statement are not cataloged.


7.64.@TEST—Test a Condition Word to Control
      Execution
        The @TEST statement tests the value of the condition word to select the particular
        control statements to be executed or skipped.

        When more than one test is to be made, the control statement is scanned until a test
        is met or all parameters are exhausted. When a test is met, the control statement
        immediately following the @TEST statement is skipped.

        Format
            @TEST f/value[/j],[f/value/j...]

        f
             Specifies the type of comparison to make. If the test is met, the next control
             statement is skipped. If the test is not met, the next control statement is
             executed.

             Permissible test types are:

              TE         Test for equal
              TNE        Test for not equal
              TG         Test for greater than
              TLE        Test for less than or equal
              TEP        Test for even parity
              TOP        Test for odd parity




7–260                                                                            7830 7949–031
                                      @TEST—Test a Condition Word to Control Execution




         value
              Specifies a positive, octal value not exceeding 12 digits to be compared with that
              portion of the condition word specified by the j field.

         j
              Specifies the portion of condition word to be tested. Permissible entries are W,
              H1, H2, T1 through T3, and S1 through S6. If you omit this field, the default is T2.
              Tests with j field of T1, T2, or T3 result in sign extension of that portion of the
              condition word for the specified test. The following diagram illustrates this:

                                                      W
                                 H1                                         H2
                          T1                          T2                            T3
                   S1            S2            S3             S4            S5             S6
             0             6              12            18             24            30         35



         Examples

             @TEST TE/6/S3

                 S3 of the condition word is tested to see whether it is equal to a value of octal
                 6; if equal, the next control statement in the stream is skipped. If unequal, the
                 next control statement is executed.

             @TEST TG/6,TE/4

                 T2 of the condition word is tested for two conditions: greater than octal 6 or
                 equal to octal 4. If either condition is met, the next control statement in the
                 stream is skipped. If neither condition is met, the next control statement in the
                 stream is executed.

             @TEST TG/10/H2

                 H2 of the condition word is tested for a greater-than octal 10 condition. If the
                 condition is met, the next control statement in the stream is skipped; otherwise,
                 the next control statement is executed. The value is treated as an octal value
                 even if the leading zero is omitted.

             @TEST TLE/4/T2

                 T2 portion of the condition word is tested to see whether it is less than or equal
                 to octal 4. If so, the next control statement in the stream is skipped; otherwise,
                 it is executed.




7830 7949–031                                                                                   7–261
@@TM—Send a Message to Another User




          @TEST TE/4000/T2

             Due to sign extension of T2, this test always results in the next control
             statement being executed.

          @TEST TOP/20/T3

             T3 of the condition word is tested to see whether the bit represented by 020 is
             set. If it is, the next control statement in the stream is skipped; otherwise, it is
             executed.


7.65. @@TM—Send a Message to Another User
        The @@TM statement sends a message (in demand runs only) to a specific run-ID,
        user-ID, or site-ID. The ID must be active to receive the message.

        If you have the limited keyin demand console mode or a higher console mode, you can
        also send terminal messages by using the @@CONS TM statement. See the Exec
        Operations Reference Manual (7831 0281) for the syntax and a description of the TM
        keyin.

        Note: The @@TM statement might not be available on your system. Check with
        your site administrator.

        The format of the @@TM statement depends on whether it is being sent to a run-ID,
        user-ID, or a site-ID.

        Formats
          @@TM run-id/R message

             Sends the message to the specified run-ID. No space is needed after the /R.

          @@TM user-id/U message

             Sends the message to all active runs with the specified user-ID. No space is
             needed after the /U.

          @@TM site-id message

             Sends the message to the specified site-ID. A space must follow the site-ID.

        Examples
          @@TM WPS/R DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A?

             Sends message DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A? to run-ID WPS.

          @@TM JAM/U DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A?

             Sends message DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A? to user-ID JAM.




7–262                                                                             7830 7949–031
                                                   @@TOUT—Change Your Timeout Period




             @@TM RE2211 DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A?

                Sends message DO YOU HAVE TAPE 3556A? to site-ID RE2211.


7.66.@@TOUT—Change Your Timeout Period
         If your terminal is idle for a certain length of time, the system assumes that you are
         not using the terminal, so it terminates the run and signs the terminal off (timeout).
         The @@TOUT statement lets you override the standard value that is normally used for
         this timeout period (typically 30 minutes).

         A timeout warning is sent after a session is idle for the period of time defined as the
         timeout period. The session is closed if it continues to remain idle after the warning
         for the same period of time defined as the timeout period.

         Not all users are allowed to use this statement. The new timeout period you establish
         with the @@TOUT statement remains in effect until you enter another @@TOUT
         statement or your run terminates (@FIN). When your run terminates, the timeout
         period is reset to the standard value.

         Format
             @@TOUT t

         t
              Indicates how long (in minutes) you want the timeout period to be. It can be from
              1 to 2047 minutes (about 34 hours). The actual limit that you work with depends on
              your site. If you do not provide a time or enter a value of 0, the system defaults to
              the standard value.

         To find out what your current timeout period is, enter an @@TOUT ? statement. This
         does not change the timeout period.

         To disable the timeout mechanism, enter an @@TOUT D statement.

         Examples
             @@TOUT 30

              The timeout period is 30 minutes.

             @@TOUT ?

              A message tells you what the timeout period is.




7830 7949–031                                                                               7–263
@@TRNS—Ignore Escape/EOT Characters




7.67. @@TRNS—Ignore Escape/EOT Characters
        The @@TRNS statement causes the escape and end-of-transmission characters to be
        ignored. (In other words, this allows you to send stop code characters without
        functioning as the stop code.) The function of this statement is similar to @@ESC and
        is for users sending file images from a host to a demand terminal.

        Format
            @@TRNS


7.68.@TTY—Change TTY Terminal Characteristics
        The @@TTY statement changes characteristics associated with the TTY terminal.

        Format
            @@TTY function-1,value-1[,...function-n,value-n]

        The function-n and value-n fields are the same.

        Example
            @@TTY W,30

        The page width is changed to 30.


7.69.@USE and @@USE—Reference a File by
      Another Name
        The @USE statement lets you reference a file by more than one file name. The
        alternate file names created with @USE are called internal (use) file names. The original
        name of a file is called the external file name. (See Section 3.3 for more information on
        naming files.) If you create more than one internal file name for a file, you can
        reference that file by any one of those internal names.

        You can want to create internal file names for the following reasons:
            To simplify file references by using a shorter internal file name instead of a long
             external file name
            To differentiate between files that have the same basic file name, but different
             qualifiers or file cycles
            To connect internally programmed file names to external file names
            To specify a directory-ID on an external file name (Most control statements that
             have a filename field do not allow a directory-ID to be specified with the file
             name.)

        Format
            @USE[,I] fname-1,fname-2




7–264                                                                              7830 7949–031
                                  @USE and @@USE—Reference a File by Another Name




         I
             Automatically releases the specified file from the run, as well as all internal file
             names associated with the file, the next time a task, such as a user program,
             terminates. (A task is a discrete processing step involving the execution of an
             absolute element.)
             The file and internal file names are released even if one of the following applies:
                Errors occur when the task terminates.
                The specified file is not assigned to your run.

         fname-1
             Identifies the new, alternate name for the file (an internal file name). This name can
             be up to 12 characters long. You cannot specify a directory-ID, qualifier, file cycle,
             or read/write keys for an internal file name.

         fname-2
             Identifies the file for which you are providing a new internal name. This can be
             either a previously specified internal (use) name or an external file name.
             If your system has Multi-Host File Sharing (MHFS), you can specify the directory-ID
             (STD or SHARED) on the fname-2 field. If your system has MHFS and you do not
             specify a directory-ID, the Exec uses the implied directory-ID (if you include the #)
             or the default directory-ID (if you do not include the #).

         Note: A directory-ID cannot be used when fname-2 is a previously specified
         internal (use) name.

         All internal file names equated to an external file name are maintained for the duration
         of the run, or until you issue an @FREE,A statement.

         Once the names are equated, you can reference the file by its internal or external file
         name from within a program or the runstream. If a conflict of file names exists, you
         must attach an internal name to the file with the conflicting external name before any
         references to that file are attempted.

         When a file is referenced, the list of internal file names is searched first. If the file
         cannot be found, the list of external file names is searched. Generally, when you use
         @FREE or @DELETE to release a file, all of the attached internal names disappear.
         However, if you try to use @DELETE or @DELETE,C on a noncataloged file in batch
         mode, the internal names remain attached to the file.

         Use @PRT,I to display the internal names of your currently assigned tapes and files.




7830 7949–031                                                                                  7–265
@USE and @@USE—Reference a File by Another Name




        Examples
         @USE FILEB,COMPANY*PAYROLL
         @USE COST,FILEB

            In the first statement, internal file name FILEB is equated to external file name
            COMPANY*PAYROLL. In the second statement, internal file name COST is
            equated to internal file name FILEB. The file can now be referenced by the
            original name (COMPANY*PAYROLL) or one of the internal file names (COST or
            FILEB).

         @USE NEWCYC,ID*FILESET(0)
         @USE OLDCYC,ID*FILESET(-1)
         @USE OTHER,QUAL*FILESET

            This example shows how you can use internal file names to differentiate
            between files that have the same basic file names, but have different F-cycle
            numbers or qualifiers. The internal file name NEWCYC identifies the current
            cycle (relative F-cycle 0) of file ID*FILESET, where OLDCYC identifies the
            previous cycle (relative F-cycle -1) of the same file. Internal file name OTHER
            identifies the file QUAL*FILESET, which has the same basic file name as the
            other file (ID*FILESET), but a different qualifier.

         @USE Q,BACKUP
         @USE BACKUP,EZ
         @USE EZ,STD#REG*FILE

            For the remainder of this run, file Q can be referenced by any of these names:
            BACKUP, EZ, and STD#REG*FILE.

         @USE MS,SHARED#MISC*FILE
         @ADD MS.

            File SHARED#MISC*FILE is given internal name MS, and then used on the @ADD
            statement. (The @ADD statement does not allow a directory-ID to be specified.)

         @USE SHAREDFILE.,SHARED#ANY*FILE
         @COPY SHAREDFILE.,BACKUP*FILE.

            This example shows you how to use an internal name to specify a directory-ID
            for a file on an @COPY statement. The @COPY statement does not allow you to
            specify a directory-ID with the file name. By associating the internal file name
            with the correct directory-ID, you can circumvent this limitation.




7–266                                                                          7830 7949–031
                                                                      @@X—Halt Processors




7.70. @@X—Halt Processors
         At times you can want to stop your current run processing to do something else. You
         can stop a processor at any time with the @@X statement.

         Format
           @@X [functions][,data]

         functions
            Let you specify what kind of stop you want. Specifying just @@X (with no function
            characters) defaults to @@X TIOCR.

            C
                  Jumps to an address previously specified in the program (remote break
                  contingency). You can use either CEND$ or CRTN$.
                  Although most requests can terminate contingency mode, the CEND$
                  request is designed for this purpose. It is the most efficient method unless
                  another request is needed.
                  The CRTN$ request removes the interrupted activity from contingency mode
                  and returns control at the address (not address+1) specified in H2 of word 0
                  of the contingency packet. This lets the user activity process a contingency
                  and return to the original execution path without destroying a register on the
                  return. This avoids the risk of another contingency interrupt overlaying the
                  packet between a CEND$, jump-indirect-on-the-packet sequence. If user
                  activity is not in contingency mode, the return is to the ER+1. When an
                  activity not in contingency mode executes this request, it has no effect.
                  If the activity is returning from a contingency that registered the RBASE$
                  function, CRTN can rebase the banks at the time the contingency occurs.
                  The CRTN$ request reestablishes the environment when the contingency
                  occurred, rebases the banks previously unbased, and returns you to the
                  return address specified in the contingency packet.
                  The data field is only available when the C function is present, either alone
                  (@@X), followed by a comma (@@X C,data), or with other function characters
                  followed by a comma (@@X CT,data). See the description of the data field
                  that follows.
                  Discards all backed-up input. This includes all images from @ADD files and
                  images entered in @@CQUE and @@INQ mode (includes FUL, PTI, and TCI).

            I
                  If the corresponding @@END INQ has not been received, the terminal
                  remains in @@INQ mode but the file is purged of all images. The next input
                  becomes the first image in the @@INQ file.

            O
                  Discards all backed-up output.




7830 7949–031                                                                             7–267
@@X—Halt Processors




            R
                    Terminates the active processor or program and all future actions of the
                    program or processor, including removal of all entries from the QECL stack.

            T
                    Terminates the program currently being executed.

        data
            Lets you pass along some unique information along with the contingency.
            The data field is only available when the C function is present, either alone (@@X),
            followed by a comma (@@X C,data), or with other function characters followed by
            a comma (@@X CT,data). Special field characters such as a slash (/), semicolon (;),
            and a stand-alone period ( . ) can never be used. The data field is case sensitive.
            The data field can be a maximum of 6 characters in length. Passing more than 6
            characters results in the error message
                     @@X ERROR - TOO MANY DATA CHARACTERS

            This keyin can penetrate wait conditions. It can be directed at a specific activity or
            activities. Distribution of this and other externally generated contingencies (those
            generated at the keyboard or the system console) are best controlled by the
            program. It is unlikely that a user sitting at the keyboard would know enough
            about where a program is executing to control which activity must field
            contingency conditions. Also, the distribution is viewed as an attribute of the run
            rather than of any particular subsystem. To help control of external contingency
            distribution, the EXTCGY$RECV is provided.
            ER II$ activities can be activated by @@X C as described in the ER Programming
            Reference Manual (7830 7899). Input can now be received in register A0 by either
            the @@X C or II keyins. Also, instead of generating the II activity with data, a
            contingency can be generated instead. Depending on when the ER II$, II keyin, or
            @X C(T) operations are performed, activating the II activity or generating a
            contingency for it is purely an asynchronous event by OS 2200.
            Normal operation is as follows:
                   An II keyin activates an II$ activity if one is present or if an II$ activity does
                    not exist, external contingencies are generated for all activities that have
                    chosen to accept them.
                   An @@X keyin both activates an II$ activity (if one is present) and generates
                    external contingencies for all activities that have chosen to accept them.

        Table 7–6 describes the conditions that affect an II activity and their respective results.
        Translation of any ASCII characters to Fieldata characters conform to those in the
        conversion table shown in the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899).




7–268                                                                                   7830 7949–031

                         Fieldata spaces if no data was     Aux = 4 ASCII characters or

           @@X CO

            This example shows how to stop output without terminating your program.

           @@X

        third examples) can corrupt common banks, database files, and user files. In general,
        you must avoid this type of program termination.


7.71. @XQT—Execute Absolute Elements or Object
       Modules
        The @XQT statement initiates the execution of an absolute element or object module.
        This element cannot reside in a Large Element Program File (LEPF).

        Format
          @XQT,[options] [filename.eltname]

        options

           Are user-specified and are initially presented to a program in a register. You can
           retrieve them with ER OPT$. (These options are also used by OS 2200 system
           processors.)
           The registers and their contents are as follows:
           A2 and A3
                  Hardware feature bit mask:

                  Bits 0-35     Unused

                  Bits 36-41    Numerical Host-ID, (1 = A, 2 = B ...)

                  Bits 42-63    Unused

                  Bit 64        VERSION3E type hardware

                  Bit 65        Unused

                  Bit 66        Queuing Architecture supported



7–270                                                                           7830 7949–031
                                 @XQT—Execute Absolute Elements or Object Modules




                 Bit 67           Unused

                 Bit 68           Unused

                 Bit 69           Basic mode

                 Bit 70           Extended mode

                 Bit 71           Unused


                 Mnemonics and values for these fields in SYS$RLIB$.ERU$ are

                 VERSION3E$       0200

                 BTPBTU$          0100

                 QARCH$           040

                 EIS$             020

                 BYTE$            010

                 BMODE$           04

                 XMODE$           02

                 FPD$             01


            A4
                 Program type:

                 4                Demand

                 5                Deadline batch

                 6                Batch


            A5
                 Bit 0            Processor was reloaded from QECL stack.

                 Bit 1            Print file is breakpointed (@BRKPT).

                 Bit 2            R11–R15 have been established.

                 Bit 3            Repeat option specified on entry of QECL stack caused
                                  reload.




7830 7949–031                                                                             7–271
@XQT—Execute Absolute Elements or Object Modules




                Bit 4            Processor was searched for in the alternate library file and
                                 the file was assigned on the user's behalf.

                Bit 5            If set, the program was called as a processor. If cleared, an
                                 @XQT started the program.

                Bit 6 - 9        Unused

                Bits 10-35       Contain the options from the @XQT or processor call (A = bit
                                 10, Z = bit 35)


          R1
                Date (in Fieldata DATE$ format in local time):

                Bits 0-11        Month

                Bits 12-23       Day of the month

                Bits 24-35       Year (last two digits)


          R2

                Current time (TDATE$ format in local time):

                Bits 0-5         Month

                Bits 6-11        Day

                Bits 12-17       Year (modulo 1964)

                Bits 18-35       Time in seconds from midnight


          R3
                Accumulated processor time for the run (in 200-microsecond increments)

          R11/12
                System type (two words, left justified)

          R13/14
                Exec master level (two words, left justified)

          R15
                System site-ID (left justified)




7–272                                                                            7830 7949–031
                                @XQT—Execute Absolute Elements or Object Modules




         filename.eltname
            Specifies the absolute element or object module to be executed. This element
            cannot reside in a Large Element Program File (LEPF).
            If you do not provide a file name with an element name (eltname), TPF$ is
            assumed. If you do not provide an element name, the system executes the
            absolute element or object module that was most recently placed in TPF$, or in
            the file name you specified on the @XQT call.
            If you specify an element name without a version name, the system executes the
            absolute element or object module with that name that has a blank version name,
            if one exists. If one does not exist, the system executes the first (not necessarily
            the oldest) nondeleted absolute element or object module in the program file that
            has the name eltname, regardless of its version name.
            For basic mode programs, when there are no absolute elements in TPF$, the
            system collects all of the relocatable elements in TPF$ (implied collection) and
            executes the resulting absolute element. The newly created absolute element is
            given the name NAME$ and placed in TPF$.

         Examples
           @XQT PAR.12C

            For an extended mode program, executes object module 12C in file PAR.

           @XQT FILEA.XYZ

            For a basic mode program, executes absolute element XYZ in file FILEA.

           @XQT

                For a basic mode program, executes the most recent absolute element placed
                in TPF$. If no absolute element is present, the Collector creates an absolute
                element (NAME$) from all relocatable elements in TPF$ and executes that
                absolute element.

         Program Load Error
         Refer to the ER Programming Reference Manual (7830 7899) for more information.

         T
             TAPE IMAGE LOST*REREAD

              Applies only to demand terminals; indicates that images were lost while inputting
              images in paper tape mode.

             TAPE LABEL FORMAT ERROR

              Tape labeling errors receive the following diagnostics:
                devnam ACCESS NOT ALLOWED ON aaa

              where devnam is the device name of the unit and aaa is the reel number. If
              read-and-write inhibit is set beyond the first label group, the following message is
              logged:
                qualifier*filename(fff) ACCESS NOT ALLOWED ON FILE n

              where qualifier*filename(fff) is the external file name and F-cycle of the tape file.
              File n is the tape file in which the error occurred.
              Errors that occur beyond the first label group are logged to the user. The following
              messages are used:
                qualifier*filename(fff) {EOF1|EOF2|HDR1|HDR2} LABEL NOT FOUND FOR FILE n

                qualifier*filename(fff) FILE n EXPED x BLOCKS REC y

                qualifier*filename(fff) I/O ERROR z ON {R|W} ON {TRL|HDR} LABEL ON FILE n

                  x              The number of blocks in the EOF1, EOV1, or HDR1
                                 labels (HDR1 in reverse processing).
                  y              The number of blocks actually read when the
                                 tape mark was received.
                  z              The actual I/O error status received (other than 0).
                  R              Read
                  W              Write




7830 7949–031                                                                                 A–25
ECL and Terminal Sign-on Messages




               TRL             Indicates trailer label group; and HDR indicates
                               header label group.
               EXPED           Expected
               REC             Received

           The first two error log messages indicate that something is missing on the tape.
           In both cases, recovery is attempted. In the case where a label is missing, the
           system tries to determine whether any type of labels exist. If so, it tries to
           position accordingly. If not, it repositions after the last valid label group or at the
           tape mark read by the user.
           In the case where file n expected x blocks and received y, the system has picked
           the block count in the EOF1 or EOV1 label, compared it to the number of blocks
           extended, and found them not equal.
           In the case where the number of blocks read by the user does not correspond to
           the block count in the EOF1, EOF2, or HDR2, the error message is logged to the
           user, and processing continues.
           If an I/O error is detected beyond the first label group and the I/O is a read, the
           input buffer is checked to see whether there was a partial read of a label. If there
           was, processing is attempted. If there was not, the file is set to read- and write-
           inhibited, and the user is informed that access to that file is not allowed.

B.1. Functional and Error Messages
         The functional and error messages are divided into the following categories:
            Messages prefixed with I/O error codes
            Messages without prefixed I/O codes

         For all commands that complete successfully with an END message (such as END
         DELETE, END REWIND, or END ERS) and can accept more than one file name on the
         command line, only one END COMMAND message will be issued upon successful
         completion even if several files were processed by the function.

         Use of the C option on any FURPUR command will prevent execution of ER ERR$ on
         error exit if FURPUR is running in breakpoint or batch. The C option should be used
         with caution because a bad result of an erroring FURPUR command could be input to a
         process later on in the runstream.

         THE END OF THE RECORDED AREA HAS BEEN ENCOUNTERED.

            The @MOVE statement you specified moves the access pointer on a diskette
            beyond the last data set recorded on the diskette. The associated message, n
            EOFs ENCOUNTERED, indicates the number of data sets actually encountered
            before the end of the diskette.

         WARNING - BUFTAP PERFORMANCE ADVANTAGE NEGATED WITHOUT THE E OPTION

            A @COPOUT, @COPY, or @MARK statement without the E option has been done
            to an unlabeled output tape that has BUFTAP buffered-write mode enabled to
            improve tape write performance. Without the E option these statements write
            two EOF marks and move backward between them. This backward tape
            movement causes the tape unit to write the data from the tape unit buffer to the
            physical tape. This negates the performance advantages of BUFTAP, which require
            constant forward tape motion and no implicit or explicit tape synchronization
            requests. Include the E option with these statements to gain the full performance
            advantage of BUFTAP buffered-write mode.

            Where n is the decimal auxiliary status code returned by SOLAR and is
            documented in Appendix F, "Conditioned File Copy Auxiliary Status Codes" in the
            Software Library Administrator (SOLAR) User Reference Manual
            (7831 0604).

B.5. Error Messages Returned by PCFP
         FURPUR calls Program-Callable FURPUR (PCFP) to perform all or part of the processing
         for the following statements:
             @COPY mass-storage-file-1.,mass-storage-2. (see Section 7.13 for all @COPY
              statement formats)
             @COPY,AORS program-file-1.,program-file-2.
             @COPY,G mass-storage-file.,tape-file.
             @COPY,G tape-file.,mass-storage-file.
             @COPY,P program-file-1.,program-file-2.
             @DELETE,UAORS program-file-1.,... (See Section 7.17.3)
             @ERS mass-storage-file-1.,… (See Section 7.24)
             @PACK large-program-file-1.,… (See Section 7.42)

         If PCFP detects errors, it returns error information to FURPUR. The error information
         includes an Extended Language Message System (ELMS) condition identifier, an
         auxiliary error code, and a file identifier.

         If ELMS message delivery is available, FURPUR calls ELMS to display the error
         message. The following is a typical PCFP error message displayed by ELMS:
             *ERROR PRA002001: Unexpected I/O status 11 was returned by a read (R$)
             request to the file with index 1.

         If ELMS message delivery is not available or if ELMS is unable to display the error
         message, FURPUR displays the error information returned by PCFP in the following
         messages:
             ELMS MESSAGE DELIVERY IS NOT AVAILABLE
             PCFP ERROR CODE: nnnn, AUX_ERROR_CODE: xxxxxxxxxxxx, ERROR_FILE: y[, SUB_ERROR_CODE: zzzz]
             REFER TO PCFP PROGRAMMING REFERENCE MANUAL (7830 9796) FOR MESSAGE TEXT


         Where nnnn is the decimal PCFP error code (part of the returned ELMS condition
         identifier), xxxxxxxxxxxx is the octal auxiliary error code, y is the file identifier, and
         zzzz is the decimal sub error code, if it is nonzero.

         The PCFP errors listed in this section are the ones that will be most commonly
         encountered for the FURPUR statements that are performed by PCFP. This is neither a
         complete list of PCFP error messages nor a complete list of possible PCFP errors that
         can occur for the FURPUR statements. Refer to the Program-Callable FURPUR (PCFP)
         Programming Reference Manual (7830 9796) for a complete description of PCFP error
         messages.

           The first error message is the @USE, @CAT or @ASG facilities statement used to

           that when FURPUR displays the variable fatal error messages with numbers
           200033 - 240033 the variable information (shown in italics in C.3) is not available
           to FURPUR and is replaced by the ‘insert indicator’ ^1, ^2, etc. For example,
           message number 203233 is shown in C.3 as ‘E:203233 device-name is not up’
           and would be displayed by FURPUR as ‘E:203233 ^1 is not up’.

         FILES $DGETAA$ THROUGH $DGETZZ$ ARE ALREADY CATALOGED

           FURPUR cannot catalog the required file on the specified pack-id because the
           676 filenames that can be used for each qualifier are all currently cataloged in the
           MFD. Any $DGETaa$ file that is not currently assigned to a run can safely be
           deleted. Deleting these unused files may also improve the efficiency of @PRT,D
           and @PRT,U.

Appendix C
Facility Request Status Codes

         The system displays facility request messages and status codes in response to the
         ECL statements for facility requests: @ASG, @CAT, @FREE, @MODE, @USE, and
         @QUAL.

         The prefixed messages are divided into three categories:

            Informational messages are prefixed with the letter I and an error number. For
             example:
                I:001433 run run-id held for unloaded file rollback for nn min.

             where run-id identifies the run being held, and nn is the number of minutes the
             run has been held so far.

            Warning messages are prefixed with the letter W and a message number. For
             example:
                W:120133 file is already assigned.

            Error messages are prefixed with the letter E and an error number. For example:
                E:200233 devname is an invalid device name.

             where devname is the character string that was supposed to be a device name.

         Table C–1 shows the message number ranges.


             Table C–1. Facility Inventory Message Ranges


             Message Number Range              Type of Message

                000133 – 002333          Variable informational
                020133 – 077733          Fixed informational
                 100033 – 12003          Variable warning
                 120133 – 177733         Fixed warning
                200033 –- 240033         Variable fatal error
                240133 –- 377733         Fixed fatal error

C.6. Facility Inventory Status Bits
        If a facility request made by one of the facilities control statements (@ASG, @MODE,
        @CAT, @FREE, @QUAL, and @USE) is in error, a status word is generated in which the
        various bits define the error. See Table C-2 for descriptions of the bit sets.


                       Table C–2. Facility Inventory Status Bits


           Bit Set                                  Description

          0*           Request not accepted; check other bits for reason.
          1*           Field error in control statement other than syntax. Option conflict
                       (for example, MHL, OE, or IB) or noise constant specification error.
                       Requested hardware not currently part of the system. CSF$
                       request returns status of 60000000000 when mass storage has
                       overflowed. (This description gave a few examples only. There are
                       other possible errors for this bit.)
          2            File specified is already assigned or cataloged (@ASG and @CAT),
                       already released (@FREE), or not assigned (@MODE). The request is
                       rejected for @CAT and @MODE statements.
          3            The file was previously cataloged.
          4*           Equipment type specified on the @ASG statement is not
                       compatible with the cataloged type, or file specified on the
                       @MODE statement is not magnetic tape.
          5            Data bank overflow attempting to acquire file-related buffer space.
                       Down pack environment full. (Either the local or shared pack status
                       table is full.)
          6            That portion of the file name used as the internal name for I/O
                       packets is not unique.
          7            X option specified; file already in exclusive use.
          8*,**        Incorrect read key for cataloged file.
          9*,**        Incorrect write key for cataloged file.
          10*          Write key that exists in the master file directory is not specified in
                       the @ASG statement (file assigned in the read-only mode).
          11           Read key that exists in the master file directory is not specified in
                       the @ASG statement (file assigned in the write-only mode).
          12*          Read key specified in the @ASG statement; none exists in the
                       master file directory.
          13*          Write key specified in the @ASG statement; none exists in the
                       master file directory.
          14*          An A option was specified in the @ASG statement, and the file
                       name cannot be found in the master file directory.

Equipment Mnemonics




       Compatibility Issues with 18- and 36-Track Tapes
       Here are 36-track tape considerations:

          A cartridge tape written on a 36-track cartridge drive can be read only on a 36-
           track capable cartridge drive.
          A cartridge tape written on an 18-track cartridge drive can be read on a 36-track
           cartridge drive.
          A labeled cartridge tape written in 36-track format will appear as an unlabeled
           cartridge tape when mounted on an 18-track capable cartridge drive. If this
           happens, the Exec displays the console message:
             IS TAPE LABELED? Y,N

           If the operator answers N to this message, the tape can be overwritten without
           tape labeling protection.

          In some cases, an 18- or 36-track tape cannot be appended. It can only be written
           from loadpoint.
          E-carts can be used only on 36-track cartridge tapes. E-carts are the size of
           standard half-inch cartridge tapes, but the actual tape length is thinner than one
           1100ths of an inch.


                                              Caution
            When you use T and HIC general assign mnemonics, be sure that you
            determine the exact device type that was allocated to you so that you can
            later use the required mnemonic to read the tape. For example, if you begin
            with "T" and are allocated a 36-track device, you must use HICM (or another
            half-inch 36-track cartridge mnemonic) to reassign and read the tape.



          A cartridge tape written on a 9840C drive cannot be read on either a 9840A or
           9840B drive.
          A cartridge tape written on a 9840D drive cannot be read on a 9840A, 9840B, or
           9840C drive.
          In some cases, 9840 media cannot be appended because it cannot contain mixed
           density. It can only be written from loadpoint if the write is on a drive with
           different density than information previously written to the tape.

Appendix E
Job and Summary Accounting Report
(Tail Sheet)

         This appendix describes the Job Accounting and Summary Accounting Report for an
         Exec-produced tail sheet. The report is generated after termination of a run.

         There is a configuration parameter, site_formatted_tailsheet, displayed in the
         “Run Scheduling” area that is entered from the initial menu displayed by COMUS. If
         the value of the parameter is TRUE, the Exec does not produce a tail sheet.

         The following is a report sample and a description of fields:

           RUNID: XXXXXX          ACCT: XXXXXXXXXXXX      PROJECT:       XXXXXXXXXXXX   HOST: X
           SITE: XXXXXX         USERID: XXXXXXXXXXXX      SYSTEM:        XXXXXXXXXXXX

                   CONSOLE MESSAGE TEXT LOCATION




           DEVICE USAGE:          REQUESTS             TRANSFERRED
                    DISK:                    0                   0 WORDS
                    TAPE:                    0                   0 WORDS
           MAX TAPES ASG:                    0
           RESOURCE WAIT:        00:00:00

           MEMORY USAGE:                     0 PAGE-SECONDS
           MAX MEMORY:                       0 PAGES

           TIME:       TOTAL:    00:00:00.000         ELAPSED:   00:00:00
                       CPU:      00:00:00.000         I/O:   00:00:00.000
                       CC/ER:    00:00:00.000         WAIT: 00:00:00.000

           SUAS USED:               0.00      SUAS REMAINING:             0.00
           IMAGES READ:           0      PAGES:       0
           START:     yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss zone      FIN:   yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss zone




7830 7949–031                                                                                 E–1
Job and Summary Accounting Report (Tail Sheet)




        The following are contained in the report.

        RUNID

            The ID of the run for which accounting data was gathered.

        ACCT

            The account to which this run was assigned.

        PROJECT

            The project to which the run was assigned.

        HOST

            The host-id (such as A, B, C, D, ...) appears if MHFS is installed, UP, and not
            reemploying.

        SITE

            The site identification number.

        USERID

            The user-id used to execute the run.

        SYSTEM

            The system identification number.

        Console Message Area

            This area contains the console messages directly issued by the run, or console
            messages issued by the Exec in response to a service request issued by the run.

            This area contains the following message types:

                  Run termination message
                  Tape/disk mount messages
                  Operator message responses
                  Log messages
                  Nonrecoverable device error messages
                  Any console message issued by the run




E–2                                                                                 7830 7949–031
                                        Job and Summary Accounting Report (Tail Sheet)




         DEVICE USAGE

            REQUESTS

                   The number of physical I/O operations to tape and disk issued on behalf of the
                   run.

            TRANSFERRED

                   The total number of words transferred to tape and disk issued on behalf of
                   the run.

         MAX TAPES ASG

            The maximum number of tapes concurrently assigned by the run.

         RESOURCE WAIT

            The time consumed in the run waiting for resources to become available. The
            value does not include voluntary waiting time.

         MEMORY USAGE

         MEMORY USAGE PAGE–SECONDS

            The number of memory pages in use multiplied by the number of seconds in use
            during the life of the run.

         MAX MEMORY

            The maximum number of memory pages in use during the life of the run.

         TIME

            Values in these fields are expressed in standard units of processing (SUP) except
            where noted. See the Exec Administration Reference Manual (7831 0323) for a
            detailed description of SUPs.

                TOTAL

                    Total of CPU time, CC/ER time, and I/O time.

                ELAPSED

                The wall clock time taken by the run, that is FIN - START, expressed in hours,
                minutes, and seconds.

                CPU

                    Actual CPU time consumed while the run was active.




7830 7949–031                                                                                    E–3
Job and Summary Accounting Report (Tail Sheet)




               CC/ER

                     The time based on standard SUP charges for control cards and Executive
                     requests.

               I/O

                     The time required for data transfer between the CPU and peripheral devices
                     based on standard SUP charges.

               WAIT

                     The wait time due to conditions other than system busy.

        SUAS USED

              The total number of standard units of accounting (SUA) consumed by the run. See
              the Exec Administration Reference Manual (7831 0323) for a detailed description
              of these units.

        SUAS REMAINING

              SUAs remaining in the account after the run.

        IMAGES READ

              The number of input images or images included in the batch.

        PAGES

              The number of output pages (print or terminal) at the default number of lines per
              page (66) or the configured number of lines per page.

        START

              The date, start time, and zone of the run.

        FIN

              The date, end time, and zone of the run.
